3fb6033e76d5.title: Start in the avatar, open into a window
3fb6033e76d5.content: Skill board-windows: Everything starts as its avatar; opening projects a window onto the board. The two mechanisms that must not be conflated, z-order, and the fixed chrome a content kind fills in. Named by: Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Everything starts as its avatar, and [x] closes a window back to it. Opening projects a window onto the board; selecting any part of a window raises it. Each content kind controls its own avatar and rendering, and opens into a full-screen panel with fixed controls such as [x], [linksrc] or [edit].

4128f34c1b14.title: TWO mechanisms, and conflating them is the defect
4128f34c1b14.content: |   | trigger | who | . | semantic zoom | the card’s rendered width crosses a declared threshold | automatic | . | open / close | [x], or opening a card | a person | . An open window is not a zoom state: it is projected onto the board rather than being the card grown large, so it survives zooming out. Only [x] closes it. Collapsing the two gives a board where a card can close itself with no action taken, and where [x] and a zoom-out are indistinguishable. Semantic zoom is the GLASS’s, not the board’s . Every board slot — a landing sticky and a todo sticky alike — is one component: the same closed square tile (--fa-sticky-tile-size) with the theme’s faded art, and the same compact icon row underneath it. A slot is its closed tile at every width, so semantic zoom does not run on the board. It decides what a card shows on the folio glass, where a card is resized freely. Do not add a width observer to the board grid: it would be a zoom with nothing to change, and the next agent would read it as the card’s state.

8efe3dad2a2f.title: One sticky, one icon row, in one order
8efe3dad2a2f.content: Under every sticky, on every panel: view, edit, pin, send to fsh-guts, as icon buttons. An icon-only control carries aria-label (what a screen reader announces) AND title (the same words on hover); they are not interchangeable. No control sits inside the card body. The open window’s bar uses the same icons for the same acts. A link the sticky cannot serve is absent, never dead.

64711a1713b5.title: Pin is a toggle onto the FOLIO glass
64711a1713b5.content: There is one store answering “what is on my glass”: the folio. A second store holding a page-level copy of the card gets no glass tools, no folio geometry and no shelve, and has to be special-cased by the glass filter and count. | Pin makes the sticky a folio asset — todo/<id> (the key the glass’s own Todos panel pulls a todo out under, so the two ways onto the glass agree) or landing/<slot> — with shown: true, drawn by the glass’s own card path and placed by placeOnGlass. A landing sticky’s theme, picture URL and text travel in the entry as data, never as stored markup. | Unpin is shelveFromGlass — the middle of the three states below. The entry stays; the same pin puts it back, where the reader left it. | The pressed state is the store’s answer (folioStateOf(key) === "glass"), never the button’s memory. The glass’s own × shelves too, and the row’s pin follows it. | .

008836be99be.title: Send to fsh-guts asks first
008836be99be.content: A control a reader has to ask about has not said what it does, so discard is named for where it goes (Send to fsh-guts, the trashcan that is kept) and opens a confirmation that names the sticky, says it is restorable and per-browser, and says where it is restored from — the fish in the navbar’s icon row. Focus starts on Cancel; Cancel and Escape do nothing but close it. A dialog whose dismissal performs the act did not ask. The window bar’s send is the same act and takes the same confirmation. The inverse is Restore in fsh-guts.

f1368e4a634b.title: The threshold is declared, inherited, and traceable
f1368e4a634b.content: schemas/kg/semantic-zoom.ts (instance data: semantic-zoom.json): a folio default (belowPx) with a per-kind override (byKind) — the repository’s inheritance rule (inherit everything, override anything; a variant states only what it CHANGES). So: . | the folio always has a number, and every kind resolves to one; | a kind that states nothing is complete, not invalid — requiredness is checked after resolution, never on the declaration; | an override carries a required because, and the resolver returns the source alongside the value, so a reviewer can tell a deliberate override from a folio default that does not fit. | . The boundary is stated once. Strictly below the number, so the declared width is the last one that still shows words. A boundary written one way in a comment and the other way in the renderer makes a card flicker.

e561c3d7dbef.title: Z-order: selecting any part raises
e561c3d7dbef.content: Windows stack, and selecting any part of one raises it — not a title bar, any part, because a reader who clicks into a window’s content has already said which one they mean. Z-order is session-only. The DI layer carries no z: a committed stacking order would make every raise a file write and every two sessions a conflict, on the most concurrently-edited state a folio has. If that proves wrong, z is one optional field in the positions document.

bf1638779d60.title: The chrome is fixed; the kind fills it in
bf1638779d60.content: A content kind declares which controls it offers, and the platform fixes the frame: . | [x] is always present and always in the same place, so a reader learns the frame once; | a declared control that names nothing known is a finding, not a missing button; | a control the environment cannot perform is hidden, and the reason reported — a dead [edit] 404s for exactly the reader who cannot edit, which reads as “this page is broken” rather than “you cannot do this”. | .

f54844405899.title: Closing must have a reachable inverse
f54844405899.content: An action whose inverse is not reachable is not a toggle. On an overlay, close may set hidden, because the launcher tile re-opens it. On a board that IS page content, hidden removes a section of the page, so the inline board collapses to a control in its own position, and focus follows it — left alone, focus lands on <body> and the keyboard position is gone. A control two clicks deep inside a collapsed launcher does not count as reachable. A default of “hidden” is allowed only with the inverse on screen. The glass’s tile strip starts slid away; its “Show tiles (N)” tab stays in view, in the strip’s own position, and the same tab hides the tiles again. See harness-tiles §”The glass strip”.

d0b4b08da4ab.title: The floor, which is not negotiable
d0b4b08da4ab.content: This layer’s declared interaction profile is low-dexterity. Every board action is keyboard-operable; drag is an accelerator and never the only way in. Targets are at least the tile size. And the board is ALWAYS collapsible to a linear, tile-based listing — a board that cannot be read linearly cannot be read by a screen reader, printed, or translated. The listing is the ARTEFACT and the board is the overlay . The board is an extra laid over a simple tile-based listing. So the floor must be correct with no JavaScript at all, not merely when the board is toggled off: notes built only by docs-ui.js from a fetch of assets/todos/index.json give a reader with JavaScript off no note, no count, and no hint that notes exist. Three checks follow: . Document order, never the board’s order. The board may stack by BPMN subprocess depth; the floor does not, because document order is what a screen reader and a printout depend on, and a floor that reordered would be a second answer to “what comes next”. Collapsed, never removed. When the board mounts it moves the listing into a disclosure so the page does not show the same notes twice. It does not delete it, hide it from assistive technology, or display: none it: a listing the board removed would have no way back while the board is open. Assert against the SERVED HTML. A test that reads the DOM passes because the board built that DOM. The assertion is on bytes the server sent — a browser context with javaScriptEnabled: false over the same renderer the generator writes with.

149b2182e9a0.title: The folio belongs to the HARNESS, not to the library
149b2182e9a0.content: A content library is something a reader browses — a replica, a published layer, any folio published as a site. A folio is the reader’s own surface: their notes, the assets they have materialised, the documents they created or linked. So the folio visualisation is cat-harness’s, available by convention on any harness, and a library never implements its own. A library may have its own landing page and its own harness; neither is licence to build a second folio. Consistency is the requirement: a reader moving between libraries must find the same folio, because the point of carrying a folio is that it does not change underneath them. A note or a todo MAY reference nodes in another KG library. The folio is not scoped to the library it is pulled down over, so a renderer must not assume local resolution.

c34fb2c42bce.title: A tile, or an avatar?
c34fb2c42bce.content: A tile is what the HARNESS declares, an avatar is what the FOLIO holds, and a theme is how either one looks rather than a third kind. The test is in harness-tiles §”A tile, or an avatar?”, and only there, because one rule with two homes is free to drift.

85cfc24d7184.title: An asset has THREE states, not two
85cfc24d7184.content: Pulling the folio down gives a glass — a surface over whatever is being browsed, carrying sticky notes and the avatars of materialised assets, including materialised KG like cat-bootstrap or cat-harness themselves. | state | where the asset is | how it got there | . | in the library | not the reader’s at all | the default | . | in the folio, not displayed | materialised into the folio’s own reproduce directories — library/ for the bytes, uploads/ for a source — off the glass | the reader closed it, “back in library” | . | on the glass | displayed in the pulled-down folio | the reader pulled it out of the library | . “In the folio” is not folio/. The folio is the reader’s REPOSITORY, of which library/ and uploads/ are declared parts — both carry dependents: "reproduce". folio/ is a different graph typology: renderable authored content. corpus-grep searches library/ only, so a node materialised anywhere else reads as ABSENT to every consumer. Closing returns an asset to the middle state and NEVER to the first. Only its display goes. Putting it back on the glass is a separate act performed from the library, not from the glass it just left. A two-state model would make closing a sticky and un-materialising an asset the same gesture, and a reader tidying their glass would silently discard work; the middle state is what makes closing cheap enough to do freely. When you implement close, check that the library offers the way back — not that the glass does. Close says where the way back is, at the moment of closing. The glass’s [x] opens a confirm that names the layer’s library and links it; Escape and Cancel leave the card where it is, and only the confirm shelves it — after which the glass says, with the same link, where the asset went. Naming the library matters because a reader holding assets from several libraries would otherwise have to remember which one each came from. The place is the card’s own, so there are three. A library card goes back to its layer’s library, a todo to the Todos board, and a landing sticky pinned to the glass to the page it was pinned from; calling a sticky “your Todos” would send the reader to a list it was never on. One function answers “where does this card go back to”, and the confirm, the status after it and the [x] button’s own label all read it, so the three cannot disagree. The confirm is the page’s one confirm dialog, shared with sending a sticky to fsh-guts, so focus-on-Cancel and Escape-cancels are stated once. Opening a library card goes to the asset’s visualizer when its index entry declares one, else to its entry page; resizing is a corner drag, with +/− in move mode and the move bar’s buttons as the non-drag path.

4b30ad1f6e2e.title: Two settings panels, two names, each points to the other
4b30ad1f6e2e.content: The glass has its own settings (theme, avatars, opacity, blur), and the page has its own under ▦ Actions (scheme, reading preferences, the Discarded fish, Declared kinds). They are named “Glass settings” and “Page settings”, so a screen reader does not read two controls identically, and each panel opens with a link to the other, as its first control, because a reader who opens the wrong panel needs a pointer to the right one. Site chrome and board state are unrelated settings but they are neighbouring places, and a reader moves between places. | The names are declared once (SETTINGS_NAMES in docs-ui.js), because each panel’s link prints the OTHER panel’s name; a panel renamed in one place only would leave the other panel’s link naming something that no longer exists. | The link must OPEN its target, not toggle it, and not open it underneath. The glass’s openPanel closes a panel that is already open, and the open glass covers the sidebar where Page settings lives. So the glass-to-page link shuts the glass first, and the page-to-glass link shuts the launcher first. In both cases focus lands on the target panel’s heading. | No link to nothing. A page with a glass and no sidebar has no launcher. Each panel registers an opener, and the link is drawn only when its target registered one. | . The same holds for any future pair of panels that share a word: name each one for what it acts on, and point each one at the other. scripts/tests/settings-labels-distinct.test.ts checks the source; test/settings-crosslinks.e2e.ts checks the rendered page at 1280×800 and 390×844, by mouse and keyboard.

0ffe44dd37fb.title: Lazy window content fetch and render safety
0ffe44dd37fb.content: Rendering the board with N cards makes 0 per-card detail fetches up front: each board slot (todoSlot / renderBoardTiles) renders only its summary tile/avatar. When a card carries a per-card detail or artifact URL (detailHref, bodyHref, artifactHref, or a non-inlined jsonldHref), opening its window (openCard / createLazyWindowLoader.openWindow) fetches that card’s content lazily on open, caches the result by card id (so re-opening uses the cached result and never pre-fetches the other N - 1 cards), and renders any body or tool/skill output through the declared renderToolOutput (RENDER_AS: text, url, markdown, json) and safeHref boundary (schemas/ui/render-output.ts, site-chrome/assets/js/docs-ui.js). A refused URL scheme (such as javascript:) is never fetched and is shown as escaped text.

673144e86ba5.title: Inputs and outputs
673144e86ba5.content: schemas/skills/bpmn-authoring/: . | in — processName (required), sourceWorkflow, existingBpmn, participants | out — bpmnFile, diagramFile, taskCount, gatewayCount, participantCount | . graphviz is a declared capability with degradation: skip — layout help degrades, authoring does not stop.

f7a3170e26c0.title: Diagram Interchange is not optional
f7a3170e26c0.content: A .bpmn with no DI section — no explicit x/y on its shapes — parses and renders blank, although the XML looks complete. bun run cat render:bpmn renders every diagram to docs/assets/img/workflows/ with bpmn-js in headless Chromium; bun run cat render:bpmn:check fails when an SVG is stale. Run the renderer and look at the SVG before you call a diagram done.

aa93787d0de0.title: Readable at 100%: check it before and after (author check)
aa93787d0de0.content: Every diagram you write or touch must, when you are done: . | fit 1400 × 900 in diagram units, so its 16px text reads at about 14px in a 1200px band without zooming; every task a fixed 120 × 120 square: boxes never grow to fit their names, and a name that does not fit is shortened (TASK_SIZE in the tools layer); | have no label on another label, on a flow (its own included), on a box or across a lane line: a gateway’s question above the diamond, its answers beside their flows, every label inside one lane; | have right-angled flows and every name inside its box, pool and lane names inside their strips; | have no crossing flows, and the lane order that keeps flows between lanes shortest: each lane sits next to the lanes it exchanges flows with, so no flow crosses a lane it does not stop in. A lane that talks to only one other lane, such as an owner who only approves the merge steward’s card, goes on the outside, next to that lane (owner, 2026-11-07: “swap owner lane down to reduce arrows across non interacting actor lanes”). | . bun run cat bpmn:detangle <file> reports all of it, and --write fixes what it can (lane order, right angles, box and lane sizes, label places). Run it before and after, and put both counts in the PR. Zero findings on every diagram you touch, or it does not merge (owner, 2026-11-02, after 63 of 80 harness diagrams were found with findings: “improve bpmn authoring process/skills so doesnt happen again”). A report nobody has to act on is how they piled up. Run bpmn:detangle <file> --check last; a finding you leave needs a reason in the PR, and only diagram-too-wide / lane-order may be left that way. Then look at the render: the check cannot yet see a box drawn across a lane line or outside its own lane, two flows drawn on top of each other, or a flow that wanders through a lane it does not stop in. Those are found only by looking. The same findings are in render:bpmn’s warnings and the process’s QA report, so a reviewer sees what the author left. The procedure, and why the budget is 1400 × 900, is bpmn-detangle.

4bb2f1d9b595.title: In this repository, a diagram is executable
4bb2f1d9b595.content: processes/**/*.bpmn are not pictures. workflow_start / workflow_next / workflow_complete run them, and workflow_complete refuses a step that is not enabled. That has consequences for how you author: . | Every activity carries <bootstrap.processes:skill ref="…"/> naming the skill that implements it, and <cat-harness.processes:bean store="beans/"/> where it touches the work plan. bun run cat check:workflow-refs fails on a ref that resolves to nothing, and bun run cat kg:audit additionally fails when the named skill exists but no package can serve it. | Every lane names a role. Declare the role once as a top-level <bpmn:resource id="<role id>" name="<title>"/> (before the collaboration and the process), and set partitionElementRef="<role id>" on the lane; the id is the role’s in scenarios/roles.json, verbatim. Lane names are free text; an explicit ref is the join that does not depend on spelling. <bootstrap.processes:role ref> is the deprecated form. A diagram using any bootstrap.processes: element declares the namespace as the first child of <bpmn:definitions>: <bpmn:import namespace="https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/v0/processes/ns/" location="https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/v0/processes/ns.jsonld" importType="http://www.w3.org/ns/json-ld"/>. | A store is not a lane. Lanes are for people and agents, the roles that act. A place where things are kept, such as the work plan (work items), a corpus, a session record, an activity log or a published bucket, is a <bpmn:dataStoreReference>. The tasks that read or write it point at it with data associations, and each task sits in the lane of whoever does it. A “Work plan — beans” lane holding “Open the bean” says the store does the work, when the agent does. | The process’s own bpmn:documentation opens with what it is for. Its first sentence is the diagram’s row on the publication-workflow page. kg-export carries it on the Process node as summary (the whole text as description), the page reads it from the published named-subgraph JSON-LD (bun run cat subgraph:jsonld) rather than from anything written by hand, and check:process-index fails when a declared diagram’s node has none. So that sentence says what the process does or answers — not who asked for it, which work item or issue it came from, or where the work got to. Those belong later in the documentation, or in the work item. | A gateway may be computed rather than chosen — see dmn-authoring. | Policy is declared on the process. <cat-harness.processes:policy enforcement="strict"/> means workflow_gate refuses a step that is not enabled; absent policy means strict. Steps marked relaxable="false" may never be relaxed by any package. | .

2cd4ced9c1cf.title: Readable diagrams: what the research supports
2cd4ced9c1cf.content: These rules are what holds up from the BPMN comprehension research, checked mechanically. kg:audit reports each rule below per process (src/workflow/diagram-quality.ts in the tools layer). The sources, and how strong each rule’s evidence is, are in the process-model-quality methodology. | Separate routing from work. A task never has two outgoing flows: put an exclusive or parallel gateway after it, or a reader must guess fork vs choice (activity-implicit-split, major). A loop-back INTO a task is fine. A gateway either joins or splits, not both (gateway-mixed). A question is a gateway, never a task: a box named “Should it leave now?” or “Separate this graph?” is a decision drawn as work. If someone must judge first, draw that as a task (“Judge whether it should leave”) or a call to Process_AskThePerson, then the question on the gateway after it. | Keep it small. Split by phase into call activities past 20 flow nodes (process-size). That 20 is house style. The only threshold with evidence is 7PMG’s 50 (process-decompose, major), and it predicts modelling errors such as deadlocks, not reading speed. | One start event per process level (process-single-start). Several named end events are fine, and the work item CLOSE pattern needs them. | A decision is a question, its branches are the answers (decision-label-question). | Label activities verb-object: imperative verb, then its object (Review the draft, not Draft review) (activity-label-verb-first). The evidence is one study of how ambiguous labels felt (29 students), so this is reported, never gated. | A name says the step, nothing else. No trailing [skill] slug: the skill is in <bootstrap.processes:skill ref>, and the page links it from there. No step numbers (“1 ·”, “Phase 2:”, “P1.1”): the flows already give the order, and a number in front breaks verb-first. A number that cites a section of a source document goes in the task’s documentation. A list of numbered steps is a sign the diagram copies a document’s outline; group the steps into phases instead. | . Split by phase: how . A diagram can be right in every step and still unreadable on its page. When process-size fires, or a diagram has a start event per lane, split it like this: . | The top-level process shows the phases. Each phase is a <bpmn:callActivity calledElement="…"> to its own process. Keep at the top only what moves the work between phases: who hands off to whom, and the decisions that send it back (rejected → revise). A loop that crosses phases is drawn at the top; a loop inside a phase stays in that phase. | A phase lives in its own file, <parent>-<phase>.bpmn, next to the parent, with its own process id (Process_<Parent><Phase>) and a first documentation sentence that says what the phase does. It becomes the phase’s row on the publication-workflow page like any other diagram’s. | A phase that ends two ways ends in two named end events, and the caller’s gateway right after the call reads which one it reached, as GW_BeanYours reads Process_BeanOpen’s. | Keep the node ids when you move nodes into a phase. A test, a schema or a skill that points at Task_X then changes only its file and process, not its id. | Open and close the work item at the top, once. A process that is only ever called runs on its caller’s work item, so a phase calls neither Process_BeanOpen nor Process_BeanClose (check:bean-calls). “Once” holds for the top as well: a process with several outcomes routes them all into one Process_BeanClose call, which decides itself whether the work item is completed, scrapped or blocked, and only then branches to its named end events. One close per outcome repeats the same box and makes the diagram wide. | A caller’s adjudication accepts looks one level down. If the judgement moves into a phase, put accepts on the call to that phase, and take it off any caller further up. | Name a call activity for the phase, verb-object like any activity (“Review the change”), not for its file. | . A phase that only one parent calls is still worth its own file: the point is the page a reader opens, not reuse. Untangle every diagram you touch . The same discipline as ArchiMate views (archimate-models §”Untangle every view you touch”), and the same geometry: a change never adds a tangle. Run bun run cat kg:audit before and after, and compare edge-crossing, edge-through-node and edge-rectilinear for the diagram, and check that no shape has a flow in and a flow out on the same point and that each lane’s rows sit at k/(n+1) of its height (bpmn-processes §”Edge routing”). Say both counts in the PR. Route loop-backs in the channel below the lane (bpmn-processes §”Edge routing”), then look at the rendered SVG. What the evidence does NOT support . Do not import these from style guides or model output; each was checked: . | Mandatory left-to-right flow. Figl & Strembeck 2015 (44 people) found no significant difference in accuracy or time across four directions. Lay out left-to-right for consistency, not because it reads faster. | A word cap on labels, a gateway fan-out cap of 4, and a fixed colour palette. No study behind them. Colouring matching split and join gateways made novices more accurate and experts faster, not more accurate (Reijers et al. 2011). | OR-gateways need no rule: the process model refuses inclusive gateways at load. | .

2b240c2266fa.title: If it has actors, activities and a control flow, it is BPMN
2b240c2266fa.content: Not a Mermaid fence. Mermaid stays for the things that are not processes — component maps, lattices, navigation graphs. The audit of which is which is on the publication workflow page, which the content core authors.

89b30e65c971.title: Why this skill is in a platform package
89b30e65c971.content: It covers both a DAK’s L2 business processes and this repository’s own processes/**/*.bpmn, and platform processes such as crdm-requirements.bpmn name it, so it cannot live in a content-type package: a platform process depending on a content-type package crosses the boundary the platform-boundary-guard subagent keeps. Its DAK material stays here rather than in a second skill, because a generic skill naming a domain worked example is ordinary, and two skills that must be read together to author one diagram are not.

d449de343285.title: When a layer above transforms it
d449de343285.content: A layer built on this one may transform an authored business process into another artefact — FHIR Shorthand, for instance — and then the BPMN is a source artefact rather than documentation of one. Author it knowing it will be transformed: names and ids you choose here appear in what is generated. That layer’s own tooling skill has the mechanics; this one names no layer above it.

2bcf6a1d4f53.title: bpmn-authoring (skill)
2bcf6a1d4f53.content: The skill bpmn-authoring as its source file cat-harness/skills/process/workflow/bpmn-authoring.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

e5c199464d24.title: Branch archaeology: what each branch holds that main does not
e5c199464d24.content: Skill branch-archaeology: Classify every remote branch against the default branch (merged, landed by squash or cherry-pick, partially landed, unlanded, undetermined) by commit ancestry, patch-id and merge-tree, not by subject line. Report only, never delete. A branch touching content or mathematics is a salvage-review item and never a delete candidate. Covers the treeless fetch that makes thousands of branches cheap, caching by tip sha, and the report’s shape. Read before answering “which branches can go?” or “what work never landed?”. Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . The question sounds like git branch -r --no-merged, and that command answers it wrong. It tests ancestry, so a branch landed by squash or cherry-pick (which is how most PRs land here) shows as unmerged forever. lsi:epics uses it to find unmerged branches, which is fine for filing and wrong for disposal. Measured in one folio, 2026-10-04: 6,480 remote branches, of which 461 held mathematics not on main. Those 461 are the reason for the rule in §2. A sweep that labelled them “stale” would have offered the only copy of proofs for deletion.

ad5d267b28dd.title: 1. The five classes, decided in this order
ad5d267b28dd.content: | class | test | meaning | . | merged | git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main | every commit is on main | . | landed | git merge-tree --write-tree origin/main <tip> produces main’s own tree, or every commit’s patch-id is on main (git cherry origin/main <tip> prints only -), or the branch’s combined diff patch-id matches a main commit (the squash case) | the CHANGE is on main under other commits | . | partial | some commits’ patch-ids are on main, some are not | part landed; the rest is unique work | . | unlanded | none of the above, and every test ran | unique work | . | undetermined | a test could not run: an object could not be fetched, or merge-tree conflicted and patch-ids disagree | not unlanded and not landed. Report it as unknown | . Some notes on the tests: . | The merge-tree test is the strongest. If merging the branch into main changes nothing, then nothing on the branch is missing from main, however it got there: squash, cherry-pick, a re-implementation with the same result, or a revert-and-reapply. A conflict proves nothing either way, so move on to the patch-id tests. | git cherry compares per-commit patch-ids. It catches cherry-picks. It misses a squash, because one squashed commit’s patch-id equals the sum of the branch, not any single commit. Hence the combined test: . base=$(git merge-base origin/main "$tip") git diff "$base" "$tip" | git patch-id --stable # the branch as one patch git log --format=%H "$base"..origin/main | while read c; do git show "$c" | git patch-id --stable # each main commit since done . | Subject lines are never evidence. Two commits titled “fix build” share nothing, and a squash usually renames. | undetermined must never be folded into either neighbour. A census that counts it as unlanded inflates salvage work. One that counts it as landed offers unique work for deletion, which is the dh4f shape: a clean report over what the tool could not read. | . Two flags sit beside the class rather than inside it: . | open-pr: #n — any branch backing an open PR is live, whatever its class. | beans: […] — work item ids named in its commit messages, the same extraction lsi:epics performs. This is the link that lets work-plan-restructure (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) close a work item whose work this census shows landed. | .

b0b8dc44de71.title: 2. Content protection: a content branch is salvage-review, never delete-candidate
b0b8dc44de71.content: If an unlanded or partial branch touches content, it goes on the salvage-review list and is never offered for deletion, at any age or size. “Content” means any path under a directory the layer declares with a content kind (folio, library), any .lean file, and the folio’s block, chapter and computation sources. Read the declaration (<instance>.json); do not use a hard-coded path list. The reason is asymmetric cost. A platform branch’s unique work can usually be re-derived from the issue that motivated it. A proof, a computation or an authored chapter often cannot, because the session that wrote it is gone and its scrollback with it. So: . | branch | goes to | . | merged / landed, no open PR | delete-candidate list, with size, age, last author and the evidence that it landed | . | partial / unlanded, no content touched | review list, with unique commits, size and age | . | partial / unlanded, content touched | salvage-review list, with the unique paths and hunks, and work item ids | . | undetermined | unknown list, with the test that failed | . | any class with an open PR | not listed for disposal at all | . The delete-candidate list is a report, not an action. deletion-requires-confirmation: the owner reads it, with sizes and ages, and says which go. A branch is the last copy of its commits once the PR is closed, and plj1 is that skill’s worked example of a workflow whose shape deleted work nobody decided to delete. The content census — “absent on main” is the signal, “differs” is not . For a branch on the salvage list, the question is which of its content is nowhere on main. Compare at three levels, strongest first: . | By name, not by path. For each Lean module and declaration, and each block label, the branch adds, search main for the name anywhere. A module that moved directories is still on main. Measured in the qou orphaned-content census, 2026-10-04: of 60 recent unlanded branches, 32 touched content and 27 carried content not on main. After excluding schema files, the residue was 12 Lean modules on 7 branches whose names occur nowhere on main. That residue is the salvage list. The other 55 files that merely “differ” are not. | Path-remapped. A branch cut before a layout move uses the old paths (qou’s branches all predate its content/ → folio/ move). Remap through the move before comparing, or every file reads as absent. Take the remap from the commit that made the move. Do not guess it. | “Differs from main” is not unique work. Main moved on after the branch was cut. Count it separately, and never as math. Only a three-way comparison against the merge-base says whose change a hunk is. | . Salvage is filed per CLUSTER, not per branch. 461 branches are not 461 work items. Work items are not sidecars, and one work item per branch is the generated-template flood work-plan-restructure exists to clean up. Group the salvage list by the subject its unique paths touch (a chapter, a Lean namespace), and propose one work item per group to the owner.

3d6c7e39d128.title: 3. Making 6,000 branches cheap: a treeless fetch
3d6c7e39d128.content: git fetch --filter=tree:0 origin '+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*' . This fetches every head’s commits without their trees or blobs: 15 s for ~6.5k branches in qou. That is enough for the ancestry test and for the commit-message work item extraction. The merge-tree and patch-id tests need trees and blobs, which the partial clone then fetches on demand, per branch. So order the work to fetch as little as possible: . | Ancestry for every branch (commits only, cheap). Most stale branches end here as merged. | Open-PR heads from the API, once. | Merge-tree, then patch-id, only for what is left. A branch whose objects cannot be fetched is undetermined (§1), not skipped silently. | .

432a4f29ae49.title: 4. Cache by tip sha, and know which classes go stale
432a4f29ae49.content: Key each row by branch tip sha and record the main sha it was computed against. | merged and landed are monotone: main only grows, so they stay true while the tip is unchanged. The exception is a revert on main, which the next full run catches. | partial, unlanded and undetermined must be recomputed when main moves, because the work may have landed since. | A changed tip invalidates the row whatever its class. | . A re-run then costs only the branches that moved plus the non-monotone rows. The full answer is never re-derived from scratch, which is the waste goal-review and the survey graph (beans/surveys/) already exist to stop.

0a8faa5504e8.title: 5. The report
0a8faa5504e8.content: For each branch: name, tip sha, main sha, class, the evidence (which test decided it, patch-ids matched of total), open-pr, beans, commits ahead, size of the unique diff, last commit date, and the last author or Claude-Session: trailer. Then the four lists in §2, each with counts, and the undetermined count stated beside the others, never dropped. Where it goes: summarised on the issue or in a work item note (bun run cat beans:note) for the owner, and the per-branch rows as a file attached to that review. A committed, declared home for a recurring census (a qa-reports sidecar) is not built yet. Do not invent an undeclared directory for it. Name the gap instead.

b865a498286a.title: What this skill does not do
b865a498286a.content: . | Delete, prune or close anything. Not branches, not PRs, not work items. | Judge whether unique work is wanted. unlanded means “not on main”, not “should be on main”. That call belongs to the owner, through salvage review. | Replace branch-freshness (your own branch against main) or coordinate (live sibling PRs). This skill is the census of everything else. | .

d487a967d77e.title: CI health — a red workflow looks exactly like a green one from in here
d487a967d77e.content: Skill ci-health: A red workflow looks exactly like a green one from inside a checkout. How to read a default-branch health report, the three verdicts that keep it honest, why a watchdog needs both a session-start print and an unattended run, and the separate external question the Pages deployments need. Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Record agent step, Review-log watch . A workflow’s outcome is invisible from the working tree. Nothing in a checkout says whether the last run passed, so a workflow can fire on every push and fail every time while the repository reads as healthy. Measured here: one publishing workflow fired on every push to the default branch and failed all 30 times over two months. The trigger was fine; the outcome was unobserved, the published site sat stale, and nothing in the repository said so.

495a63b7472a.title: Read the report, and read it by these three rules
495a63b7472a.content: check:ci-health reports each workflow’s state on the default branch — consecutive failures, days since the last green, and whether it has run at all recently. The session-start sweep prints it, so it lands where you already look. | “Could not check” is never rendered as green. A watchdog that has gone blind must not read as good news. | A red that has not re-run in a week is possibly stale, not an active fire. The distinction is what stops a dead workflow consuming attention a live one needs. | A red whose workflow file changed after the failing run is superseded. The version that failed is gone, so the verdict is stale. superseded is never rendered as green and never counted as a live failure: a later edit is evidence the failing version is gone, not evidence the new one works. | . That third rule is not hypothetical. Two workflows here failed to parse on one day — which is why the platform ran them on push despite both being dispatch-only, and why their runs are named by path rather than by their declared name. They were fixed the next day, and they only run on dispatch, so nothing will ever run them on the default branch again. Without the rule they are red forever. Do not “fix” a dispatch-only workflow by dispatching it. Some fail by design in the repository you are standing in — a folio-shaped job preflighting on a manifest the platform does not carry, or a computation step needing a directory only a folio has. A red you caused by running something that was never meant to run here is worse than the stale verdict you were trying to clear.

67f0eb93a66e.title: For ONE commit, zero checks is not a pass
67f0eb93a66e.content: check:ci-health reads workflows across history. When the question is one commit (may I merge this PR, must I fix it, or do I not yet know?), the tool is bun run cat ci:watch <sha> or ci:watch --pr <n>. It answers in three states, and undetermined has its own exit code, never 0. The trap it exists for arrives as good news. A conflicted pull request gets no pull_request run at all. GitHub checks out refs/pull/N/merge, which it does not build for a head that conflicts. So the notification that “every check suite completed and none failed” can be true of zero suites. “No suite failed” over nothing that ran is not green, and neither is a partial set (a push-triggered job finished, the PR’s gate workflow never registered). Before reading an event as a pass, ask the head’s merge state. A merge ref that exists can still have been built for an EARLIER head (GitHub leaves the old one in place when a new head conflicts), so the ref must have been built from the current head. The tool enforces this (verdictForCommit, mergeStateForHead); an agent reading PR events without the tool applies it too. qa-publish is a job in the gate workflow, and it is not a gate . Code quality gates carries one job that judges nothing: qa-publish, which runs after gates whatever they concluded and stores the run’s QA results on the orphan qa-reports branch (main/<sha>/ on a push, pr/<n>/<sha>/ on a same-repository PR). Read its outcome as a statement about the evidence, not about the commit: . | red — the record for this commit was not stored. The gates’ verdict is untouched (it is a separate job for exactly that reason), but a later --against this commit will read UNKNOWN, so it is still a red to fix, and a workflow-level red in this report. | green with a ::notice on a fork PR — skipped by design: a fork’s token cannot write. Stated, never silent. | green with the gates red — the red commit’s evidence was stored. That is the point of always(), not a contradiction. | . The merge policy counts it like any job: a PR is handed to the Merge Steward only when CI is green on every job (continual-progress §”Green means handed to the Merge Steward”).

171a4e875e4e.title: The report answers about the default branch — and Pages is not on it
171a4e875e4e.content: A Pages build outcome is not repository state. It is a fact GitHub holds about the repository, and it changes the repository’s status without changing a single byte of it. So the tool must look external, cache nothing: a committed answer would be right when it was written and silently wrong from then on. The default-branch query cannot see it, for three reasons at once, and all three have to be answered together: . | property | why the default-branch query misses it | . | runs on the publish branch | ?branch=<default> excludes them outright | . | raised by github-pages[bot], event dynamic | there is no file in .github/workflows/ to be a row about | . | its workflow has no file | it is addressable only by a per-repository id | . Measured here on one day: the default-branch page held zero deployments while the publish branch held 51 cancelled and 49 succeeded, of which 25 were self-inflicted. None of it was visible from anywhere. Two more, for the question the three above do not cover . Deliberately not numbered 4 and 5: the three rules are the three rules, for reading the default-branch report, and they are quoted by that count in several places. These are a separate pair for a separate question — which is itself the rule about never letting a count in prose go stale. | cancelled is a THIRD state. A cancelled deployment neither shipped nor broke: the previous preview stays up, so the site is stale rather than down, and nobody is owed a fix. Folded into success the report says the preview shipped; folded into failure it sends somebody after a build that was merely superseded. Both readings are wrong in a way the reader cannot detect — which is rule 1 again, wearing different clothes. Crucial exception: staleness is benign only when falling back to an existing live preview, never when the previous state is a deletion (where “stale” manifests as a 404). When PR N’s merge cleanup removed branches/<slug>/ and PR N+1’s staging deploy was cancelled, the live site serves the deletion rather than a previous preview. Staleness is safe only when what you fall back to actually exists. | Say WHOSE contention it is. One workflow pushing twice and cancelling its own build is a fixed defect; several sessions racing for the publish ref is a different, open one. A merged cancellation count cannot show whether the first fix held — so the self-inflicted ones are named by slug, and a slug still appearing is a branch running the workflow from before the fix. | . Report the counts; grade only a floor . There is no calibrated threshold for “too many cancellations”, so the report states the numbers and does not grade the share — no percentage, no verdict word. That is the same refusal that stopped a PDF heuristic inventing a size threshold with nothing to calibrate against. One statement is graded, because it is a floor rather than a threshold: deployments happened and not one succeeded. That needs no calibration, the way “the build directory is empty” needs none.

58583c975132.title: A report is only read by someone in the room
58583c975132.content: This is the part that gets designed wrong. The session-start print covers every day somebody is working — and the failure being guarded against is a quiet stretch with nobody looking, which is exactly the stretch in which no session starts either. A report alone cannot cover its own worst case. So the watchdog has a second half: the same check runs on a schedule and maintains one tracking issue, which is . | opened when the default branch has a live failure, | edited in place while it persists — an edit does not notify, so a long outage stays one unread item rather than a stream, | closed automatically when the branch is clean. | . It deliberately does not send another email. The platform already sent 30 and the premise of the whole exercise is that nobody reads them. Live badges at the top of the README are the same state at the front door. Two properties of that scheduled run are load-bearing rather than incidental: . | It needs full history. The superseded rule asks when a workflow file last changed, and a shallow clone cannot answer — which would resurrect exactly the false fires the rule exists to retire. | On “could not check” it leaves the issue untouched and fails its own job, rather than closing it. A watchdog reporting that it cannot see must not read as good news, and its own red is reported by the next scheduled run. | . The second instance: merge-main’s in-place comment . The same edited-in-place doctrine governs merge-main.yml (implemented by cat-harness-tools/scripts/merge-main-comment.ts). The workflow fires on every push to main and runs across open PRs; one failing PR must not email the maintainer on every push across the day. So the bot’s PR comment is the record and is edited in place, and a failure whose signature the comment already holds stays quiet. Three conditions stay loud (failing the aggregate step so the run notifies): . | A new failure — the first failure on this PR head. | A changed cause — the failure signature changed even on the same head. | A systemic failure — every selected PR failed, not made up entirely of repeats (or a member failed to classify itself). | . Quiet is not silent. A failure that does not notify still maintains four records: . | Its PR comment (edited in place, carrying the failure signature). | Its line in the job summary. | A warning annotation on the run. | Its own red member job in the matrix (findable in GitHub Actions UI). | .

fa34de81cde0.title: The opposite defect
fa34de81cde0.content: This covers a workflow that fires constantly and fails every time. The complementary failure — a workflow that never fires at all — is not visible to this check, because a workflow with no runs and a workflow with no failures look identical in the run history. Both are “could not check”, and the first rule applies.

0c070363ba79.title: A superseded PR run is cancelled — and only a PR’s
0c070363ba79.content: A run on a PR head that a newer push replaced judges a commit nobody will merge, and it still waits for and holds a runner. So a workflow that runs on pull_request declares . concurrency: group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' && github.event.pull_request.number || github.sha }} cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }} . Two halves, and the second matters as much as the first. A PR’s runs share one group, so the newer cancels the older. Every other event is grouped by its own sha and never cancelled: a push to main keeps its verdict, so this report’s history of main is not thinned by cancellations, and a cancelled on main keeps meaning contention rather than housekeeping (the third state above). A cancelled run on a PR’s OLDER head is therefore expected and is not a finding. The merge guard judges the head, and the head’s run is never the one cancelled.

6d8b314e1fae.title: A green step can be a SKIPPED one: the CI cone
6d8b314e1fae.content: cat-harness-tools/scripts/ci-cone.ts lets a pull request skip a bun run cat <check> gate step whose inputs are unchanged since main’s last green run. Such a step prints SKIPPED — inputs unchanged since <sha>, and the job summary lists it under CI cone. Read it as “not asked here”, never as “passed here”. It is built but NOT wired into the workflow. Measured 2026-10-07 on the 53 candidate steps of gates-kg and gates-docs: . | It saves almost nothing. The 36 checks it could record skip on a beans-only or one-script PR, but they are the cheap ones: about 30 runner-seconds a run. Deciding costs about 0.5 s a step, roughly 22 s for those steps. | Recording would slow main a lot. The expensive checks cannot be recorded: kg:audit:check and kg:audit:all:check read the qa-reports store, and skill:register:check has an unannotated site. Tracing them anyway would add minutes to every main run (kg:audit:all:check: 74 s untraced, 782 s traced). | . Wire it in when those checks become recordable. The rule it follows: an input set is declared or derived, never inferred, and derived is preferred (no drift, no extra data fields). | Declared is a task-io row. It is checked by the input-site audit. | Derived is computed from the run itself and never stored as authored data. A green run on main traces the check under strace and records what that run read: the files, the directory listings, the absent paths it probed, and the read-only git commands it ran, with their answers. A PR skips the check only when every recorded path and every git answer is the same, and so is the script fingerprint (import closure, audited environment, tools and --against baseline). | Inferred is a guess about what a check reads. It is never used. | . Why the derived set is enough. The verdict and its read set come from the same run. A PR run with the same code and the same recorded inputs takes the same path, so it reads the same files and gives the same answer. A data-dependent read is covered by the same argument: the file that chose the path is one of the recorded inputs. What a trace cannot enumerate is never skipped. Each of these is recorded as undetermined, so the check always runs: . | a write inside the checkout; | a git command that is not read-only; | a traced input site the run reached; | a relative path with no known directory; | a trace over 256 MiB; | more than 20,000 paths. | . A failed traced run is asked again untraced, so the verdict is always the check’s own.

082860da8fee.title: A slow workflow can be mostly waiting: fold tiny serial jobs into one
082860da8fee.content: Owner ruling, 2026-11-13 (card “A. Collapse into one job”, then “update skills and processes to see when need to do so”). Each job waits for its own runner, so a chain of small jobs pays that wait once per link. Measured: one content layer’s run took 23 minutes for about 2.5 minutes of work. Its five small serial jobs each queued for a runner, for 9m29s, 1m, 1m45s, 3m43s and 4m22s. When to act. A job is a candidate to become a step of its neighbour when either holds: . | its median queue wait is longer than its median run time; or | it is one of more than 2 jobs in a serial chain (needs:) that each run in under 1 minute. | . How to see it. Measure each job from the Actions API (GET /repos/<owner>/<repo>/actions/runs/<run>/jobs): . | its wait is started_at − created_at; | its run time is completed_at − started_at. | . Take the median over the workflow’s recent runs on the default branch, not one run, because a single wait says more about the runner pool that minute than about the workflow. The tools layer will add the report. Until it does, the weekly review below measures by hand. What stays a separate job, even when it is small: . | a heavy job, or a set of parallel shards: folding them makes the run longer, not shorter; | a job that needs different permissions, a different runner, or a different environment; | a job whose check name something reads: merge:guard, branch protection’s required checks, or verdict reuse. Fold it only together with every reader of that name, in the same change. | . Who looks, and when. The weekly CI health review (ci-health-watch.bpmn, the check:ci-health step) also looks at job shape. When a workflow crosses either threshold, it opens a work item naming the workflow, the jobs, the measured medians, and which of them must stay separate. The fold itself is an ordinary PR.

377295aa04c5.title: Step names describe what the check does, not merely its passing invariant
377295aa04c5.content: A CI step named solely after its passing invariant misdescribes any failure where the check could not run or the baseline was absent. A step named viewer pages keep the navbar they had that goes red when its audit sidecar is absent misleads a reader to investigate page layouts when zero pages regressed. Where a check has both a subject-invariant branch and an audit/baseline-reachability branch, the step name in the workflow must cover both (e.g. viewer pages keep the navbar they had, and audit is reachable).

d96ee019fe11.title: The accidental-repair trap on derived gates
d96ee019fe11.content: A green outcome on a derived gate (such as readme:subgraphs:check, docs:harness:check, or other verify/write pairs) must never be read as “was never broken”. Because PR branches run merge:main which regenerates derived files, an unrelated PR branch may happen to carry a freshly generated artefact. When that PR merges into main, it incidentally repairs main, creating an illusion in CI history that the commit before it was clean. The guard: The post-merge regeneration pipeline (.github/workflows/post-merge-regen.yml, scripts/post-merge-regen.ts) audits derived artefacts when dispatched on main and warns when they are stale; dispatched for a PR, it commits the regeneration to that PR’s branch, and the release build regenerates into what it publishes (merge-queue.md §”Where derived artefacts are regenerated”). When inspecting CI health on main, do not treat an accidental green as evidence of health: verify that post-merge checks run and derive their state consistently. Full details in merge-queue.md (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”The accidental-repair pattern”.

c09a428c23df.title: Compiled Artefact Cache
c09a428c23df.content: Skill compiled-artefact-cache: The general pattern for caching expensive compiled artefacts (Lean .oleans, FHIR ASTs) across builds. Defines branch-based storage, validity checking, exit code protocol, safety guards, and the restore→build→contribute loop. Named by: Authoring a document, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Draft, review and publish, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Review and publish a folio . This skill documents the generalisable pattern for caching compiled artefacts (such as Lean caches and FHIR ASTs). It is the shared contract that specific implementations (e.g. lean-cache-restore and ig-ast-delta) adhere to.

9620b661e939.title: The restore→build→contribute loop
9620b661e939.content: The cache is not a maintenance chore but the output of every authoring session. Every session should leave the cache warmer than it found it: . restore ──▶ draft / edit ──▶ build ──▶ contribute ▲ │ └───────── next agent starts here ─────────────┘ .

8b3d40b61953.title: Branch-based storage
8b3d40b61953.content: Artefacts are stored on orphan branches named for their package and toolchain (e.g. lake-cache/<package>-<toolchain>). This keeps the repository clean while persisting large derived outputs across builds. A branch that keeps every seed grows by what each seed’s writer changes. Write seeds by git-friendly-churn: the same bytes when nothing changed, and a stable path for each file, so a new seed costs deltas, not copies.

05b8f6b86fd9.title: Validity checking (3-valued)
05b8f6b86fd9.content: The validity of a cache is not a simple boolean. It relies on the CompiledInputsSchema defined in the content core’s schemas/materialization.ts. Validity is checked BEFORE use via compiledValidity() and returns one of three states: . | valid: The cache matches the current inputs (e.g. toolchain, source revision, input digest). Restore and build. | stale-inputs: Identifies exactly which input changed. The cache cannot be used as-is; restore for the current toolchain instead, or build cold. | cannot-tell: The cache record lacks required input fields. Never a pass. Build cold or find the missing inputs first. | .

7af3c5d11035.title: Exit code protocol
7af3c5d11035.content: Scripts managing the cache must adhere to a standard exit code protocol. Branch on these codes rather than grepping the output: . | Code | Meaning | Next | . | 0 | present / restored / published | proceed | . | 1 | miss — no such branch | build cold, then contribute | . | 2 | usage or environment error | stop the run, read the message, do not fallback to full build | . | 3 | found but unusable (corrupt, won’t link, wrong toolchain) | repair or reseed | .

a91332f9defb.title: Safety guards
a91332f9defb.content: When contributing a build back to the cache, it must be safe to run unconditionally. The contribution is refused unless it passes these guards: . | Non-empty: There must actually be artefacts to cache. | Own-package: Artefacts must belong to the package itself, not just its dependencies. | Trace coverage: There must be sufficient metadata (e.g. >90% traced) for the build tool to use the cache effectively. | No-shrink: The new result must not be materially smaller than the incumbent cache, preventing partial builds from destroying a fuller cache. | . For cold starts, seeding the cache uses a test-branch staging approach: the cache is seeded to a -test branch, and a restore is verified from a clean clone before touching production.

490c5a68989f.title: The warm-start principle: Cache the intermediates, not just the output
490c5a68989f.content: The core value of the cache is that an expensive step’s intermediate outputs survive across builds. The pattern is: a cache branch carries not just the final output but also the intermediate build artifacts that prevent the build system from re-deriving them: . | cache type | final output | intermediate artifacts | what they prevent | . | Lean | .olean files | .trace files | Lake rebuild + eviction | . | FHIR AST | AST JSON + edges | txcache/ (tx.fhir.org expansions) | Publisher re-hitting tx.fhir.org for every ValueSet | . input-cache/txcache/ goes on the fhir-ast branch alongside the AST files. Preserving these intermediates is what makes subsequent incremental builds (such as those in ig-incremental-build.bpmn) fast: a warm build with cached packages and terminology runs several times faster than a cold one.

45bd416db89a.title: Instantiations
45bd416db89a.content: | Aspect | Lean Cache (lean-cache-restore) | FHIR AST (ig-ast-delta) | . | Artefacts | .olean files, .trace files | Per-resource AST JSON, dependencies.json, txcache/ | . | Inputs Schema | CompiledInputsSchema | CompiledInputsSchema | . | Key Inputs | toolchain (Lean version), sourceRevision | toolchain (Publisher version), sourceRevision, inputDigest | . | Storage Branch | lake-cache/<package>-<toolchain> | fhir-ast/<ig-package-id> | . | Service Script | lake-cache.sh (9 verbs) | ig-cache.sh (7 verbs) | . | Refreshed by | an agent’s lake-cache.sh contribute | a reusable workflow of the IG layer, on a runner (the Publisher needs Java and a 10 GB heap), which each IG repository dispatches; a site build refuses an AST that is not valid | . | Cone Engine | Lake’s .trace-based dependency graph | SUSHI’s fsh-index.json (forward: file → resource) + fsh-cone.ts (reverse: who uses this file) + AstPlanCli | . | Incremental | lake build (only stale modules) | IncrementalBuildCli (cone rebuild loop) | .

785792d3dc58.title: The file-to-resource mapping comes from the toolchain, not from us
785792d3dc58.content: Do not reimplement what the compiler already knows. SUSHI already writes fsh-generated/data/fsh-index.json on every run — the authoritative mapping from source .fsh file to output FHIR resource, with source locations. The AST exporter copies it into the AST directory; the incremental planner reads it there. No modification to SUSHI is needed. fsh-cone (a Tool node, declared by the FHIR IG layer) provides the reverse half — who depends on a file — so a changed RuleSet- or Alias-only file (which produces no resource itself) can be traced to the resources it affects. These two maps together give the planner a complete cone. Without fsh-index.json the planner can only plan a full build; with it, a single-file change rebuilds only the resources in its cone, which is a small fraction of an IG.

a11b021b9aae.title: A confirmation can be waived — by the person who is owed it
a11b021b9aae.content: Skill confirmation-waiver: A human may waive a confirmation they are owed — for a session, for a process run, or until a stated time. Covers what a waiver is made of, where it is recorded (the context graph, never the work plan), the gates that can be waived and the rules that cannot, why every waiver carries an expiry, and the one thing an agent may never do: grant itself one. Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Several rules here stop an agent and hand a decision back: merging to main, removing a durable artefact, spawning a swarm, closing a work item whose evidence the session could not re-derive, re-entering a process it fell out of. The person who is owed a confirmation may give it in advance, for a stated scope. That is the same decision, made earlier, by the same person — never an agent making an exception for itself.

f5c4814446e0.title: A waiver is five fields, and none is optional
f5c4814446e0.content: | field | what it carries | why it cannot be omitted | . | granted_by | the person, by the identity the repository already knows them by | a waiver with no grantor is an agent’s own decision wearing a hat | . | quote | the grantor’s own words, verbatim | the agent’s paraphrase is the thing under suspicion; a summary can widen a scope without anyone noticing | . | gate | which gate class is waived (below) — never “everything” | a blanket waiver is indistinguishable from no rule, and nobody can audit what it covered | . | scope | session:<id>, process:<instance-id>, or until:<ISO-8601> | an unscoped waiver outlives the situation that justified it | . | expires | a timestamp, always | same argument bean-blocking.md (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) makes for a block: a waiver with no expiry cannot be told from one nobody remembered to withdraw | . A waiver missing any field is not a waiver, and the gate stands. An agent that finds a malformed one asks, exactly as if none existed.

d45e725cf4c7.title: The gates that can be waived, and the rules that cannot
d45e725cf4c7.content: A waiver relaxes a rule whose text is ask first. It can never relax a rule whose text is never. Never delete a work item is such a prohibition: no waiver reaches it, and the non-destructive move (scrapped, with reasons) is always available. | gate class | the rule it relaxes | waivable | . | merge-to-main | merge-to-main (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) — the owner’s authorisation for each merge (and crdm-requirements-workflow §Phase 6) | yes, for green heads only: a head in a repository with no CI is never covered | . | bean-close | bean-coordination §”When you cannot re-derive it yourself” — the ready-to-close batch | yes | . | deletion | deletion-requires-confirmation — report and wait | yes, per artefact class, never blanket | . | swarm-spawn | swarm-management — asked every time, per swarm | yes, with the agent count and model level named in the quote | . | process-reentry | process-state — confirm before re-entering | yes | . | issue-close | issue-working — an agent never closes an issue on its own say-so | yes; the waiver names the issues | . | agent permission grants | agent-permissions — a person grants what a coding agent may do | no — never self-granted, and granted per permission | . | hand-edited agent config | harness-projections — consent per change to .claude/settings.json and the like | no — consent is per change | . | work item deletion | todo-manager, never delete a work item | no — a prohibition, not a gate | . | fabricating evidence | anywhere a rule says re-derive rather than quote | no | . A never that somebody wants waived is a change to the skill that owns it — not a waiver.

09274bfe1078.title: Where a waiver lives — the context graph, never the work plan
09274bfe1078.content: A waiver is context: read at the start of a turn, consulted by whatever gate is about to fire, and never produced by the work it governs. That is the context layer as content-context-and-state-graphs defines it, so a waiver is a node under memory/waivers/ — the same graph an agent’s durable memory lives in. Not beans/. The work plan is state: it records what is being worked on and where it got to. A waiver is not work, has no Done-when, and must be readable by a gate that fires before any work item is opened. The work plan is also branch-local, so a session-scoped waiver filed there could be invisible to the session it was granted for. Not the interaction node (memory/interaction.json) either: that is read at session start and never written by a process, and a waiver is granted mid-session.

eb3a011dd705.title: Consulting one — the three-state read, as everywhere else
eb3a011dd705.content: Before a gate fires, look for a waiver in scope. There are three answers: . | A valid waiver covers this gate, in scope, unexpired → proceed, and say in the turn report which waiver you are acting under, quoting its words. A waived action is still an announced one. | No waiver → ask, exactly as the gate’s own skill says. | Could not determine — memory/waivers/ unreadable, a malformed node, a clock you cannot trust → ask. A gate that cannot read its waivers has not been waived. | . An expired waiver is kept, never deleted, as a scrapped work item is: the record of what was permitted, to whom and when, makes the next grant reviewable.

e781e39e99c0.title: What an agent may never do
e781e39e99c0.content: . | Grant itself a waiver. A waiver whose quote is not the grantor’s own words does not exist. If you are composing the sentence, you are the grantor, and you may not be. | Widen one. session: does not reach the next session; process: does not reach a sibling layer; deletion for build artefacts does not reach content. When the scope does not plainly cover the case in front of you, it does not cover it. | Infer one from tone. “go ahead”, “yes”, “do it” discharge the gate they were said to — that is an ordinary confirmation, and it needs no waiver node. A waiver is a standing grant over future gates, and it is recorded only when the owner says something that plainly is one. | Treat a waiver as a reason to skip the work. merge-to-main waived still means green CI and no conflict; bean-close waived still means the evidence is quoted in the work item. A waiver removes the asking, never the doing. | .

fa75bb408e51.title: Checked, not trusted
fa75bb408e51.content: bun run cat check:waivers reads every node under memory/waivers/ and fails on a missing field, a gate outside the table above, a scope that names a non-existent session or layer, and a waiver over a non-waivable rule. It reports expired waivers as inert, never as findings — they are history. The check reads the same table this skill publishes, so a gate class without a row is refused and the vocabulary cannot drift into “everything”.

1a287ebbc20b.title: Don’t hand off on a workflow nobody ran
1a287ebbc20b.content: Authoring is not finished at “it builds here”. Before the PR, push and dispatch the repo’s verification workflow against your branch (gh workflow run <wf>.yml --ref <branch>, or actions_run_trigger), wait for it, and put the run URL and conclusion in the PR body. Red → fix and re-dispatch. If you lack actions: write, state that in the PR along with the command a maintainer should run. Check when that workflow last ran, too: a CI file that nothing dispatches can sit red on main while the content it checks stops compiling, and nothing catches it because nothing runs.

ecbb5f35127c.title: Committee review of a content change
ecbb5f35127c.content: Process_ContentChangeReviewCommittee · strict (defaulted) · 10 step(s) . Called from content-change-review when the author submits. Which end it reaches is what the caller’s GW_CommitteeApproved reads. Organising the review is the review coordinator’s lane and deciding it is the committee’s. Merging is not here: it is a separate, confirmed act in content-change-review-publish. i i i i i i i i i i

ae91ae1166f3.doc: Committee review of a content change
ae91ae1166f3.title: Lanes — who acts
ae91ae1166f3.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Review Committee | reviewer | Compares staged against main, reviews the slices it is assigned (review-task.bpmn, one call per slice), takes a disputed finding to adjudication, judges the impact assessment, and decides. Task_Approve records the approval; merging is a separate, confirmed act in the publish phase. A rejection ends this phase with changes requested, and the caller routes it to Task_Iterate in the agent’s lane rather than to the author. | . | Review Coordinator | review-coordinator | Organises a review large enough to need organising, and decides nothing about the content: ingests the reviewers’ tagged comments, slices the change into pieces a reviewer can hold, assigns each slice to a review lane, and watches coverage until every changed block has a verdict or a reasoned waiver. A separate role from the editor: organising a review and deciding its outcome are different accountabilities. | .

b1e28a79a054.doc: Committee review of a content change
b1e28a79a054.title: Steps
b1e28a79a054.content: Every one of the 10 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Compare main vs stagingTask_CompareBeforeAfter | Review Committee | staging-reviewvisual-diffrendered-impact | The review starts from the Change Set’s RENDERED list (skillrendered-impact): every rendered file the change alters, predictedfrom each renderer’s dependency cone and checked against the build.The reviewer opens every content page on it, not only the pages theauthor mentions; index files are listed but not reviewed. An inputthe renderer could not place is shown as not known, never as nochange.Review committee opens both URLs side by side:- Main site: <pages-url>/ (current published state)- Staging: <pages-url>/branches/<branch-slug>/The staging banner shows the commit SHA so they can verifywhat they are reviewing matches the PR. A changed figure, diagramor table is also pictured before and after on the review page,with the share of changed pixels in words (skill visual-diff,Tool folio-block-screenshots). Anything the staging job cannotpicture (page chrome, scroll behaviour, a PDF page, an IG page) isin the agent’s before/after preview (skill before-after-preview). | . | Ingest tagged review commentsTask_IngestComments | Review Coordinator | review-comments | Every PR conversation comment that starts with block: <label> becomes a review-comment/1.0.0 todo (open), idempotently, and is published with the preview as review-comments.json. The staging workflow runs this on every push and on every tagged comment; the coordinator owns that it has run before slicing, because the slices are cut around what reviewers have already said. This is the ingest transition of REVIEW_TRANSITIONS. Uses folio-review-comments. | . | Slice the change and assign reviewersTask_SliceAndAssign | Review Coordinator | review-heatmapstaging-reviewrendered-impact | From the ChangeSet, its rendered list (skill rendered-impact: each changed rendered page is assigned like a changed block) and the heat map on the review page: cut the change into slices a reviewer can hold (usually a section, or a run of sections where the heat map clusters), and assign each slice to a review lane by what it contains — clinical content to a clinical SME, a decision table to a QC reviewer, prose to a narrative reviewer. A block that needs no review (a pure rename, say) is WAIVED here with a written reason, which is what the coverage gate counts. Re-entered from GW_Covered when coverage is incomplete: the uncovered blocks become new slices. | . | Review each sliceCall_ReviewSlices | Review Committee | calls Review taskcontent-reviewreview-comments | review-task.bpmn, once per slice, in parallel lanes by role. What kind of thing changed decides which review the slice descends into; the reviewer takes on that inner lane’s role for the call only. Each reviewer gives the slice’s blocks a verdict, and comments on the pull request with the block: tag where something needs saying. | . | Withdraw a review commentTask_WithdrawComment | Review Committee | review-comments | The reviewer who made a comment takes it back (it was a misreading, or a later slice answered it). Recorded with folio-review-comment-move --to withdrawn, committed to the edit-set’s feature branch like every status change. This is the withdraw transition of REVIEW_TRANSITIONS. | . | Adjudicate the disagreementCall_Adjudication | Review Committee | calls Adjudicationadjudication | adjudication.bpmn. When the editor and a reviewer, or two reviewers, disagree about a finding, an adjudicator settles it and records why; the review comment moves to adjudicated with the Decision that closed it.Permitted answers: stands — the finding is right and the author addresses it; withdrawn — the finding is wrong and the comment closes. Recorded on the comment, not branched: either way the flow goes on to the coverage check. | . | Review the editorial dependenciesTask_ReviewUses | Review Committee | uses-editorial-review | uses[] is what a READER must have read to follow the block — neverpopulated from the formal dependency graph. Once every changed blockis covered, the committee checks the editorial dependencies of thechange as a whole before judging its impact. Reading order is aproperty of folio content, so the step belongs to the contentprocess, which reaches the harness’s review by calling DOWN intoreview-task. | . | Review impact assessmentTask_ReviewImpact | Review Committee | content-review | Committee reviews the agent’s impact assessment:- Were all downstream effects identified?- Are the indicator changes acceptable?- Does the logic change match the narrative intent? | . | Request changesTask_RequestChanges | Review Committee | content-reviewcontent-review | Committee provides feedback. PR stays open.Author and agent iterate further. | . | ApproveTask_Approve | Review Committee | decision-audit | The committee approves the change: the judgement, recorded with theevidence it rests on. Approving is not merging: a self-authoredchange cannot be approved through GitHub’s own review (the approvermay not be the PR’s author), and a merge needs the owner’s explicitconfirmation whoever approved. | .

2fac4f8627a0.doc: Committee review of a content change
2fac4f8627a0.title: Decisions
2fac4f8627a0.content: Every one of the 4 decision(s) is documented. | decision | what decides it | branches | . | A comment withdrawn?GW_Withdraw | Asked after the slices are reviewed: did a reviewer withdraw a comment? Yes records the withdrawal first; either way the flow then asks whether a finding is disputed. | Yes → Withdraw a review commentNo → GW_Disputed_Join | . | A finding disputed?GW_Disputed | Is any finding disputed between author and reviewer? Yes goes to adjudication; No goes on to check that every changed block was reviewed. | Yes → Adjudicate the disagreementNo → GW_Covered_Join | . | Every changed block and page reviewed?GW_Covered | Computed, not chosen: decisions/review-coverage-gate.dmn reads uncoveredBlocks (changed blocks with neither a verdict nor a reasoned waiver) and openDefects, and, where the build published a rendered impact, unreviewedPages, undeterminedInputs and missedPages with their rendered and measured statuses (skill rendered-impact). Resolved comments are not coverage, and coverage is not approval — that is GW_Approved. | no → Slice the change and assign reviewersyes → Review the editorial dependencies | . | Changes approved?GW_Approved | The committee’s decision on the impact assessment. No requests changes; Yes approves. | No → Request changesYes → Approve | .

46b38bc7aefc.title: Content Change and Review
46b38bc7aefc.content: Process_ContentChangeReview · strict (defaulted) · 11 step(s) . Getting a change to a folio’s CONTENT from a request into a published rendering: the author says what they want, an agent works out its scope and makes it, a review committee accepts or refuses it, and the pipeline deploys. You are in this process when what is changing is a folio — a chapter, a block, a piece of deterministic logic — rather than the platform that renders it. code-change-review is the same shape for the platform: a content change is accepted by a REVIEW COMMITTEE on editorial grounds, a platform change by a code reviewer on engineering ones. Two things this is not. It is not the feedback workflow: todo-review triages what readers said about content that already exists. And the rendering the author reviews is a STAGED one, because a person cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it. The diagram shows the phases and the hand-offs between them; each phase is its own process. Making the change is content-change-review-make, staging it is content-change-review-stage, the committee’s review is content-change-review-committee, and merging and deploying is content-change-review-publish. This follows bpmn-authoring’s rule of one phase per call activity. i i i i i i i i i i i
