43a1caec7172.title: Feature-request detection (CRDM trigger)
43a1caec7172.content: Skill crdm-detect: Detect when a request needs requirements agreed before anything is built, and which of the two parallel requirements methodologies governs it. Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Detect when a user request is a feature request (platform capability change) rather than a content request (writing, editing, reviewing folio content). When a feature request is detected, the agent works through requirements rather than implementing directly.

b5daa2b01eb6.title: Applies when
b5daa2b01eb6.content: Requirements that come from stakeholders who must sign them off, on work tied to a folio’s domain — WHO SMART Guidelines, an IG, a programme’s content. The requester is a content developer working through a BA, and the answer depends on what the folio says. Not for a platform capability change raised by somebody building the tooling with a content-agnostic answer — that is spec-kit.

f98fc408415d.title: Which requirements methodology — the fork this detection now carries
f98fc408415d.content: Detecting a feature request does not select CRDM by itself. There are two parallel requirements methodologies, and methodology-adoption forbids blending them. The signals below tell you a request needs requirements; this fork tells you whose. |   | governs | requester | the answer depends on | . | crdm — this methodology | stakeholder-facing WHO/IG work: needs assessment, BPA, stakeholder sign-off | content developers, via a BA | a folio’s subject matter | . | spec-kit (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | folio-assistant feature development; software-development best practice, closer to a scrum process | tool developers | nothing a folio says — content-agnostic | . Most of the signals listed below are spec-kit’s, not CRDM’s — the “Platform-level change requests” and “Direct capability requests” categories especially, since both describe somebody building the tooling. Read the categories as this needs requirements, then apply the fork. Two things bind under either methodology and are not a reason to pick one: the issue-association rules at the end of this file, and the spec-before-code gate.

bdac484b0cc4.title: Detection signals
bdac484b0cc4.content: Scan every user request for these categories of phrasing. A single match is enough to flag; two or more from different categories is high confidence. Direct capability requests . Phrases where the user explicitly asks for new functionality: . | “I need a way to …”, “can you add …”, “we need a tool that …” | “there should be a skill for …”, “add a QA check for …” | “the renderer should support …”, “make the pipeline do …” | “can we add a new block kind for …”, “we need a content type for …” | “it would be great if the agent could …” | “the agent should …”, “the agent needs to …”, “we will need to …” | “build me …”, “create a tool …”, “develop a feature …” | . Workflow gap descriptions . Phrases where the user describes a process that does not work today: . | “right now I have to manually …”, “there is no way to …” | “the current process for … is broken”, “this workflow doesn’t handle …” | “we can’t do … yet”, “it’s missing …”, “it doesn’t support …” | “every time I need to …, I have to …” (manual workaround pattern) | “other people need to be able to …” | . Platform-level change requests . Phrases that imply changes to folio-assistant itself (not folio content): . | “change the schema to …”, “modify the pipeline …” | “add a new adapter …”, “the constraint should …” | “update the CI to …”, “the workflow should fire when …” | “the MCP tool needs to …”, “register a new tool for …” | “the upstream change requests to …”, “upstream asks” — a change asked of a tool this platform DEPENDS ON is still a platform change; the folio is not where it lands either way | References to files under schemas/, pipeline/, adapters/, src/, scripts/, .github/workflows/ | . Cross-cutting concerns . Phrases that affect multiple folios or content types: . | “for all papers …”, “every folio should …”, “across all content types …” | “when any user …”, “the platform should …” | “this needs to work for both document and paper folios” | . Review-surfaced needs . Phrases that emerge during content review: . | “this review process would be easier if …” | “we need a way to triage these comments …” | “the feedback workflow should …” | “stakeholders need to be able to see …” | “can we make the review process more …” | . A request for a plan . A request for a plan ALWAYS produces a requirements document and a work plan for review before implementation. | “plan”, “make a plan”, “plan the …” | “approach”, “what approach would you take” | “proposal”, “propose …” | “how would you …” | “come up with …” | . A plan request needs requirements under either methodology, and content requests are not exempt: “plan the edits to chapter 3” triggers it as surely as “plan the new validator”. The fork above still decides WHOSE requirements — this signal never selects a methodology and never blends them. The operation is the same for both and lives in the content layer, in the plan-request-gate skill (skill_fetch plan-request-gate): produce a requirements document and a work plan, put them where this methodology says (CRDM: committed under docs/proposals/), hand both over as absolute GitHub permalinks, and stop until sign-off is recorded on the issue. The definition of a requirement both methodologies share is the requirement-definition skill (skill_fetch requirement-definition). Self-declared genre . The mirror of "Migration record: …" below. Some documents say what they are in their own first line, and a proposal or a design document argues for a change that does not exist yet — which is a feature request whichever category its sentences fall into. | “Proposal: …” as a document’s OPENING line | “design document for …” | . Anchored to the opening line. On the adjudicated corpus an unanchored proposal adds no false alarm and catches one more item (a change register for pipeline changes not yet built). The anchor stays until an owner decides, because changing a detector to fit its own 27-item eval set is tuning to the test.

058a7052f51a.title: What is NOT a feature request
058a7052f51a.content: Do not trigger CRDM for: . | “Write the next section of chapter 3” — content authoring (but “plan the next section” is a plan request — see §”A request for a plan”) | “Fix the typo in the overview” — content editing | “Run content_validate” — tool invocation | “What does this block kind mean?” — information request | “Review chapter 5” — content review within existing workflow | “Create a bean for …” — work-plan management | “Migration record: …” — a record of work already DONE, not a request for work; the tense is the signal | Bug reports about existing features (unless they imply a redesign) | .

6c072ae7890f.title: On detection — what to do
6c072ae7890f.content: Do NOT use the term “CRDM” with the user. It is internal methodology jargon. If new session and the first request is a feature: . | Acknowledge the request as a feature/capability change | Explain that you will help them work through the requirements before building | Start Phase 1 (needs assessment) | . If existing session and the user is already in a CRDM cycle: . | Incorporate the new request into the current requirements document | Continue with the current phase | . If existing session and the user is doing content work (not in CRDM): . | Synthesise what you have heard as a feature need | Ask the user: . | “This sounds like a platform change rather than content work. Would you like to pause and work through the requirements now, or should I note it for later?” | If pause: enter CRDM Phase 1, return to content work when done | If later: create a work item with as much context as possible, linking to any relevant GitHub issue | . | .

5a6812707cb3.title: Issue association
5a6812707cb3.content: Feature work should be linked to a GitHub issue: . | Scan open issues for a match — search by title/body keywords | If match found — ask user: “This looks related to #NNN — should I add your requirements there?” | If no match in open issues — scan recently closed issues | If no match at all — ask the user to create an issue (do NOT create without permission) | Do not proceed without an issue link — the issue is where stakeholders do feature sign-off; without it, there is no review surface | . Requirements may span multiple issues. The agent should link to all relevant ones and note the relationship.

151009708cd9.title: After implementation
151009708cd9.content: When a PR is merged that addresses a feature from this process: . | Post a summary comment on the linked GitHub issue describing what the PR accomplished | PRs are for code review (agent and human coders, code reviewers) | Issues are for CRDM stakeholders — the requestor, the BA, and updates from the coding team for feature sign-off | Many work items per issue — they are not synonymous | .

f5b8fcd2c19e.title: A feature is a COLLABORATION you are joining, not a fix you are making
f5b8fcd2c19e.content: When a feature comes up in conversation, it starts or joins a collaborative design between this user, other users and authors, and other agents. It is not a one-off fix: put it into epics and stories, create or update the artefacts it needs, and link them from the owning harness’s docs/ page. The default that is wrong . A feature surfaces mid-conversation, the agent understands it, and the agent builds it, with the conversation standing in for requirements. Everything needed to review the decision — the alternatives, the reason, who else it affects — stays in a chat log nobody else will read. What to do instead . 1. Assume the conversation is not the first. Before treating a feature as new, look for the collaboration it belongs to: an open issue, an epic, a work item, a sibling session’s branch, a spec. This repository has many of each and they are cheap to search. A feature that arrives without a home usually has one. 2. There are OTHER PARTICIPANTS, and they are not all present. Other authors, other users, other agents working other branches. Two consequences: . | the record has to be legible to somebody who was not in the conversation — which is what the issue is FOR, as against the PR (code review) and the work item (work plan); | a sibling session may already be solving it. Check before you build, and if their answer differs from yours, that is a design discussion to have on the issue rather than a merge conflict to win. | . 3. Structure it: epics and stories, not a task. A feature that is worth doing is worth a place in the roadmap. This store’s hierarchy is milestone → epic → feature → task, and check-bean-parents enforces that every open work item has a home. A feature filed as a bare task with no parent lands in the roadmap’s Miscellaneous section, where it stops being planned. An epic cannot parent an epic here. When the subject already has an epic, the new work is a FEATURE under it — a second epic beside it splits one subject across two roots, which is how a roadmap becomes unreadable. 4. Write the artefacts, and LINK them from docs/, because an artefact nobody can navigate to is one nobody reads. The harness that owns the capability owns the link — so a change to cat-harness’s pipeline is linked from cat-harness’s docs/, not from wherever the agent happened to be working. Which harness owns it is usually answered by which layer declares the directory the change lands in. The test . If this session ended now, could somebody who was not in it pick the feature up — find what was decided, what is still open, and who else is affected — without reading the chat? . If the answer is no, the collaboration has not been joined yet, whatever has been built. What this does NOT mean . It does not mean every small change becomes an epic. The trigger is the same one opening-brief uses: irreversibility and surprise, not size. A one-line fix to a typo in a generated file is a fix. A one-line change to a schema that three layers resolve against is a feature, because other people have to live with it. Nor does it mean stopping work to do paperwork first. continual-progress still holds — branch, commit, push, open the PR from commit #1. The point is that the record is collaborative, not that the work pauses.

624f9a994273.title: Related work first
624f9a994273.content: When a requirement is initiated or updated in chat, find the related work before anything else. That means work items, issues and open PRs, each categorized and summarized, followed by one question to the user about whether and how to coordinate. The procedure is related-work-coordination (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc), and crdm-issue-linking.bpmn calls it as Process_RelatedWork.

320d661e985e.title: Phase 4 — Impact analysis (detail)
320d661e985e.content: Skill crdm-impact-analysis: Guide for CRDM Phase 4 — Impact Analysis and Migration Planning. Systematic scan across 7 dimensions: schema, pipeline, adapter, folio, skill, migration, and test/documentation impact. Produces a structured assessment for posting to the GitHub issue. Named by: Guideline Updates . This skill expands the Phase 4 summary in crdm-requirements-workflow.md.

a251d34c0fae.title: The 7 impact dimensions
a251d34c0fae.content: 1. Schema impact . Scan schemas/*.ts: . | types.ts — are any types added, removed, or changed? | block-kinds.ts — does a block kind change? (triggers adapter cascade) | constraints.ts — new or modified constraints? | builders.ts — new or modified builders? | folio-config.ts — does the config schema change? (affects all folios) | . rg "YourChangedConcept" schemas/ . 2. Pipeline impact . Scan pipeline/*.ts: . | Validators (validate.ts, profile-check.ts) | Renderers (render-markdown.ts, render-latex.ts) | Extractors/codemods (pot-extract.ts, po-inject.ts, citations.ts) | Content graph (content-graph.ts) | QA criteria (qa-criteria-registry.ts) | . 3. Adapter impact . Check adapters/ routing and inheritance: . | PaperContentAdapter extends DocumentContentAdapter | adapterForKind must stay total and unambiguous | Adding a kind: which adapter owns it? | Profile vs adapter distinction (AGENTS.md §”Content types, and starting a folio”) | . 4. Folio impact . For each active downstream folio: . | Does it use the changed schema/pipeline? | Does it need a migration? | Will content_validate still pass? | Is init-folio affected? | . 5. Skill impact . rg "affected_file_or_concept" cat-harness/skills/ . Check .claude/agent-memory/ for rules/traps that reference the changed area. 6. Migration assessment . | Does this need a codemod? (codemod-*.ts) | Schema version bump? (schemas/package.json) | Data migration for existing folios? | Rollback strategy — what if the migration fails? | . 7. Test and documentation impact . | scripts/tests/ — which tests need updating? | E2E tests — affected scenarios? | Jekyll docs under cat-harness/docs/ — pages to update? | BPMN diagrams in cat-harness/processes/**/*.bpmn — workflows affected? | .

b18f1630ad77.title: Structured output format
b18f1630ad77.content: Post this table to the GitHub issue: . ## Impact assessment — [Feature name] | Dimension | Affected? | Files | Risk | Migration needed? |---|---|---|---|---| Schema | Yes/No | `schemas/types.ts` | High/Med/Low | Yes/No | Pipeline | Yes/No | `pipeline/validate.ts` | ... | ... | Adapter | Yes/No | `adapters/paper/` | ... | ... | Folio | Yes/No | `qou`, `who-smart` | ... | ... | Skills | Yes/No | `skills/process/crdm/` | ... | ... | Migration | Yes/No | — | ... | ... | Tests/Docs | Yes/No | `scripts/tests/` | ... | ... | ### Consumer impact - [List fields added/removed from published artefacts] - [List IRIs or filenames that move] - [List conventions a consumer must learn] ### Test plan - [Tests to add or update] .

d63e17757c83.title: Scanning checklist
d63e17757c83.content: # 1. Schema rg "CONCEPT" schemas/ # 2. Pipeline rg "CONCEPT" pipeline/ # 3. Adapters rg "CONCEPT" adapters/ content/adapters/ # 4. Folios # Check folio.config.json in each active folio # 5. Skills rg "CONCEPT" cat-harness/skills/ # 6. Tests bun test 2>&1 | tail -20 # 7. Docs rg "CONCEPT" cat-harness/docs/ .

0ed181ef65ea.title: Phase 1 — Needs assessment (detail)
0ed181ef65ea.content: Skill crdm-needs-assessment: Facilitate Phase 1 (Needs Assessment) of the CRDM requirements workflow. Guide the BA through stakeholder identification, source material gathering, and synthesising a domain-language needs statement. Post to the GitHub issue and iterate until the BA confirms the need is correctly captured. Named by: Guideline Updates . This skill expands the Phase 1 summary in crdm-requirements-workflow.md. The agent facilitates; the BA provides domain knowledge.

f4e1e52cbe6f.title: Identifying the requester
f4e1e52cbe6f.content: Determine who is asking and their role: . | Role | What they bring | . | BA / Feature Requestor | Domain knowledge, stakeholder access, sign-off authority | . | Content Author | First-hand experience with the gap | . | Managing Editor | Cross-folio perspective | . | Technical Reviewer / SME | Deep subject-matter expertise | . | Programme Lead | Strategic priority, resourcing | . The requester is the BA for this CRDM cycle. They interact with the agent; stakeholders interact with the BA.

8ca1664547cb.title: Identifying stakeholders (systematic 4-step approach)
8ca1664547cb.content: . | Check each active folio’s <name>.config.json roles — authors, editors, reviewers, contributors, affiliations | Check .github/CODEOWNERS — subsystem ownership | Check recent activity — gh issue list --search "...", gh pr list --search "..." for who’s been working in the area | Ask the BA directly: “Who else is affected by this change?” | . Categorise stakeholders: . | Approvers/Governance — must sign off (e.g. review committee) | Direct Operators — will use the feature daily | Downstream Consumers — affected indirectly (e.g. country adaptation teams) | .

3d18f0e30241.title: Gathering source material
3d18f0e30241.content: The request may arrive through any of these channels: . | Source | How to access | . | Chat messages in the current session | Current context | . | GitHub issue body or comment | gh issue view <number> | . | Uploaded document (Word, PDF) | uploads/ directory | . | Referenced document in library | library/ directory | . | Issue comment attachment | Download via gh | . | Pasted Teams/email discussion | Current context (motivation, not spec) | . Probing discipline: begin with the end in mind. Distinguish: . | Symptoms vs root causes | Workarounds vs missing capability | One user’s need vs shared need | .

f8587969e025.title: Synthesising a needs statement
f8587969e025.content: Every needs statement follows this structure: . | Current state — what exists today (specific, not vague) | Gap — what is missing or broken (the actual problem) | Desired outcome — what should happen after the feature | Who benefits and how — named roles, concrete improvements | Workflow rationale — how this fits the broader process | . No jargon (STRICT) . Write for business stakeholders and domain experts, not developers: . | ❌ Avoid | ✅ Use instead | . | Zod schema validation | “the system checks the structure” | . | AST traversal | “scanning the document” | . | TypeScript types | “the data format” | . | Pipeline stage | “processing step” | . | CLI flags | “options” | . | MCP tool | “assistant capability” | .

de2cd43f6b41.title: Posting to the issue
de2cd43f6b41.content: . | Scan for existing issue first — gh issue list --search "..." | Never create an issue without BA permission | Post the needs statement as a comment: gh issue comment <number> --body-file /tmp/needs-statement.md . | .

9f5a54d89ae4.title: Requesting feedback
9f5a54d89ae4.content: After posting, ask the BA: . | “Does this capture what you need?” | “Are any stakeholders missing?” | “Is the desired outcome specific enough to test?” | . The BA coordinates with stakeholders. The agent does not contact stakeholders directly.

d23b9fab1f9d.title: Exit gate
d23b9fab1f9d.content: BA confirms the needs statement before proceeding to Phase 2.

5f187a11b3d1.title: Requirements from a recorded walkthrough
5f187a11b3d1.content: Skill crdm-recorded-walkthrough: Turn a recorded requirements walkthrough (a video call where a business analyst demonstrates a feature and a stakeholder asks for changes) into CRDM Phase 3 requirements with evidence: transcripts compared, an independent transcript where one can be made, screenshots cut at the moments the speakers point at the screen, and every requirement traced to a timestamp. Use when someone uploads a meeting recording, a Teams/Zoom transcript (.vtt, .docx) or both, and asks for requirements from it. Named by: Guideline Updates . A walkthrough recording is the best source a CRDM round can have: the stakeholder reacting to a working thing, in their own words. It is also easy to over-trust, because a transcript reads like a record and is not one. The tool is cat-harness-tools/scripts/meeting-recording.py (stdlib + ffmpeg; --help per subcommand).

68b3c52cea1d.title: 1. Inventory what was actually uploaded
68b3c52cea1d.content: List the files before promising anything, because a request can promise a video that was not uploaded. A Teams .docx transcript never contains the shared screen; its images are speaker avatars. Say what is missing, do what can be done, and list what waits for the missing file.

5899bc44a66b.title: 2. Two exports of one recognition are one transcript
5899bc44a66b.content: meeting-recording.py compare A B gives word similarity and where they differ. | pair | similarity | what the differences were | . | Teams .docx against its .vtt | 0.980 | interjections in another cue; words joined at a .docx line break | . | Vosk small-en (independent) against Teams | 0.802 | mostly Vosk’s errors, but also Teams’ (“Lightner” → Leitner, “philtres” → filters) | . The first number is not confirmation: both files carry every word Teams misheard. Only an independent recognition can disagree with it. A lower similarity from a weaker model is expected and still useful, because what you read is where they disagree, filtered with --keys to names and domain terms. Record the names the recogniser mangled (“Tini”, “Jiun” for Chinni; “Saroop” / “Swarupu” unresolved) in the requirements document, and ask rather than guess any name neither transcript settles.

9c4af8467681.title: 3. An independent transcript, offline
9c4af8467681.content: meeting-recording.py transcribe VIDEO --model DIR --out vosk.json needs the vosk package (PyPI) and a model directory. It downloads nothing. In a sandbox whose proxy refuses Hugging Face and the Vosk model host, find a model already packaged somewhere the network allows, take only the model files, and never run code that came with them.

d13536424723.title: 4. Screenshots: where the screen changed and where a speaker points
d13536424723.content: . | scenes VIDEO --min-gap 10 lists when the shared screen changed. | Grep the transcript for deictic phrases: “you can see”, “here”, “this”, “looking at the screen”, “select these”. Their timestamps are the candidates; a scene change a second or two later is the frame to take. | frames VIDEO --at 1:52,2:26 --out DIR --crop W:H:X:Y --width 1280 --webp. Crop out the participants’ camera tiles: a requirements document needs the screen, not the faces. Check the crop on one frame first. | Look at every frame you keep. A frame cut for one thing can show a defect or a requirement that is already half-built, and either changes the requirements document. | WebP at quality 80 cut nine 1280-wide frames from 2.8 MB to 476 KB. | .

3c4e579e0fca.title: 5. From transcript to requirements
3c4e579e0fca.content: Follow crdm-requirements-template. In addition, for a recording: . | Every requirement cites a timestamp, and every defect the demo exposed is listed separately from the requirements, with the timestamp and “not yet reproduced” until it is. | Say what already exists (Today:) for each requirement, measured against the code or the data, not recalled. | Who signs off is part of the requirement set. Ask who it is if the recording does not say. | Do not build from the recording. A speaker telling the recording agent “implement them on a staging site” is a requirement about the process (P-1), not approval of the requirements. | .

61c317f0961e.title: Phase 3 — Requirements definition (detail)
61c317f0961e.content: Skill crdm-requirements-template: Guide and template for CRDM Phase 3 — Requirements Definition. Helps the agent structure requirements from conversation using a REQ-### format with acceptance criteria, priority, and traceability. Named by: Guideline Updates . This skill expands the Phase 3 summary in crdm-requirements-workflow.md and applies the crdm methodology.

c1bb7062d429.title: Requirement format
c1bb7062d429.content: One definition, shared with spec-kit: a statement, a conformance level, a source, at least one success criterion with its verification method, and a sign-off owner — the requirement-definition skill (skill_fetch requirement-definition) in the content layer. The fields below are CRDM’s rendering of it; Acceptance criteria are the success criteria. A requirement with none is not ready to post. Each requirement has: . | Field | Format | Example | . | ID | REQ-### | REQ-001 | . | Title | Short phrase | “Beans filtered by epic type” | . | Description | Plain language, no jargon | “The agent can filter work items by their type (epic, story, task)” | . | Conformance | SHALL / SHOULD / MAY / SHALL NOT (RFC 2119 / RFC 8174) | SHALL | . | Acceptance criteria (= success criteria, ≥ 1) | Testable, measurable, each with a key and a verification method (test / inspection / review / analysis) | “SC-1 (test) — Given an epic with 3 child stories, when filtered by epic, then all 3 appear” | . | Sign-off owner | Who says it is met — a named person or role | “The BA” | . | Priority | Must-have (High) / Should-have (Medium) / Nice-to-have (Low) | Must-have (High) | . | Source | Phase 1 needs statement / Phase 2 process activity ref | “Needs statement §2 — BA cannot see work grouped by release” | . | Impact | Phase 4 footprint | “Schema: new type field on bean. Pipeline: none” | . | Estimated scope | Work item count / PR sizing | “2 beans, 1 PR” | . Priority scale and conformance keywords . CRDM separates implementation priority (how essential a requirement is when sequencing work or trading off scope) from normative conformance (how strictly an implementation must behave once it claims conformance to that requirement): . 1. Priority scale (High / Medium / Low = Must-have / Should-have / Nice-to-have) . Aligned with PHII’s Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, p. 2) and PATH & PHII (2012) (library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm, p. 1): . | Priority label | PHII / PATH CRDM scale | Meaning | . | Must-have (Must) | High | Essential to the core business process; the system cannot satisfy the process goal without this capability. | . | Should-have (Should) | Medium | Important for operational efficiency or completeness; expected in standard operation, though a temporary workaround may exist. | . | Nice-to-have (Nice-to-have) | Low | Desirable enhancement that improves convenience or secondary workflows when resources permit. | . 2. Normative conformance keywords (SHALL / SHOULD / MAY / SHALL NOT) . While PHII’s informal prose grammar phrases requirement statements as “The system must or should…” (phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, p. 1), the separate Conformance field uses uppercase normative keywords governed by IETF BCP 14 — library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels (RFC 2119) and library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words (RFC 8174, specifying that only UPPERCASE words carry RFC 2119 normative meaning): . | SHALL (MUST) — mandatory requirement of the specification | SHOULD (RECOMMENDED) — recommended; valid reasons may exist in particular circumstances to ignore, but full implications must be understood and weighed | MAY (OPTIONAL) — truly optional capability | SHALL NOT (MUST NOT) — absolute prohibition | .

d946871c68ab.title: Generating from conversation
d946871c68ab.content: 4-step elicitation . | Listen and deconstruct — identify the nouns (entities), verbs (capabilities), and adjectives (qualities) in the BA’s description | Disentangle what from how — “I need to see beans grouped by release” is a requirement; “use a Jekyll page” is an implementation choice | Formulate testable criteria — every requirement must have a Given/When/Then or a checkable statement | Validate with the BA — read it back. “Does this capture what you need? Anything missing?” | .

e24c09e41c71.title: The document is a requirement set
e24c09e41c71.content: The requirements document as a whole is a RequirementSet (bootstrap-tools/schemas/requirement-set.ts, published as bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json): reqset:<slug>, the methodology, the issue, a stage — draft → proposed → approved → planned → in-progress → delivered → accepted, or rejected, cancelled, superseded — its members (req: references, each with its own decision), its work plan (work item ids) and its sign-offs. Commit it beside the proposal as <slug>.requirement-set.json, or as a requirementSet: key in the proposal’s front matter; check:requirements judges it. The set’s stage and each member’s status are independent — a requirement outlives the document that proposed it — with one link enforced: a set is accepted only when every member it approved is in-force. The stage moves only through a sign-off (Phase 5’s BA_Signoff, close-out’s BA_Confirm), and check:requirements refuses approved/accepted without a human sign-off, planned without work items, and cancelled without a reason.

952e9bf984dd.title: Grouping requirements
952e9bf984dd.content: By workflow area . | Area | Examples | . | Ingestion | Document upload, structure extraction | . | Authoring | Block editing, chapter management | . | Validation | Schema checks, QA criteria | . | Rendering | PDF, HTML, Markdown output | . | Review | Staging, before/after comparison | . | Translation | PO extraction, machine + human translation | . | Release | Versioning, changelog, release gating | . By architectural layer . | Layer | Examples | . | Schemas | Type definitions, constraints, builders | . | Pipeline | Validators, renderers, extractors | . | Adapters/Tools | Block-kind routing, MCP tools | . | Skills | Agent guidance, workflow definitions | .

127a9bf1dd80.title: Posting to the issue
127a9bf1dd80.content: Format as a markdown checklist: . ## Requirements — [Feature name] ### Must-have - [ ] **REQ-001** (SHALL) — Beans filtered by epic type - _Source:_ needs statement §2 - _Acceptance:_ `SC-1` (test) — Given an epic, when `beans list --type epic`, then only epics appear - _Sign-off owner:_ the BA - _Scope:_ 1 bean, 1 PR - [ ] **REQ-002** (SHALL) — Release lifecycle skill - _Source:_ needs statement §3 - _Acceptance:_ `SC-1` (inspection) — Skill exists at `cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/release-lifecycle.md` - _Sign-off owner:_ the BA - _Scope:_ 1 bean, 1 PR ### Should-have - [ ] **REQ-003** — ... ### Deliverables summary | ID | Title | Priority | Beans | Status |---|---|---|---|---| REQ-001 | Beans filtered by epic type | Must | 1 | ⬜ | REQ-002 | Release lifecycle skill | Must | 1 | ⬜ | . UI / wireframe . Every requirement set carries this section, filled or marked not applicable. When a requirement changes a rendered surface (a page, a visualiser, the navbar, a form, an app screen), the wireframe is designed and chosen before implementation, by wireframe-design-review in Design use; its output (schemas/skills/wireframe-design-review/output.schema.json) supplies every row: . ### UI / wireframe - _Surface:_ the review page's heat map (REQ-004, REQ-005) - _Candidates:_ `docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/` — assets of this proposal - `a.html` — [staging](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6) · web ![](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6/checks/a-web.png) · mobile ![](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6/checks/a-mobile.png) - `b.html` — [staging](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6) · web ![](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6/checks/b-web.png) · mobile ![](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6/checks/b-mobile.png) - _Chosen:_ `b` by @requester ([where they chose](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6): the conversation, the issue or the PR), because …; `a` rejected because … . Or, when no requirement changes a rendered surface: . ### UI / wireframe N/A — no rendered surface.

3837ceeeb199.title: Traceability
3837ceeeb199.content: Every requirement traces in both directions: . Needs statement (Phase 1) ↓ "Source" field Requirement (Phase 3) ↓ "Impact" field Impact assessment (Phase 4) ↓ bean reference Bean (Phase 5) — names its REQ / req: statements; `## Done when` copied from their acceptance criteria ↓ PR link PR (Phase 6) .

1e25c61023fa.title: CRDM requirements workflow
1e25c61023fa.content: Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Guideline Updates, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Once a feature request is detected (see crdm-detect.md), the agent follows this workflow to gather, validate, and implement requirements collaboratively.

c9d088b5dc38.title: Method origin and how this workflow adapts it
c9d088b5dc38.content: This workflow adapts the Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) developed by the Public Health Informatics Institute (PHII) and applied to health information systems by PATH & PHII (2012) — see the crdm methodology node and the canonical SKOS glossary concept https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/glossary/platform/collaborative-requirements-development-methodology: . | PHII (2021/2023), Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM): A Collaborative Approach to Public Health Systems (library/phii-2023-crdm) | PHII (2016/2021), 5. Analyzing Technical Options: Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide) | PATH & PHII (2012), Common Requirements for Maternal Health Information Systems: Produced with the Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm) | . The relation to PHII and PATH CRDM is adapts: . | Phases that follow PHII & PATH CRDM: . | Phase 1 (Needs assessment) and Phase 2 (Business process analysis & redesign) follow PHII’s first two concentration areas (1. Business Process Analysis — think: How do we do our work now? and 2. Business Process Redesign — rethink: How should we do our work?), using swimlane task-flow diagrams across pools and actor lanes and a business process / gap matrix. | Phase 3 (Requirements definition) follows PHII’s third concentration area (3. Requirements Definition — describe: How can an information system support our work?) and PATH (2012)’s separation of activity-linked functional user requirements from cross-cutting non-functional / general system requirements, together with PHII’s priority scale (High / Medium / Low = Must-have / Should-have / Nice-to-have) and validation walkthroughs (Desk checking, Walkthrough, Peer review). | . | Phases and mechanisms that are the platform’s own extensions: . | Agentic BA-only facilitation channel: An LLM agent facilitates the process with the human BA (Role_BusinessAnalyst) over issues and pull requests rather than a multi-day in-person workshop. | Phase 4 (Codebase impact analysis): 7-dimension impact analysis across the repository’s schemas, skills, BPMN/DMN models, UI components, pipelines, tests, and downstream consumers (crdm-impact-analysis.md). | Phase 4b (Capability area dependency ordering & formalize-first rule): Grouping requirements into capability areas (CA-1, CA-2, …) ordered by a dependency DAG and formalizing existing implicit behavior before adding net-new features. | Phase 5 (Work-plan decomposition & specification filing): Creating agent work items (beans/) and human todos (todos/), and filing proposals from docs/proposals/<slug>.md to docs/requirements/<slug>.md. | Phase 6 (Implementation, branches/ preview & merge sign-off): Feature-branch delivery, automated verification gates, branches/<branch-slug>/ review, and explicit human owner confirmation before merging (merge-to-main.md). | . | .

6591b5b50f89.title: Actors
6591b5b50f89.content: | Actor | Role | Swim lane | . | BA / Feature Requestor | The person who identified the need and coordinates the CRDM process. Acts as Business Analyst: interacts with the agent, reviews increments, translates stakeholder feedback into agent-actionable direction. May be an author, editor, programme lead, or reviewer. | BA / Feature Requestor | . | Agent | The LLM agent running in the folio-assistant harness. Facilitates the process, synthesises inputs, implements on feature branches, posts summaries to the issue. Interacts with the BA only, not with stakeholders directly. | Agent | . | Stakeholders | The people affected by the feature who must review and approve it. They participate at defined checkpoints (needs confirmation, requirements approval, MVP testing, feature sign-off) — not in the day-to-day development loop. Examples: review committee, country programme managers, IT teams, end users. | Stakeholders | .

16b5a3af1f76.title: BPMN reference
16b5a3af1f76.content: processes/process/crdm-requirements.bpmn is the outer process — detection, the Feature? decision, then six phases, each a real subprocess in its own file: . | phase | file | what happens | . | Link the work to an issue | crdm-issue-linking.bpmn | scan, then link or ask; never create without permission | . | Phase 1 — needs | crdm-needs.bpmn | stakeholders, needs statement, loop until recognised | . | Phases 2–4 — BPA + requirements | crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn | current workflow, requirements, impact, loop until approved | . | Phase 4b — prioritization | (inline in Phase 4 exit) | dependency-order capability areas, formalize-first rule, BA confirms | . | Phase 5 — work items + sign-off | crdm-signoff.bpmn | requirements become work items, BA signs off, branch announced | . | Phase 6 — implement + acceptance | crdm-deliver.bpmn | implement, review increment, share MVP, take findings | . | Close-out | crdm-close.bpmn | stakeholder sign-off, BA confirmation (an adjudication, recorded as a requirement-signoff attestation that moves the set to accepted), then the close | . workflow_complete takes step ids such as A_Implement, A_Close and BA_Signoff by name; the interpreter enters a phase by itself and workflow_next tells you which one you are in (inside: Phase 6 Implement + acceptance). You cannot complete a phase — a phase is done when its steps are. Phase 6 is one subprocess, because a rejected increment, an MVP that is not ready, and stakeholder findings all route back into implementation, and a subprocess has one exit and cannot be re-entered once finished.

78dc4b947ecc.title: Every question you put to the BA carries its context first (STRICT)
78dc4b947ecc.content: Every phase of this process hands the BA a decision they were not inside the analysis for. The ordering rule in interaction-modality.md §4.1 governs this whole workflow, not just its explicit checkpoints: context → options → recommendation → question. Its test applies unchanged: . Can the BA answer without opening anything? . Terms the agent coined during its analysis feel defined to it and are new to everybody else. Three traps: . | An option name you invented. “Prefix-at-rest or prefix-at-install?” names two things that exist nowhere outside your own head and your own issue. Describe what each one does instead, and put the coined name in parentheses if it earns its place at all. | A question that resolves to “go read the issue”. The issue is where the BA goes for depth. It is never where the question’s terms are defined, and a question that needs it read turns a quick decision into a long one. | Options without their costs. “A or B” is not a choice; “A, which changes nothing here, or B, which rewrites every bootstrap.processes:skill ref in the diagrams” is. The BA is deciding on the consequences, so the consequences are the question. | . This applies to every surface this workflow uses: the chat, the summary comment posted to the issue after each round, the PR body, and a work item’s ## Done when.

707fd3d58ffb.title: Phase 1 — Needs assessment
707fd3d58ffb.content: Input: the feature request (from chat, issue, discussion, or upload) . | Identify the requester — who is asking? | Identify stakeholders — who else is affected? Check: . | <name>.config.json roles across active folios | GitHub CODEOWNERS | Recent activity on related issues | . | Gather source material — the request may come from: . | Chat messages in the current session | A GitHub issue body or comment | An uploaded document (Word, PDF) in uploads/ | A referenced document in library/ | An attachment to a GitHub issue comment | . | Synthesise a needs statement — write a clear, jargon-free statement of what is needed and why, with rationale linking to a concrete workflow | Post to the issue — the synthesised needs statement goes on the GitHub issue as a comment, not in chat | Request feedback — ask the requestor and stakeholders to review | . Loop: iterate until the needs statement is approved.

435286b8502d.title: Phase 2 — Business process analysis
435286b8502d.content: Input: approved needs statement . | Find the current workflow — check processes/**/*.bpmn for existing process diagrams that cover the affected area | Map the gap — where in the current workflow does the need appear? Identify the specific activity or decision point | Document current state — if no BPMN exists, document the as-is workflow in prose or create a new BPMN fragment | Identify bottlenecks — probe for the real pain point behind the stated request | . Post to the issue: current-state workflow description with gap identified.

828a419d2cc8.title: Phase 3 — Requirements definition
828a419d2cc8.content: Input: current-state analysis with identified gap . For each requirement: . | Functional requirement — stated as “SHALL” / “SHOULD” / “MAY” | Proposed implementation: . | Skill file (name, location, description) | MCP tool registration (if applicable) | Schema changes (Zod types, block kinds, constraints) | Pipeline changes (validators, renderers, scripts) | . | Acceptance criteria — testable conditions | Consumer burden — see below. A requirement that shifts work onto the consumer is not done. | Cross-references — link to related documentation pages under docs/source/, existing skills, existing workflows | Wireframe candidates, when a requirement changes a rendered surface — a page, a visualiser, the navbar, a form, an app screen. Before anything is built, run wireframe-design-review in Design use (Call_Wireframe in crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn): at least two candidates, each with a web and a mobile layout, committed as assets of the proposal under docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/ on the feature branch, and shown where the requester will look, chosen from context — the conversation, the issue the request came from, the PR, or several — each place carrying the same branches/ deep links and screenshots (feedback-deep-links, point 5). The candidates are the options Phase 4’s comparison lays out; the requester or BA chooses one at the review. Record “N/A — no rendered surface” in the template otherwise. The wireframe is part of the design process for adjudication (wiregen). | . Consumer burden is a requirement, not a nicety (STRICT) . Every requirement states what a downstream consumer must do to use the result — and the target is nothing. The standing rule: a downstream consumer must never have to string-manipulate, re-derive, or assume a rule in order to use what we publish. If an artefact makes a consumer parse a name, strip a prefix, substitute a base URL, or know a convention that is written down only in prose, the requirement is not met. Ask it in this form, because the failure is always phrased as a saving: . “We don’t need to emit X — it can be derived from Y.” . That sentence is the smell. A rule a consumer has to know is a rule a consumer can get wrong, and the cost is paid by someone who cannot see the code that made the assumption reasonable. Emitting the derivable field costs bytes in a regenerated artefact; the derivation rule costs correctness in every consumer. So emit the derivable field. For example, a preview knowledge graph’s nodes each carry an explicit prov:alternateOf link to their canonical counterpart, rather than relying on a documented base-URL substitution: a consumer should follow a link, not implement a substitution. Three checks that catch most of it: . | Would a consumer in another language need our source to understand this? If yes, emit the field. | Is the convention stated anywhere a machine can read? Prose in a skill is not machine-readable. A typed term in a @context is. | Does the artefact answer “what am I?” from itself? A preview that needs an external convention to be told apart from the canonical version fails this. Put it in the type, not in a filename or a path segment. | . This is also why the declaration file keeps a fixed name while artefacts are stub-named: a consumer must be able to open a repository it has never seen without first deriving a filename. See directory-conventions §Naming. Post to the issue: structured requirements with acceptance criteria.

f0984aa759e6.title: Phase 4 — Impact analysis
f0984aa759e6.content: Input: defined requirements . | Schema impact — which types, constraints, builders change? | Pipeline impact — which scripts under pipeline/ are affected? | Adapter impact — paper, document, dak? Does it ripple? | QA impact — new criteria? Modified criteria? Registry changes? | Folio impact — which active folios need migration? | Consumer impact — what must every downstream consumer change, and what must it now know? An impact analysis that lists only our own files has measured half the change. Enumerate: fields added or removed from published artefacts, IRIs or filenames that move, conventions a consumer would have to learn. A convention added is an impact, even when no file changed shape. | Test plan — what tests to add or update? Include at least one that asserts the consumer-facing contract, not only the internal one — a test over the emitted artefact, not over the function that built it. | Migration plan — steps, rollback, what breaks without it | . Post to the issue: impact assessment and migration plan. When the analysis yields more than one viable approach . Phase 4 often ends with a choice rather than a plan, and that is the moment the BA is handed a decision. Not a list of approach names with the analysis linked: a comparison, per decision-comparison — per option its pro, its con, what it changes downstream and how reversible it is, laid out where the rows can be read against each other, then one recommendation and a stated default. Items 1–6 above enumerate the downstream question for the change as a whole; the comparison asks it once per option, so an empty downstream column discards work already done.

d7b2433c1c11.title: Phase 4b — Prioritization and dependency ordering
d7b2433c1c11.content: Input: impact analysis complete, possibly multiple capability areas identified . When a feature request decomposes into more than one capability area (as most non-trivial requests do), the agent must explicitly order them before creating work items. This is not optional: a flat work item list has no implementation sequence, so the next session either guesses the order or asks the BA a question the analysis already answered. The prioritization protocol . | Identify capability areas — each is a coherent cluster of requirements that can be implemented and reviewed independently. Name them. | Map dependencies — draw the dependency graph: . | Does area A define concepts that area B assumes? | Does area A produce artefacts that area B consumes? | Does area A change structure that area B builds on? If yes, A must precede B. | . | Apply the formalize-first rule — within the dependency order: . | Structural/organizational work first (taxonomies, indexes, schemas) | Process/policy formalization second (skills, workflows, conventions) | Implementation third (code, pipelines, tools) | Visualization/UI last (dashboards, pages, views) | . Only the UI’s build comes last. Its wireframe is designed and approved in Phases 3–4 (step 6 of Phase 3), so the order fixes when it is implemented, not when it is decided. This is not arbitrary — a visualization built before the process is formalized will be rebuilt; a process formalized before the structure is organized will reference the wrong paths. | Present the order to the BA — as a dependency chain, not a list: Area 5 (structure) → Area 2 (process) → Area 3 (review) → Area 4 (planning) → Area 1 (visualization) . With one sentence per arrow explaining why the dependency exists. | BA confirms or reorders — the agent proposes, the BA decides. The BA may override the dependency order (e.g. “I need the visualization first even if it’s throwaway”) — that’s a legitimate business decision, and the agent records it as such rather than arguing. | . What this step produces . | A numbered list of capability areas in implementation order | A dependency rationale for each ordering decision | An estimate of scope per area (work item count) | A recommendation for which areas constitute the MVP release | . Post to the issue alongside the impact analysis. This becomes the input to Phase 5’s work item creation — work items are created in dependency order, not in the order the BA mentioned them. Cross-domain applicability . This step applies identically to code features, paper milestones, and project deliverables. The formalize-first rule is domain-independent: a paper’s structure (chapter order, block kinds) must precede its content (prose), which must precede its presentation (PDF layout).

d776a49c1eb6.title: Phase 5 — Sign-off and bean creation
d776a49c1eb6.content: Input: requirements + impact analysis reviewed and approved by stakeholders . | Post sign-off summary on the issue — what was agreed, what was deferred — and record it. BA_Signoff is an adjudication: the BA answers approve, amend, reject, defer or cancel, and A_RecordSignoff appends a requirement-signoff attestation for the requirement set (who, when, scope, outcome, the stage it moves the set to, the reason, and the permalink to the issue comment). GW_SignoffRecorded reads it back, so the phase cannot continue on a sign-off nobody recorded. An agent records the BA’s decision; it never makes it. | Create work items for each implementation unit — each naming the req: statements it delivers, with ## Done when copied from their success criteria, and listed in the set’s workPlan (a set at planned with no work items is refused): . | Follow the check-before-create protocol (see todo-manager.md) | Scope to a single PR-sized unit | Reference the parent issue in each work item | . | Offer the knowledge-graph destinations for the agreed set — A_OfferKg, BA_ChooseKg, A_RecordKg in crdm-signoff.bpmn. This step is not optional and its default creates nothing. See below. | . The agreed set is an ASSET, and Phase 5 is where it gets a home . The agreed set is a design-memory asset, so it goes into docs/; when it relates to a harness, feature or tool, its detailed design and planning go into that harness’s docs/. Without this step requirements end as an issue and a conversation: requirements are produced while building, and they are not the thing built. Three rules, and the first is the one a run skips: . | Ask; never pick silently. The destinations are DERIVED from the owning layer’s declared graphs at the time of asking, none is a listed answer, and if nobody answers nothing is created and “asked, answered none” is recorded. kg-contribution-offer carries the option set and the question that identifies a design-memory asset. | It goes in the OWNING layer’s docs/ — a cat-harness feature’s reasoning in cat-harness/docs/, a folio’s subject matter not in the platform at all. placement decides where inside it: architecture/ for why it is shaped this way, guides/ for how a person does something with it, reference/ for generated material that is never hand-edited. | Not fsh-guts. That is the declared non-rendered trashcan and its content may be thrown away or lost. A design record’s whole value is that it survives the conversation that produced it. | . What separates the record from the skills the same phase produces: a skill carries what a competent practitioner needs in order to do the task; everything past that line — background, options not taken, how to reach a data source, an API’s full surface when the task touches three calls — is documentation. Both directions fail silently, so state which one you are writing before you write it. A harness feature’s documents: proposed in docs/proposals/, filed in docs/requirements/ (STRICT) . When the feature is the harness’s own, the documents this process produces (initial analysis, MVP, the options, the agreed requirements) live and are updated under docs/, in two declared sub-graphs of it. | stage | where | what it is | checked by | . | Phases 1–5, and while building | docs/proposals/<slug>.md | the argument: needs, options, MVP, what was agreed | — | . | the feature ships | docs/requirements/<slug>.md | the promise: its front matter is a Requirement | check:requirements | . The directory says what KIND of document it is; the stage is a field. The requirements document is a RequirementSet whose stage (draft … accepted, or rejected, cancelled, superseded) is recorded in the set and moved only by a recorded sign-off. The directory follows the stage — a set reaching accepted is when its proposal is filed — but does not stand in for it, because a file’s location records neither the decision nor who made it. Both kinds, proposals and requirements, declare within: "docs". Every list of kinds (the navbar’s Folders among them) therefore draws them inside the Docs row, folded shut until the reader opens it. That is general behaviour for any kind declaring within, not a special case for these two. One proposal per feature, updated in place, never forked. A later phase edits the same page rather than writing a second one, so the history of the argument is git log on one file. Filing on ship is a MOVE, never a copy. In Phase 6, once the owner has said to merge: . | git mv docs/proposals/<slug>.md docs/requirements/<slug>.md, so git log --follow walks the requirement back through its argument. | Add the Requirement fields to its front matter, from bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json: . | id: req:<slug>. The id IS the file name. | status: in-force | proposedIn: the old path. | actors, description. | statements: one per agreed requirement, each with a key, a conformance level (SHALL, SHOULD, MAY or SHALL NOT) and one requirement sentence a reviewer can say yes or no to. A functional statement may add activity, capability (“I want”) and benefit (“so that”). A non-functional one may add a category. Keep the body: the reasoning stays with the promise it produced. | . | Point the feature’s test runs at the statements they check, in folio-test-run/v1’s requirements array, as req:<slug>#<key>. The test points at the requirement, never the reverse. | bun run cat check:requirements. It refuses a slug that is in both sub-graphs (a copy, or a proposal landing on an existing requirement), an id that is not its file name, and front matter the schema rejects. | . The schema names no outside concept. It lives in bootstrap, so every harness has it, and check:bootstrap-concepts fails if any bootstrap schema names a derivative’s content model, layer names, organisation or interchange standard. A harness that follows a particular standard maps that standard’s fields onto these fields in its own layer, never in the base. How filed requirements are organised, traced, superseded, and retired: . | The assessment of open requirements standards is in methodologies/requirements-standards-assessment.md, and the literature search, adopted/rejected methodologies, and the BPMN filing workflow (Process_RequirementsFiling, sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)) are in methodologies/requirements-filing-and-organisation.md. | Physical files stay flat at docs/requirements/<slug>.md (id: req:<slug>, statement keys req:<slug>#<key>), organised in docs/requirements/index.md under the eight canonical concern groups (code-lists/concern-group.json), with three-axis traceability (proposedIn, derivedFrom, dependsOn, beans, skills, processes, test/attestations/) and an immutable lifecycle (proposed → in-force → superseded | retired, never git rm). | . A folio’s features are not filed here. This applies to the harness’s own feature work. A folio’s subject matter lives in the folio, as Phase 5 already says.

a70805ed6384.title: Phase 6 — Iterative development
a70805ed6384.content: Input: work items . For each work item: . | Create feature branch — always, no exceptions. Before the first edit, run the collision review in coordinate (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”Starting new work”. | Implement — following the accepted requirements, and, where a requirement changes a rendered surface, against the wireframe candidate the requester or BA chose in Phases 3–4. The delivery summary links the chosen candidate beside the after-screenshot. | Open PR — link to the work item and the parent issue | Deploy staging preview — the feature-staging.yml workflow auto-deploys to branches/<branch-slug>/ on gh-pages. The magenta “FEATURE BRANCH” banner at the top of every page links to the source branch and provides a “compare with main” link. | Post before/after comparison to issue — use the staging-review skill. Every changed page gets a before (main) and after (staging) URL pair in a Markdown table. See schemas/staging-comparison.schema.json for the schema: | Page | Before (main) | After (staging) | What changed |---|---|---|---| Landing | [main](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6) | [staging](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6) | Added badge | . | Iterate on PR feedback — code review is on the PR; visual review uses the staging preview URLs. When the change touches a folio’s blocks, the page a reviewer opens is the preview’s review page, branches/<slug>/review/: every changed block before and after, with the heat map and outline. The review itself runs through content-change-review.bpmn. The review coordinator slices the change and assigns the slices, reviewers work them in review-task, disagreements go to adjudication, and the coverage gate must pass before sign-off. | Ask user for explicit confirmation before merging to main. This is the merge-to-main (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) sub-process, called from crdm-close.bpmn (Call_MergeToMain) once the sign-off is recorded and before the issue is closed, and run the same way for any increment the owner asks to land earlier. A stakeholder sign-off or the BA’s confirmation is acceptance of the feature, not authorisation to merge it. | Update documentation — the OWNING layer’s docs/ pages and the workflow BPMNs. For the harness’s own feature, file its proposal as its requirements once the merge is agreed: see “A harness feature’s documents” above. If Phase 5’s offer chose a docs/ destination, this is where that page is written and kept true; if the implementation diverged from what was agreed, the divergence is recorded there rather than smoothed. | Staging cleanup — a merged PR’s preview goes away on its own: the merge is the confirmation, since the main site now shows the same thing. Everything else is retained by default. While a PR that will not be merged is open, the user adds the staging:cleanup label; once it is closed the label can no longer reach it, and removal is a feature-staging.yml dispatch the user runs with cleanup_slug and a matching cleanup_confirm (see staging-review). Never remove a staging preview any other way, and never on your own initiative. | . Theme and UI review is NOT a Phase 6 step — it happens at ingestion . theme-ui-review runs only at ingestion of graphical assets for a website or app design, from ingest-theme.bpmn. GW_StakeholderOK’s accepted branch in crdm-deliver.bpmn closes the phase directly. Accessibility, branding and locales for a UI are checked there, not here, because at ingestion a finding is a decision about what the assets will be rather than a defect in something that shipped. When a round of implementation is complete (one or more work items resolved): . | Post a round summary comment on the issue — addressed to the BA and stakeholders, containing: . | What was accomplished in this round | What remains to be accomplished (open work items) | Links to updated content for review (staging URLs, docs pages) | Before/after comparison table for changed pages | . | Never close the issue without explicit authorization — the BA or stakeholder closes it, or the agent closes it only when the BA explicitly says to. An agent must never assume completion. | .

b2d2d3915bb2.title: Staging links
b2d2d3915bb2.content: When a staging preview exists, every request this skill makes for feedback, review or sign-off carries it: one deep link per changed page, to the anchor where the change sits, with the same page on main as before. Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: feedback-deep-links.

7aa01e084623.title: crdm-requirements-workflow (skill)
7aa01e084623.content: The skill crdm-requirements-workflow as its source file cat-harness/skills/process/crdm/crdm-requirements-workflow.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

2405f99fc106.title: Data modelling — the entities, before the fields
2405f99fc106.content: Skill data-modelling: Build a data model: identify the entities a body of work is actually about, the relations between them, and the cardinalities — then declare it where the tools can read it. Process-agnostic technique; the CRDM phase that invokes it is crdm-data-model. Named by: Guideline Updates . One question, and everything else follows from it: . What are the things, and what is true of each of them exactly once? . A model is wrong in a way no schema check can catch when a fact that belongs to one thing is written on another. Typical shapes: a fact about a capability (what substitutes for it) copied onto every skill that uses it; a fact a BPMN diagram already states executably (which role takes over) repeated on a skill; a field naming performers in a vocabulary that resolves against nothing. Each is a field on the wrong entity, or a second copy of a fact that already has a home. Modelling first catches them, and costs far less than unwinding them later.

5ddb750e965f.title: The procedure
5ddb750e965f.content: 1. Name the entities, as nouns a domain expert already uses . Not the tables you expect to build. If the people who do this work say “attestation”, the entity is Attestation, even when it will be stored beside something else. A name you invented is a name nobody will look up. Stop when two candidate entities have the same identifier. They are one entity with two names, and carrying both is how a codebase ends up with a Role registry and an actor-id vocabulary that do not resolve against each other. 2. For each entity, say what identifies it . An entity with no identifier is an attribute of something else — that is the test, and it is decisive. If you cannot say what makes two of these the same one, you have found a field rather than a thing. 3. Put each fact on the entity it is about . For every fact, ask whose property is this? The question that settles the hard cases: . If this entity disappeared, would the fact still be true of anything? . What substitutes for X survives the disappearance of every skill that uses X, so it belongs to X. What this skill does when X is missing does not — it is the skill’s. 4. State cardinality in both directions, and mean it . “One attestation per report” and “one report per attestation” are different claims, and a model that states only the first cannot tell you whether a re-signature is an update or a second row. Write both. Where the answer is “many”, say what ORDERS them or admits there is no order. 5. Say which facts are derived, and never store those . A derived fact stored is a cache, and an unvalidated cache is worse than no cache. If a value can be computed from the model, computing it is the declaration — the role a process falls back to, for example, is recoverable from the diagram that executes it. 6. Declare it where a tool can read it . A model in prose is a proposal. A model in the declaration is a model. In this repository that means a graph typology in <name>.json, a Zod schema under the declared schemas directory, and a node kind that kg-export knows — placement is the skill that decides which. And ship a reader in the same change, because a field that is only documentation goes inert. A field with no consumer is not a model, it is a comment with punctuation. 7. Model VARIATION as inheritance, and earn a new kind with BEHAVIOUR . Two things are nearly the same. Do they get one type with a discriminator, two types, or one type and an override? . A new KIND is earned by a BEHAVIOUR difference — a consumer has to DO something different. Everything else is an OVERRIDE on an inherited default. So the default posture is inherit everything, override anything. A variant declares what it CHANGES; every unstated field comes from its parent. A variant that states no new behaviour is not a new kind, however different it looks. The test is on the consumer, not the values. Ask: does any reader of this model take a different code path? Different colours, sizes, labels or thresholds are the same behaviour with different inputs — one kind. Different FIELDS, different units, or a field whose meaning changes — the reader must branch, and that is a kind. Worked example: Theme . Theme dresses three surfaces: sticky notes, a website, a print publication. | variant | kind? | why | . | iris-web vs the default web theme | no | different hex values, same fields. Nothing branches. An override. | . | publication vs sticky | yes | a sticky theme’s geometry is {minWidth, padding, fontScale} across laptop \| mobile \| card; the WHO style guide states A4 \| A5 \| A5 landscape with trim size and margin, and no column width anywhere in 66 sections. minWidth means “before the grid reflows” — a fixed page does not reflow. A renderer MUST branch. | . Reusing {minWidth, padding, fontScale} for print, reading minWidth as trim width, would typecheck and mean nothing. A shape that typechecks is not a shape that models. And the palette stays SHARED across all three kinds, which is the other half of the rule: three kinds each with their own palette vocabulary would be three spellings of “accent colour”, free to disagree about what an accent is. What inheritance costs, and what it must not hide . A required field stays required after resolution, never before. “All three layouts, or invalid” is a property of the RESOLVED variant; a declaration that states one and inherits two is complete. Checking requiredness on the declaration instead is how inheritance turns into optionality by accident. And an inherited value is still a fact somebody must be able to trace. A variant that overrides a value cites why, the same as any other asserted fact — otherwise the model records what the value is and loses where it came from, which is the failure the uses[] rule exists to prevent elsewhere. 8. Point from the dependent at the general node . A relation between two entities is written on ONE of them. Write it on the entity that DEPENDS, pointing at the one it depends on. A general, reused node never holds a field naming the things that use it. The test is the step-3 question applied to the relation: if every user of this node disappeared, would the node still be complete? A skill with no task implementing it is still a skill; a task with no skill is not a task. So the pointer lives on the task. | relation | written on | never on | why | . | a task implements a skill | the BPMN task (<bootstrap.processes:skill ref>) | the skill | a skill is reused by many tasks in many processes; listing them makes every new process an edit to the skill | . | a voice speaks for a role | the voice (activeIn.roles) | the role (voice) | a role is what an actor does in a lane; how it sounds is a separate, swappable thing | . | a lane names a role | the lane (partitionElementRef) | the role (lanes) | the role names diagrams it cannot know about | . | a user story is for a role | the story (role, in scenarios/stories.json) | the role (useCases) | stories are added by whoever writes them, not by editing the role | . | a Tool satisfies a skill | the Tool (satisfies) | the skill (scripts, validators, mcpServices) | several Tools may satisfy one skill, and a script is added without editing the skill | . | a skill or capability discharges a requirement statement | the skill’s front matter or the capability (satisfies: req:<id>#<key>) | the statement (satisfiedBy) | a requirement is written once; what discharges it arrives later | . | a skill says how to read a graph typology | the skill’s front matter (graph-typologies:) | the kind (skill) | a kind is registered once; skills that read it come and go | . | a skill takes and produces a contract | the skill’s front matter (input:, output: — a path into the layer or an https IRI) | a directory named after the skill | the skill can then say its contract is elsewhere, and a contract no skill names is visible as unclaimed | . | a test checks a skill’s contract | the test run (skill, with its cases checked against the skill’s input:/output:) | the skill | tests come and go; the contract does not | . Prose counts. A skill body that says “the only step of initialize-harness” knows its caller just as surely as a field does, and goes stale the same way. Say what the skill does, not who calls it; the caller’s own declaration says the rest. The general node owns its CONTRACT. What a skill takes and returns is a fact about the skill, so it is declared there: an input and an output schema reference, each either a KG schema or a pinned external schema. Tasks, Tools and tests point at the skill and are checked against that contract. That is how a general node stays complete without naming its users. Declare which nodes are general, and let the audit hold the line. Which nodes are general is a modelling decision, so it is written down: the schema declaration’s doc comment carries @general. The general nodes are Role, Skill, Requirement statement, Graph typology, Capability, Actor and Process. kg:audit’s arrow-direction criterion then reports two things: a @general schema whose @ref names a declaration that is not general, and a BPMN <folio:…> element pointing from a process at anything but a skill, role, decision table, convention or precondition. It cannot see a bare string field with no @ref (step 9 is how those become visible) or prose, so a clean run is a claim about declared pointers only. Prose may name a dependent; data may not. The rule governs references, the things a tool follows. A general node’s prose can still name a dependent to explain itself. For example, a process’s documentation may say “feature-staging.yml publishes the branch” so the reader knows why a step exists; deleting such an explanation loses the reason a step exists. If the relation matters to a tool, it must also exist as data held by the dependent, like a workflow’s # bpmn: line. The prose then explains that data and does not replace it. What prose cannot do is notice a rename, so kg:audit’s advisory prose-names-resolve criterion lists a named path whose directory exists and whose file does not. A bare name that nothing in the repository carries is left undetermined, because it could be a run’s output, a folio’s file or an example. 9. Make every cross-node reference a typed KG reference . A reference is a claim that another node exists. A bare string makes that claim in a vocabulary nothing resolves: a typo, a rename or a deleted node reads exactly like a valid name. So a field that names another node holds a KG reference: the target’s kind and id, resolvable in the knowledge graph, and projected by kg-export as an @id link, never a literal. The IRI that link carries is <doc dir>/<kind>/<id>, never ….jsonld#<kind>/<id> — minted by the exporter, not by the model; kg-export §”Subject IRIs — a path, not a #fragment” owns that rule. Use the helpers that already exist rather than inventing one: . | helper | shape | for | . | KgRefSchema (schemas/kg/carried-note.ts) | {kind, id, note?} | any KG node | . | TaskRefSchema (schemas/kg/carried-note.ts) | {process, task} | a BPMN task: the pair, never a bare task id | . | VoiceRefSchema (schemas/content/voices.ts) | {instance?, voiceId} | a voice, possibly in another layer | . | SkillNameSchema (schemas/tools/tool-types.ts) | kebab id | a skill id, where a whole ref is not needed | . | module#Export, instance:module#Export (parseValidatorRef) | string with a checked grammar | a schema | . A reference that crosses into another layer says which layer. And a reference is resolved by a check, not trusted: the audit that reads the field fails on one that points at nothing. Free text stays free text only when it is not a claim about another node: a description, a note, a persona. Free text that names things the graph cannot point at is a reference that should be a node.

253b6f1d4b2b.title: What falsifies a model
253b6f1d4b2b.content: Write these down as you go and check them at the end. A model nobody tried to break is a diagram. | test | what it catches | . | name two layers that differ only in a field you called an identifier | the identifier is not one | . | find a fact you would have to update in two places | it is on the wrong entity, or duplicated | . | find a relation whose cardinality changes under a plausible future | the model states today’s data, not the domain | . | count the facts nothing reads | the part you modelled for its own sake | . | find two kinds whose consumers take the SAME code path | one of them is an override wearing a discriminator | . | find a required field a variant can never state | requiredness is being checked before resolution, not after | . | delete every user of a general node; is it still complete? | a field on the general node names its users (step 8) | . | rename a node; does anything still read as valid? | a reference is a bare string, not a KG reference (step 9) | .

7a4ad0687ec3.title: What this skill is NOT
7a4ad0687ec3.content: Not a storage design. Tables, files, indices and formats come after, and a model that assumed one of them has usually smuggled a storage constraint in as a domain fact. Not domain content. folio-assistant is the platform. A model of clinical recommendations, FHIR profiles or any one folio’s vocabulary belongs in that folio — this skill is the procedure, and the procedure carries no subject matter. See the platform-boundary rule in placement.
