7c8ba57abf2a.title: Editing and HCI validation
7c8ba57abf2a.content: Process_Editing · strict · 17 step(s) . What happens to one proposed change to one content block: drafted, validated mechanically and by review, shown to the editor, and committed to the corpus only if accepted. i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i

3faa42300f8d.title: How it connects
3faa42300f8d.content: . | Called by: Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish | Calls: Close the bean, Open the bean, Evidence for a recommendation, Options analysis | Presented on: no docs page section shows this diagram | Running instances: none recorded | .

1af88aaad6fe.title: Lanes — who acts
1af88aaad6fe.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Editor / author (person) | author | Every act the requesting party performs personally rather than through the agent lands here: stating the change, retrieving its evidence, and — once every validation path has reported — ruling on it. The gate sits at Task_ReviewFindings, once the findings exist. | . | Authoring agent (system) | authoring-agent | Produces the proposed change and, once findings exist, weighs the options for it — accept, revise, discard — but stops short of choosing: Call_OptionsAnalysis records that the options were weighed, Task_RecordDecision in the editor’s lane records what was chosen, so one party never both analyses and decides. | . | HCI validation pipeline (system) | validation-pipeline | Forks validation into its four parallel paths and, once every one reports, collates mechanical results and review findings into a single report. It checks nothing itself; it makes sure none of the four is missing before the editor sees anything. | . | Mechanical validation (system) | validation-pipeline | Runs the three checks that need no judgement call — schema and constraints, syntax and link resolution, build and QA gates — in parallel with the non-mechanical review rather than gating on it. | . | Non-mechanical validation (review agent or SME) | reviewer | Supplies the half of validation no checker can perform: whether the change says what the editor meant. Gateway_ReviewerKind escalates from agent review to a human SME specifically when the judgement needed turns clinical or scientific rather than editorial. | .

05454e25c934.title: Steps
05454e25c934.content: Every one of the 17 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Describe the intended changeTask_DescribeChange | Editor / author (person) | — | The editor states the change in natural language; no content has moved yet. | . | Open the beanTask_ClaimBean | Authoring agent (system) | calls Open the beanbean-coordination | Process_BeanOpen: check before you create, find out whose the bean is, and claim it — or leave it alone when it is someone else’s. The one place a claim is drawn; the gateway after this reads which end it reached. | . | Gather and verify the evidenceCallActivity_Evidence | Editor / author (person) | calls Evidence for a recommendation | Before anything is drafted: the author reads the guidance ALREADY in this content, frames the question as PICO, retrieves candidates across the three evidence classes, and has each candidate’s authority resolved against its publisher’s own API. A recommendation reaches the drafting step with its evidence attached, or with the gap recorded.This step has nothing to do for content that carries no recommendations – a mathematics folio has none, and a figure redrawn from its own source adds none – and the subprocess’s first gateway (Gateway_RecommendationInPlay) ends it there at its own event, recording the answer, rather than satisfying the search vacuously. | . | Draft the block editTask_DraftEdit | Authoring agent (system) | content-authorbefore-after-preview | The authoring agent produces a PROPOSED change. Nothing is written to the corpus yet. For a rendered change it also produces the before/after preview (skill before-after-preview) here, before Gateway_ValidationFork, so the preview exists when the parallel review starts. | . | Schema and constraint checksTask_SchemaValidate | Mechanical validation (system) | content-validate | Block schema, label prefixes, required fields, constraint rules. | . | Syntax, spelling and linksTask_SyntaxSpell | Mechanical validation (system) | content-validate | Syntax, spelling, cross-references, citation and link resolution. | . | Build and QA gatesTask_BuildGates | Mechanical validation (system) | content-test | Lean build and proof status, LaTeX compile, FHIR/SUSHI validation, QA axes. | . | Agent review of the changeTask_AgentReview | Non-mechanical validation (review agent or SME) | content-review | A review agent judges what no checker can: accuracy, voice, exposition, whether the change says what the editor meant. | . | Human / SME reviewTask_SmeReview | Non-mechanical validation (review agent or SME) | content-review | Escalated to a human reviewer or subject-matter expert when the change turns on clinical or scientific judgement. A rendered change reaches the reviewer with its before/after preview (skill before-after-preview). | . | Collate findings into a reportTask_CollateFindings | HCI validation pipeline (system) | content-validatecontent-validatecontent-validate | Mechanical results and review findings are merged into one report against the proposed change. | . | Log findings on the beanTask_LogFindings | Authoring agent (system) | todo-manager | Findings are appended to the bean, so the next agent or human sees what is outstanding. | . | Review the findingsTask_ReviewFindings | Editor / author (person) | decision-auditdecision-auditdecision-audit | THE GATE: the editor sees every finding BEFORE anything reaches the corpus. | . | Options analysis accept · revise · discardCall_OptionsAnalysis | Authoring agent (system) | calls Options analysis | On the edge out of Task_ReviewFindings and before Task_RecordDecision: the findings are the evidence, so the options can only be weighed once they exist, and after Task_RecordDecision the decision is already written down.Not between Gateway_EditorDecision and Task_RecordDecision: Flow_21b runs Task_RecordDecision -> Gateway_EditorDecision, so the gateway reads a decision already recorded.In the Agent lane: the subprocess records that the options were WEIGHED (its own decision-audit note), and Task_RecordDecision in Lane_Editor records WHAT WAS CHOSEN. The analyst is not the decider. (CallActivity_Evidence is in Lane_Editor because the author performs the retrieval.)On the trigger: A_Frame opens the subprocess on opening-brief’s trigger — irreversibility and surprise — and leaving there is a correct outcome. A spelling fix that reached Task_ReviewFindings with one mechanical finding exits immediately; a revise-or-discard on a block other content depends on does not. | . | Record the decision and audit noteTask_RecordDecision | Editor / author (person) | decision-audit | A decision is an act ABOUT the findings, not a finding. Record the outcome, every finding it weighed, every finding it overrules — and an audit note saying why it was made, or why a finding in it was left. Each note cites corpus evidence: a witness, another finding, a QA report, a block, a file range. An overruled mechanical finding stays on the record; a gate whose findings vanish when somebody disagrees with them cannot be audited. An agent may assemble the citations and is recorded as proposed_by; the author is whoever decided. | . | Revise the proposed changeTask_ReviseEdit | Authoring agent (system) | content-authorbefore-after-preview | The editor chose revise: rework the proposed change against the findings the editor reviewed, then send it back through validation as a new proposal. The before/after preview is refreshed with it (skill before-after-preview). | . | Commit into the corpusTask_Commit | Authoring agent (system) | corpus-commit-contract | Only now does the change become corpus content, together with its QA sidecars. Subject to the commit-hygiene requirement. | . | Close the beanTask_ResolveBean | Authoring agent (system) | calls Close the beantodo-manager | Process_BeanClose: end the bean in a state that says why — complete and archive it, scrap it with its reasons and archive it, or record the blocker and hand it back. The one place resolve and archive are drawn; placed straight before the end so the engine’s resolve sees nothing left but the archive step. | .

f2f1aa073506.title: Evidence Appraisal
f2f1aa073506.content: Named by: Authoring a document, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Evidence for a recommendation, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Public comment on a review draft, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Board: place a note . Appraise and grade a body of evidence against the grading system the folio declares. This skill supplies the procedure; it does not supply the system.

ab6b205cd1d5.title: Why this skill names no grading system
ab6b205cd1d5.content: Which grading system applies is a methodological commitment of the folio and the body that publishes it; the platform holds no subject matter, and a hardcoded system would leave every folio that uses another one working around the platform. An evidence-retrieval process in the content layer judges certainty “per the grading system the folio declares”. This skill covers what appraisal is, what it attaches to, and what has to survive as a record afterwards. Domain layers supply concrete grading systems as refinement skills and code lists (certainty levels, rating reasons, recommendation strength). Each applies only when declared, never as a default; with nothing declared, appraisal is refused.

69db44a6a528.title: Responsibilities
69db44a6a528.content: . | Appraise the body of evidence assembled for one question, not a citation | Record the grade with its reasons, not as a bare label | Distinguish “the evidence is weak” from “there is not enough to judge” | Re-appraise when the body changes, and say what moved the grade | Refuse to grade when no system is declared, rather than picking one | .

7e1ee13e6ac5.title: The unit is the body, not the citation
7e1ee13e6ac5.content: The grade attaches to the body of evidence for one PICO question. This is why appraisal sits after retrieval’s parallel join and not inside the fan-out: the three retrieval classes (trusted L1 sources, trusted L2/L3 content, data repositories) contribute to one judgement; grading each branch separately would produce three numbers that answer no question. A single citation does not carry a certainty grade.

f8b74a4dd532.title: “Cannot appraise” is a third state
f8b74a4dd532.content: Three outcomes; “not appraisable” is not a low grade: . | outcome | means | . | graded | the body was appraised and carries a certainty | . | not appraisable | too little retrieved, or no declared system, or the question was not framed as PICO | . | gap recorded | nothing authoritative was found, and that is the finding | . Never collapse “not appraisable” into the lowest grade: “we looked and the evidence is poor” is not “we could not look”. A recommendation resting on the first is weak; one resting on the second is unsupported.

326bcfd5d452.title: Inputs
326bcfd5d452.content: . | The framed PICO question — without it the search is not reproducible and the appraisal is not checkable | Candidates that passed an authority check, so authority is a resolved fact rather than an assertion in the citation | The grading system declared by the folio | .

d1337b56df41.title: Outputs
d1337b56df41.content: . | A certainty judgement for the body, in the declared system’s own vocabulary | The reasons, in enough detail that a later reader can tell whether they would still hold (decision-audit); a grade without them cannot be reviewed, only re-litigated | Any gap, recorded as a gap rather than as a low grade | .

59728974a904.title: This has nothing to do with formal content
59728974a904.content: A graded body of empirical evidence is never an input to a formal deductive proof. In a content type with a formal proof layer, a formal claim’s assertion is discharged by its machine-checked proof sibling and by nothing else; certainty grading belongs to empirical guidance about the world, where the question is what the evidence supports. An empirical grade in a formal proof obligation is a category error.

795281c70a4f.title: Actors
795281c70a4f.content: . | Author / guideline developer (lead) | Domain SME (domain judgement, supplied by the content-type layer) | Content Reviewer (checks the grade’s reasons survive, not the grade itself) | .

ee9bf9135fc8.title: Evidence for a recommendation
ee9bf9135fc8.content: Process_EvidenceRetrieval · strict · 10 step(s) . Frame a question for a recommendation, retrieve and appraise evidence from trusted sources, and either attach it or record the gap; a change that states or alters no recommendation ends at its own event before any search. Evidence comes from three classes (trusted L1 sources, trusted L2/L3 content, data repositories), and each candidate’s authority is verified against the publishing body’s own API. STRAWPERSON: registries, grading system and API bindings are not fixed here. i i i i i i i i i i

6c71b2cd846c.title: How it connects
6c71b2cd846c.content: . | Called by: Editing and HCI validation | Calls: none | Presented on: no docs page section shows this diagram | Running instances: none recorded | .

0fd2848ab59a.title: Lanes — who acts
0fd2848ab59a.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Author / guideline developer (person) | author | Brackets the machine work rather than doing it: frames the PICO before Lane_Agent fans out across evidence classes, then is the only lane that grades what comes back and decides whether it is sufficient for a recommendation; retrieval and authority-checking are delegated. | . | Evidence agent (system) | evidence-agent | Fans out in parallel across the three evidence classes and joins the candidates. It owns coverage, not judgement: grading is Lane_Author’s call and authority is Lane_Trusted’s. | . | Trusted registries and observatories (external) | external-registry | Task_VerifyAuthority and its gateway sit here rather than with Lane_Agent because the decision is a readout of what the external API returns, not this layer’s call; when that answer is uncertain or absent, a bean is opened rather than a verdict invented. | .

d375a74bc782.title: Steps
d375a74bc782.content: Every one of the 10 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Review the existing guidanceTask_ReviewExisting | Author / guideline developer (person) | content-review | The author reads what the document, DAK or IG ALREADY says on this question, before looking outward. A recommendation that contradicts a sibling recommendation in the same artefact is a defect no external evidence will reveal. | . | Frame the question as PICOTask_FramePico | Author / guideline developer (person) | content-author | Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome. The PICO is what makes the search reproducible and the evidence auditable: without it, ‘we looked for evidence’ is not a claim anyone can check. WHO guideline development states the question this way before any retrieval. | . | Search trusted L1 sourcesTask_L1Sources | Evidence agent (system) | document-intake | Ingested primary literature under library/: the sections/*.md tree and, where a document was scanned, ocr/page-NNN.txt. NOTE the known blind spot — a document OCR’d but never re-run through pdf-structure.py has only a stub in sections/, so a sections-only search misses it. | . | Search trusted L2 and L3 contentTask_L2L3Content | Evidence agent (system) | document-intakedocument-intakedocument-intake | Already-adjudicated guidance: WHO SMART DAKs at L2 and FHIR Implementation Guides at L3. A recommendation adopted in a published DAK is evidence of a different kind from a primary study – it is a prior decision, with its own provenance, and must be cited as that rather than laundered into primary evidence.NOT YET SKILL-BACKED: no skill searches adjudicated L2/L3 content forevidence. corpus-grep is a different task (checking that a gap is reallyopen). | . | Query data repositories and statistical datasetsTask_DataRepos | Evidence agent (system) | document-intakedocument-intakedocument-intake | Indicator and microdata sources. Distinct from the two above because the unit of evidence is a MEASUREMENT with a population, a period and a method, not a claim in prose. | . | Verify authority against the registryTask_VerifyAuthority | Trusted registries and observatories (external) | registry-authority-contract | Each candidate is resolved against the standard API of the body that publishes it, so that ‘authoritative’ is a RESOLVED FACT rather than an assertion in the citation. What is checked: that the identifier resolves at the publisher; that the retrieved record matches what the citation claims; that the version and date are the ones cited; and that the publisher is one this folio has declared trusted. STRAWPERSON: the concrete registry list and endpoints are not settled here – see the cat-harness.processes:policy note. | . | Open a bean for the unverified citationTask_RecordUnverified | Author / guideline developer (person) | todo-manager | An unresolvable citation is not dropped and not silently kept. It becomes a tracked item, so the gap is visible in the work plan rather than surviving as a footnote nobody re-checks. | . | Appraise and grade the body of evidenceTask_AppraiseGrade | Author / guideline developer (person) | evidence-appraisal | Certainty of evidence per the grading system the folio declares. The grade attaches to the BODY of evidence for one PICO question, not to an individual citation – which is why this step is after the join and not inside the fan-out. | . | Record the evidence gapTask_RecordGap | Author / guideline developer (person) | todo-manager | Insufficient evidence is a RESULT. It is recorded as such – an honest gap the guideline can state – rather than being closed by weakening the recommendation until the available evidence supports it. | . | Attach the evidenceTask_AttachEvidence | Author / guideline developer (person) | content-author | The PICO, the graded body of evidence, each verified citation and its resolved authority record are written onto the recommendation block, so a reader can retrace the whole chain from the sentence back to the source. | .

4ff5ba46ffa8.content: Every one of the 3 decision(s) is documented. | decision | what decides it | branches | . | Does the change state or alter a recommendation?Gateway_RecommendationInPlay | The author answers before any search starts. yes: the change states a recommendation or alters one, and the evidence is gathered as below. no: the change carries none – a mathematics folio has none, and a figure redrawn from its own source as a computable graphic adds or changes none – so there is nothing to frame as PICO. f2bcff97708e.title: Evidence review — the same rule, a second instance
f2bcff97708e.content: Skill evidence-review: Evidence review as an instance of untainted verification — the separation of the appraising party from the drafting party, what recurring surveillance in a living guideline shares with a stale QA verdict, and which of guideline methodology’s rules are fenced rather than shipped. Named by: Make a decided public comment change, Contributor feedback on a working draft . Skill id: evidence-review · Package: folio-core . untainted-verification states a generic discipline. Evidence review — the appraisal of the evidence behind a recommendation — is one instance of it; the translation round trip is another. Two unrelated instances are evidence that the discipline is generic, where one would only be an example.

420f0d080d1c.title: The rule
420f0d080d1c.content: The party that drafted the recommendation does not write the evidence appraisal for it. Guideline methodology already separates the systematic review team from the guideline development group for the same reason: a party assessing its own output is comparing a thing with its own paraphrase of itself. | untainted-verification | here | . | producer | whoever drafts the recommendation | . | checker — given the artefact, and nothing that would let it shortcut | the appraisal, given the question and the evidence, not the draft’s conclusion | . | adjudicator — given the intent and the checker’s output, never the artefact | the evidence-to-decision judgement | . An appraiser shown the drafted recommendation is told the answer before being asked the question; its “the evidence supports it” measures the instruction, not the literature.

299ff1413991.title: Recurring surveillance is staleness, generalised
299ff1413991.content: A living guideline is updated as evidence appears, so its appraisal is a verdict with an expiry. A QA verdict is hashed to its subject and stales when the subject is edited; a living-guideline verdict stales when the evidence base changes, even though the subject did not. The field_hash covers only inputs in the repository; an external corpus is not covered. Either way, “verified on DATE against THESE inputs” is a different claim from “verified”, because a reader given the second cannot tell a current verdict from a lapsed one. A folio implementing surveillance gives each verdict an explicit expiry, as bean-blocking (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) does for a block: a verdict with no expiry cannot be told from an abandoned one.

e8d3a2d2b09b.title: The fencing analysis — which rules are the platform’s, and which are not
e8d3a2d2b09b.content: Run through domain-fencing (opt-in cat-harness.kg-ops)’s three questions, in order, first-to-answer wins: . | candidate rule | Q1 rationale survives translation? | Q2 domain in mechanism or vocabulary? | Q3 needs the domain installed? | verdict | . | appraiser ≠ drafter | yes, word for word | vocabulary | no | platform — it IS the spine | . | a verdict carries what it was verified against, and when | yes — it is the field_hash argument | vocabulary | no | platform | . | a finding is upheld by opening the cited source, never by trusting the rule’s wording | yes | vocabulary | no | platform — and already the practice in voice-who-guideline-development | . | certainty rated across the GRADE domains | no | mechanism | yes | fence | . | PICO question formulation | no | mechanism | yes | fence | . | evidence-to-decision framework tables | no | mechanism | yes | fence | . | a search strategy is re-runnable — databases, dates, query recorded | yes in rationale | mechanism is bibliographic | yes | fence the mechanism, keep the rationale (it is the row above) | . Three rows are platform rules; the four fenced rows are a folio’s methodology, not a backlog. Nothing is shipped for the fenced rows — empty criteria would let a consumer scan nothing and report a clean run. A folio that wants them declares them in its own repository.

fe106e5db0be.title: What this skill does NOT do
fe106e5db0be.content: It asserts no clinical or empirical claim, and the platform must not. The mechanism carries process — who may rule on what, given what. The evidence is the folio’s and the judgement is the guideline group’s; a platform that shipped a default answer to either would be asserting on their behalf.

e71546bd923a.title: External registry — the role’s contract
e71546bd923a.content: Skill external-registry-contract: The contract the external-registry role is held to: what a trusted registry outside this layer must provide for a portal to verify what it received, and what the verifier does when it cannot. The narrowest contract the diagrams require. A mechanical role’s skill is a contract to test against, not instructions to read. Named by: Evidence for a recommendation . external-registry in scenarios/roles.json is played by an external actor: trusted registries and observatories outside this layer’s control. A role played by something we do not run is still a role, and its skills are its contract: what we rely on it to do. A contract is not an instruction; it is what the diagrams assume.

42c2642f1e54.title: Where the diagrams lean on it
42c2642f1e54.content: One lane names this role: Lane_Portal in processes/kg/kg-to-portal.bpmn, holding P_Verify and GW_Verified. What that lane’s documentation, the task’s, and kg-to-portal §”Trust” require of the registry is the whole contract — nothing more is claimed.

c714c765e9c0.title: What it must do
c714c765e9c0.content: . | Publish the trust anchors a verifier resolves a signer’s key from — for GDHCN, a WHO SMART Trust DID trustlist (did.json), served as static JSON (PROD: tng-cdn.who.int/v2/trustlist/…). | Serve a slice by its hierarchical path, …/$domain/$participant/$usage/did.json, with - as a wildcard, so a verifier fetches only what it needs. | Nothing else. 2cc37ed341fa.title: What the verifier does when the contract is not met
2cc37ed341fa.content: An unreachable registry is unknown, never a pass: GW_Verified routes it as it routes a mismatch, to the last good version (End_Rejected). This side of the contract is ours, and it is what makes relying on a party we do not control safe. Needs the owner’s review: this contract is inferred from one diagram. The test in tested-by: holds the side of it that is ours: one lane names this role, it holds P_Verify and GW_Verified, and GW_Verified serves the bytes only on a match, sending every other answer to End_Rejected. Lines 1 and 2 above are the registry’s own behaviour on a network this repository does not reach, and nothing here tests them.

fb604266bb6d.title: Feature-branch staging
fb604266bb6d.content: Skill feature-staging: Manages feature-branch staging deployments under gh-pages/branches// for before/after publication review comparison. Handles branch creation, staging deployment, commit SHA stamping, and cleanup. Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Record agent step, Review-log watch .

9098902b3156.title: When to use this skill
9098902b3156.content: When a content change is being reviewed and the reviewer (or the author) needs to see the rendered result before merging. The staging deployment puts the feature branch’s rendered site at: . https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/branches/<branch-slug>/ . A preview is the general publication step with a different root. The push itself is render-kg-to-cdn with branches/<branch-slug>/ as the publication root URL and the gh-pages Tool as the target — the same step a release takes with the site root. What this skill owns is everything around that call: the slug, the banner and staging.json, the render log, the PR comment, and taking the preview down. Which site — the repository the change lives in . <owner>/<repo> above is the repository that holds the change, not the repository of the index the agent happens to be working in. Read that repository’s index.config.json first: . | the change lives in | its preview is at | published by | . | a repository with its own site (its index.config.json has a site entry) | https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/branches/<slug>/, and the root from its default branch | that repository: stage-local.ts --repo . from its checkout when it declares site.agentRun (below), else its own staging.yml | . | a layer an index mounts and publishes as part of its own site (no site of its own) | branches/<slug>/ on the index’s site | a staging re-pin: a pull request on the index that points the mount at the branch’s commit, recorded with bun run cat mount:remote --staging (basis staging, no consent needed) | . A repository with a site of its own is previewed there, even when an index also mounts it. The index’s site shows it as one layer among its layers, which is the wrong page for that repository’s reviewers. If the repository’s own build cannot run yet (its publisher refuses for a missing cache or an undeclared input), say what is missing and ask. Never fall back to the index’s site in silence.

17d5d9964b19.title: How it works
17d5d9964b19.content: 1. Feature branch → staging deployment . When an agent pushes to a feature branch with an open pull request, drafts included, feature-staging.yml automatically: . | Builds the docs site (Jekyll + TypeDoc + BPMN diagrams) | Writes the build’s facts — commit SHA, timestamp, branch, PR, issue, build log — once, to staging.json at the preview root | Injects a constant staging banner at the top of every HTML page, which reads those facts in the browser | Comments on the PR that the preview is staged and queued, with the earliest push time and when it should be live | Waits for the rate-limit window (§8), then deploys to gh-pages/branches/<branch-slug>/ only the files that differ from the live site (staging-share.ts apply). The preview’s staging-sw.js serves the rest from the live site in the browser and puts the banner back on its pages; the live site’s root 404.html (staging-share.ts write-404, written by docs-site.yml) installs that worker for a deep link opened before it exists. A page is shared only when it matches the live one once the per-preview edits are set aside (banner, SEO strip, fa-staging and fa-search-index, TypeDoc’s title suffix); anything else keeps the preview’s own copy. The footer build stamp is filled in the browser on every build, the live site’s from build.json, so an unchanged page is byte-identical across deploys | Rewrites the same comment: pushed at a time, live by about five minutes later | . 2. The staging banner . Every staged page carries a muted-sage banner: . 🔀 FEATURE BRANCH — claude/update-schedule · commit a1b2c3d · built 2026-09-18T00:30:00Z · PR #42 · issue #215 · compare with main ↗ · build log . Its colour, #4F6F52, measures 5.63:1 against its white text, above the 4.5:1 WCAG AA threshold. Check any replacement the same way; the pale decorator sages (#9CAF88, #87A96B) land near 2.5:1. The facts are fetched, not baked — and that is a storage decision . cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-banner.ts injects a fragment that is byte-identical on every page and across every rebuild, and the browser derives its preview root from location.pathname, fetches staging.json and fills the banner in. A per-build value in the fragment makes every page unique on every build, so each re-push adds the whole site to gh-pages as new objects. Three rules: . | Nothing per-build may go back into the fragment. staging-banner-constant.test.ts runs two builds with different facts and compares the emitted bytes, so any leak fails regardless of how it is spelled. Add the fact to staging.json instead. | A failed fetch must still say PREVIEW. The static markup carries “FEATURE BRANCH” before any fetch happens, and the fetch only ever ADDS detail. “Could not determine” is never rendered as “this is the real site” — the same third-state rule the rest of the repository runs on, and here the failure mode is a reviewer approving the wrong artefact. | Every value from the JSON goes in as textContent, never as markup. Git ref names may contain <, > and " — they are not in git’s forbidden set, which stops at space, ~, ^, :, ?, *, [, \ and the control characters. staging-banner.e2e.ts pins this with a branch name carrying an onerror payload. | . Pages still differ between previews, because Jekyll’s relative_url prepends the baseurl to ~235 hrefs per page and the fa-translation-index island publishes site.baseurl to JavaScript. Both are coupled to the language switcher. 3. Commit SHA stamping — and the four fields staging must NOT write . Both builds write docs/_data/build.yml, and they do not write the same fields. The difference is deliberate: it is the second half of the deduplication above. |   | docs-site.yml (main) | feature-staging.yml (a preview) | . | sha, short_sha, built_at, run_url | written | DELIBERATELY ABSENT | . | branch, staging, staging_slug, pr_number, search_index | — | written | . Why staging omits them. site-chrome/_includes/footer_custom.html renders short_sha, built_at and run_url into the footer of every page, so writing them per build changes every page on every deploy. The client fills those three in from the same staging.json the banner already fetches — one request, two consumers — and a failed fetch leaves Jekyll’s | default: 'dev' in place rather than blanking the footer, which is the same third state §”The facts are fetched, not baked” requires of the banner. On main there is one copy and nothing to deduplicate, so the include’s own reason stands: “a stale browser cache and a deploy that has not run look identical.” . Adding a per-build field back to the staging stamp will not fail a test. staging-banner-constant.test.ts compares the banner fragment, which is genuinely constant; the footer is not in it, because it lives in a Jekyll include rather than in the workflow’s injection step. Check the deploy commits on gh-pages, not the code, to confirm pages do not differ across rebuilds. A Jekyll layout can read site.data.build.sha to display the deployed version — on main. Under a preview, read it from staging.json. 4. Before/after comparison . The reviewer opens both URLs side by side: . | Surface | URL | What it shows | . | Main (current) | <pages-url>/ | The published state on main | . | Staging (proposed) | <pages-url>/branches/<slug>/ | The feature branch’s changes | . The commit SHA on each page confirms exactly what is being compared. 5. Cleanup . When the PR is merged or closed, the cleanup job in feature-staging.yml removes branches/<slug>/ from gh-pages so stale previews don’t accumulate. The full retention rules — merged vs closed-unmerged, the label, the dispatch — are in staging-review §”Staging retention”. 6. The cap — 3 GB of previews in total, the oldest rotated off . Previews are capped by size, at 3 GB in total, and the oldest are rotated off. The cap is by size rather than count because one preview can run to hundreds of megabytes. Per-PR cleanup bounds nothing in total, every preview is a full copy of the site, and a gh-pages branch past GitHub’s 10 GB Pages limit freezes the live site. So every stage run, inside its push loop, runs cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-rotate.ts: it stamps the preview it is staging (branches/<slug>/.staged-at), keeps that one plus the most recently updated others while the total fits MAX_PREVIEW_BYTES (3 GB, 3 x 1024^3 bytes, defined there and nowhere else), and removes the rest, oldest first — each with a removed render-log entry, its record retired into branches/_retired/, and a line (slug, age, size) in the commit message and job log. _retired/ and non-preview entries are never touched. Two things to know when editing it: . | The push loop re-reads gh-pages on every attempt; it does not rebase. The commit carries removals decided against one read of the branch, and a replayed removal is a stale one — it could delete a preview another run has just refreshed. Same shape as publish-gh-pages.sh. | A rotated-off preview is regenerated by the next push to its PR branch. It can reach an OPEN PR’s preview; the cost is a 404 until the author pushes, not lost work. Detail and the reviewer’s remedy: staging-review §”The cap”. | . 7. The cone — a preview rebuilds only what a changed file can reach . A preview rebuilds only the dependency cone of the changed files, at FILE level, with each derived directory’s generator declared as writer. The rule is general across rendered kinds. A rendered directory is in the cone when a changed file is . | under its own path (its pages, or its source data), or | in the import closure of a writer it declares, or under a writer directory (a path ending in /: what a generator reads, such as its templates, rather than imports), or | in a directory it is derivedFrom, transitively (check:derived-from --downstream <instance/id> prints that half on its own). | . cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-cone.ts computes it; compose-docs.ts carriedInstances applies it to the composed layers. Three rules: . | Any doubt carries. No file list, a writer that does not exist, or an import that does not resolve carries the directory, with the reason in the build log. A preview missing the pages under review misleads a reviewer, while an oversized one only costs bytes. | A computed import() is bounded, not ignored. It can load only a module, so it carries on a changed module file and never on a page. The two such sites a generator reaches today (harness-config.ts’s contributes loader and block-module.ts’s block loader) have DECLARED targets and are walked exactly; DECLARED_COMPUTED_IMPORTS lists them. | The instance-prefix match is a floor. The cone can only add to it. Narrowing below it is a separate decision, made once the cone has been measured in previews. | . A skill-only change carries no IG; a change to gen-ig-pages.ts or to the DAK layer’s themes/chrome.json carries all three. staging-cone.test.ts holds these cases as tests. Built sites follow the same rule. An IG’s own Jekyll site and its AST site are BUILT in the preview from an upstream repository pinned in the layer’s own files, not composed from the checkout. stage-ig-sites.ts and stage-ast-sites.ts take --changed-files and stage only the layers siteInCone reaches. Its reasons, in order: no file list; a change to the build environment (SITE_ENVIRONMENT: the docs Gemfile and this workflow); a change under the layer; the cone reaching any of the layer’s directories (a theme change arrives this way); or a change in the stager’s closure. Each decision is printed with its reason. When you add a generated directory, declare its writer and derivedFrom. Without them the cone cannot reach it through code or data, and the prefix floor is all it gets. 8. The rate limit — a preview never cancels the main site’s Pages build . Staging previews are pushed to gh-pages at a limited rate. GitHub’s pages build and deployment keeps only the NEWEST run, so every push cancels the build in flight, the main site’s included; a build takes about three minutes. So before each push attempt the stage job re-reads gh-pages and runs cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-push-gate.ts gate, which holds the push until the branch tip is old enough: . | tip of gh-pages | wait until it is | . | a staging commit (staging(...)) | STAGING_WINDOW_MS — 5 min | . | anything else: the main-site publish, publish.yml, any other publisher | MAIN_WINDOW_MS — 10 min | . The numbers live once, in that script. Exit 75 means it slept until the window should open (plus up to a minute of jitter) and the loop must re-read and ask again; exit 1 means the job has waited MAX_WAIT_MS (two hours) and fails rather than pushing; exit 2 is an unreadable tip, never read as open. Three things to know when editing it: . | git’s fast-forward rule is the lock. Two jobs that both find the window open both build on the same tip; one push is rejected, re-reads, finds a tip younger than the window, and waits. So at most one staging push lands per window with no shared state. A rejection whose tip MOVED is therefore a lost race, sent back to the gate without spending one of the three attempts; only a rejection with the tip unmoved counts as a failure. | No concurrency group, and none should be added. Every waiting preview would pend in one group and each arrival would cancel the last. The per-branch group at the workflow level stays: a newer push to the same PR cancels a preview still waiting at the gate, so a superseded preview is never pushed at all. | A staging push BEFORE a main-site push is harmless; only one AFTER it cancels the build that matters. The main push then cancels the staging build, and the build that runs carries both. That is why the gate looks at the tip, and why it does not wait for docs-site runs that have not pushed yet. | . A rate limit is used rather than a batching flush job because the gate is one script and one loop whose correctness rests on git, while a flush job needs a second workflow, an artifact round trip per preview, a record of what is deployed, a best-effort schedule and a write token over content built from a pull request. The cost is latency under load: with K previews waiting, the last one pushes about 5 × K minutes later, and the PR comment gives its own estimate. The cleanup and cleanup-dispatch jobs do NOT pass through the gate. They push once per closed PR rather than once per push. 9. Build types — preview and full . There are two build types. A public comment (PC) build is a full build, and so is a release. | build type | used for | builds | . | preview | every pull request’s branches/<slug>/ preview | only what the change can reach (the cone, §7); every whole-corpus index is main’s copy, put back rather than rebuilt | . | full | the main site deploy, a public comment release, a release | everything; every index rebuilt from the tree being published | . An index is computed over the whole corpus: the search index, the LSI viewer, the SQLite slices, the handler index, the glossary pages, the translation status pages and the node-kind pages. A builtAtPublish entry says so with index: true; a writer is borrowed only when every entry it writes says so. Rebuilding an index in a preview shows the reviewer almost nothing and costs minutes, so in a preview derive:publish puts back main’s copy from main’s writer-cone recording and logs borrowed <writer>; the search index is served from main the same way (§”Serve the published search index” in the preview workflow). So a preview of a glossary, translation or node-kind change shows main’s copy of those pages: review such a change on a full build (dispatch with build_type: full) or in its source. The switch is CAT_BUILD_TYPE (cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/build-type.ts). Any doubt builds full: unset means full, and a value that is neither word is refused. A preview whose main recording holds no copy of an index builds it. A public comment release must be frozen from a full build. A frozen release is cited by page and line for the whole comment period, so its search and slices must describe the draft, not main. Dispatch the preview workflow for the branch with build_type: full, then run pc:release freeze. Freeze refuses a copy whose staging.json says buildType: "preview", and records the build type in release.json. 10. Agent-built previews — deferred on the critical path, verified by a full CI rebuild . When an agent builds and pushes a preview with stage-local.ts, it writes branches/<slug>/_build-record.json (scripts/preview-record.ts) recording builder: "agent", the git tree hash tree of the source tree it built (HEAD^{tree} or the merge tree with origin/main), the head and base commit SHAs, and the SHA-256 of every deployed file outside the per-build metadata (staging.json, _build-record.json, .staged-at, build.yml). When feature-staging.yml runs on the pull request: . | Defer on the critical path. conflict-gate checks branches/<slug>/_build-record.json on gh-pages. When builder is "agent" and record.tree equals MERGE_SHA^{tree} (refs/pull/<n>/merge), the preview is already live for that exact merge tree: the workflow sets the preview/agent-build commit status on the PR head to pending, posts a <!-- preview-build-verify --> notice on the PR, and skips the critical-path stage build so the runner is free. Any missing record, CI-built record, or tree mismatch (including when main moved under the branch) builds on the critical path as usual. | Verify off the critical path. preview-verify-sweep.yml (triggered when feature-staging.yml completes and on a 15-minute schedule) checks that no Feature Staging run is queued or in progress, finds the oldest open PR whose head commit has preview/agent-build in state pending, and dispatches feature-staging.yml with verify_pr=<number>. | Compare or replace. The verify run rebuilds refs/pull/<n>/merge in full and runs preview-record.ts compare against the agent’s _build-record.json on gh-pages: . | Files match (same=true): nothing is redeployed; preview/agent-build is set to success (or failure if a built-site check failed) and the PR comment records the verified tree. | Files differ (same=false) or the base moved (same=stale): CI’s build is deployed to branches/<slug>/ (guarded so a newer preview tree is never overwritten) with a rendered log entry, and when the agent’s build differed, preview/agent-build is set to failure with the differing file paths listed in the PR comment. | Merge guard: merge-guard check 5 (src/coordinator/merge-guard.ts) reads preview/agent-build alongside check runs; pending holds the PR as not ready, and failure refuses the merge. | . | .

46c0d711e3ea.title: Agent workflow
46c0d711e3ea.content: When an author requests a content change: . | Detect scope — use content-graph and integration-watcher to identify affected blocks and downstream implications | Create feature branch — branch from main, open PR immediately | Make changes — edit content blocks, deterministic logic, translations | Push — on a folio whose staging.yml runs on push, the staging deployment happens automatically. On an agent-run repository, run stage-local.ts (below). | Report staging URL — tell the author the preview is at <pages-url>/branches/<slug>/ | Iterate — each push updates the staging deployment with a new SHA | . The BPMN for this workflow is the content core’s processes/content/content-change-review.bpmn. Publishing without a runner — stage-local.ts, one command . When the Actions queue is backed up, the agent can build and publish itself: it already has the checkout, the platform and bun. On an agent-run repository (below) this is not a shortcut. It is the only publish path. It is one command for a preview and for the main site, for a folio and for a FHIR IG: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --plan # what it would do; nothing built bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --dry-run # build, compose the commit, push nothing bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> # build and push bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --artifact <dir> . It prints its plan first, every time: which workflow it mirrors, where the output lands, what it replaces and what it keeps, the commit message, and what it does not run. The size review. Owner, 2026-11-10: “add size review as part of authoring process”. Every build, preview or main, prints a size report before its push (site-size.ts, bun run cat site:size). The report gives the total against the published root, the top directories, the size by extension, the biggest files, byte-identical duplicates, source maps, the directories named after another layer of index.lock.json, and the directories the shared-assets host could serve. It writes site-size.json beside the build, never into the site. The review is advisory: growth over 10% or 10 MB is a warning, and nothing is refused. Read the report before you hand over the preview. The usual culprits each have one fix: . | another layer’s pages copied in: link that layer’s own site; | the same bytes under several names: publish one index, and serve each file once; | vendored libraries: serve them from the shared-assets host; | .map files: do not publish them. | . When the growth holds and none of these fixes applies, raise a decision card with the owner, with the comparison line and the top contributing directories on it. Which publisher is read from the repository’s own workflow files, from the reusable workflow each one calls: . | a caller of folio-staging.yml is a folio. The build inputs (build_command, site_dir, publish_branch, …) are read from that caller. | a caller of a reusable workflow that a mounted layer declares as a site publisher is that publisher’s kind. The IG layer declares one: a caller of its fhirbuild.yml or ghbuild.yml is an IG, published by that layer’s own code, which stage-local.ts reaches through the layer’s declared site-publisher-ig pipeline slot and never by path. The reusable workflow is fetched at the ref the caller names, and its build job is run step by step as written: run: blocks with the environment a runner gives them, docker:// steps in their image. Steps that read a secret, push to the source branch, or need an Actions runtime are skipped, and the plan names each one with its reason. fhirbuild.yml itself only triggers build.fhir.org’s auto-build, so the Pages build is the ghbuild.yml beside it, and the plan says so. | a repository that calls both (smart-ra carries an IG under input/) gets the folio, unless --publisher ig is given. The folio owns the publish root. An IG’s root deploy is a clean one, and it is refused on a publish branch that holds a folio’s branches/, _render-log/ or _main-site.json. | . Main site or preview follows the branch, as the workflows do. The default branch publishes the main site; any other branch publishes a preview. --main says the same explicitly, and it is refused off the default branch. The main site is published only from a HEAD that is the pushed tip of the default branch. |   | folio | IG | . | preview | branches/<slug>/, replaced wholesale; held by the rate-limit gate (§8); commit staging(<slug>): from <sha>; render log staging-preview | branches/<last path component>/, nothing deleted; commit Deploy candidate branch | . | main site | the root, through publish-main-site.ts: only the files the last publish’s _main-site.json lists are replaced, and branches/, _render-log/ and anything a person put at the root are kept; commit main-site: from <sha>; render log main-site for / | the root, cleaned except for the deploy step’s clean-exclude (branches, sitepreview) and the action’s own exclusions; commit Deploy main branch | . Every path refuses an empty build before it deletes anything. | Pushing removes the first wait and not the second. Pages deploys on a runner, so say the page is live once that deploy has run, never sooner. | --artifact <dir>: no GitHub at all. It writes the same build as a bundle for a claude.ai Artifact: index.html plus the files listed in <dir>/artifact.json. Publish that, and it is live in about a minute, private until shared. | An Artifact holds at most 254 files plus the page per publish. Whole top-level directories are left out to fit, the ones with the most files first. artifact.json names each one, and links into a left-out directory 404. | Before publishing a folio whose content belongs to a real organisation (a WHO draft, say), ask the author: an Artifact is a new place that content appears. | . | What it does not do, and says in its plan: . | the folio preview’s QA sweep, screenshots, review-comment ingestion and PR comment (the banner says the preview was built locally); | the IG workflow’s PR comments, its branch-history page and README write-back (each reads a token, or writes the source branch); | the IG deploy action’s single-commit, which force-pushes one orphan commit and erases the publish branch’s history. This path commits on top and never force-pushes. | . | An IG build needs what its workflow needs. The workflow runs IG Publisher in a Docker image, so a machine with no Docker daemon gets the plan from --dry-run, and a real run stops naming the missing prerequisite. | An IG repository’s own site is built from its AST, not from the Publisher’s HTML. The repository declares site.build in its index.config.json entry (inline — never a <instance>.config.json), and that recipe’s first step restores the AST from its cache branch and refuses one that is not valid for the commit. The cache is refreshed by a Publisher run on a runner, through the IG layer’s reusable refresh workflow. It is the one workflow an agent-run IG repository dispatches, and only a person, or an agent the owner names for that run, dispatches it. The layer that owns IG builds owns the rule and the workflow; this skill names no IG step. | . Agent-run repositories — the GitHub Actions path is documented, not run . A repository is agent-run when it says so in its own index.config.json: "site": { "agentRun": true }. An agent builds and publishes its site, and its publish workflow keeps only workflow_dispatch. This skill keeps no list of them: the declaration is the list, and stage-local.ts says in every plan whether the repository declares it. For these repositories the GitHub Actions path is documentation. It says what the workflow does, so that the agent path can match it. It is not a fallback for an agent to take. | what | agent path | GitHub Actions path (documented, not run) | . | a folio preview at branches/<slug>/ | stage-local.ts from the branch | folio-staging.yml job stage | . | a folio’s main site at the Pages root | stage-local.ts from the default branch | folio-staging.yml job publish-main | . | an IG preview at branches/<branch>/ | stage-local.ts from the branch | the IG publisher’s ghbuild.yml, “Deploy candidate” | . | an IG’s main site at the Pages root | stage-local.ts from the default branch | the IG publisher’s ghbuild.yml, “Deploy main” | . | QA sweep, screenshots, review comments, PR comments | not run (the plan says so) | jobs in the workflows above | . Never dispatch the workflow, to cover a gap or for any other reason: a dispatched run contradicts the repository’s agent-run setting. When the agent path cannot do a step, say which step it is and ask. Skills that drive GitHub Actions are not to be implemented. Document what the workflows do, here and in the workflow files, so that an agent-run step can be checked against them — stage-local.ts reads the workflow files rather than restating them, so a change to a workflow’s build or layout is a change to the agent path too.

4a2f655c1fba.title: Staleness detection
4a2f655c1fba.content: The SHA stamp means staleness is always detectable: . | Staging matches PR head → the staging preview is current | Staging SHA ≠ PR head → the staging preview is stale (push again) | Main site SHA = merge commit → the publication is current | Main site SHA ≠ latest main → docs-site.yml needs to run | .

7230337e0683.title: Example — a change that spans several blocks
7230337e0683.content: An author needs to change the immunization schedule: . | Agent detects the change affects: . | Narrative content in the immunization chapter | Decision logic (CQL) for scheduling the next visit | Indicators that count doses administered | Referral logic for follow-up visits | . | Agent creates feature/update-immunization-schedule | Agent edits all affected blocks, assesses downstream impact | Push → staging deployment → author reviews | Author submits to the guidance review committee | Committee compares main vs branches/feature-update-immunization-schedule/ | Committee approves → merge → staging cleaned up → main site updated | .

6ae95b0e3dcf.title: Before you hand a staging URL to a person
6ae95b0e3dcf.content: Check the ref, then say how long and come back. A preview push is not a served page, and the bot’s “Staging preview” comment reports at most the first, not the second — and while it says queued, not even that. List branches/<slug>/ on refs/heads/gh-pages before relaying the URL; quote the comment’s own push and live-by times (the rate limit in §8 can hold a push for several windows), or say the stage job takes about 22 minutes plus the wait and Pages adds 3 to 4 on top; schedule the re-check rather than promising it. The three states, and why the third is not yours to assert, are in staging-review §”Before you hand a staging URL to a person (STRICT)”. It is the same rule and it is written once, there.

6f612da814aa.title: Before you report a staging URL as broken
6f612da814aa.content: Look at the publish ref, not the site. A staging URL is LOOKED UP in gh-pages under branches/<branch-slug>/, never composed from the source path — cat-harness/docs/guides/x.md publishes to /docs/cat-harness/guides/x.html, and composing it from the source path yields a 404 for a page that is there. From an agent container a curl against a Pages URL fails on the proxy regardless, so a failed fetch is not evidence either way. Full rule: github-state-inspection (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc).

be7b3f276931.title: Write capability requirement and read-only degradation
be7b3f276931.content: folio-init is a writing verb: it creates directories, writes manifests and agent stubs, and (when git is available) prints the command that seeds the cat/<instance>/beans and cat/<instance>/todos orphan state branches. Before invoking folio-init to write, check that at least one write capability is present (scenarios/capabilities/): . | git-push — local filesystem write plus git remote push capability for the target repository and its state branches. | github-api — GitHub API token (gh / REST / GraphQL) able to create or populate the target repository and refs. | github-connector — MCP GitHub connector able to push the scaffolded files into the target repository. | . When no write capability is available (a read-only container or an unauthenticated session), folio-init degrades cleanly via --dry-run (dry_run: true on the MCP tool): it computes and returns the complete Markdown report of every directory, manifest, builder shim and config file it would write, without touching the filesystem or git refs. Never attempt a partial write when write capability is absent, and never report a failed capability probe as a completed scaffold.

Writing the path to the harness once in the shim means re-linking a folio (submodule ↔ sibling ↔ remote mount) is a two-file edit rather than a sweep across every block manifest. | The link back to the platform (--link) — links the harness via sibling (--assistant-path ../folio-assistant) or submodule, and writes .mcp.json and the .claude/ session-start hook (bun run cat state:mount) pointing at that link. | The agent instructions — AGENTS.md and the one-line CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md stubs pointing to it. | The work-plan state branches — declares beans and todos on the cat/<slug>/beans and cat/<slug>/todos branches and prints the seed command; once it has been run, bun run cat state:mount mounts a working store on the first session start (directory-conventions §”Where a NEW layer’s state lives”). | .

baae7c84f022.title: “NOT clean” is a verdict about the RUN, not about your diff
baae7c84f022.content: Skill gate-tree-mutation: Reading bun run cat gates’ “NOT clean” verdict. Why every gate can pass and the run still exit 1, the two causes and how to tell them apart in one command, and the question that settles whether a churning field is a defect in the writer: does it describe the SUBJECT or the RUN? . Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . bun run cat gates snapshots the tree before the first gate and after every one, so a gate that repairs something on its way past is named. Every gate can pass and the run still exit 1: . ✗ every gate passed, and the run is NOT clean — 1 gate(s) changed the tree. The gates that ran after the mutation were handed the repaired tree, so their verdicts describe a state you have not committed. No gate can observe what another gate did, which is why the detector can only live in the runner (gate-tree-guard.ts) and why its predicate is a per-gate delta rather than “the tree is dirty”: running gates over your own uncommitted work is the normal case. A failure to read the tree is carried as undetermined and reported rather than thrown, because undetermined is not clean. Two causes, and they are answered differently. Read git status --short before you decide which one you have.

e24447c7359d.title: Cause 1 — you changed an input and did not regenerate
e24447c7359d.content: The ordinary case, and platform-gates §”What a *:check failure is telling you” is the whole of it: run the generator, commit its output, and run the gates after the last edit. Never hand-edit the artefact into agreement.

6cd6724f7b8c.title: Cause 2 — the artefact records the RUN, and your run differs
6cd6724f7b8c.content: This is the one that looks like cause 1 and is not. The generator is behaving correctly, the input has not changed, and the file still gets rewritten — because a field in it describes the run that produced it rather than the subject it is about, and your run is not the last one. The question that settles it: . Does this field describe the SUBJECT the artefact is about, or the RUN that produced it? Only the first is a reason to write. A field that records the environment — a timestamp, the checked-out HEAD, the runtime version — will differ on every machine, so counting it as a reason to write makes the artefact churn everywhere and reports that churn as though an input had moved. Example — QA script sidecars . The committed QA script sidecars under cat-harness-tools/pipeline/script-sidecars/ carry three run fields: . last_run_at wall-clock time of this run last_run_sha the checked-out HEAD engine_version `bun-${Bun.version}` — the local runtime . saveQaScriptSidecar writes only when a substantive field moved, and none of the three counts. Counting engine_version would make a run under any other Bun rewrite every sidecar whose recorded engine disagrees, so that bun test dirties the tree and bun run cat gates ends NOT clean on every branch. Two measures are kept, and they answer different halves: .bun-version pins Bun for CI (check:bun-pin holds every oven-sh/setup-bun site to it), which makes the recorded engine consistent where the repository controls it; the comparison skip stops any other engine — an agent container’s image, which a repository cannot pin — from rewriting a file whose checker did not change. “A verdict produced by a different engine is a different verdict” is true, and about a different artefact. A script sidecar holds no verdict — it records a checker’s source file, its hashes and its dependencies; verdicts live in block sidecars. No reader consults a script sidecar’s engine_version for freshness: entryIsFresh compares field_hash and the script hashes, nothing else. The same field can be load-bearing in one artefact and pure provenance in another, so check the argument against the artefact in front of you. Where the rule is already implemented . | where | the guard | . | scripts/qa-results.ts writeQaResult | compares withoutTimestamp(prior), so only updated_at differing is not a write; shared by every *.qa-results.json family | . | pipeline/qa-sweep.ts | wroteSomething = verdictChanged \|\| metadataDrifted, and updated_at advances only then | . | qa-utils.ts saveQaScriptSidecar | content-derived fields only; engine_version and the two last_run_* fields are excluded | . writeQaResult’s docblock states the principle: the timestamp answers “when were these findings established”, not “when did somebody last run the script”. A churn you meet is more likely a family that MISSED this rule than a new question — look for the nearest of these three before designing anything.

8c260906d322.title: If you meet a churn whose writer has not been fixed yet
8c260906d322.content: Discard it rather than committing it, and then fix the writer: . git checkout -- <the churning paths> . Committing such a churn stamps whatever your environment happens to be as though it were a fresh measurement — with an older local runtime, a downgrade. The generator records your container correctly, and your container is not the repository. Discarding is a workaround, not a fix. A signal that is always red is one nobody reads, and then it cannot report the next real in-run repair. So the sequence is: discard, ask the question at the top of cause 2, and fix the comparison. Do not add the paths to an ignore list — that removes the signal instead of the cause.

ebbf61ba82aa.title: Do not read past the line
ebbf61ba82aa.content: Cause 2 has a narrow signature. If NOT clean names paths outside the artefact family you expect, or fields other than the run-provenance ones, it is not this: the gate is telling you something new, and cause 1 is the likelier answer.

91de723528b6.title: Generalise the fix, then attack the generalisation
91de723528b6.content: Skill generalise-the-fix: You have a fix. Before it ships, ask what CLASS of defect it belongs to and whether the fix sits at the right layer — then attack your own answer: name what the fix now catches that the bug did not. Two axes go wrong, SCOPE and STATE, and widening either past the problem is how a fix becomes the next defect. Applies to a bug fix, a schema change, a detector, or a claim in a paper. Use after the fix works and before the pull request. Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . A fix that repairs one instance and leaves its siblings is half a fix. A fix widened past the problem it solves is the next defect. This skill is the pass between those two, and it is two moves in order — generalise, then adversary — because the adversary has no subject until a generalisation exists. Run it when the fix works and before the pull request. Not while debugging: this asks what the defect was, which you cannot answer until you know.

a85db8d4a15a.title: Move 1 — what class is this?
a85db8d4a15a.content: Three questions, in order. The first is the one that is usually skipped. 1.1 What was the defect, as opposed to the symptom? . The symptom is where you noticed it. The defect is the rule that was wrong. They are rarely the same, and the fix belongs at the defect. Symptom: two work items reported as having no options. Defect: the counter recognised one markdown form — top-level list items — while MADR, the authority, is format-agnostic. The corpus was fine; the detector had invented a requirement. Fixing the two work items would have left the rule free to misjudge the next one. The tell that you are fixing a symptom: the fix names a specific instance — two work item ids in a rule, document-ingestion.html in a selector, one filename in a condition. 1.2 What else has this shape? . Look, do not guess. The corpus answers this and your memory does not. The same detector. A twelve-bean sweep over the store found ten using list items, two using bold enumerations — and one using subheadings and being over-counted ten for four options. The sweep found a second error direction nobody had reported, and it changed the design: three forms, most structured wins, never summed. A fix designed from one example handles one example. A fix designed from the sweep handles the class, and the sweep is usually one command. 1.2a A sweep must report its own coverage . The sweep in 1.2 is a measurement, so it answers to the same rule every other measurement here does: say what you covered, or a silent under-match reads as a clean corpus. Sweeping the health checks for more findings whose action could not clear them. The first pass regex-matched action: followed by string literals and reported 6 actions, all sound. The file has 15. The nine it missed included a ternary, and the pass would have concluded the class was closed after seeing 40 % of it — while looking for exactly that kind of blind spot. The fix is one line of output: parsed 15 of 15. The count of subjects found against the count that exist, printed beside the verdict. So a corpus sweep prints the denominator. grep -c for the crude marker, parse for the real one, and show both — if they disagree, the parse is the thing to fix before reading anything into the result. This is rendered-verification’s “assert the conditions” rule with the browser taken out of it: a check that cannot tell an empty walk from a clean one is not a check. 1.3 Is the fix at the right layer? . Walk outward from the symptom until you reach the thing that is actually wrong, and stop there. Both directions are failures: too deep and the siblings stay broken, too high and see Move 2. The search field was 44 % of its panel. Our rules said width: 100 % and flex: 1 1 auto and they were all correct — walking the box chain found the theme’s own .search-input-wrap at max-width: 536px, two layers above where the change felt like it belonged.

b52a3f7f5844.title: Move 2 — the adversary
b52a3f7f5844.content: Now attack what you just wrote. One question, and answer it in writing: . What does this fix now apply to that the defect did not? . If the honest answer is “nothing”, say so and move on — the pass is cheap when it passes. If it is anything else, that is the list to justify or narrow. The two axes, and they go wrong independently . Most over-generalisation is one of these, and the worked case below is both at once. | axis | the question | widened past the problem looks like | . | SCOPE | which things does it apply to? | the fix names a container when the problem was one child | . | STATE | when does it apply? | the fix is unconditional when the conflict only arises in one state | . The worked case. A rule was written so ONE panel could paint over a full-bleed figure. It was applied to the whole sidebar (scope) in every state (state), as :root.fa-has-fullwidth .side-bar { z-index: auto }. At specificity (0,3,0) it beat the open-nav rule’s (0,2,0) always — so on every page with a wide figure the navigation opened behind the page content, which the open-nav rule’s own comment had predicted in as many words. Neither axis needed widening. The panel is position: fixed; only the panel was in conflict; and only while a figure was expanded. Four tells, all cheap to check . | The fix names a container, the bug named a child.side-bar when the problem was .fa-qr-panel. | The fix is unconditional and the conflict is not. Ask when the defect can occur. If the fix is broader than that window, narrow it or say why not. | You summed where you should have chosen. Recognising three forms is right; adding their counts gave one work item 14 options where it has 4. When alternatives are alternatives, take the most specific present — do not add. | The label is doing work the relation should do. A stale-claim check keys on parent rather than type: epic, because type is a label a work item sets about itself while parent is a fact another work item asserts about it. Keying on the label would also have forced a ruling on what feature means. | . Keep the discrimination the check exists for . A generalisation that excuses everything has deleted the check. Name the case that must STILL fire, and test it. The stale-claim check excuses a claim whose child moved recently. The case that must still fire: a parent all of whose children are also quiet — 8 open children, none moving — and it has a test of its own. Without it the change would have excused every parent. The strongest outcome is when the adversary reverses you . Expect to find a trade, and measure it rather than reasoning about it. The sidebar case. I expected z-index: 100 to fix the nav at the cost of the panel the old rule protected, so I synthesised that panel and measured. Under auto it was not visible at its own centre — covered despite its z-index: 1200. Under 100 it was. The old value failed the case it was written for, so the new one was better on both counts and there was no trade to weigh. An adversarial pass that only ever confirms you is not being run.

247f9400ccd6.title: Move 3 — falsify the guard
247f9400ccd6.content: A guard that would not have caught the bug is worth nothing, and you cannot tell by reading it. Reintroduce the defect, watch the guard fail, restore, watch it pass. Two commands. The sidebar case: sed the value back to auto → both assertions fail; restore → 25 pass. A health finding: it fired before, is silent after, and the adjudicated group is still counted so “never created” and “all resolved” cannot read the same. If the guard cannot be falsified — because the defect needs a state you cannot produce — say so where the guard lives, and say what does cover it instead.

23d63efbb999.title: Where this is NOT a bug fix
23d63efbb999.content: The moves are the same; only the vocabulary changes. | A schema or model change. Scope is which records must now satisfy this; state is from when. A field made required is a fix applied unconditionally to every record ever written — the sidebar shape in a schema. | A detector or gate. Its class is the set of inputs it judges. Sweep the corpus (1.2) before changing the rule, or you will tune it to the two examples in front of you. | A claim in a paper. The generalisation is the theorem’s hypothesis; the adversary asks which objects now satisfy it that the proof does not cover. The falsification is the counterexample you look for on purpose. Widening a hypothesis past what the argument supports is over-generalisation with a different name. | .

6ccf694227df.title: What this deliberately does not do
6ccf694227df.content: It does not ask you to generalise everything. “Nothing else has this shape” is a complete and common answer to 1.2, and one worked example is not a class. The cost of the pass is a few minutes; the cost of inventing a class that is not there is a rule nobody can satisfy. It does not replace rendered-verification or a test. It asks whether the fix is aimed correctly. Whether it works is a different question and comes first. It does not decide a trade the owner should decide. When narrowing the generalisation costs something real — say, a corner magnifier under the staging banner, where raising it defeats the banner and lowering it costs the position — report the measurement and the two options rather than picking.
