A stage is done when its gate is green, never when the work looks finished. | # | stage | lane | gate | . | 0 | Brief, measure the signals, claim | authoring-agent | signals in the work item; bun run cat beans:claim <id> | . | 1–3 | Declare in place, detangle, isolate | authoring-agent | graph-detanglement — all its gates | . | 4 | Identity: name, version, iriBase, needs, nodeSchemas in the declaration; move the base once | platform-authoring-agent | iri:sync -- --from <old base> then iri:sync:check; check:node-iris | . | 5 | Hosted outputs out of the content | platform-authoring-agent | the content leak test’s pending list is empty | . | 6 | Split content from tools: create <name>-tools/ as a sibling, move the code, cut its import cone | platform-authoring-agent | FR-7 (content holds no code); check:tools-closure; generated files byte-identical before and after | . | 7 | Publication plan: every identifier the content mints is a file some step publishes, at /v<major>/ | publication-manager | check:node-iris; the site layout in instance-publication §”The release site” | . | 8 | Rehearse standalone: copy content + tools alone into a temporary directory and run the tools’ checks there | build-pipeline | green with nothing else on the path; an empty tree exits non-zero | . | 9 | Authorise — report what moves, sizes, what breaks, and wait | administrator | the owner’s answer (deletion-requires-confirmation) | . | 10 | Seed: the owner creates the repositories; once the source has settled, seed main, then the content and tools as reviewed PRs, with history | administrator, then authoring-agent | bun run cat seed:ready --layer <name> --rehearse answers settled for each layer, at seed time; then the seeding PRs reviewed and green | . | 11 | Parent consumes, additively: pin (a SHA while staging, a version once released), repoint imports, keep the parent’s copy. After any move of files between the pair, run the post-move sweep first (below) | platform-authoring-agent | the parent green with the dependency declared; check:published-refs; every gate in the sweep table | . | 12 | First release: tag, publish /v<major>/ | publication-manager | check:version-bump; every identifier dereferences (publish-verification (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)) | . | 13 | Cutover: the one commit retiring the parent’s copy into fsh-guts as a verified archive (the deposit state:seed --cutover makes: it must extract to the exact tree removed, with a provenance note), deposited into the PARENT’s fsh-guts before the removal, frozen, never refreshed or rendered: a relocation, not a deletion (sub-kg-lifecycle stage 13 has the steps) | administrator | only after 11 and 12 are green; DONE only when bun run cat separation:cutover:check --site, run in the separated repository, exits 0 (Tool separation-cutover-check: mounts, declarations resolve, no monorepo wiring, layer direction, the site builds from the mounts alone) | . | 14 | Independent refinement: each new release adopted by the parent as a reviewed step | authoring-agent | upstream-version-adoption | . Nothing is committed to the new repositories before stage 10, and stage 10 starts only when the owner says so. Until then the pair is staged as sibling directories in the parent (bootstrap/, bootstrap-tools/). Ready to seed? — asked at seed time, not at rehearsal . A seed is a snapshot: one commit that names the source sha, with no history. Every open PR whose diff touches the layer when the snapshot is taken is orphaned into the monorepo: after cutover its change is in neither the seed nor anywhere that reads it. Stage 8 asked whether the layer stands alone, but the tree has moved since. So GW_SeedReady sits between creating the repositories and seeding them, and asks again: . bun run cat seed:ready --layer cat-harness --rehearse --text # exit 0 settled, 1 not yet, 2 unknown . | criterion | not yet when | . | heavy movers | an open PR labelled heavy-mover touches the layer or the next one up | . | next layer | any open PR touches the next layer up, which imports this one | . | layer load | more than five open PRs touch the layer | . | moves | an open PR deletes a file in the layer, or renames one into or out of it. A generator’s own names do not count: an owned-tree path in merge-conflict-patterns.ts (content-hashed payloads, rail data) is renamed by every regen, so moving one changes what no seeded path means | . | standalone | bun test is red with only the layer and what it needs beside it, as sibling directories | . | upward paths | a path DECLARED in the layer — a Tool module, a QA criterion source, a render target — resolves only in a layer above it, so it breaks the day the layer stands alone | . A test about the WHOLE CHECKOUT lives at the top. A test that reads several sibling layers at once, or the aggregate root itself (.github/, .gitignore, the root declaration, beans/, todos/, memory/, fsh-guts/), is red in every layer it is placed in, so it goes in the root layer’s DECLARED test home — folio-assistant-tests in folio-assistant.json, at test/ — never in a layer and never at a path a runner hardcodes. Whatever names every layer belongs at the top, so each layer below stays standalone-green. Split a file when only some of its tests read the checkout, keep the fixture tests with their layer, compose the moved paths from ORIGIN_DIR (the directory the test was written in), and move a corpus describe whole when it carries a vacuity guard: a sibling left behind passes standalone over nothing. A test reading an UPPER layer’s files moves to that layer. It is red standing alone for the same reason, one level down: the file it reads is not in its layer’s closure. It goes in the upper layer’s DECLARED test home, which may import the lower layer — never the reverse — and it is split, pointed back to and composed from ORIGIN_DIR exactly as above. Check first that the file it reads really IS the upper layer’s: a path written from the checkout root (cat-harness/src/… read relative to the working directory) is red standing alone over a file the layer does hold, and the fix there is to resolve it from the test file, not to move it. A test that reads the checkout’s GIT asks which of two things it is. A standalone layer is a fresh clone with no origin and one commit, so a test handed this checkout’s remote, HEAD or origin/main fails there on a missing input. A test of LOGIC that merely reads git — address derivation, an upload URL’s shape, a commit IRI, resolving a short sha — builds a throwaway repository whose facts it sets (gitFixtureRepo in cat-harness’s test/support/git-fixture.ts) and passes that root, with every assertion exactly as strict; a function that resolves its root internally gains an optional root parameter defaulting to today’s. A check that THIS repository is configured right — its own Pages address, its committed pages’ banners — keeps its assertion verbatim and moves to the top-level test home above. upward paths counts what breaks, not what is out of sight. It counts declared paths that resolve above the layer, not dependents discovery cannot find: discovery is checkout-local on purpose, so a count of what it cannot see never reaches zero, and the risk is paths, not layers. A seeding pair is not upward. A higher layer’s Tool nodes may resolve into their implementer below through needs; the two are seeded in the same step, so none of those paths can break on seeding day. The HIGHER layer says so, seedsWith: [<lower>] in its declaration, because a lower layer naming one above it is the wrong direction. seed:ready states such paths in its note and does not count them; a path into any other layer above still counts. Four things to keep straight: . | The layer map is read off the declarations: livesAt.path is the directory, the longest needs chain is the depth, and the next layer is every layer one level up that needs this one. Nothing in the tool names a directory. | Every threshold is in the decision table, processes/kg/decisions/seed-readiness-gate.dmn. The script works out each criterion’s verdict by evaluating the table with the other facts at zero, so changing “five” is a one-line edit to the table. | heavy-mover is a label a person applies. With none on the layer, the criterion passes. If the label cannot be read, the answer is could-not-determine. | The rehearsal runs only on request, with --rehearse. It copies the layer and its needs into a scratch workspace (~150 MB and ~8,000 tests for cat-harness) and refuses to start with less than 3 GB free. Without --rehearse, the standalone criterion is could-not-determine, so seed:ready cannot answer settled until a rehearsal has run. That consequence is the one constant SETTLED_REQUIRES_REHEARSAL. | . Could-not-determine is never clean. GitHub lists at most 3,000 files per PR, so a criterion that the unseen files could change is undetermined, and the gateway answers unknown and stops. An unknown only withholds settled, though. It never hides a finding that is already certain, so the table tests the not yet rows first. not yet goes to Drain: land, close or re-target the PRs it named, then ask again. The tool only reports. It never seeds, labels or comments.

aa1e908eabf5.title: The owner’s decisions
aa1e908eabf5.content: An agent asks these; it does not settle them. | Separate at all, and where the boundary is — after the signals are measured. | The address base for the extracted graph’s identifiers: under the parent, or the new repository’s own. | Where verdicts about it live: hosted in the harness, or in the content. | What the tools repository owns, and how its checks run (agent, package, described workflow). | Authorise the extraction (stage 9). | Whether the first release is a draft with a tag, or the first formal publication (instance-publication). | The cutover (stage 13). | .

5aea13619a63.title: Identifiers and versions
5aea13619a63.content: One iriBase and one version in the declaration. Identifiers a program reads and pages a person reads are both <iriBase>v<major>/…; the exact release is the pin’s (bootstrap-tools/schemas/release-iri.ts). A base move is bun run iri:sync -- --from <old base>, once. A $schema tag carries its schema’s own semver. The exported graph’s own @id moves only when the new repository actually publishes. A published node’s identifier must be its file’s path (check:node-iris).

de9e74a3df7d.title: Versions of the pair — same scheme, same start, then independent
de9e74a3df7d.content: . | At the split, both start at the content’s current version, for simplicity — bootstrap was 0.1.0, so bootstrap-tools starts at 0.1.0. | After that each is versioned on its own, by the same rules: semver, the bump computed from the exported surface (check:version-bump). | Tags are plain v<major>.<minor>.<patch> in each new repository: a standalone repository holds one layer, declared at its root, so the tag needs no name. check:version-bump reads the plain form only there; a repository of several layers — the parent while the pair is staged — keeps <name>-v<major>.<minor>.<patch>, because a plain tag could not say which layer it released. | A tools release says which content versions it handles as a list of supported MAJOR versions (bootstrap: [0]), never a range expression — instance-versioning rule 2 forbids range syntax, and within one major a newer minor or patch only adds (tagCompatible). A tool asked to work on a content major it does not list refuses rather than guesses. | .

f90ed7aaff65.title: How the parent consumes the pair
f90ed7aaff65.content: No git submodules, ever (remote-mount.md). | mechanism | when | details | . | Remote mount (remoteMounts) | staging & development | A declared directory fetched at a pinned 40-character SHA with a committed lock (index.lock.json) and consent record. Downstream checkout .gitignore automatically ignores mounted directory trees. | . | NPM KG retrieval (kg-retrieve-npm) | packaged distribution | package.json declared in <instance>.json (role: "package-manifest"). Tarball packed via pack-tarball with a folio-binary-release/v1 integrity record, downloadable via npm install or GitHub binary releases (unhydrated source vs hydrated store). | . | Package import | published tools | The parent imports the tools’ Zod schemas and pipeline writers as an npm package dependency. | . | Upstream pins | maintenance | upstream-pins.json, maintained by upstream-version-adoption.bpmn. | . Separation lessons . | Downstream Gitignore Contract: When remote mounts populate a layer directory in the consumer repository, the consumer’s .gitignore must ignore the mounted paths. Otherwise, git treats external files as uncommitted local files. index.config.json automatically includes all remoteMounts paths in the generated .gitignore. | Folded Layer Aliases: When a layer or subgraph is folded into another (e.g. cat-openapi folded into cat-harness as named subgraph openapi), external forks or dependencies may still carry needs: ["cat-openapi"]. schemas/kg/harness-config.ts maintains FOLDED_INSTANCE_ALIASES to resolve these. | Asset Permission & License Validation: Pre-separation audits must verify library/withheld.json and copyright gates. Materializing or mounting a separated catalogue without verified asset clearance causes 404s and broken links on published documentation. | NPM Manifest in the KG: package.json is an authored pre-packaging asset in the Knowledge Graph (role: "package-manifest"), and .tgz release tarballs are tracked as folio-binary-release/v1 state documents with SHA-256 integrity digests. | No Relative Directory Climbing Across Repositories: Once separated into standalone checkouts, climbing ../.. escapes the repository boundary into .claude/worktrees/ or the parent filesystem and fails with Cannot find module. All cross-repository imports MUST be authored as package imports (e.g. @litlfred/cat-harness/... or via package exports), or resolved through package specifiers / tsconfig paths, NEVER through escaping filesystem ../.. traversals. | No Fixed-Depth Repository Root Assumptions (REPO): const REPO = resolve(import.meta.dir, "..", "..") points at the checkout root in a monorepo and above it in a standalone repository, so the script cannot find <instance>.json or scans sibling worktrees. Resolve the root dynamically — search upward for <instance>.json, index.config.json, or .git. | Clean Standalone Manifest (package.json) and Tooling Scaffolding: When extracting a layer to an upstream repository, package.json must be normalized: . | Operational commands must live under "scripts", not leftover monorepo "checkoutScripts". | Script definitions must NOT hardcode monorepo subdirectory paths (e.g. "bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/..." -> "bun run scripts/..."). | A standalone tsconfig.json must be present to prevent tsc from walking up to the monorepo root. | Explicit dependencies and devDependencies must be declared. | . | Fan-Out Recursion Guard in declaringInstances: When a mounted dependency carries its own nested remoteMounts, consumer remote fan-out must not mount sub-layers into roots that are already locked mounts of the parent checkout (!lockedMountPaths(checkout).has(rel)). Otherwise remoteFanOut mutates the child checkout’s tree and treeDigest verification fails. | Relative Directory Symlink Handling in Staging & Tarball Scripts: Recursive copies (cpSync(..., { recursive: true })) of trees with internal symlinked directories can recurse forever. Staging, site compilation, and packaging scripts must copy symlinks with { dereference: false } or use archive utilities (such as tar or rsync -a) that preserve symlink references. | Purely Declarative Ontologies vs. Companion Toolsets (FR-7): Purely declarative base repositories (such as litlfred/bootstrap) contain zero runtime execution code, zero test suites, and zero package.json manifests (FR-7). All graph compilation (JSON-LD export, BPMN diagram rendering, site staging, and schema validation) is executed by the companion tooling repository (bootstrap-tools). The declarative repository marks its render exemption (renderExemption: true) in its root manifest, and tooling scripts accept an explicit target repository argument (--repo <dir>). | Toolchain Decentralization (package.json, tsconfig.json, bunfig.toml): Tools and harness subgraphs must possess full standalone toolchain autonomy. package.json must be a standalone package manifest (e.g. @litlfred/<tools-layer>), bunfig.toml defines test preloads per layer, and tsconfig.json must set "noEmit": true and omit rootDir/outDir to prevent error TS6059: File is not under rootDir when cross-subgraph schemas or utilities are imported. See bun-use. | Monorepo Coordinator Demotion: Once tools and code are extracted to their respective packages, the root package.json is demoted to a private coordinator ("private": true) with narrowed tsconfig.json (test/**/*.ts). The root platform coordinates development workspaces, mounts, and integration tests, but never directly exports or publishes tool implementations. | Ephemeral File Purging and Root Hygiene: Ephemeral generated directories (_kg/, build/, test-results/) must NEVER be committed to the root repository or left unignored. Build outputs belong to the tool that produces them. | Layer Memory Preservation: Root directories beans/, todos/, and fsh-guts/ are the layer’s own durable working memory (the agent’s plan, the user’s todo queue, and the archival store). They are never overlaid across layers, never extracted to downstream packages, and stay at root by design. | A cutover is not done until the layer has re-pointed and can publish itself: livesAt is not a comment — remote-mount.ts takes livesAt.path as the mount path and seed-ready reads it as “still staged”. A path that was only ever a mount inside the parent’s site build serves nothing on its own, and generated pages keep absolute links to the parent’s paths, which 404 once the bytes move. Before stage 13: livesAt is gone, iriBase is declared, and the layer’s own site builds from its own repository. | The replayer must never live inside a layer it replays: if every workflow (and every downstream folio’s staging build, through a reusable workflow) bootstraps by running a script inside the directory being retired, the cutover breaks the first step of every job. Before stage 13, grep every workflow the parent ships for paths into the directory being retired, and give the parent a bootstrap entry point that lives in the parent and needs nothing mounted (a dependency-free .github/mount-from-lock.sh that fetches the pinned replayer). | A downstream’s CI is part of “green” for a cutover: a reusable workflow called @main (uses: litlfred/folio-assistant/.github/workflows/folio-staging.yml@main) runs the PARENT’s current workflow in the DOWNSTREAM’s repository. A cutover that is green in the parent can therefore be red in every folio at once, and the red lands on whatever pull request the folio author opens next — it reads as their failure. Stage 12’s “green” includes one dispatched staging run of at least one downstream folio after the cutover commit. | A separated checkout must run its own tests and type-check its own subgraphs: run them in a fresh standalone clone. A test that reads <checkout>/../package.json fails with ENOENT outside the composed tree (lesson 6 by another route), and a tsconfig.json whose include omits named subgraphs (openapi/, archimate/) is green while never reading them. A test or type-check that silently depends on the composition, or silently skips part of the repository, is not evidence the separated repository works. | The kinds a declaration is judged against come from the checkout being read, not from where the harness module sits: the graph-typology registry reads the checkout under inspection first (defaultTypologyRoots; $REPO_ROOT still overrides), then its own; a kind both declare is shadowed and reported, never merged. Otherwise two layouts give two answers about one correct declaration. Every path a declaration names is resolved in one run by check:declaration-resolution, and separation:cutover:check uses it as its declarations condition. | .

2acfaa64288c.title: After a move lands — the post-move sweep
2acfaa64288c.content: Moving files between the pair is one reviewed commit in each repository; making the repositories that consume the move work again is most of the work. Run the sweep after a move lands and before the parent re-pins (stage 11), and do not call the move done until every gate in this table is green in a composed checkout at the matched pins. When another layer links into the moved path, declare the move first, so the layers can re-pin in any order: two-phase-move. | what still names the old home | the gate that catches it | the fix | . | A Tool node’s invoke.shell | kg:audit criterion tool-invoke-path-resolves (CRITICAL) | rewrite the invokes in each tools/<id>/<id>.json | . | Prose and commands in skills, guides, READMEs, BPMN documentation, workflows | check:command-paths | the rewrite rule below | . | A script’s own usage string | check:usage-paths | rewrite it in the receiving layer | . | Printed and RUN commands: “Run: …” remedies, generated banners, shell hooks, an e2e global setup | check:published-instance-exports, check:invocation-parity, security:gate (all three match paths by text), and the unit tests | rewrite the strings in the receiving layer | . | A wrapper generator’s list of the scripts it wraps | bat:sync / bat:sync:check (the writer errors on the first missing file) | update the list | . | Partition rules naming moved files | check:partition (“exact rule(s) name a file that is not in …”) | remove the dead rules | . | A kind-validator node pointing at a moved module | check:kind-validators:require-all | open: how a node in one layer names a module in the other | . | A writer’s claims in qa-refresh: files the writer used to rewrite became output it writes | qa:refresh (“N file(s) no declared writer claims”) | update the writer’s claims | . | A visualiser route a generator computed by hand | uml:overview inside skill:register (“no glossary page at …”) | use the declared route (declaredRoute(<core>, "glossary-page")) | . | A browser bundle importing a node-only module through a package import | navbar:assets (“Browser polyfill for module node:url …”) | move the constant into a node-free module | . | A directory declared inside another declared directory in the receiving layer | check:layout-norms (it stops qa:refresh) | move it out of the enclosing declared directory | . | A file left in BOTH layers | slice:sqlite / slice:sqlite:check (the KG export mints the same IRI twice and the slice dies on a UNIQUE constraint); node-kinds:check and kg:export do not refuse a duplicate on their own | delete the copy in the layer that no longer owns it, archived to fsh-guts/retired/ | . | Paired artefacts a move split across repositories | skills:docs (“page(s) produced by NO source”), check:declared-dirs (“absent — declared and not on disk”) | pin the receiving commits WITH the removing one (below) | . The rewrite rule . Rewrite a path only where the file exists in the destination and not in the source, and never in a record. The first half keeps a placeholder or a typo from turning into a different wrong path; the second keeps a file that moved and was later re-created from being redirected. Records say what was true when they were written, so they stay as written: proposals, todos, agent memory, work items, provenance (library figures, terminologies), upstream pins, vocab mappings, QA results and test fixtures. Generated files are rewritten by re-running their generators, never by hand. The rule is a Tool: rewrite-moved-paths (bun run cat paths:rewrite-moved --from-name <old> --from-root <dir> --to-name <new> --to-root <dir> --prefix <moved dir> … [--keep <glob>]). It reports with file and line by default, applies with --write, and with --check is the gate for a sweep that should be finished. Its test proves it never opens a proposal, a memory or a fixture. Pin the pair together, and record each consent first-hand . A move that removes files from one repository must be pinned together with the commit that adds them to the receiving one. A parent that pins the new source with the OLD pin of a receiving repository has the moved artefacts in neither, and the gates say so only indirectly. Before a re-pin, list what each new commit removes and confirm the receiving repository’s pin contains it. Every pin is a trust decision with its own consent (rule H8, remote-mount): trust.consent names who, when, the exact ref and the evidence, and mount:remote refuses a ref nobody consented to. A consent relayed by another agent is not the owner’s consent, so it is not recorded from the relay alone; record it when the owner’s answer to a question naming the exact SHAs is relayed verbatim with its time. A standing consent (“pin any main commit of these repositories that includes a fix merged in this session, listed in the PR”) covers only the repositories and the window it names, and each pin made under it is listed where the owner will read it. When a consented ref turns out not to do (a consented main with no declaration of the layer), do not substitute another ref: keep the previous pin and report it. The order that worked, and the rules for several sessions at once . | Fix the tools (the receiving layer): paths, the checks that matched paths by text, bundles, layout. | Fix the content (the source layer): prose, Tool invokes, declarations, partition rules. | Regenerate the content at matched pins, in a composed checkout laid down from the parent’s lock, to a fixed point (qa:refresh COMPLETE, then bun run cat regen, then every --check green on a fresh lay-down). | Re-pin the parent to those commits. | Run bun run cat gates on a fresh lay-down of the parent. | . When several sessions work on one separation at once: . | Hold pushes on a branch another session is superseding; hand over what is unpushed instead of racing it. | Announce which gates each session takes before starting, and re-check the open PRs and recent merges of a repository before opening one there. | Verify on the lock of the PR that will land, in a fresh scratch copy, never on another session’s checkout. | A measurement-only workaround stays local (for example a baseline entry needed to run qa:refresh while a decision is pending), is never committed, and is deleted once the real fix lands. | .

4d2f9bdb131c.title: Rollback
4d2f9bdb131c.content: Until the parent is green with the extraction declared, the extraction is additive and the parent keeps its copy; the cutover commit is the one unit worth reverting, and since the copy is ARCHIVED in the parent’s fsh-guts rather than deleted, the archive restores the exact tree that was removed. After a release, a tagged version is never reused: roll back with a new patch release and move the parent’s pin back.

7f142fb0ebe3.title: Worked examples
7f142fb0ebe3.content: 1. bootstrap + bootstrap-tools . | Stages 1–5: wrong facts, folio-only names and root-relative paths removed; graph typologies, $schema tags and QA moved out; IRIs under https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/ with semver. | Stage 6: bootstrap-tools/ created as a sibling; the Zod source moved down; the import cone cut to zod only; check:tools-closure and check:node-iris added, each watched failing on a planted violation. | . 2. cat-harness + the tools layer . | cat-harness (litlfred/cat-harness): owns the knowledge graph, declarative schemas, content adapters, and BPMN/DMN processes. | The tools layer: owns the MCP server (src/server.ts), concrete tool implementations (src/tools/), ambient moddle type definitions (types/), standalone package.json, tsconfig.json, and bunfig.toml. | Consumed through an index.config.json remote mount, locked in index.lock.json. The move of the harness’s remaining code into the tools layer is the case the post-move sweep was written from. | .

09e0b1380129.title: kg-separation (skill)
09e0b1380129.content: The skill kg-separation as its source file cat-harness/skills/kg/graph-management/kg-separation.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

71907d3afc4b.title: Subscribing to a knowledge graph
71907d3afc4b.content: Skill kg-subscription: Subscribing a folio or harness to an external knowledge graph — a substrate — and walking its parts from referenced to materialised, one at a time and only through the shared materialisation gates. When to subscribe, what makes a repository a substrate, choosing subgraphs, assets and harnesses, the five gates, instantiating a harness so it reaches the navbar, moving the pin, and what never to do. Named by: Getting started, Public comment on a review draft, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Publish extracted statements with source links, Board: open and close content, Board: place a note, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . A folio layer, or any harness, can subscribe to an external knowledge graph: choose to materialize some or all of its subgraphs and assets locally, and instantiate one or more of its harnesses so they appear in the navbar. A subscription is not a new mechanism. It is the relation that joins pieces this repository already has: the materialisation record, the shared Process_MaterializeRemote, the refresh, and the harness tile. This skill is the walk between them; each piece keeps its own rules, and where this file and one of them disagree, that one wins. |   | where | . | the process | subscribe-kg.bpmn | . | the entry | SubscriptionSchema in cat-harness/schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts | . | the held-bytes record | the folio-materialization/v1 record (MaterializationSchema, owned by the content layer) | . | the gates | materialize-remote and its process | .

f7d89e5326e9.title: When to subscribe — and when not to
f7d89e5326e9.content: Subscribe when your graph consumes another repository’s graph and you want to hold some of it, or just to pin exactly which version you are reading. | you want | relation | . | to load a layer fully, with its skills overlaid | needs | . | to point at a harness and never load it | associatedHarnesses | . | to consume a remote graph, holding the parts you choose | subscriptions | . A subscription sits between the other two and moves: every part starts referenced and becomes materialised only when chosen and let through the gates. The schema refuses an id that is also in needs or associatedHarnesses, because two relations to one layer is two answers to “do we hold it”.

de3171d98583.title: The substrate rule
de3171d98583.content: You can subscribe only to a substrate: a repository whose root declaration . | parses as bootstrap’s KnowledgeGraphDeclarationSchema (bootstrap-tools/schemas/graph.ts), and | declares at least one instantiated harness. | . Both are answered by the declaration file alone, so validate with a sparse, shallow fetch of that one file — never a full clone. “Could not fetch” is a third answer, never “conforms”. A repository that fails either point is not subscribed; record the reason and the pin you asked at, and write no entry. Known substrates are derived from each staged layer’s repository and each associated harness, with hand rows (knownSubstrates, schema KnownSubstrateSchema) only where no declaration names one. Start from that registry before asking the person for a repository name.

2a681b1d0fd1.title: Pin, always
2a681b1d0fd1.content: ref is a full 40-character commit SHA. Never a branch, never an abbreviated SHA, never “latest”. An unpinned subscription is how two subscribers see two different graphs under one name, and the schema refuses anything else — the same rule sync-remote-skills.ts enforces for remote skills. A tag replaces the SHA only once the substrate publishes releases.

7abc24519a9e.title: The entry holds the choice, never the state
7abc24519a9e.content: "subscriptions": [{ "id": "<iris-replica>", "repository": "litlfred/<iris-replica>", "ref": "<40-char sha>", "subgraphs": ["catalogue"], // CHOSEN; everything else stays referenced "assets": { "policy": "on-demand" }, // none | on-demand | all "harnesses": ["<iris-replica>"] // CHOSEN for instantiation }] . Whether catalogue is held is answered by its materialisation record, not by this list. Writing “materialised: true” on the entry would be a second answer free to disagree with the record — so do not add one, and do not read subgraphs as “what arrived”. A subgraph not listed is referenced, not absent: the visualizer still shows it.

a8083a413958.title: Choosing parts
a8083a413958.content: Show the person everything the cached declaration offers — every subgraph, asset class and harness, each with its state — before asking what to hold. A reader who sees only what was chosen cannot tell “not offered” from “not taken”. Then follow interaction-modality: context, options, recommendation, question. | Subgraphs — by the substrate’s directories[].id. Choose the smallest set that serves the folio; each is a separate trip through the gates. A nested subgraph is chosen by its parent’s id and materialised by its path (next section). | Assets — none, on-demand (each asset through the gates when first asked for), or all (every referenced asset walked now). on-demand is the sensible default for a large binary library; all on a catalogue the size of IRIS is a size-gate refusal waiting to happen. | Harnesses — only those whose needs are held here, locally or by another subscription. The process checks this before any byte moves and sends the choice back if not: subscribe the missing dependency first, or leave that harness referenced. | . Choosing nothing is legitimate. A subscription with no parts chosen is a pinned reference.

5d32d5abf950.title: Materialising: the five gates, via the shared process only
5d32d5abf950.content: Every chosen subgraph or asset goes through Process_MaterializeRemote, called — never re-implemented. Purpose first (working or archival), then the five gates in order: . | size — what fraction, and what the whole costs; refuse when you cannot tell | restrictions — “none known” is a state, not a green light | copyright — per bitstream, and separately for the derived work | retention — what expires this copy | source loss — what survives if the origin goes; only an archival copy discharges it | . unknown on any gate keeps the part referenced. That is the process working, not failing: record the refusing gate’s basis and continue with the next part — one part refused is not the subscription refused. The bytes that do arrive carry a materialization.json with fixity, and check:materialized-fixity covers them. A nested subgraph: chosen by its parent, materialised by its path . Some subgraphs are declared from within another directory. skills/voices, for example, is declared in skills/skills.json. To hold only that part, choose its parent’s id in subgraphs and ask for the part by path: . bun run cat kg:materialize <subscription> skills/voices # `skills` is chosen . The snapshot is not changed and nobody re-subscribes. The snapshot holds the root declaration only, so a nested id cannot be checked against it offline. The parent’s id can be, and the path is checked against the parent’s declared path. The part goes through the same five gates and its record names the parent’s id and the nested path. It is held beside the parent’s own part, which it never disturbs. A path under no declared directory is refused, and so is a path whose parent is not chosen.

b7312c77d221.title: A subgraph’s nodes without its bytes: metadata mode
b7312c77d221.content: To know what is in a subgraph — every node of sdlc/skills, typed, labelled and linked — you do not need its files. Ask for its published index.hydrated.jsonld instead (kg-export §”Named subgraphs”): . bun run cat kg:materialize --nodes <subscription> <subgraph-path> # e.g. --nodes cat sdlc/skills . | It fetches one file at the pin, <docs>/subgraph/<HARNESS>/<path>/index.hydrated.jsonld. Here <docs> and <HARNESS> come from the cached declaration. The file is validated against SubgraphHydratedSchema, and its root @id must be the subgraph you asked for. | It is held under <snapshot dir>/<subscription>/nodes/<path>/, beside a nodes.json record with its sha256. kg:materialize:check re-hashes it. | The root is refused. A harness root publishes index.jsonld only, so read that for the child subgraph IRIs, then ask for a child. | Only size applies, as a measured cap (--max-bytes). The four person gates guard copies of somebody else’s content. This is published graph metadata, with every body left as a pointer, and it can be fetched again from the pin at any time. The reasoning is in the header of the content core’s scripts/kg-materialize.ts. | It is not a substitute for the byte copy. When you need the files themselves, choose the subgraph and run it through the five gates above. | .

bb91594553e3.title: Instantiating a harness
bb91594553e3.content: kg:instantiate writes the state directories the harness declares and its config. The state directories go under the subscriber’s own subscribed-harnesses directory (graph typology subscribed-harnesses, holds: state), at <state dir>/<subscription>/<harness>/; a subscriber that declares none is refused, with what to declare. They never go at the repository root, where a harness named after a staged layer would write into that layer’s directory, and never under the snapshot directory, which holds upstream’s bytes and is declared readOnly. Where the checkout has a root index.config.json, the config goes INLINE in a new instances[] entry and no <harness>.config.json is written: the index is the one config, and it is then what reads as instantiated. Only a checkout with no index gets a root <harness>.config.json. The rule is index-config’s. Instantiation is what harness-tiles reads, and what puts the harness in the navbar’s bottom region. check:instance-render must be green afterwards; a config that renders nothing is a navbar entry pointing nowhere. A harness already instantiated at this pin is skipped, not rewritten.

7b9e655a44b7.title: Moving the pin is refresh, not re-subscribe
7b9e655a44b7.content: To move ref: validate the substrate at the new commit, then run every held part through Process_RefreshMaterialized — what changed upstream, what changed locally, what to do when both did; an archival copy is fixity-checked and never re-fetched. Only then rewrite ref and re-cache the declaration. Moving the ref first leaves the records of parts not yet refreshed describing a commit the entry no longer names. Afterwards, review again: the new pin may offer subgraphs the old one did not.

35c4afdba38f.title: Do not
35c4afdba38f.content: . | Materialise without the gates. No copying a subgraph by hand, no git archive into the tree, no “it’s only a few files”. Every byte arrives through Process_MaterializeRemote, or it is an unrecorded fork of upstream. Metadata mode (--nodes) is not an exception to this, because it copies none of the subgraph’s bytes: only the graph description that the substrate publishes. | Subscribe unpinned. No branch, no short SHA, no follow-latest. | Record state on the entry. State lives on the materialisation record. | Treat a refused part as failure and retry it with the gate relaxed. The refusal is the answer until the fact behind it changes. | Instantiate a harness whose needs are not held. Subscribe them first. | Subscribe to a non-substrate because its content looks useful. Without a conforming declaration there is nothing to pin subgraphs against — reference it instead. | Delete a materialised part to “unsubscribe” it on your own initiative. It is a durable artefact; report what would go and wait (deletion-requires-confirmation). | Skip a step because its tool is missing. Perform it by hand following the process — least of all the gates. | .

1d89495c6b29.title: kg-subscription (skill)
1d89495c6b29.content: The skill kg-subscription as its source file cat-harness/library/skills/large-datasets/kg-subscription.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

b86f3577ebc8.title: L1 document ingestion
b86f3577ebc8.content: Skill l1-document-ingestion: The detailed method for turning a DOCUMENT in uploads/ into a complete L1 entry in library/<bib-slug>/ — which rung reads it and why, what a complete L1 entry holds, why an inferred structure is refused rather than guessed, and the archive, dataset, narrative, image and vector-label arms. Refines the harness’s basic library-ingestion flow; one entry point: bun run cat ingest. Named by: L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure . This is a refinement, not the entry point. The harness’s library-ingestion skill carries the basic flow every asset takes — an upload is accepted, its metadata goes into the knowledge graph, and the asset lands in library/ if it is materialized — together with the two entry points, the upload’s retirement to fsh-guts/, and the remote half. This skill is what happens next when the asset is a document whose text and structure are wanted as L1 source content: reading it into sections, blocks and sidecars that check:l1-complete can judge. The rung code — scripts/ingest-document.ts, the pdf-*.py rungs, notebook-structure.ts and OCR — lives in the harness. This skill is the METHOD that chooses among them; invoking harness code from here is a downward edge. The executable form is collab/processes/library/l1-document-ingestion.bpmn, which calls the harness’s basic Process_Ingestion first and then the four ingest-* phases beside it.

7a97b51d4a21.title: The whole path is two commands
7a97b51d4a21.content: bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.pdf --library <lib> # rung + every derived arm, into ingest-staging/ bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.pdf --library <lib> --promote # the L1 gate, then into <lib>/<slug>/ . Staging prints the second line for you, built from your own arguments. --promote writes the entry’s JSON-LD nodes, for that entry only, with the same buildEntryNodes the corpus generator uses. They are minted for the destination, not for staging: an entry’s layer is read off where it sits, and ingest-staging/ belongs to whichever layer holds it. You do not need gen-library-jsonld or check:l1-complete --write after promoting — the first is done, and the second’s verdicts live on the qa-reports branch rather than on main.

0157a604b596.title: Which rung, and why there is more than one
0157a604b596.content: | rung | when | what it produces | . | pdf-structure.py | any PDF with a text layer | the outline’s chapters; with no outline, the inferred contents when it is trusted, else one section per page | . | pdf-pages.py | a page tree by hand: --first-page-label, or --from-ocr text | one section per page | . | pdf-ocr.py | text extraction yields almost nothing | a text layer to then page-split | . | pdf-tables.py | tables or figures matter | what pdf-structure/v1’s Section does not carry | . | slides-structure.py | the package declares a PPTX or ODP deck | one section per slide, images.json, accessibility.json | . | referenced-source.py | --reference given: the licence forbids a copy | referenced.json only — identity, sha256, outline; no text | . | text-structure.ts | the source is text files — Markdown, MDX, XML — usually fetched from a repository at a commit | text-structure/v1: a Markdown file divided by its own ATX headings outside fenced code, any other file one verbatim section, located by file and line range; images recorded by digest, never sectioned | . | notebook-structure.ts | the file is JSON with a numeric nbformat and a cells array — a Jupyter notebook, decided by content, never by the .ipynb name | notebook-structure/v1: one section per markdown heading, located by cell range; code kept as fenced code and never run; outputs not kept, and structure_note says so | . A notebook is a variant, not a PDF with odd pages. structure.json has a shared base (cat-harness-tools schemas/content/document-structure.ts): the PDF format is one variant, unchanged, and the notebook format is the other. A reader that needs only sections reads either through structureOf(), which says where a section is as {pages} or {cells}. A page-aware reader gets nothing from a notebook, rather than a cell index mistaken for a page number. The decision is mechanical: . | toc_source: outline → pdf-structure (9789241548960-eng, 250 sections) | toc_source: none, source.text_source: embedded → pdf-structure, which keeps its inferred contents only when they pass the trust tests and otherwise writes pages (wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng lands on pages that way) | a junk outline (milnorlink) → pdf-pages: pdf-structure would read the outline it found rather than infer one | toc_source: none, source.text_source: ocr → pdf-ocr then pdf-pages --from-ocr (who-pub-tps-931) | .

5d9f8a85d523.title: Slide decks — PPTX and ODP
5d9f8a85d523.content: A deck is a zip that declares its type ([Content_Types].xml, or ODF’s mimetype member), so it routes on the sniff, before the archive rung, exactly as a workbook does. slides-structure.py writes the same pdf-structure/v1 shape a paged PDF gets — one section per slide, page_start == page_end == <slide>, granularity: "slide" — so l1-blocks.ts, the manifest and check:l1-complete read it unchanged. Two differences from the PDF rungs: . | A slide’s title is its title placeholder, or it is Slide N. Never the largest text box: that is the inferred-TOC failure below in a new format. It is also an accessibility finding, because a slide with no title placeholder cannot be navigated to by name, so the two questions share one answer (title_source: placeholder | none in each section’s front matter). | No image is a page-scan. A full-bleed picture alone on a slide is the slide’s content, not a scan of text already extracted. | . accessibility.json reports, per check, what the package can answer — slide titles, alt text (with editor auto-captions such as “Description automatically generated” counted as failing, since nobody wrote them), decorative marks, language tags, document title, speaker notes — and says undetermined for the three it cannot: reading order, images of text, contrast. It gives no overall score. A single number would weigh a missing title against a missing alt text, and nothing supports that weighting. Two copies of one deck? Compare before you choose which to ingest: . python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/slides-structure.py --a11y-only DECK.pptx DECK.odp . Prefer the copy that wins the per-check comparison. An export can lose what the author wrote (an ODP export of Google Slides can drop all alt text and keep the language only on the default style), and the format’s reputation does not tell you which way a particular export went. Image descriptions go in the library’s image-verdicts.json as for a PDF. Put the inspector in attribution.<doc-id> when they are not the file’s inspected_by; without it the deck inherits the first inspector’s name and date.

8f2faaa66515.title: A source whose licence forbids a copy — record it, do not ingest it
8f2faaa66515.content: Some sources may be read but not reposted. The OMG BPMN and DMN specifications permit use on condition that a copy “will not be copied or posted on any network computer or broadcast in any media”. A normal ingest commits every section’s text to a public repository, which breaks that condition. It does so silently, because nothing in the text layer says so. bun run cat ingest FILE.pdf --reference IDENTITY.json --library <name> . IDENTITY.json holds the title, version, document number, date, publisher, URL and the licence clause, read off the document. A missing field is refused, never guessed. The entry holds referenced.json — the exact bytes’ sha256, the embedded outline (clause titles and pages, so a citation can still name a clause), a folio-materialization/v1 record in state referenced, and why the text is withheld — plus a manifest with an empty contains, and a licence.json quoting the clause. The choice is the caller’s, never inferred. Whether a licence permits posting is a reading of the licence, not of the bytes. check:l1-complete knows the kind, and refuses a referenced entry that holds sections/, blocks/ or images/. That would be the copy this kind exists not to make. A publication, not a file — an external reference. A FHIR implementation guide is a website and a package, not one PDF, so there are no bytes to hash. Its referenced.json takes the published variant of source (schemas/referenced-source.ts): kind: "published", url, canonical, package_id, version, and read_from / read_at naming the local record the identity was read off — no sha256, rather than a made-up one. links names where a reader goes instead (the publisher’s page, and a site_path on this site such as the layer’s artefact index), and the library viewer shows them on the entry’s row. Write it by hand — there is no file to run referenced-source.py on — then gen-library-jsonld.ts --entry for the manifest. The licence follows the usual rule: stated only with a basis, else unknown with where you looked. Example: the WHO SMART Trust IG’s entry in the DAK layer’s library/.

3ac454b49a96.title: A source published as text in a repository — read it at a commit
3ac454b49a96.content: The Gherkin reference, the MCP specification, the hmans/beans README and FHIR R5’s TestPlan resource are published as Markdown or XML in git repositories. Printing one to PDF so a PDF rung can read it makes the recorded sha256 identify a rendering nobody published, so they take their own rung instead: . bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.md --text --library <lib> # rung + l1-blocks, into ingest-staging/ bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.md --text --library <lib> --promote # the L1 gate, then the entry and its KG nodes . --text is the CALLER’s statement that the file is text: text has no magic bytes, so the extension is never read, and a binary handed in as text is refused as undetermined. Through cat ingest it takes the notebook’s derived arm (l1-blocks), and --promote writes the entry’s JSON-LD nodes, as for every rung. Do not stop at the rung. Run alone, text-structure.ts leaves an entry with no manifest.jsonld and no section or block nodes. A source read at a commit, with its upstream.json and several files, still runs the rung directly: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/text-structure.ts -o <library> --doc-id <slug> \ --base <checkout> --upstream upstream.json [--title T] [--image F]... FILE... and then, without fail, l1-blocks.ts -o <entry> and gen-library-jsonld.ts --entry <entry>, as for a notebook. What it decides: . | Divided by the author’s headings, or not at all. A Markdown file splits at its own ATX headings, outside fenced code. A # comment inside a gherkin block is not a heading. Any other text, and anything that opens with <, is one section, fenced verbatim. Nothing is rendered: shortcodes and JSX stay as written, and structure_note says so. | upstream records the exact revision: repository, 40-hex commit, ref, path, and in words whether that revision is the published text or a working copy. A default branch is often neither, and a reader cannot tell which from a URL. Keep the clone out of the repository tree. The bytes can be fetched again from the commit, so none go to uploads/ or fsh-guts/. | Several files are one source when the publisher ships them as one, as with a specification version that is a directory of pages. Each file keeps its own sha256. The source’s sha256 is the sha256 of their sha256sum listing, so sha256sum -c against a checkout verifies the entry without this code. | .

259f3528cb74.title: From a library entry to a folio document — seed it, and its graph comes with it
259f3528cb74.content: A folio whose working document starts from a source (an outline, a draft, a report) is SEEDED from the library entry, not from the raw file: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/seed-folio-from-library.ts \ --entry library/<doc-id> --slug <folio-doc> [--title T] [--author A]... [--force] . Any structure.json variant works. The top heading level becomes the chapters, deeper levels nest as sections, and a section’s own text becomes one prose block. No kind is guessed: a persona or a requirement is the folio’s own enrichment step. Every block carries meta.source (library, section, locator, method: "library-seed"), and the seed ENDS by writing each block’s .jsonld with gen-block-jsonld’s own code. A folio-specific seed script that writes blocks must end the same way, or its site publishes no graph. A seed is one-time: an existing document is refused unless --force, which discards hand edits. The original is never touched: the library entry and the folio’s nodes are DERIVED, and both are checked (gen-library-jsonld --check, gen-block-jsonld --check) so neither can drift unseen.

ff17d548c495.title: A source’s glossary and abbreviations — candidates, read by one tool
ff17d548c495.content: Every L1, DTH and DAK source reads its glossary the same way, with the Tool glossary-from-source, never with a script of its own: . bun run cat glossary:from-source --out glossary/<scheme>.glossary.json \ --id <scheme> --title "<title>" --from library/<doc-id>/sections . --from reads every section whose title names a glossary, definitions, terms, abbreviations or acronyms, and each numbered section under a glossary section (a specification that prints one term per heading). A folio block can be named with --terms or --abbreviations. Each row becomes a candidate term, verbatim, with source: <file>#L<line>; an acronym becomes the notation of the term it expands. The scheme is merged: a term a person has adopted or edited is never changed. Only a person moves a term to authored (glossary-terms). --check keeps the candidates in step with the L1 entry.

5456894fd7bf.title: A source’s reference list — its own bibliography, read by one tool
5456894fd7bf.content: Every source that prints a reference list gets its own bibliography, read the same way with the Tool references-extract (step Task_References of ingest-build-l1-kg.bpmn), never with a script of its own: . bun run cat references:extract --instance . [--entry <doc-id>] [--check] . It reads the L1 sections of each library entry. A list is a whole section whose title is a reference-list heading, or the lines after such a heading inside a section (chapter-end lists), in the six UN languages and Portuguese (References, Bibliography, Further reading, Références bibliographiques, Referencias, Литература, المراجع, 参考文献, …). Numbered lists are split on their own numbers; unnumbered ones where an entry closes and the next opens. Page numbers, running heads and section tabs between entries are skipped; a list ends at an annex, chapter or glossary heading, a table or figure, or a contents leader. Each entry becomes a folio-reference/v1 node in the instance’s declared references directory, keyed <doc-id>.<section>.<n>: provenance: extracted, derivedFrom the section file, and printed the entry exactly as the source prints it. Only fields read without guessing are set: URL, DOI, ISBN, issued (the work’s year, not the access date), accessed, and type: article-journal for a journal’s year;volume:pages. No title or author is parsed, because WHO, Vancouver and author-year styles disagree on where a title ends; the bibliography shows printed instead. A cited IRIS handle the library holds gets heldAt. An entry longer than any citation (the list ran into the text after it) is left out rather than kept wrong. The bibliography page lists the nodes under the document they came from (bibliography/library/<doc-id>/). Re-run the tool after a section is re-derived; --check fails when a node is stale or has no list left to come from. Nodes with any other provenance are never touched.

90a7326aa565.title: Requirements and normative statements — every DAK and DTH source
90a7326aa565.content: Requirement extraction is a general part of L1 ingestion for DAK and DTH sources, as a Stage B aspect: cat ingest runs extract-candidates.py --aspects-only on every staged entry, and each requirement the source states becomes a typed node in the entry’s graph, derivedFrom its L1 section. A folio’s requirement block then CITES that node. It does not restate it with an id of its own. The mount is the gate. The requirements aspect lives in the DAK layer (its scripts/extractors/dak-requirements.py), so it runs in DAK and DTH repositories and nowhere else. With no aspect mounted the arm writes nothing. No new schema: the existing kind that fits the source. Requirement schemas come in more than one style, some core and some the DAK layer’s: . | the source prints | kind | layer | . | a DAK requirement row, <CODE>.FXREQ.<n> / .NFXREQ.<n> | functional-requirement / non-functional-requirement | DAK layer | . | a system’s shall/must/should in prose (“The registry shall …”) | functional-requirement, no id | DAK layer | . | a row of a table of system functions | functional-requirement, source_kind: function-table-row (by hand today) | DAK layer | . | a row of a table of information needs, an item of a list of reports or functions, a figure caption naming a function | functional-requirement, source_kind: information-need-table-row, function-list-item, figure-caption (by hand today) | DAK layer | . | an indicator | indicator | DAK layer | . | any other normative sentence | recommendation, strength in rfc2119-requirement-level or grade-recommendation-strength | core | . Ids come from the source or there are none. number is the id exactly as printed, and it lands in the node’s meta.source_number. A requirement that prints no id has none. The node’s @id is derived from the section and the order the items appear in (<kind>-<section>-NN), never from a made-up label such as an agent-assigned FR-xx. A requirement from a source is a reference, not a definition: it contributes to a definition but does not make one. The nodes carry provenance: ingested and route_to: l2-dak-authoring. The folio that cites one decides what it means for its own system, and a person promotes it. Then account for everything. Run l1-coverage with the entry’s requirement candidates as --captured. Every normative sentence the aspect did not propose is either a missing capture or an exclusion a person signs off. A requirement written by hand, from a table no extractor reads yet, uses the same candidates.json shape: kind, source_kind, number (or null), name, statement verbatim, section_file, section_title, pages, formalization_candidate: false, route_to. Leave out document_class, validated and disposition. Those describe the WHOLE document, and the manifest reads them as such. Then run gen-library-jsonld --entry.

30f170230e78.title: An inferred chapter tree is refused, not guessed
30f170230e78.content: The failure this rule prevents is silent. Without an outline, a heading-detector can infer a table of contents — and an inferred TOC is confidently wrong in a way the output does not show. Two cases: . | WPR-RDO-2020-003-eng.pdf — 11 of 13 inferred sections were named after a different publication, because page 22 reproduces a sample table from one as a design example. | WHO_PUB_TPS_93.1.pdf — inferred entries took page numbers from the contents pages, so 26 of 42 sections came out under 500 characters while 37,923 characters landed in one section misnamed 18-usetul-reference-books. | . So pdf-pages claims no chapter tree and says so in structure_note. A page is a determined division; an inferred chapter was not. Same third-state rule the rest of this repository keeps: a structure that could not be determined is never rendered as one that was. The route pdf-structure.py takes itself . With no outline, the inferred contents is used only when it passes all three tests, in order (inferred_toc_trust): . | concentration: at most 60% of its entries may start on the two commonest pages — a list read off a page is not the document’s structure; | mean confidence ≥ 0.6 (TOC_MIN_MEAN_CONFIDENCE), each entry’s confidence being how much independent evidence agreed — a contents page, the body, a heading style, a numbering run; | headings with bodies: from 5 sections up, no more than 25% of the sections the tree would cut may hold under 50 characters (TOC_MAX_EMPTY_SHARE, TOC_EMPTY_SECTION_CHARS), front matter not counted — a tree of empty sections is logo lettering, a sample table’s column heads or a cover’s address block, not chapters. | . Otherwise — refused, or nothing inferred — the entry is split one section per page (page-001, “Page 1”, the shape pdf-pages.py writes), with granularity: "page", toc_source: undetermined or none, toc_undetermined_reason, and a structure_note saying why. Both inputs are recorded whether or not they passed: diagnostics.toc_inferred_entries and diagnostics.toc_inferred_mean_confidence and diagnostics.toc_inferred_empty_share. What the floor does and does not catch. The mean is a weak predictor of quality. A mean of exactly 0.60 means no entry was corroborated by anything but its style, and “at least 0.6” lets it through, so read a font TOC at 0.60 before citing it. The floor’s real work is on the regex fallback, whose entries carry no confidence and count as 0. The third test is the one that catches a poor font tree; a poor tree with an empty share just under 25% is too close to good ones to separate by this measure.

b64594f4c6a8.title: A text layer that is not text
b64594f4c6a8.content: Owner, 2026-11-11 (who-iris, card Q-ODD-1 = A): “force OCR when a page’s text layer fails a quality check”. A text layer can carry plenty of letters and still not be the page’s words, and the character count the router used to look at cannot see it. cat-harness-tools/scripts/_text_quality.py checks EVERY page against the document’s languages (--lang-hint, else the catalogue’s dc.language.iso). Each check was measured on an IRIS PDF: . | The text layer | Seen on | What the check counts | . | accents through the wrong code page (“dΘclaration”) | 10665/231031, French | words mixing Greek and Latin letters, in a Latin-script document | . | Persian in the wrong Arabic code points | 10665/94830-per | Arabic-script letters outside the language’s alphabet | . | words split by kerning (“au g m ente”) | 10665/83270, French | a lone lower-case letter between two lower-case words | . | fake bold, each word printed twice | 10665/66977-chi | words equal to the word before | . | a font with no Unicode mapping | 10665/232378, Arabic | letters among characters that are not digits or table punctuation | . The router runs the check in its probe. When any page fails, the document goes to pdf-ocr+pdf-structure: pdf-ocr.py reads every page and pdf-structure.py --ocr takes the OCR text for the failing pages only, keeping the outline and the text layer of the rest. They are listed in structure.json source.ocr_pages, each with its reason; text_source stays embedded. When most pages fail and there is no outline, the whole document is read from OCR (pdf-ocr+pdf-pages), as for a scan. A page that holds two scripts. OCR reads a page in the script its detector names, so a French article’s Arabic abstract (10665/117378) came out as “er ie obus AU ball”, and the Latin URLs in an Arabic toolkit’s references (10665/75211-ara) as Arabic letters. A page whose mean word confidence is under 70 is read again with each other installed script added (ara+eng, fra+ara), and the most confident read is kept when it gains 10 points. On the Arabic references page the confidence went from 54 to 86 and the URLs read correctly; a page of plain Arabic keeps its first read.

499ae2f46131.title: An outline that is not contents, and a section too long to be a block
499ae2f46131.content: Owner, 2026-11-11: “split single blocks that hold a whole book”. Eight IRIS PDFs came out as one section of 10,000 to 101,000 words, every one because an outline was present, was taken as the document’s answer, and located no heading on any page: . | Word bookmark names: _tyjcwt, _Hlk62546849, _GoBack, _TOC_250000 (10665/353150, 353151, 259268, 341997); | “Blank Page” (10665/385385), or the names of the files merged into the PDF (10665/44118: 9789241547727_eng_Chapter1-4); | a Russian edition carrying its English outline (10665/331525-rus). | . pdf-structure.py drops machine bookmark names from the outline, and sets the outline aside when nothing is left or when under half of what is left names a line the pages print (diagnostics.outline_rejected says which). The contents are then inferred, and must pass the three tests above, else the document is split by page. A section that still holds more than half of a document of 20 pages or more (and over 8,000 words), or over 20,000 words anywhere, is cut at the headings inferred inside it, else one section per page (diagnostics.oversized_split). A re-ingest renumbers the section ids of an entry cut this way, so its block summaries go stale and are redrafted. Titles that do not match their text . Four IRIS entries had section titles that did not match the words under them. pdf-structure.py now tidies an INFERRED table of contents before it splits (diagnostics.headings_tidied; an outline entry is never touched): . | A title cut to its last line (“sanitaria universal”, 10665/354399): a title that opens in lower case is rejoined with the lines above it, up to the bare number that opens it (“1.2 Función de la salud digital … cobertura sanitaria universal”). With no number above it, it is dropped. | A body word set apart by a font (“un”, “comme”, “On”, 10665/264857), and a reference’s first author in capitals (“YOUNG,”): dropped. | A diagram’s labels (an annex flowchart, 10665/329296): two or more sections on one page, each with fewer than 30 words, are dropped as headings and their words stay with the section before them. | . A page whose PDF draws its side panel and body before its headings (10665/342236) put every section one heading late. When the outline’s first heading on a page sits in the later half of the page’s text, and the page read in print order (top to bottom, a band of columns left column first) puts it near the top, that page is read in print order (diagnostics.pages_read_in_print_order). The document’s language is recorded, not read from the slug . structure.json source.languages holds the languages the ingest was given (--lang-hint). A reader asks it, not the slug: an item’s first edition keeps the bare slug whatever its language, so 10665/202203, which is Russian, has no -rus.

9040488e2bc5.title: Footnotes and their marks
9040488e2bc5.content: Owner, 2026-11-11: “also foot notes/marks”. The pdf-footnotes.py arm reads the page layout after l1-blocks.ts and writes footnotes.json (folio-document-footnotes/v1, schemas/content/document-footnotes.ts): . | a mark is a superscript span (or one small and raised) whose text is 1-3 digits, a letter, or * † ‡ §; | a note is a line in the lower 40% of the page, smaller than the body text, that opens with a mark; the small lines after it continue it; | a mark calls the note with the same mark on its page, else on the next. | . Only a note that a mark calls is a footnote, with every marks[] place that calls it (page and the words before the mark) and the block that holds its page. A small line opening with a number is as often a table row or a running footer (10665/311941: 159 such lines, none called), so those are kept as uncalled_notes, and marks with no note as unlinked_marks; nothing is dropped. The section text is not changed. OCR’d pages have no fonts and are listed in pages_unread. check:l1-complete reports the counts (footnotes) and fails only on a file that will not parse or names another entry. Numbered citations ([12], or a superscript 12 whose reference is in a list at the end) are not footnotes; a superscript one shows up in unlinked_marks, where a reference-list extractor can pick it up.

c12feeba7e7f.title: Errata: errors in the source’s own text
c12feeba7e7f.content: Owner, 2026-11-11 (card Q-ODD-1 = A, and “add to L1 doc schema errata”). Reading the blocks to summarise them finds errors that are in the publication, not the extraction: a workshop report titled June 2006 whose introduction says June 2005 (10665/205022), a Spanish edition announcing “nueve recomendaciones” where the English lists ten (10665/354399). The block is never changed. The agent records each one in library/<bib-slug>/errata.json (folio-document-errata/v1, schemas/content/document-errata.ts): . | Field | What it holds | . | id | e1, e2, … never reused | . | kind | error, inconsistency (two places or two official editions disagree), residue (a placeholder, an editor’s comment, contents page numbers “xx”), translation (an official translation says what its original does not) | . | block / page | where it is printed; at least one | . | quote | the words as printed, verbatim | . | reading | the reading the evidence supports, when there is one | . | evidence | what shows it, in a form a person can check | . | narrative | the note a reader sees, a draft naming its model until a person confirms it in bun run cat narratives | . The file is authored, so a re-ingest keeps it. An extraction defect (garbled OCR, a block cut in the wrong place) is not an erratum: re-derive the entry. Decisions about a document (personal data in a participant list, a “do not distribute” notice) are not errata either; ask the owner. check:l1-complete reports errata (errata) and fails only on a file that does not parse, names another entry, or points at a block the entry does not have.

67793c4129ad.title: What a complete L1 entry holds
67793c4129ad.content: library/<bib-slug>/ structure.json "$schema": "pdf-structure/v1" — doc_id, toc_source, granularity, sections[], structure_note, source{} (see below; source.text_source says embedded|ocr) sections/ one Markdown file per section, front matter + body blocks/ the block projection consumers read manifest.jsonld @id, @type folio:SourceDocument, contains[], provenance summaries.json agent summaries of prose blocks, a QA sidecar (see below) footnotes.json footnotes and the marks that call them (pdf-footnotes.py arm) errata.json errors in the source's own text, authored (never a rung's) images.json raster images and their role (figure | decorative | ...) vector-figures.json drawn figures rendered to figures/vfig-pNNN.png tabular.csvw.json transcribed tables (CSVW) and tables/*.csv extraction.json "$schema": "folio-library-extraction/v1" — what each kind's step found (see "Every kind says what was extracted") ocr/ page-NNN.txt, only where the source was scanned . Every kind says what was extracted . Owner, 2026-11-14, on a one-page notice whose page showed no references and no glossary: “why no biblio, glossary, etc here”. A blank says nothing: “none in the source”, “not extracted yet” and “never looked” all look the same. So every entry records, per kind — contents, sections, figures, tables, references, glossary, footnotes, summaries — one of: . | state | means | . | found (+ count) | the step ran and kept N | . | partial | fewer kept than the text declares (e.g. 15 figures captioned, 3 kept), or sections split per page rather than by heading | . | none | the step ran and the source has none — never written for a step that did not run | . | not-extracted | the step has not run for this entry | . The ingest writes extraction.json: {"$schema":"folio-library-extraction/v1","kinds":{"<kind>":{"state","count"?,"note"?,"tool"?,"version"?,"at"?}}}. The library viewer’s What was extracted line reads it and, for any kind it does not name, derives the state from the files present (entryCoverage in cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/library-document.ts). A check:l1-complete pass is not this. The gate checks the files an entry must hold; it does not check headings, captions, tables, references, glossary or figure blocks. An entry can pass the gate and still be page-granular with fifteen figures nobody can see — 205 of who-iris’s 211 entries passed while 89 were split per page (audit, 2026-11-14). When an entry needs re-ingesting — and how it is done . Re-ingest an entry when any of these holds; each is visible on its page: . | granularity: page on a born-digital PDF (sections are “Page 1…N”, the Contents tree is flat) — the current pdf-structure.py may now trust an inferred contents the older run refused; | figures captioned in the text but none kept, or vector figures kept but no figure blocks (they are invisible to the knowledge graph); | a references or glossary heading in the text but its entries not extracted; | tables captioned but none transcribed. | . The order is fixed (owner’s card, 2026-11-14): fix the tools first, re-ingest a pilot of about three entries, check them on their pages, then batch. Re-ingesting writes new derived files; the source PDF is frozen evidence and is never edited. Re-splitting a page-granular entry makes its block summaries stale: they are kept and marked stale, English is redrafted in the batch, and the other five languages are left to the summary drain. bun run cat check:l1-complete is the gate. It reports three states, never two: a requirement met, unmet, or not yet derivable — the last because the per-format arms (images, audio, tables, archives) are tracked separately and a check that cannot run must not read as a pass. Then publish its statements. Once the entry is complete and promoted, every statement extracted from it is published in the folio’s working artifact and in the shared extraction viewer, each linked to the entry and its section, and CI keeps those pages current. That is a standard step, the same for every content type: publish-extracted-statements.

32778529b3d0.title: A manifest’s title — the authority order, and never the page-1 parse
32778529b3d0.content: A library entry’s manifest.jsonld title is the first of these the entry has: . | rank | meta.title_source | read from | . | 1 | dc-record | dc.title of the Dublin Core record that the catalogue node naming this entry (libraryId) points at through metadataRef | . | 2 | referenced | referenced.json identity.title | . | 3 | pdf-info | structure.json metadata.docinfo.Title, the PDF Info /Title, when it is not junk | . | 3 | text-heading | structure.json metadata.title of a text or notebook structure: front-matter title:, --title, or the level-1 heading | . | 4 | slug | the entry id. Nothing better exists, and check:library-qa reports it as title-missing | . The page-1 front-matter parse is NEVER a title. On a pdf-structure/v1, metadata.title is parse_front_matter’s guess at which lines of page 1 are the title, and it guesses wrong (a running head, a repeated word, a status block). A plausible wrong title passes every check that has no second source. A slug is honest about being a placeholder and gets flagged. The parse may still feed search and the section files’ doc_title. text-heading shares rank 3 because it is the same kind of fact as /Title (the source naming itself, in its format’s own metadata). The two are exclusive by variant, so no entry ever has both. A tabular record’s title is its source file name, which is never a title. Junk /Title (pdfInfoTitleJunk): shorter than 3 characters or no letters; untitled and its kin; Microsoft Word - …; an arXiv stamp (arXiv:0909.4061v2 [math.NA] …); anything ending in a file extension; the source’s file name or stem; the slug. A junk value falls through to the next source. It never becomes the title. Records (ranks 1–2) are taken as written, because a cataloguer’s choice is not a program’s default. Record the Info dictionary at ingest. pdf-structure.py and pdf-pages.py write metadata.docinfo. Backfill an older entry with python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-pages.py --docinfo-into <entry> <pdf>. It refuses unless the PDF’s sha256 is the one the entry recorded. One resolver, cat-harness-tools/pipeline/library-title.ts (resolveLibraryTitle, TITLE_AUTHORITY), is used by both gen-library-jsonld.ts and check-library-qa.ts. The manifest records meta.title_source and meta.title_from, and the QA check re-derives the order from the entry’s files. So a manifest that claims pdf-info while a catalogue record exists is reported as title-implausible, not believed.

cd49b3328c10.title: source{} — the technical facts, written by whichever rung ran
cd49b3328c10.content: Every rung writes source on structure.json, from the single definition in scripts/_tech_meta.py: file, full 64-hex sha256, bytes, mtime (the SOURCE’s, UTC to the second — not the ingest time, because what tells you a re-fetch got something new is the file changing), mimetype_sniffed and mimetype_source. Both rungs add text_source, embedded or ocr: ONE field and ONE vocabulary for where the section text came from. pdf-structure also adds pages and extractor. The mimetype is sniffed from the leading bytes and never falls back to the extension. An extension is a claim by whoever named the file; the magic bytes are what the content is, and a .pdf that is really an HTML error page extracts to nothing while every downstream verdict is about the wrong document. Unrecognised bytes give mimetype_sniffed: null with mimetype_source: "unrecognised": a guess that agrees with the filename is indistinguishable from a real sniff. bun run scripts/ingest-document.ts <pdf> --refresh-meta backfills an existing entry. It reads the indent off the file rather than choosing one: the two rungs write at different widths, and hardcoding either reformats every entry the other authored.

0fc3ff676bc8.title: provenance — who wrote it, and the closed union that makes omission impossible
0fc3ff676bc8.content: Every block declares how its text came to be. The vocabulary is schemas/attribution.ts, and it is closed: . | the literal "ingested" — verbatim source text. There is no author to name; the document it came out of is recorded by source{} above. | an Attribution — kind (script | agent | human), id, and optionally version, model, session, date, skill. | . An agent must name its model, structurally. “A model described it, version X” is what a reader needs to weigh a narrative, and what makes the set re-generatable when that model is superseded, so AttributionSchema refuses an agent attribution with no model. The vocabulary is the QA reviewer’s, not a second one. block-qa.ts re-exports ATTRIBUTION_KINDS as QA_REVIEWER_KINDS; the same three participants review and author. What is not shared is QaReviewer itself, most of which is about whether a criterion’s cached verdict is stale. What the gate can and cannot enforce . check:l1-complete checks two things per block, and the second is the point: . | provenance parses as a Provenance. An open string, a malformed attribution, an agent with no model — all unmet. | A block of an authored kind must not claim "ingested". | . LIBRARY_BLOCK_ORIGIN classifies each library block kind as extracted or authored, and a test asserts it is total over what actually occurs in library/ — so a narrative arm cannot land a new kind without classifying it, and classifying one authored arms requirement 2 immediately. Closing the union does not stop an arm asserting something false. It makes the omission impossible: a new arm has to choose, and choosing "ingested" for a generated description is a false statement rather than a missing field.
