A zero narrative count is reported, never silent. The authored branch is proved to fire by fixtures in scripts/tests/attribution.test.ts, not by the corpus, and each of the three branches is mutation-checked — removing it fails a named test.

0bdf19c3ee9b.title: Archives — the entry list is data, and the rung is chosen by CONTENT
0bdf19c3ee9b.content: A tar or zip in uploads/ is opaque to every grep in the corpus: a search for a filename inside one finds nothing, and that absence is indistinguishable from the file not being there. scripts/archive-contents.py writes library/<slug>/contents.jsonld — one schema whatever the container (schemas/archive-contents.ts), so a consumer reads archives without knowing whether it was tar or zip. Per entry: path, bytes, sha256, mtime, mimetype_sniffed, mimetype_source — the source{} vocabulary above, reused verbatim, because an archive entry is not a different kind of thing from a loose file. The mimetype is sniffed from the entry’s own leading bytes, never from its name, for the same reason it is outside an archive. Four entry states, not two: a directory carries no size and no digest (a zero would be a measurement nobody made); an unreadable member is mimetype_source: "unreadable", which is not an empty file; a symlink or special is listed with its kind rather than dropped. Dropping directories would make an archive of empty ones indistinguishable from an empty archive. A file the sniffer does not recognise as an archive is refused — an empty entries[] would read as an empty archive, a different fact. The rung is chosen before anything opens the file as a PDF . planFor sniffs first, so a zip is never reported as a PDF with a missing backend. A file named .pdf that is really a zip takes the archive rung, which is the case only a sniff can decide. What the gate checks, and the determined zero . Which entries the requirement applies to is derived, not guessed: source. mimetype_sniffed is already on every entry, so “this came from a zip” is a recorded fact. An archive entry must carry a contents.jsonld that validates against the declared schema. An entry that is not an archive reports not an archive (<mimetype>) — said out loud rather than passed in silence, because “nothing to check here” and “the check never ran” are different facts. The requirement is proved to fire by fixture archives built in scripts/tests/archive-contents.test.ts, and each of its four branches is mutation-checked.

221de78efbdf.title: Datasets — findable by their headers, and the narrative nobody wrote
221de78efbdf.content: scripts/tabular-records.py writes library/<slug>/tabular.jsonld: sheet names, the header row, and the shape of each sheet. header_vocabulary is the union across sheets, and it is the field a grep for a column name lands in — without it a dataset is stored but not findable, and a failed search is indistinguishable from the dataset not having that column. The record is real JSON-LD, and so is contents.jsonld. Both arms emit the published content context (the URL lives once, in scripts/_content_context.py, pinned to CONTENT_CONTEXT_URL by a test), and every key is a declared term. The facts a consumer queries across documents — format, the counts, header_vocabulary — are real terms; the nested structures that are ours — sheets, entries, the technical metadata, the narrative — are @json literals, because that is how their nulls survive: rows: null means “could not be counted” and narrative.text: null means “nobody has written one”, and JSON-LD drops a null anywhere else. The schemas still accept an older record with no @context, since folio repositories hold them. Stdlib only (zipfile + xml.etree, csv). This repository declares no Python dependencies — no requirements.txt, and CI installs only ruff — so a tool needing openpyxl would pass locally and fail there. Everything this arm needs is in xl/workbook.xml and each sheet’s <dimension>. The narrative is a state machine — drafted by an agent, confirmed by a person . cat-harness-tools schemas/content/narrative.ts: not-authored → draft → confirmed, with rejected as a real fourth state. Two attributions, because they are two acts. drafted_by is who wrote the words; confirmed_by is who accepted them. The question a reader most wants answered is not “did a machine touch this” but “has a person agreed to it”. An agent cannot confirm its own draft — confirmed_by.kind must be "human", structurally. Without that, confirmed degrades into “an agent said so twice”. But a rule about who may act cannot be enforced by a rule about what is written. In an agent container git config user.name is the agent’s, so the CLI could record the agent as a human reviewer and the schema could not see it. reviewer() therefore refuses outside a terminal: a person confirming at a prompt has one, an agent’s subprocess and CI do not. This stops accident, not fraud — it makes it impossible to confirm a narrative while going about other work. rejected keeps its reasons. A rejected draft silently re-offered wastes the reviewer’s time; one that vanishes lets the next agent redraft the identical thing. Reviewing: bun run cat narratives . Numbered list, numbered reasons: a review step that demands a typed sentence is one that will not happen, and then confirmed means “nobody got round to objecting”. bun run cat narratives # what is waiting on you bun run cat narratives:confirm 1 bun run cat narratives:reject 1 --why 2 # or --why-text "..." . check:l1-complete’s narrative-review validates every narrative-bearing file. A draft is reported, not failed: it is work waiting on a person, and failing it would make an unreviewed queue indistinguishable from a broken arm. A null rows/columns is likewise not an empty sheet: shape_source says whether the shape was read, counted, or undetermined. Summarising prose blocks — a QA sidecar, drained slowly . The block stays verbatim. A prose block is the source’s text, provenance: "ingested", and re-ingestion regenerates it. A summary is an agent’s account of that text, so it lives beside the blocks in library/<slug>/summaries.json (folio-block-summaries/v1, schemas/block-summary.ts): one record per block, holding block, source (the section file), source_hash and a narrative. That narrative is the state machine above, not a second one: draft, confirmed by a person only, rejected with a reason, and an agent author must name its model. source_hash makes a changed source read as STALE. It is the sha256 of the section text the summariser was shown (proseBody). Re-ingest a document and any section whose text moved puts its summary back in the queue, marked stale. bun run cat narratives shows it and refuses to confirm it. The queue is derived, so nothing enqueues. Every prose block in every declared library is in it until it has a current draft or confirmation. A rejected draft is back in it, and its rejection reason travels with it. bun run cat summaries # the backlog, per entry bun run cat summaries:next -- --n 5 [--entry <slug>] # next K blocks WITH their text, as JSON bun run cat summaries:record -- drafts.json # write drafts; validated, all or nothing . drafts.json is {drafted_by: {kind: "agent", id, model, session}, drafted_at, lang?, drafts: [{block, source_hash, text, lang?}]}, with source_hash echoed from summaries:next. lang is a BCP 47 tag and defaults to en. record refuses a state other than draft, a hash that no longer matches, and a block that already has a current summary IN THAT LANGUAGE. A draft in a language the block does not have yet is added beside the others, which are kept unchanged. Drain K at a time during ingestion work, not all at once: a thousand unreviewed drafts at once is a buried reviewer. Write in your own words, from the block’s text only, adding nothing from outside it. Length scales with the source: . | source text | summary | . | under ~150 words | 1 short sentence | . | ~150–600 words | 2 sentences, short to medium | . | ~600–2,000 words | 3 medium sentences | . | over ~2,000 words | 4 sentences, medium to long | . If the extraction put the wrong text under a heading, summarise what is there and say so. The backlog is reported by check:l1-complete (block-summaries) and on the library page. It is advisory, never a gate. What the gate does fail is a sidecar that does not parse, names another entry, or holds a record for a block or source that is not there. Special pages get one sentence saying what the page is: a cover, title page, copyright or cataloguing page, a blank or near-blank page, a table of contents, an index, a reference list. Garbled OCR, text in the wrong script, or text that does not match the block’s title is summarised as far as it can be, and the summary says so (“the extracted text of this page is garbled OCR; it appears to be a table of …”), so a reviewer sees an extraction defect instead of a confident account of noise. A block too long to read whole (a whole book extracted as one block) is summarised from its start, its headings and its end, at the 4-sentence length, and the scope is taken from the headings. Report the block as an extraction defect: it should have been split. Summaries in every language . A block’s summary is owed in every configured language: the layer’s translation.supportedLocales, which defaults to the six UN languages (ar, zh, en, fr, ru, es) (owner, 2026-11-11). The slot holds one narrative per language, each reviewed separately in bun run cat narratives. The order is: . | English first, from the block’s text, as above. | The document’s own language, when it is not English, also written FROM THE SOURCE TEXT, not from the English. It uses the document’s own terminology and checks the English against the source; when the two disagree, the source wins and the English draft is reported for redrafting. An edition in a language outside the configured set (Portuguese, Persian…) still gets one in its own language. | Every other configured language, translated from the current summary, as below. | . bun run cat summaries # also prints the translations owed, per language bun run cat summaries:next -- --lang fr --n 50 [--entry <slug>] # summarised blocks with no fr summary, WITH their current summaries bun run cat summaries:record -- drafts-fr.json # drafts carry lang: "fr" . check:l1-complete reports the missing languages in its block-summaries detail. Like the summary backlog, it is advisory. Translating a summary . Say the same thing, in the same length. Translate the current summary faithfully and naturally: nothing added, nothing dropped, and its notes kept (garbled text, blank pages, a figure that does not match). It is a translation of the summary, never a new summary of the block. Use WHO’s established terms in the target language (ВОЗ, منظمة الصحة العالمية, 世界卫生组织, OMS; World Health Assembly as each language’s official name). Proper names, test and drug names (Xpert MTB/RIF, PrEP) and document codes (A42/10, EB95/8) stay as written. A title with no official translation stays in its original language. Use the target’s own conventions: decimal commas in fr, es and ru, logical-order Unicode for Arabic and Persian (Persian letters ی and ک), Simplified Chinese with full-width punctuation. Check before recording: every block and source_hash copied exactly, the text is in the target script, and it is not the source summary unchanged. Record one language per file: record refuses the same block twice in one file. The Document panel — what a reader browses . Every entry carrying a structure.json gets a Document panel in the library viewer, built from the ingestion schema by cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/library-document.ts and published as assets/library/entries/<id>.doc.json (folio-library-document/v1) by bun run cat library:viz. Tabs: Contents (the TOC as a tree, collapsed below the first level that branches, each inferred entry’s confidence, linking to its section), Pages (physical page, printed label, sections starting, figures), Figures & tables, Sections (the summary, else an extract — the section’s own opening text, labelled as such and cut at a word), Checks (contents vs body, numbering gaps, page-label conflicts). Because it reads the schema, a new field in structure.json reaches every library at once; a field an older ingestion lacks shows “not recorded — re-ingest”, never an empty table. Above the tabs: the entry’s own listing row (the same columns the whole library shows) and the What was extracted line. Figures are a list, one per row: a lazy thumbnail, a short name taken from the description’s own “Fig. n, ‘Title’”, and the page; selecting the thumbnail opens it large with its description (owner, 2026-11-14). Block summaries sit behind a disclosure labelled with their state, so an unconfirmed agent draft is readable and still says it is one. Printing loads everything first (owner, 2026-11-14: “make sure printing loads all of the content before it renders the PDF”): the panel’s Print / PDF button and the browser’s own print both switch lazy images to eager and wait for them, write each figure’s description under it, and open the contents tree and every disclosure. For a withheld entry the panel keeps structure, page labels, figure and table captions (labels, like TOC titles) and our summaries, and omits only section body extracts. Keywords — from the LSI weights, per section and per document . Keywords are extracted content, so they never live in the ingest record (cat-harness#1144). bun run cat library:keywords builds them at publish into the derived keywords graph: one folio-keywords/v2 JSON-LD node per entry under the site’s assets/keywords/<instance>/<slug>.jsonld, with an index.json beside them. Nothing is written inside library/<slug>/; the route is declared builtAtPublish, and derive:publish runs the writer. Up to 12 for the document and up to 8 per section, fewer for a short section (one per ~20 content tokens, at least 3). Each node holds six variants side by side, so they can be compared: . | Variant | Method | Weighting | Terms scored | . | lsi-log-entropy-surface (default) | lsi | log-entropy | the words the text uses | . | lsi-tfidf-surface | lsi | tf-idf | the words the text uses | . | lsi-log-entropy-latent | lsi | log-entropy | latent scores, any term of the library | . | lsi-tfidf-latent | lsi | tf-idf | latent scores, any term of the library | . | lsi-log-entropy-latent-rerank | lsi | log-entropy | latent scores, only the words the text or its headings use | . | ca-latent | correspondence-analysis | raw counts | latent scores, any term of the library | . The default is read from the same log-entropy matrix the LSI index is built from (keywordsOf in pipeline/lsi.ts), so a keyword means “frequent here, rare across this library” exactly as the index does. A latent variant scores terms by the rank-k reconstruction (k = 100), so it can propose a term the text never uses (synonymy, Deerwester et al. 1990); it scores the top 300 candidates. Correspondence analysis tends to favour rare proper names (authors, publishers), which the comparison shows. The Document panel computes the default variant in memory and shows it as chips, green where a heading also names the term (evidence: ["heading"]): the document saying it of itself. Withheld entries show them: they are derived terms, like captions, not the text. The library-keywords check in bun run cat health reports entries without keywords and any legacy keywords.json still committed. What the scoring does: . | Two-word phrases from truly adjacent tokens said at least twice; a stop word, punctuation, or a line break before a capital (a table cell, a heading) breaks the run — “Development” over “Systematic review team” is two cells, not “development systematic”. | A word said once in a text of 100+ tokens is not a keyword, unless the section’s heading names it; heading-named terms score double. | Generic words the index keeps but that say nothing about a topic (“anyone”, “aims”, “take”, “-ly” adverbs) are excluded from keywords only. | Plurals fold: “evidence reviews” does not follow “evidence review”. | . Limits: no part-of-speech tagging, so a rare verb can still surface in a short section; a library of fewer than 3 sections gets none. A WITHHELD entry in the viewer — its summary, else the gate, never “no content” . An entry whose library root’s withheld.json names it is listed but publishes no verbatim text: gen-library-viz reads its blocks with verbatim: false. “Not ours to show” must not look like “nothing was extracted”: . | A row shows the section’s summary when one exists, labelled as a summary and never as the source text. Summaries are our writing and stay published. | Otherwise, a withheld row says the gate: “Withheld — copyright not granted”, naming every gate that refused (“copyright and restrictions not granted”), with a link to the catalogue record — its published page first, its upstream URI second, no link rather than a guessed one. | Anything else with no content keeps the neutral “(no content carried)”, because for those it is true. | A banner tops a withheld entry: why the text is not shown, which gate refused, the record link, and how many sections have summaries (“0 of 121 sections summarised”). No banner on any other entry. | . Withheld is READ, never inferred from emptiness. The flag, the gates and the record come from withheld.json — folio-withheld/v1 carries an optional structured gates[] and record{id, page, uri} beside the reason sentence, which the layer’s generator writes from its own data (the IRIS catalogue: gen-iris-pages.ts, from the catalogue’s publication gates). A list that carries only the sentence still works: the row then says the sentence. The row and banner code is scripts/lib/library-withheld-view.ts, embedded in the page verbatim so library-withheld-view.test.ts runs the same text the browser does; library-withheld-viewer.e2e.ts opens the rendered page. Drafting the summaries is a separate backlog: bun run cat summaries:next -- --entry <slug> serves a withheld entry’s text to the summariser like any other. Describing a document’s images — and why it is an ARM, not a step you run . pdf-images.py classifies by geometry, which answers exactly one question: is this image the whole page, or something on it. It cannot tell a logo from a chart. The finer roles come from LOOKING, and that judgement is data — <library>/image-verdicts.json, one entry per image, reviewable line by line. bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.pdf --library <lib> # stage; reports what is unmet # look at ingest-staging/<doc-id>/images/, write the verdicts into # <lib>/image-verdicts.json, then: bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.pdf --library <lib> # re-stage: the arm applies them bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.pdf --library <lib> --promote . Re-running ingest is the second step, not a separate apply command. --promote refuses an entry whose image-descriptions requirement is unmet, and the stand-alone narrative writers (apply-image-verdicts.ts, narratives.ts) resolve their targets through directoriesForGraph(root, "library"), i.e. only in promoted libraries. Applying the verdicts as an arm in staging is what lets a document be both described and promoted. Applying by hand works exactly once. pdf-images.py opens the sidecar with "w" — no existence check, no merge — so the next ingest overwrites the descriptions, and overwrites them quietly: the file still parses and still validates, it simply has no narratives in it any more. Running the application as the fourth arm, after pdf-images.py, makes a re-run RE-APPLY instead — the sidecar is rebuilt from the PDF and the committed judgement is laid back over it. --staging <entry-dir> --library <lib-dir> is available directly if you need it, and --library is required: a staging directory does not say which library a document is being promoted into (a queue does not determine a library). An absent verdicts file exits 0, because the first ingest necessarily runs before anybody has looked at the images; image-descriptions is the gate that refuses, not that script. An orphaned verdict — one naming an image the sidecar does not have — still fails, in either mode. Every narrative it writes lands as draft. Only a person confirms one. A role threshold is OPTIONAL, and its default is NONE . A coverage cutoff may sort images into roles (figure vs furniture) only when a caller supplies one. | By default nothing is thresholded. With no value supplied, every role call comes from an inspection verdict as above, naming who looked. | A caller may supply one. An image whose role it decides must record that basis: the value, and that the value was caller-supplied rather than inspected. A thresholded role must never be readable as an inspected one. | Ship no number. No config default, and no value in docs, tests or examples presented as recommended. Per-image coverage does not separate the classes, and a cutoff placed in one corpus’s empty stretch is fitted to that corpus and says nothing about others. | . Reading a figure: the text layer is not the figure . Two traps, both of which produce a wrong description: . A diverging axis’s SIGN cannot be read from the text layer. get_text returned 0.2 0.4 0.6 below the zero of a Delta Pass Rate bar with no sign at any codepoint — matplotlib draws U+2212 as a vector path, so the minus exists in the rendering and not in the text. Rendering the region showed -0.2 -0.4 -0.6 plainly. A verdict trusting the extraction would have called a -0.6 endpoint +0.6. And the direction is a fact about the axis, not about the colours. The recorded inspection said a bar ran “blue low to red high”. Its ticks said Pass Rate, 1.0 at the top in dark blue: blue was HIGH. A reader given the original sentence reads every heatmap in the paper inverted — worse than no description, because a missing one is visibly missing. So: render the region and read the ticks. Two images that look alike need the same check each: a third “repeated legend” can be a different, signed scale. The figure that is DRAWN — pdf-vector-labels.py, the other arm . pdf-images.py answers “what does this page PLACE”. A WHO conceptual figure — a framework, a maturity model, a taxonomy, a process flow — is drawn in path operators and text, so it places nothing, and the raster arm is silent about it truthfully. 9789240120747-eng declares six captioned figures, places zero images, and image-descriptions reported “0 image(s), 0 describable and all described” over it: a determined empty that is true about raster and misleading about figures. The vector arm runs beside the raster one in withDerivedArms and writes vector-labels.json — every positioned text line on a page that declares a figure, with its rectangle in the visible frame, its fonts and sizes, and whether it intersects a drawing. Read the sidecar, not a count. Three things it deliberately does not do: . | It does not say which labels belong to the figure. intersectsDrawing is recorded and never filtered on. On 9789240120747-eng page 34 it separates perfectly; on 9789240010567-eng page 25 it is false for thirty labels that are plainly figure content, because they sit in the white space between the drawn boxes. | It does not group above the MuPDF LINE. A block on that same page holds six circled numerals 200 pt apart across three different diagrams. | It does not compare its counts to anything. Declared figures and recovered labels are not commensurable. | . So when you describe such a figure, the labels are your evidence and the grouping is your judgement — which is the same split as image-verdicts.json, one level over. The rule from the section above holds here with more force, not less: render the page and look at it. The arm recovers what the text layer says; it cannot tell you that the arrows run clockwise. The determined empty is still meaningful: who-rhr-1806-eng records zero pages because it contains no Fig. or Figure mention at all. A document with no text layer returns pages: null with a reason instead — the one place this arm could otherwise report a clean run over an unread scan. An .xlsx IS a zip — ask the container . The magic bytes of an OOXML or ODF document say application/zip, which is true and useless: it would send every spreadsheet to the archive rung to be listed as a bag of XML parts. The magic cannot tell them apart, so _tech_meta.sniff_zip_package asks the container, which declares itself — OOXML by [Content_Types].xml plus the part names, ODF by its mimetype member. Same principle as the byte sniff, one level in. sniff_effective_mimetype is the single answer the router (planFor) and the recorder both ask, so they cannot disagree. A CSV has no magic bytes at all, so routing one cannot be a sniff and must not become an extension guess. is_tabular_text asks the only content question available: do the first rows split into the same number of fields, more than one? Prose, a single column and anything ragged all answer no — a one-column “table” is indistinguishable from a list of lines. Proved on fixtures built at test time, all five branches mutation-checked.

edf34805628c.doc: L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph
edf34805628c.title: Steps
edf34805628c.content: Every one of the 16 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Basic ingestion (harness)CallActivity_Basic | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/library-ingestion | The harness’s document-ingestion.bpmn: accept the upload by a declared route, extract its metadata into the KG, and catalogue the asset in library/ — placed if materialized, recorded as referenced if not. Everything below refines that result for a document. Called, not copied. | . | Detect media type, mint a doc idTask_Detect | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Sniff the media type rather than trusting the extension, and mint the doc id from the page-1 arXiv stamp where there is one, else from the filename. | . | Establish the licence from the uploadTask_Licence | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | EARLY: before any derivation, because library/ is holds: content and anything derived first is committed, so refusing it later is a deletion nobody may take unasked. This step sees only the upload itself — the licence recorded in its intake.json (the same stated / unknown record a library manifest carries) and whether a LICENSE file sits beside it. It never infers a licence from extracted text. The verdict is stated, unknown, or UNDETERMINED, and undetermined is never reported as cleared: the pipeline proceeds and says so, because a licence that only extraction can reveal is a later check’s to find. | . | Extract structureCallActivity_Extract | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Ingestion subprocess — extract structuredocument-intake | See ingest-extract-structure.bpmn. | . | Derive content from the assetsCallActivity_Derive | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assetsdocument-intake | See ingest-derive-content.bpmn. Most of this subprocess is not implemented yet. | . | Ingest the themeCallActivity_IngestTheme | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Ingestion subprocess — ingest a themetheme-art-intake | See ingest-theme.bpmn. The subprocess derives one Theme node with kind sticky|webpage|publication, and refuses a source it cannot complete rather than emitting a partial theme. | . | Open the beanCall_BeanOpen | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Open the beanbean-coordination | Process_BeanOpen: check before you create, find out whose the bean is, and claim it — or leave it alone when it is someone else’s. The one place a claim is drawn; the gateway after this reads which end it reached. | . | Close the beanCall_BeanClose | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Close the beantodo-manager | Process_BeanClose: end the bean in a state that says why — complete and archive it, scrap it with its reasons and archive it, or record the blocker and hand it back. The one place resolve and archive are drawn; placed straight before the end so the engine’s resolve sees nothing left but the archive step. | . | Build the L1 knowledge graphCallActivity_BuildKg | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graphdocument-intake | See ingest-build-l1-kg.bpmn. | . | L1 completeness gateCallActivity_Gate | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gatel1-document-ingestion | See ingest-l1-completeness-gate.bpmn.Skill-backed by l1-document-ingestion: its section“What a complete L1 entry holds” names check:l1-complete as the gate andstates its three results.The gate contains one adjudication (Task_FlagDrift: real, spurious or source-wrong), and its own Task_Verdict records the answer as a reason against the verdict before returning. So both answers reach this step, and nothing here branches on them; Gateway_Complete branches on the gate’s completeness verdict instead. | . | Record the gap as a beanTask_OpenBean | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | todo-manager | A missing derived artefact is a tracked gap, not a silent omission. The document stays in uploads/ until the gap closes. | . | **Move into library//**`Task_Promote` | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | The folder name IS the bibliography citation key, so a citation and a directory are the same string. | . | Publish the extracted statementsCallActivity_PublishStatements | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Publish extracted statements with source linkspublish-extracted-statements | THE ENTRY IS COMPLETE HERE, so its statements are published here. Every statement the extraction captured from this entry (a recommendation, a requirement, a candidate a person still has to rule on) becomes readable in two places: the folio’s working artifact, in the pages its content profile renders, and the shared extraction viewer. Each one links back to the library entry and to the section it came from.WHY IN INGESTION AND NOT LATER. A statement nobody can read beside its source is reviewed from memory, or not at all. Publishing when the entry is promoted means a reviewer can check every extracted statement against its source the moment it exists.The sub-process is the same for every content type. The content type decides only how its pages look, through its adapter. An entry that yields no statements (a referenced source, a dataset) passes through it with nothing to publish, and says so. | . | Summarise prose blocks, in every languageTask_SummaryQueue | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | l1-document-ingestion | A QA sidecar of general document ingestion, drained slowly.Nothing is written to ENQUEUE a block: the queue is derived (every prose block in every declared library, minus those whose summaries.json record is a current draft or confirmation), so a promoted entry is in it the moment its blocks are. A re-ingested document whose text changed re-enters it on its own, because the record’s source_hash no longer matches.What an agent doing ingestion work does here is DRAIN a few: bun run cat summaries:next -- --n K hands it the next K blocks with their text, it writes a short summary of each in its own words, and bun run cat summaries:record writes them into library/<bib-slug>/summaries.json as drafts naming the agent and its model. The block itself stays verbatim and ingested.A library can ask for a summary in more than one language (the six UN languages for a WHO publications library, owner 2026-11-11): the English draft, one in the document’s own language read from the source, and translations of the English into the rest, each its own narrative in the block’s slot. Method: skill l1-document-ingestion, “Summarising prose blocks”.ADVISORY, never a gate: this step does not hold up Task_Citeable, and check:l1-complete reports the backlog (block-summaries) without failing on it. Confirming or rejecting a draft is a person’s act, in bun run cat narratives. | . | Record errata in the source’s own textTask_Errata | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | l1-document-ingestion | Owner, 2026-11-11 (card Q-ODD-1 = A, and “add to L1 doc schema errata”). Reading the blocks to summarise them finds errors that are in the publication itself, not in the extraction: a title that says June 2006 over an introduction that says June 2005, a Spanish edition announcing nine recommendations where the English lists ten. The block stays as printed. The agent records an erratum in library/<bib-slug>/errata.json (folio-document-errata/v1): the kind, the block or page, the words as printed, the reading the evidence supports, the evidence, and its note as a draft narrative a person confirms in bun run cat narratives. An extraction defect is not an erratum: it is fixed by re-deriving the entry. ADVISORY: check:l1-complete reports errata and fails only on a file that does not mean what it says. Method: skill l1-document-ingestion, “Errata: errors in the source’s own text”. | . | Available to cite as an L1 sourceTask_Citeable | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Every knowledge-graph reference to this source now resolves through library/. Authoring and review consume it from here – see authoring-a-document.bpmn. | .

23912e88721a.title: Library ingestion — the basic flow
23912e88721a.content: Skill library-ingestion: The BASIC ingestion flow every asset takes: an upload is accepted, its metadata goes into the knowledge graph, and the asset lands in library/<slug>/ if it is materialized. The two entry points (a drop in uploads/, or materializing an asset a remote graph lists), what happens to the upload afterwards, and why content-type methods refine this flow from above rather than living in it. Command: bun run cat ingest. Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Public comment on a review draft, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Publish extracted statements with source links . uploads/ and library/ are two stages of one pipeline. uploads/ is the incoming queue — raw files as dropped, not L1 and not greppable as corpus. library/<slug>/ is where an ingested asset lives, and every knowledge-graph reference to a source resolves through it. Why that bites: the corpus-grep checklist searches library/ only, so a file still in uploads/ makes a clean grep mean “nobody has done this” when the source is right there. That is how a held result gets re-derived.

c79628ce9027.title: The flow — four steps, and no content-type decision
c79628ce9027.content: cat-harness holds only the basic, high-level ingestion workflow, with very little process context assumed: the uploaded asset’s extracted metadata goes into the KG, and the asset into library/ if materialized. library/processes/document-ingestion.bpmn (Process_Ingestion) is that flow, executable: . | Accept — the bytes reach the declared uploads/ queue by a declared route (upload-routes; names per upload-naming; arrival noticed by uploads-watch). | Extract metadata into the KG — asset-extraction: a container’s INDEX goes in, its contents do not unless asked for. | Materialized? — the state vocabulary is schemas/kg/materialization-state.ts: referenced, materialized or unknown, with no default. | Place in library/<slug>/ — this skill. A referenced asset is still catalogued: its record says where the bytes are and that we hold none. | . The flow calls no subprocess and decides nothing about content type. Which reader a PDF needs, what a complete L1 entry holds, how images or datasets are described — those are refinements, and they live in a layer above this one. The mechanism is inversion: a higher-layer process CALLS Process_Ingestion as its first step and continues with its own work. Nothing here names a refinement, because there is no BPMN extension point in the corpus and a harness process naming a higher one would be an upward edge. methodology-from-source.bpmn’s Call_Ingest is a harness caller of the same flow.

998ab43f006c.title: TWO entry points
998ab43f006c.content: Things enter the library through uploads/ → library/ document ingestion, or through materializing an asset listed in an external KG that a dependent harness declares. |   | drop | materialize | . | the source is | a file somebody put in uploads/ | an asset listed in a remote graph a dependency declares | . | decided first | how it is read (a refinement’s choice) | the five gates, and a purpose | . | entry | bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE | materialize-remote.bpmn | . Neither is a shortcut past the other. A materialized asset still arrives as bytes that have to be read, so it re-enters at exactly the point a dropped file does. Materialization adds what happens before there is a file: may we hold it, what does holding it cost, for what purpose, and what if the source goes away. Entry one is bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE (--dry-run says what it would do, and why). Entry two starts from remoteGraphs in a layer’s declaration (schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts, RemoteGraph): assets listed there are referenced — we know they exist and where, and hold none. materialize-remote.bpmn asks purpose (working or archival), then the five gates, then fetches; the asset lands in library/ with its provenance and fixity, and a refusal leaves the node referenced rather than failing. A reference is not a fetch: the KG viewer follows a remote graph to show its hierarchy without materialising anything — navigable without being held. Who owns which half . | This layer owns the basic flow and the reading CODE — the pdf-* rungs, ingest-document.ts, notebook-structure.ts. Reading bytes is platform work, and OCR stays here. The method that chooses among them is a refinement above. The flow itself cannot move up: uploads and library are graph typologies this layer declares, and a flow above would make the harness’s own library writable only from a layer above it — a wrong-direction, and circular, dependency. | The remote half’s gates belong to the content layer above. Only the state vocabulary lives here; the five gates, the purposes and the record binding them stay with the layer that owns content, because each gate is a decision about content. A harness that cannot hold content must not own the vocabulary for deciding to acquire it. | The large-datasets package owns the question before both (library/skills/large-datasets/): how to enumerate a corpus and ask it for a subset (source-descriptor.ts). Neither entry point can start until something says what is out there. | Further down the tree, a dependency’s declared remoteGraphs is what makes the second path reachable at all, inherited the way directories are. | .

534b309d8abb.title: A held PDF gets its page-1 cover BEFORE the upload is retired
534b309d8abb.content: The picture of a PDF entry is library/<slug>/cover.png, page 1 rendered by pdf-cover.py — never its first figure, which can be any picture from deep in the document. With no cover, the entry shows the book glyph. | A new ingest writes it: ingest-document’s cover arm runs last. | An entry without one gets it from bun run cat library:covers. Run it in the checkout that holds the PDF (the composed index, whose uploads/ may be another repository’s), and commit the cover into the repository that holds the entry. | Run it before the upload is retired. Once the PDF moves to fsh-guts/uploads/, library:covers no longer finds it and skips the entry as “not held”. | bun run cat library:covers:check fails on a held, unwithheld PDF that has no cover. | .

d3f1411964c1.title: After ingestion the upload is RETIRED — never left, never deleted
d3f1411964c1.content: Three places, and only uploads/ is temporary: queued uploads/FILE; derived library/<slug>/, which may not hold the source bytes (check:l1-complete reports an unexpected child); archived fsh-guts/uploads/FILE beside a folio-fsh-guts/v1 sidecar whose movedFrom and movedOn are load-bearing. Never rm an ingested upload: it is the only working-tree copy of the source. bun run cat check:uploads-retired finds unretired ones by sha256 against every declared library, never by filename, and refuses rather than passes when no library records a hash. It reports and never moves anything. Rename an upload before its first ingest — the slug follows the name. The full rule — why the library cannot be the destination, the sidecar convention, the blocking and advisory families, and renaming — is in library-ingestion/uploads-retirement.md.

06750a40b146.title: When an ingested document names what else the library needs
06750a40b146.content: Some documents say what they rest on, by number, in a section the content type defines — and then the library is not complete until it holds those too. The flow above is run again for each, and the citing document’s graph is regenerated once they are in, so a cited source the library HOLDS is described from its own metadata rather than from a one-line reference. The content type owns which section that is, how its citations resolve, and how a cited source is acquired (for instance from a DSpace repository); it says so in its own authoring skill. This layer owns only the rule: the flow above runs once per cited source, and the citing document’s graph is regenerated after.

1e5163155d12.title: A second representation sits DOWNSTREAM of the entry
1e5163155d12.content: A content type may describe an ingested document a second time, in its own schema — a WHO guideline is also an L1 knowledge graph. The library is upstream of L1: L1 points upstream, never downstream. So that representation is derived from the entry and points at the entry’s nodes (the source document, its sections, its blocks); nothing in the library points back, and the entry is never rewritten for it. It inherits whatever sectioning this flow produced, so a better reader here improves it without a change there. Whether a document gets one is recorded on its intake (classifications), by a person, by the process that acquired it, or by a rule — the content type owns which, and its skill says how.

685386e51f4e.title: Liquid templates — layout only, every fact from the graph
685386e51f4e.content: Skill liquid-templates: Authoring a Liquid template in this repository — a README template the subgraph-readmes Tool renders with liquidjs, or a Jekyll include on the just-the-docs site. Where templates live (inside a declared directory, reached through its id), what a template may read (only what the Knowledge Graph hands it), the leading comment the generator reads as the file’s description, includes, whitespace control, escaping, and regenerate-then-commit with the --check gate. Read it before adding or changing any .liquid file or anything under docs/_includes/. Named by: Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Two engines run Liquid here, and they produce different kinds of output. Know which one you are writing for before you write a line: . |   | README templates | site templates | . | engine | liquidjs, run by bootstrap-tools’ subgraph-readmes (jekyllInclude: true, strictFilters: true) | Jekyll, run by docs-site.yml with the pinned just-the-docs remote_theme | . | lives in | templates/readme/ beside the writer, in the tools repository (bootstrap-tools/scripts/templates/readme/) | cat-harness/docs/_includes/ — just-the-docs’ extension points (head_custom.html, footer_custom.html, nav_footer_custom.html) plus our own | . | output | <directory>/README.md, committed, read on GitHub where no Liquid runs | _site/, never committed, published to Pages | . | data | only what the generator passes: subgraph, instance, kg, files, subdirs, summary | site, page, include, and _data/*.json written by the pipeline | . | verified by | bun run cat readme:subgraphs:check — the diff is the output | building the site: rendered-verification, bun run cat preview:site | .

2d157c1e3041.title: Where a template lives
2d157c1e3041.content: Beside the writer that renders it, in the tools repository. The README templates are part of bootstrap-tools’ scripts/ subgraph, at bootstrap-tools/scripts/templates/readme/, and the writer finds them with TEMPLATES, a path relative to its own file. A template is part of the toolset: somebody who wants different READMEs uses a different toolset over the same content, and a harness that wants its own layout passes its own templates directory to plan(). They are files OF the scripts/ subgraph, not a directory of their own: a declared directory nested inside another is refused by check:layout-norms. Never an inline template string in a .ts file and never a .liquid file outside a declared directory: a template nobody declared is one no checker looks at, and its README row cannot say what it is.

e9fdbeebfba2.title: What a template may read — and what it must not compose
e9fdbeebfba2.content: A template arranges facts; it never states one. Every word that is not layout comes from a variable the generator read from the Knowledge Graph: the directory’s declared title and description, each file’s own account of itself, a relation a diagram records. No count, URL, name or claim typed into a template — each is a second answer free to drift from the first, which is readme-sections §”Resolve links; never compose them” one level down. | Computation belongs in the generator, where it is tested: counting, grouping, choosing a link target, collapsing a long list. The template sees results (subdirs[].count, summary), not inputs to derive them from. | A missing value is shown as missing, never papered over: {{ subgraph.title | default: subgraph.id }} and “No description is declared for …” are the pattern. The generator records the gap as a QA finding in test/results/subgraph-readmes.qa-results.json (a derived result, stored on the qa-reports branch by qa-publish); the template must not make it look filled. | A new variable is a generator change first. Add it to the object passed to renderFile, list it in the template’s comment, then use it. | .

9e62169aa48f.title: Versions are variables, never numbers
9e62169aa48f.content: A version typed into a template is stale on the next bump. Read it: . | README templates get release: version (every layer declares one), and — for a layer declaring an iriBase — major, agent (for identifiers) and human (for pages), both <iriBase>v<major>/. Empty strings where not declared: test with != "", and show nothing rather than a guess. | Site templates read site.data.harness.releases.<instance> — the same four fields for every layer, written by sync-docs-harness into _data/harness.json under the docs:harness:check gate. | . Link a person to human and name an identifier with agent. They are one address today — every address carries the major only, and the pin, not the address, fixes the exact release (instance-publication §”Release IRIs”) — but the field still says which audience a link is for.

2acfb8af4071.title: The leading comment IS the file’s description
2acfb8af4071.content: Open every template with a {%- comment -%} block. Its first sentence is what the directory README’s “what it is” column shows for the file (describe() in bootstrap-tools/scripts/readme-graph-sections.ts), so write it for a reader of that table — “The file table: files directly in the directory, then its subdirectories.” — and put the variables it reads in the lines after. No comment and the row says only “a template”.

281c22f09786.title: Includes
281c22f09786.content: jekyllInclude: true gives Jekyll’s syntax: {% include files.liquid %}, the file name unquoted and with its extension. An include with no parameters sees the including template’s variables (files.liquid reads files directly); a parameter passed as {% include x.liquid key=value %} is read as include.key, as in Jekyll. Split a template when a part is reusable or when a reader would want its own row for it — not to hide logic.

59af41261feb.title: Whitespace — check the output, not the template
59af41261feb.content: {%- and -%} strip the whitespace on that side of the tag, and that is how a template emits clean Markdown. It is also how a separator the output needs disappears — a stripped space between two HTML attributes makes the page print its own markup as text, past every gate (continual-progress §”A template is not a page”). Strip freely inside a tag’s own lines; think before stripping next to a table row’s newline, the blank line before a heading or table, or an attribute boundary. subgraph-readmes also collapses three or more newlines to two, so do not fight blank lines with stripping.

7ca7091d4253.title: Escaping
7ca7091d4253.content: . | strictFilters: true — an unknown filter is an error, not a silent pass-through. No custom filter is registered. | A value bound for a table cell is escaped before it reaches the template — the generator’s cell() turns | into \| and folds newlines. A new cell-bound field goes through it; a raw | from a file’s description splits the row. | Liquid syntax in prose that Jekyll will build must sit inside a raw block. gen-skill-docs wraps every skill page in one, so a skill may quote {{ }} and {% %} freely — but never the closing endraw tag itself, which ends the block early. A generated README that sits under a site source (cat-harness/docs/, root docs/) may be read by the site build too; if a KG value there can carry Liquid, build the site and look before assuming either way. | .

1dcf8ece63c0.title: An undefined variable is a message, not silence
1dcf8ece63c0.content: Jekyll renders an undefined variable as the empty string and says nothing; strict_variables says something by FAILING the build and by changing what renders (the exception aborts the whole tag, else branch included). docs/_plugins/liquid-undefined-warn.rb does neither: every lookup runs as Liquid runs it, and at the end of the build each path that was ABSENT is printed as a warning with its count and pages, site.data.* first. A lookup inside a condition or under | default is not reported — there the template asked — nor an include’s own parameter (include.x, optional by convention), a field of a variable that is there and nil (its cause is reported once, where it went undefined), or a path liquid_undefined_ignore in _config.yml lists: a THEME’s optional settings, which site-chrome/_config.yml names for just-the-docs. Without those exclusions the report is mostly noise over a few real gaps. FOLIO_LIQUID_UNDEFINED_REPORT=<file> writes the same record as JSON; liquid_undefined: off in _config.yml turns it off. It runs only where plugins do (bundle exec jekyll, as an IG repository’s own site and preview:site build); the github-pages build is safe mode and loads none.

21cd5774f2b6.title: Markers — the platform owns the region, the folio owns the file
21cd5774f2b6.content: subgraph-readmes writes only between <!-- kg:subgraph:begin --> and <!-- kg:subgraph:end -->, creates a README holding just that region when there is none, and leaves an unmarked README alone and reported. The rules are in readme-sections; do not restate them in a template.

d9cd534dea0f.title: Regenerate, commit, and the gate
d9cd534dea0f.content: bun run cat readme:subgraphs # render every declared directory's README + the QA sidecar bun run cat readme:subgraphs:check # fail on a stale README or sidecar — CI and the pre-commit hook . Changing a template changes every README it renders; commit them with the template, in one commit. So does adding or removing a file in any declared directory — that directory’s table changed. readme:subgraphs:check runs in code-quality-gates.yml and in cat-harness-tools/scripts/git-hooks/pre-commit; it is part of bun run cat gates.

c4bb27a1b939.title: On the site specifically
c4bb27a1b939.content: . | Pages need front matter to be pages — title, and parent / nav_order for just-the-docs’ sidebar, which it builds from front matter at build time. | baseurl is /folio-assistant; a link or asset path goes through relative_url, never a literal /…. | Override just-the-docs through its extension-point includes, not by copying a theme layout — a copied layout silently stops tracking the pinned version (upstream-version-adoption). | A generated reference directory (reference/skill-instructions/, reference/skills/, auto-docs/) is never hand-edited; change its generator. | .

2b3fd271afad.title: liquid-templates (skill)
2b3fd271afad.content: The skill liquid-templates as its source file cat-harness/skills/ui/ui-core/liquid-templates.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

9866501c0084.title: Materialize on demand
9866501c0084.content: Skill materialize-on-demand: After bootstrap, a person asks for part of a remote subgraph to be held locally. Check what is already here (cache:index), put a number on the ask before anything is fetched, then run materialize-remote. Eviction is a report, never an act. Named by: Public comment on a review draft, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Publish extracted statements with source links . Bootstrap brings an agent to a working harness. It does not bring the corpus, and must not: a remote source such as IRIS runs to about a million files and hundreds of gigabytes. What arrives is the reference; a person asks, as they come to need it, for parts of subgraphs to be materialized. This skill is that ask. The gates are not here; they are in materialize-remote, once.

55e0c027f037.title: 1. What is already here
55e0c027f037.content: bun run cat cache:index # summary and eviction candidates bun run cat cache:index --all # every copy . Read the columns for what they are: . | column | values | what it means | . | size | recorded · measured · directory · absent | measured is the file now, not when it landed. A directory is counted through its parts. absent is not zero. | . | fetched | a date, or not recorded | only the record’s materializedAt | . | last read | not recorded, always | nothing records reads; file access times are not used, because they are often off or reset by a checkout. | . | freshness | fresh · expired · no-expiry · permanent | from freshness(). no-expiry is a finding: a working copy nobody gave a lifetime. | . If what they want is already held and fresh, stop: point them at it.

dd6ba91c5437.title: 2. Put a number on the ask BEFORE anything moves
dd6ba91c5437.content: Asking must not mean hundreds of gigabytes arrive without a number first. Before calling materialize-remote: . | Name the subset in the source’s own terms: its identifiers, or a subset strategy its descriptor (in the owning layer’s declared sources/, e.g. the IRIS replica’s sources/) supports. | Close it over dependencies if the descriptor says the subset is not self-contained (subsetIsSelfContained: false, mathlib). The size that matters is the closure’s. | State the size and its basis: from the descriptor’s enumeration, or a measured listing. If neither gives a number, say that. The SIZE gate refuses on an unknown, and so should this conversation. | Say what it would add to the cache total from step 1. | . Then ask the person, with the number in front of them.

3045ead25b90.title: 3. Materialize
3045ead25b90.content: Run Process_MaterializeRemote. Its five gates decide; this skill does not second-guess them. A refusal leaves the content referenced, with the reason recorded. That is the process working, not failing.

97227a908762.title: 4. Eviction is a report
97227a908762.content: cache:index lists candidates: expired first, then no-expiry working copies, largest first. An archival copy is never a candidate. Nothing is removed by the tool or by you. Show the list with sizes and reasons, and let the person decide (deletion-requires-confirmation).

b118922d74f0.title: materialize-on-demand (skill)
b118922d74f0.content: The skill materialize-on-demand as its source file cat-harness/library/skills/large-datasets/materialize-on-demand.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

a88c6efac80a.title: Materializing remote content
a88c6efac80a.content: Skill materialize-remote: Landing remote content locally — the five gates, the three states, and the two purposes. One process, shared by catalogue import and harness bootstrap, plus the refresh that is not a re-import. Named by: Getting started, Public comment on a review draft, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Publish extracted statements with source links, Board: open and close content, Board: place a note, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . One process for every caller that lands remote content locally. | caller | remote source | held locally | refresh | . | the IRIS replica | IRIS | selected items | refresh-materialized | . | bootstrap | a harness | the cat-harness checkout | upstream-pins.json | . bootstrap/workflows/initialize-harness.bpmn fetches a harness that is remote content and lands it locally; upstream-pins.json exists because that copy goes stale. Diagrams: materialize-remote.bpmn and refresh-materialized.bpmn. Schema: the folio-materialization/v1 record (MaterializationSchema, owned by the content layer above this one — named here, not linked). Nothing here restates either — where they disagree, the schema wins and this file is wrong.

f5a080e96366.title: Ask the purpose FIRST
f5a080e96366.content: working or archival, before any gate, because three of the five mean different things under each. |   | working | archival | . | what is kept | derived content — sections, OCR | the original bytes | . | retention | expires; re-fetchable | no expiry, by design | . | sourceLoss | unanswered | discharged | . | fixity | not needed | required | . A process that gated first and asked afterwards would be judging a copy whose obligations it did not yet know.

404c80e1f02f.title: The five gates
404c80e1f02f.content: Each is a decision a person makes; none is answerable from a file. A gate that only warns is a gate nobody fails. | Size — what fraction, and what the whole would cost. Refuse when you cannot tell: “three items” with no denominator is not a size answer. | Restrictions — “no restrictions known in context” is a state, not a green light. unknown is never rendered as permitted. | Copyright — per bitstream, and separately for the derived work. LICENSE-CONTENT.md exists here and the ingestion pipeline does not read it. | Retention — what expires this copy. A copy with no expiry cannot be told from an abandoned one. | Source loss — what survives if the origin goes. Only an archival copy discharges this. Origins do disappear: a regional repository instance can be merged away, taking its handles with it. | .

2fbec28a444b.title: Three states, and no default
2fbec28a444b.content: referenced (it exists, we know where, we hold no bytes) · materialized · unknown. A node that has not declared one is invalid, not unknown — “the author did not say” and “the author said they could not tell” are different facts, and only the second is actionable. A refusal is the process working. The node stays referenced, the graph still knows it exists, and the refusing gate’s basis is recorded so the next agent does not re-litigate it.

6654977eb102.title: Refresh is not re-import
6654977eb102.content: Three answers, not one: what changed upstream, what changed locally, and what to do when both. A materialized copy edited in place is not a copy — overwriting it destroys work whose existence was never established; check:materialized-fixity detects it. An archival copy is never refreshed. Re-fetching it discards the state it exists to keep. It gets a fixity check instead — has our copy rotted — which is a different question with a different remedy: restore from backup, never re-download.

0e9883d35579.title: Before you enumerate anything
0e9883d35579.content: cat-harness/schemas/library/source-descriptor.ts answers the question that comes before the gates: how to enumerate a corpus and ask it for a subset. Check subsetIsSelfContained first — when it is false (mathlib), close the request over its dependencies before gating, because the size being gated is the closure’s, not the request’s.

64b8a89a8920.title: materialize-remote (skill)
64b8a89a8920.content: The skill materialize-remote as its source file cat-harness/library/skills/large-datasets/materialize-remote.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

9b2409d9498d.title: Merge-conflict patterns — what a merge may resolve on its own
9b2409d9498d.content: Skill merge-conflict-patterns: Merge the base branch in and resolve, without a person, only the conflicts a DECLARED pattern covers — generated files, generated README regions, QA sidecars — then prove the result with the gate set. Refuses the whole merge when any conflict is authored or undeclared. Use for “merge main”, “resolve the conflicts”, “the PR is conflicted again”, “auto-resolve”, and when adding a pattern for a new kind of churn. Also governs what a merge steward does with a merge-train member it had to refuse: one deduplicated work item under the PR’s own epic, a hand-back to the owning session with a fail condition, one dispatched agent when nobody owns it, one PR comment, and the close. Named by: Guideline Updates . bun run cat merge:main is the command; sdlc/processes/merge-base.bpmn is the process it executes, called from Task_PrepareMerge in code-change-review.bpmn. The patterns themselves are data in cat-harness-tools/scripts/merge-conflict-patterns.ts. This page says what each one is FOR, so a reader can tell a deliberate refusal from a gap. Most main-into-branch merges that conflict do so only on generated files, and every one of those resolves the same way — take the base’s copy, regenerate — so resolving them by hand costs an agent a round and the PR another CI run for nothing.

26c3f90f793c.title: The three rules that make it safe
26c3f90f793c.content: . | All or nothing. Every conflicted path is classified before anything is touched. One refusal ABORTS the merge and restores the tree. Resolving nine generated files and leaving one authored conflict half-done reads as progress, and is not. | Proved, not assumed. After resolving, bun run cat regen asks the checks the CI workflow runs (under merge:main, those whose inputs either side changed since the fork point; --full-regen asks every one) and runs each stale one’s writer until the tree settles. Anything unrepaired aborts the merge. No pattern names its own check: the gate set is derived from the workflow and cannot drift, a hand-kept list of check names can. | Classify with the BASE’s patterns, not your tree’s. pathClass reads PATTERNS from the checkout it is running in. A branch that forked before a pattern was declared therefore classifies by the OLD declaration, and every path in a newly-declared family reads authored — the one verdict that routes work to a person. | . A path that no pattern names is refused. Adding automation is adding a pattern, deliberately, with its reason — never widening a glob on a hunch. Applying rule 3 . A stale tree can be wrong in either direction. A pattern the base has added makes it over-report authored conflicts, which sends a person work the base already declares mechanical. A pattern the base has narrowed, reordered or retired makes it under-report: it takes a side on a path the base now refuses. So git fetch, and classify with the BASE’s own merge-base.ts (from a worktree of the tools at the base, git worktree add --detach <dir> origin/<base>), run against your checkout with --root <your checkout> --base origin/<base> (add --dry-run to classify and change nothing). merge-main.yml does the same: it checks out main’s tools and runs main’s merge-base.ts --root on the PR’s branch. The number that decides whether a human is needed must come from the declaration the merge will actually be resolved under.

4b0547be2d7c.title: A merge round — run each check ONCE
4b0547be2d7c.content: Most of a round of folding main into a PR is the same question asked twice. What each step costs and adds: . | step | cost | what it adds | . | merge:main, including its own regen | 5–10 min — regen 238–309 s with nothing stale, 601–639 s when a writer runs | THE regen; rule 2 above | . | skill:register | 1–2 min | the derived artefacts the merge left owed | . | a standalone regen after merge:main | 4–5 min | nothing for the merge — same tree; it can only add a pair already stale on both parents, which CI reports anyway | . | full local bun run cat gates | ~24 min (1429 s), nearly all bun test (~21.8k tests) on 3–4 local cores | what CI’s sharded run says in ~5 min, 4 ways | . | regen again in a fresh checkout, to prove a no-op | 4–5 min | what CI’s own clean checkout already proves | . The timings in this section were recorded by 2026-10-08, when cat-harness was seeded. Re-measure with bun run cat measure:merge-round before you quote them. Three of five rows repeat a measurement somebody else, or the same command, has already made. So: . When every conflict is generated — the trimmed round . “Generated” means every conflicted path was resolved by a declared take-base, region or sidecar pattern below, and the merge brought in no authored change of yours to reconcile. | bun run cat state:mount, then bun run cat merge:main. merge:main’s regen IS the regen. Do not run another one after it. | bun run cat skill:register until bun run cat skill:register:check passes. The chain can need two passes: one writer’s output is another’s input. | Targeted checks, and only these: . | skill:register:check and kg:detangle:check — the two reds a generated-only merge actually hit in CI; | subgraph:jsonld:check — a merge or edit that changes a skill also changes its payload hash; skill:register does not run subgraph:jsonld, so run the writer (bun run cat subgraph:jsonld) when the check is red; | check:declared-paths (never with --update here) and check:process-index; | bun run typecheck, and bun run cat lint at 0 errors; | the deletion audit — git diff --name-status --diff-filter=D HEAD^1 HEAD -- '*/test/results/*' must list only files main itself deleted. A gitignored-but-tracked file is dropped by a merge silently, local checks stay green because the writer recreated it on disk, and CI’s fresh checkout fails. merge:main refuses such a drop itself (§”When one side deleted the file”); after a hand merge, restore each one main still tracks with git checkout HEAD^2 -- <path>; | submodule pins equal to main’s — git ls-tree HEAD bootstrap bootstrap-tools against git ls-tree origin/main bootstrap bootstrap-tools. Not git submodule status: merge-queue §”git add -A after a merge silently reverts the submodule gitlinks” says why it cannot see this; | the fsh-guts mount is not committed — git diff --stat origin/main HEAD -- fsh-guts is empty; | git merge-tree --write-tree origin/main HEAD reports 0 conflicts, with the exit status captured on the next line (prepare-merge step 4). | . | Push, never with force. CI’s sharded run is the full gate set. Skip the local full bun run cat gates and the fresh-checkout regen for this kind of merge: each repeats something CI does better. | . When it is NOT generated-only — keep the full local run . An AUTHORED file conflicted, or the merge touched code (a script, test, schema or workflow that conflicted or that you reconciled by hand, on either side): run the full local bun run cat gates before pushing, and read prepare-merge §”What a green LOCAL run entitles you to claim” before quoting it. The targeted list above is chosen for a merge that changed only artefacts with one right answer; it cannot see a semantic conflict such as an import of a module the other side moved (merge-queue §”A train admits only members that STACK cleanly”). Four things a round needs to know . | merge:main has no “continue after a manual fix” mode. When one path blocks it, it aborts and restores the tree (rule 1). Do its steps by hand: git merge origin/main, fix the blocking path, then resolve each declared path by its own pattern’s strategy, never with one command for all of them, and stage each with git add -f <path>: . | take-base: git checkout --theirs <path> when main kept the file; git rm <path> when main deleted it, since a modify/delete has no stage to check out (§”When one side deleted the file”). | owned-tree: take each parent’s committed blob, as takeOwnedTree does (§”subgraph-index and subgraph-payload”). Never --theirs: in a rename/rename it writes conflict-marked bytes under a hash name. | readme-generated-regions: edit the conflict markers in place, hunk by hunk, as resolveGeneratedRegions does. A hunk inside a generated region may take either side, because regen rewrites the region. A hunk outside one, or one that moves a region boundary, is an authored conflict. Never --theirs: it replaces the whole README and drops the branch’s own edits to it, including the ones git merged cleanly. | . Then run the regen it would have run, and both droppedInMerge checks it would have run: once after resolving, and once after regen and git add -A, before committing. Each path git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=D HEAD lists must be one main deleted since the merge base, and each path git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=D MERGE_HEAD lists must be one the branch deleted since the merge base. After regen, a writer’s own deletion also passes, but only when the file is gone from disk too. | Give the regen a long leash. Cold, it needed ≥1200 s of wall time (recorded by 2026-10-08; bun run cat measure:merge-round re-measures). Run it in the background rather than under a default 2-minute tool timeout, which kills it part-way and leaves a half-written tree. | merge:main commits with git’s default message. Amend that commit to add the session’s trailers (git commit --amend) before pushing — it is your unpushed commit, so this is not a rewrite of shared history. | Do not fold main in while another big PR is minutes from landing. Wait for it. Merging now buys a second round the moment it lands (merge-queue). | .

abe9e7234fbf.title: A pattern is not always the answer — ask what the file’s record is
abe9e7234fbf.content: Read this before declaring a pattern for a path that already has one. The registry answers how a conflict is resolved. It never answers whether one arises, and reaching for it a second time on the same path is the move to stop and check. A declared pattern settles a file whose content is a function of the TREE, and settles nothing about one whose content is a function of the machine that built it — there, take-base is a loop. This section is about a third case: the content is tree-determined, the pattern does resolve it, and the path still conflicts on every merge. The LSI indexes are the example: a one-sentence edit to one skill rewrites most of skills.lsi.json (an SVD rotation is globally sensitive), so the file conflicts on nearly every merge, and the pattern only makes each conflict cheap — and no check on main judges those bytes. So the question to ask is not which strategy, it is: . What is this file’s record, and is main it? . | main is the record — an authored file, or a generated one a reader navigates to by name. Declare the pattern; that is what the registry is for. | main is not the record — the file’s record is the qa-reports entry for its commit, or a build output, and the copy on main is a duplicate kept in step by a gate. Then take it off main, and keep the declaration for the branches still carrying it, where the base has deleted the file and take-base resolves that too (see the next section). | Part of it is, and part is not — the common case, and the one to look for before concluding either of the above. Cut by what each value is a function of: a value the TREE determines stays committed and is reviewable; a value determined by some other artefact’s CONTENT is produced where that artefact lives. docs/lsi/index.md is the worked example — front matter, prose and the verdict table stay, each index’s size, poles and findings go — and the front matter is why it could not be taken off whole: it declares the harness tile, so an uncommitted page is a page with no way in. | . The trap on the way out. Taking a page off its store and leaving it committed can make it worse: a page computed from qa-reports at main reads the latest published entry, so the committed copy goes stale whenever anyone else pushes. Whatever stays committed must be computed from the tree.gitattributes reached the same conclusion from the -merge side and states it plainly: “Removing these conflicts, rather than tidying them, needs the files off main altogether.” Two things make that safe rather than merely tidy, and both are checks, not care: every reader must already cope with the file’s absence, and something must still PRODUCE it where its record lives — qa:refresh decides that per writer, so a family can be removed on its own.

24bd4803f5b9.title: When one side deleted the file
24bd4803f5b9.content: A modify/delete conflict has no stage for the side that deleted it, so checkout --theirs (or --ours) has nothing to take. Every resolving strategy takes the base’s side of the deletion instead: its copy when the base kept the file, git rm when the base removed it — takeBase in merge-base.ts. Regeneration recreates the file if it is still produced. Classification is by path, so an authored path in a modify/delete conflict is refused exactly like any other conflict on it. The owned-tree patterns are the exception. They read which parent commits hold the path rather than which stages exist, because in a rename/rename “no stage 3” does not mean the base deleted anything (see subgraph-payload below). Taking a deletion is the ONLY way a merge may drop a path, and merge-base.ts checks this before every merge commit. droppedInMerge compares the index with the merge base and both parents. A path either parent tracks that the result lacks is a drop, unless one side deleted it since the merge base. A path both parents hold, or one a side added, must survive. The check runs twice. Right after resolution, before anything else is staged, every drop is refused. After regen and add -A, only a drop the disk still holds is refused, because a writer may delete what it owns: subgraph:jsonld replaces a content-addressed payload when the merge changes its node, and its :check proves that. The check exists because of the gitignored-but-tracked files under */test/results/. Once one of them leaves the index, regen rewrites it on disk and git add -A does not stage it again, since it is now untracked and ignored. The failure signature is green locally, red in CI, with the check reporting the file missing (“has none”). git add -A is not what removes such a file: it only fails to restore one that something else (such as a git rm) already removed from the index. The refusal line says when the dropped file is still on disk, which is the case that local checks cannot see.

2c21727e694f.title: The patterns
2c21727e694f.content: kg-qa-manifest — take the base, regenerate . **/test/results/**/kg-qa.manifest.json. One per layer (hosted ones one level deeper), holding only the auditor’s script hash, so any change to kg-audit.ts restamps every one at once. It holds no attestation. qa-results — take the base, regenerate . **/*.qa-results.json. Whole-artefact QA results, rewritten whole by their producer. They change whenever any finding does. derived-results — take the base, regenerate . kg-qa sidecars, LSI indexes, detangle sidecars, tool-run records and translation-qa sidecars under test/results/. Recomputed from the whole corpus, so any concurrent skill or schema change touches them. Attestations live in test/attestations/, which no pattern names and a merge therefore refuses; test/results/ is not committed on main, and a branch still carrying a sidecar takes the base’s side. The LSI half is untracked on main; the globs are kept for branches still carrying it (§”A pattern is not always the answer”). auto-docs — take the base, regenerate . The generated docs index pages, already -merge in .gitattributes. One page per directory, so a new file anywhere changes one. uml — take the base, regenerate . Generated overview diagrams and their SVGs. prov-qaqc — take the base, regenerate . The PROV-O QA/QC report (docs/prov-qaqc/) and its per-instance logs (docs/assets/prov/). Generated WHOLE from the workflow instances under beans/workflows/, so any branch that records an instance — which every branch doing process work does — rewrites the index page and adds a .prov.jsonld. The globs are instance-agnostic (**/docs/prov-qaqc/**), like derived-results and unlike glossary: a dependent folio runs prov:qaqc over its own instances and writes the same two shapes under its own root. It names no check of its own, per rule 2: regen runs prov:qaqc because check:prov-qaqc is a workflow gate, and a pattern that named its own check would be a hand-kept list able to drift from the workflow. glossary — take the base, regenerate . The generated glossary and LSI pages: whole-corpus aggregates where concurrent term additions always collide. The LSI page’s per-index detail is added by the docs-site build rather than committed, and what is left is a function of the tree. The glossary page has no equivalent split: every number on it is a term count over the whole corpus, so there is no half that only the tree moves. That is the second branch of §”A pattern is not always the answer” — main is still the glossary page’s record, and declaring the strategy is all there is to do. translated-glossary — take the base, regenerate . cat-harness/docs/{ar,es,fr,ru,zh}/glossary/index.md. The per-locale glossary pages glossary-page.ts writes whole beside the English one (check:glossary), so they collide exactly when it does. Only the glossary page is named: the rest of each locale directory is authored translation, and a locale no generator writes (de/) is refused. viewer-pages — take the base, regenerate . docs/external-schemas/index.md, docs/methodologies/index.md, docs/processes/*.md, docs/qa/index.html and docs/translation-status/index.html: whole-file viewer pages, each with its writer’s --check in the CI workflow (external-schemas:viz, methodologies:viz, processes:viz, state:visualizer, translation:status). A new schema, diagram or translation anywhere rewrites them.
