Conflict resolution belongs on the member’s branch, never in the train, and never in the steward’s time. Resolving conflicts inside a train blocks everything else from landing. The overlapKind table above still says what a collision NEEDS; the steward provides only the none row. Every other kind goes back to its owner.

c0f36b4805e2.title: The automated merge train (folio-assistant, work item folio-assistant-hd58)
c0f36b4805e2.content: Where a repository runs merge-train.yml, as it does in folio-assistant, the steward’s hand train is a workflow. A person opts a PR in by adding the merge-train label (a bot’s label does not count) or by approving it. Every 15 minutes, when there is work, the train: . | judges the open train PR (merge-train-batch) as the re-pin train is judged: every check finished, the full tier ran, and no check fails that passes on main, check by check. When green, it merges the train PR with a merge commit, and every member is then on main; | on red, ejects a batch of one (label removed, failures listed), or splits a larger batch in halves and tests the first half next (about log₂ k extra runs for one culprit); | otherwise stacks the ready opted-in PRs on main with merge:train (in folio-assistant) and opens ONE train PR, which CI judges once. | . Owner ruling, 2026-11-05 (“Resolve generated only”). For the automated train this supersedes §”A train admits only members that STACK cleanly” for GENERATED paths only. A conflict that a declared generated-path pattern covers is resolved mechanically at train time and proved by the candidate’s CI. A conflict in any hand-written file ejects that PR with a comment, and it waits for its author. No person resolves conflicts in the train. Owner ruling, 2026-11-05 (off switch). A PR that changes .github/workflows/ rides the train only when the repository variable MERGE_TRAIN_CARRIES_WORKFLOWS is true and a bot token with the workflows permission is present. Until then, workflow PRs are merged one at a time when green (owner, 2026-11-05, option 1). subscriptions/ never rides. merge-main.yml skips PRs labelled merge-train: they are integrated once, at train time, never on each push to main. Owner ruling, 2026-11-07, card “Train”, A. When the owner approves a folio-assistant PR that does not change .github/workflows/, the merge manager adds the merge-train label instead of merging it, so the train lands it in a batch with one CI run. Merging one PR at a time cost about 6.7 runs per merged PR. Workflow PRs, and repositories with no train, merge directly, and a workflow PR needs no approval beyond the batch card (card “Workflow PRs”, A).

6e830017d5d7.title: Regenerate on a clean tree, and check it
6e830017d5d7.content: git status --porcelain is empty before a member is merged and the tree regenerated. Checked, not assumed, on Task_Admit. Generated directory READMEs carry a per-subdirectory file count, and the writer counts the files git would commit — git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard (bootstrap-tools/scripts/git-files.ts:23). --exclude-standard keeps ignored junk out, which is the __pycache__ case that drove that line, but --others still counts an untracked file nobody has ignored. So a transient written by an earlier train step moves a committed count, readme:subgraphs:check goes red, and the red belongs to nobody. The precondition does not make the count stable: two members each adding a file still write different integers to one line. merge:main resolves them under readme-generated-regions; a merge made by plain git does not. Not -merge and not a merge driver — both are refused in .gitattributes, the first because it tidies conflicts without removing them and the second because it needs per-checkout git config.

cf321081052a.title: A red train ejects one member, not the train
cf321081052a.content: . | Retry only a declared-flaky gate, and only once (Task_RetryFlaky). A deterministic gate retried learns nothing. | Attribute from each member’s own CI first (Task_Attribute). A member whose own CI is red, or never ran on its head — GitHub runs no pull_request CI while a PR conflicts — is the prime suspect, at no cost. | Bisect only when every member is green alone (Task_Bisect). | Eject and hand back with the reason (Task_Eject, then merge-refusal.bpmn). The ejection is written on the member’s entry; the rest re-run without it. The owning session fixes and re-signals ready; it is never merged on its behalf. | .

053a00339f55.title: A PR lands only through merge:guard (STRICT)
053a00339f55.content: Every merge a steward makes goes through bun run cat merge:guard <pr> --merge --session <your session id>. Never gh api -X PUT …/pulls/<n>/merge, never the web button, never merge_pull_request from an MCP tool, and, while a Merge Manager is active, never by marking a PR ready or labelling it yourself first (with none active, see §”When no Merge Manager is active”). The script (cat-harness-tools/scripts/merge-guard.ts) is the merge: it evaluates eight checks over GitHub’s live facts, and performs the PUT, pinned to the head it evaluated, only when every one passes. A direct PUT lands a PR whatever its state. When no Merge Manager is active, elect one; only it merges . Owner ruling, 2026-11-13: only the merge manager merges (merge-manager-watcher §”Only the merge manager merges and re-pins”). With none active, the siblings elect one first, and a lone session is elected alone. A PR’s own session lands its PR only when it is that merge manager, once the owner has said to merge, and still through the guard: . bun run cat merge:guard <pr> --merge --session <your session id> --no-merge-manager . --no-merge-manager lifts one thing: check 2’s refusal of a merging session that marked the PR ready itself. Every other check still applies, and so does check 2’s own-session attribution. In particular, the ready: <head sha> marker signed by this session, ready-to-merge, green owed CI and a clean merge are all still required. The verdict says the separation was lifted, so the landing is auditable. Where the guard cannot run (for example a cloud sandbox whose gh has no usable token), do not merge: hand the landing to a session that can run it, or ask the owner. No workflow posts a merge-guard commit status, so there is no posted verdict to read in its place. How to tell whether a Merge Manager is active: the owner says so, or a live session holds the merge-steward lane (§”Address the ROLE, never a session”, step 1). If you cannot tell, apply the rules of merge-manager-watcher §”The sibling’s side: find the merge manager first”: with none active, the siblings elect one by its fixed rule, and a lone session is elected alone (owner rulings, 2026-11-07 and 2026-11-13). Do not assume none. A stale memory of “there was one yesterday” is not an answer in either direction. “The owner said merge” is still required. Submitting to main is the owner’s call (§”Ask the user before submitting”), and this does not change that. The eight checks, each named in a refusal by number and id: . | base — open, based on main, and the base is not the head branch of a merged PR. A stacked PR is retargeted by its owning session first. | ready-for-review — not a draft, and the latest ready_for_review event is attributable to the PR’s own session, never to yours. When the merge manager lands a PR of its own, --no-merge-manager lifts the “never to yours” half (§”When no Merge Manager is active”). | ready-marker — a ready: <sha> comment signed with the PR’s own session link (the one in its body), naming the head, or with only merge-main bot merges after it. | labels — ready-to-merge present, needs-merge-human absent. | ci — gates a release only (--release, or the release label; owner, card Q-CIB-4 A, 2026-11-08). On any other merge the judgement below is made and reported, and the check passes as advisory. The judgement: every pull_request run on the head is success or skipped, and every workflow owed for that event ran. A workflow_dispatch run counts only as the stand-in for a pull_request run GitHub held for approval (action_required) on a head that is a merge-main bot merge: merge-main has already merged main into that head, so the head IS the merge, and a dispatch on it judges the tree that would land. The latest dispatch of the same workflow on the head decides — green counts, running is not-ready, red is a defect. Held with no dispatch: not-ready if merge-main.yml’s for wf in … ; do gh workflow run line names that workflow’s file (the dispatch is still owed), reported not judged if it does not (Feature Staging, preview-only), and unknown if that line cannot be parsed. A green dispatch never rescues a pull_request run that executed and went red, and anywhere else it is reported and not counted. Feature Staging is judged, never waited for: a staging run still in flight, or not started, is not a refusal — its deploy is held by the gh-pages rate limit — and the verdict says so as not waited for. Once it finishes, red still refuses, since stage runs real checks before it deploys — unless the only failed step is the deploy itself (DEPLOY_ONLY_STEP): a push window that never opened, or three rejected pushes, is not a verdict on the tree. The guard reads the run’s failed steps to tell; if it cannot read them, red refuses as before. The list is NOT_WAITED_FOR_WORKFLOW_FILES in merge-guard.ts. | checklist — no unticked - [ ] in the body. | open-question — no comment after the marker asks the owner or the Merge Manager a question (a heuristic; its limits are on openQuestions in the script — a fresh ready: after the answer moves the window). | mergeable — GitHub says the head still merges cleanly into main Check 5’s runs tested the head merged with main as main was when the head was pushed; once main moves, a stale green head with a valid marker can pass checks 1-7 while it conflicts. The PR API’s mergeable: false (mergeable_state: dirty) refuses not-ready — merge main into the head and re-sign ready:. mergeable: null means GitHub has not computed it yet: the guard re-asks for up to 14 s, then reports unknown, never a pass. unstable and blocked pass here, because they are about checks and reviews, which check 5 and the owner judge. A verdict is a snapshot and can go stale on exactly this check when main moves; --merge re-evaluates live. | . Exit 0 is pass (or merged), 1 refused, 2 could not determine — never a pass. A refusal is handed back to the owning session through merge-refusal.bpmn with the check’s text; the steward does not fix the PR to make it pass. What the OWNING session does, so a finished PR passes: mark it ready, then post ready: <head sha> signed with its session link — https://claude.ai/code/session_… in the footer — within ten minutes of each other, and apply ready-to-merge. Every session acts with the owner’s token, so the timeline’s actor is always the owner and cannot tell sessions apart; the signature is the only thing that can. An unsigned marker is refused. A verdict has four states, and red means wrong, not unfinished. A PR that is merely not ready yet (a draft, no marker, no label, an unticked box, CI still running, an open question, a conflict with main) is pending. Only a defect is failure: a base that is not main or is dead, needs-merge-human, red CI on the head, or a marker or ready-flip by a session other than the PR’s own. success is pass and error is could-not-determine. Red on every draft would teach readers to ignore red. Only success lands. No workflow runs it. The guard is the script alone, and --merge evaluates live at the moment it lands. Rule_NotReady in merge-priority.dmn applies the cheap half of checks 1-3 at placement (readiness, from LivePr.draft, baseRef, readySha, readyBy), so an unfinished PR is handed back before it is put in a train rather than at the PUT.

4be231559fc6.title: When the authors stall: the steward dispatches unblockers
4be231559fc6.content: Authors’ sessions can hit usage limits together, so the whole hand-back column can go quiet while every member in it is one small fix away from admission. The steward may dispatch agents for small unblocking fixes, without using up the CI budget. This adds a second actor to step 4 above. It changes nothing else. An unblocker fixes the head. It never merges, never adds ready-to-merge, and never posts a ready: marker. The author still vouches for the PR, and the steward still lands it only after the author signals ready, or under the owner’s explicit release. Who goes: the PRs merge:steward routes to hand-back. Leave out drafts, PRs whose author was active in the last 15 minutes, PRs another session has claimed, and PRs under an owner block (a ruling such as “this blocks the PR” is a judgement about content, and fixing the code does not lift it). Group them into a few agents, each in its own worktree. The general swarm rules are in swarm-management. Every unblocker gets the same rules, written once and handed to all of them: . | rule | why | . | at most ONE push per PR, after bun run cat gates locally — or, when every conflict was generated, after the targeted checks of merge-conflict-patterns §”A merge round — run each check ONCE” | each push runs full CI and deploys a staging preview into gh-pages, which has a size budget. Pushing speculatively spends both | . | no workflow_dispatch, re-run, empty commit or close/reopen | the same budget, and a dispatched run is not an owed run (above) | . | the merge manager re-runs only a PR it is about to merge, never held content, never in a batch, never during a GitHub outage, and refreshes a re-pin PR’s pins first (merge-manager-watcher §”Re-run policy”) | every failed run emails the owner; re-runs were most of the 11-11 failure emails (card Q-RERUN-1 B) | . | merge commits only: no rebase, amend or force-push | it is somebody else’s branch | . | authored conflict → resolve only dead code, or a pure addition carried over verbatim; otherwise quote both sides and stand down | choosing between two behaviours is the author’s call | . | git submodule update --init and bun run cat state:mount before regen | without the submodules merge:steward cannot load. Without the mount, fsh-guts:viz:check exits non-zero (it judges that the mounted graph renders; the page itself is built at publish) and audit:coverage:strict goes red | . | delete the worktree’s node_modules at the end | four parallel installs run out of the container’s disk | . | one comment per PR: root cause, the commit it pushed or the reason it stood down | the author comes back to an explanation, not a mystery commit | . missing-required is often a head that CI never started, not a slow one. The causes to check, in order: . | the PR edits a workflow file and GitHub cannot parse it, so no run is created at all; | the head was pushed with GITHUB_TOKEN, which starts no pull_request run; | the run is held at action_required. | . The first one is not visible in the check list, so look at the YAML. After any merge of main, check for silently dropped files. Some files under */test/results/ (LSI indexes, QA and detangle sidecars) are gitignored but still tracked. Once a resolution step removes one from the index, regen rewrites it on disk and git add -A does not stage it again. Local checks still pass, but CI’s fresh checkout fails. merge:main and the merge-main bot refuse such a merge and name the paths (droppedInMerge in merge-base.ts, see merge-conflict-patterns §”When one side deleted the file”). A hand git merge gets no such check. After one, run git diff --diff-filter=D HEAD^1 HEAD -- '*/test/results/*', and restore anything that main still tracks with git checkout HEAD^2 -- <path>. Stalled for days, with no handover report: write it, then hand it to a takeover agent . An unblocker suits a short pause. When the authors are gone for days, the steward does something else: . | Writes the handover report each author did not. It goes as one comment per PR, headed ## Takeover plan, in the handover-report format and measured, not recalled: intent with the owner’s rulings quoted; head SHA, conflicts split into authored and generated, owed CI; done and remaining; approval and any scope drift; ordered next steps with their falsifiers; owner questions; couplings with other open PRs. This step is read-only apart from the comment. | Gives the owner one paste-able brief for the takeover agent: the cold start, the work order across PRs (the couplings decide it), the merge rules, and the open owner questions. The owner starts that agent, possibly on another account, so the brief must stand alone. | The takeover session becomes each PR’s owning session. merge:guard accepts a ready: marker only from the session the PR body names, and check 2 keeps the merging session from vouching for its own landing. So the takeover agent edits the body’s session line to its own session, records “taken over from . (stalled)", claims the work items, and then signs. The steward never signs for it, and there is no one-time bypass. | . A PR that is green but refused by checks 3 and 4 (no marker, no label) is waiting-on-author in the queue, not active, until the takeover session signs it.

c9624736ceb3.title: Landing
c9624736ceb3.content: Re-run merge:steward after every merge, before the next one. Each merge moves main. A member admitted against the old main can turn dirty and then cannot land at all: its tested head is still green, but GitHub refuses to merge a conflicted PR, so it waits for its merge:main round and fresh CI on the new head. Only with the owner’s release, which is the authorisation half of merge-to-main (Call_MergeToMain in merge-train.bpmn): explicit, or a standing ruling quoted verbatim with its date, and only through bun run cat merge:guard <pr> --merge --session <id> (section above). What lands is exactly the SHA CI tested — the guard pins the PUT to the head it evaluated, so GitHub refuses it if the head moved; if main moved after the train’s CI started, re-run rather than land. A standing release covers the queue AS IT STOOD, not every PR that arrives later. New PRs need the owner’s explicit approval. So on every sweep the steward lists the PRs opened since the release, and puts them to the owner in one question, with the table’s verdict on each. One answer (“approve all 6”) may cover the whole batch.

ec9169432f66.title: Post-merge asymmetry: why main needs its own regeneration pipeline
ec9169432f66.content: .github/workflows/merge-main.yml runs bun run cat merge:main on an opted-in PR branch when main moves, resolving declared conflicts and regenerating. There is a structural asymmetry in the other direction: after a PR merges into main, nothing in that workflow regenerates main. So any merge changing an enumerated or counted directory can leave main red on a hard gate, even when the PR merged cleanly with zero git conflicts. The only reason it usually does not is an accident: the PR branch happened to regenerate against a base that had not moved yet. When that accident does not hold, main goes red and stays red until somebody notices. The accidental-repair pattern . A PR that adds files without regenerating a counted README breaks main; a later, unrelated PR whose branch carries a regenerated README repairs it incidentally; a web-UI upload breaks it again with no generator run at all. The trap: A green on a derived gate must NOT be read as “was never broken” or “the commit before it was clean”. Unrelated PR branches that happen to carry regenerated files incidentally repair main, creating untrustworthy gate histories. Why this halts development: While main is red on a hard gate, every open PR inherits that red, so no PR can show green, and nothing can be merged on green CI. PR sessions start debugging their own diffs for failures that belong to main. Where derived artefacts are regenerated . No automation pushes to main and none opens a repair PR: the automation/post-merge-regen-<sha> branches and their PRs piled up with no CI once Actions could no longer open PRs here, and they are gone. A full regen composes and regenerates the whole index, 50-80 minutes of runner time, so it runs only when a person dispatches it or the release build calls it. No pull request, push or schedule event starts one. | For a PR, by hand, before it merges. Dispatch post-merge-regen.yml with pr set to the PR’s number or branch (gh workflow run post-merge-regen.yml -f pr=<n>). It runs the regen writers at the PR’s head. When a tracked file changed, it commits ONE chore(derived): regenerate derived artefacts for <sha> to the PR’s own branch; for a fork’s PR it commits nothing and fails with the command to run. The PR’s checks judge that commit, so the regen reaches main through the normal, tested merge. Pushed with GITHUB_TOKEN, the commit starts no CI and the run fails saying so; a REGEN_PUSH_TOKEN secret lets the checks start by themselves. A head that is itself a regen commit and still regenerates fails (no fixpoint), so it cannot loop. | At release, automatically. release-npm.yml regenerates into the package it publishes (a patch applied to the release checkout, never committed) and publishes nothing when a check is unrepaired. | On main, by hand: verify and warn. post-merge-regen.yml with pr empty regenerates in its runner, warns with what was stale, and commits, pushes and opens nothing. NEGATIVE CONTROL: a main with nothing stale warns about nothing. | . Branch and staging preview builds do not regenerate. Merge steward procedure: post-merge verification . | A PR carries its own regen. When a PR changes the inputs of a derived file, its author (or the steward) dispatches the regen for it before it merges. The PR’s own gates report a stale derived file as they always did. | Main stale on a derived gate: dispatch the verify run to see what is stale, then dispatch the regen for the next PR in the queue, or for a PR opened only to carry it, which is admitted with priority under merge-priority.dmn as an unblock-main repair. | A red regen run is that PR’s failure, like any other check: a fork PR runs the regen it names, and a regen commit pushed without CI needs one more push before the PR’s checks run. | .

7b933e2cbdf8.title: ACK every PR that enters the queue, on its bean (STRICT)
7b933e2cbdf8.content: A submitter who hears nothing cannot tell “queued” from “lost”, and the work item is where the next session looks. When a PR enters the queue (first seen on a sweep, or approved by the owner), the steward writes three things in the same change: . | The queue entry, beans/queue/<owner>--<repo>--<pr>.json. It holds the table’s placement, a reason that begins ACK: and says what the PR waits on, and beans, copied from the PR body. Validate it against MergeQueueEntrySchema. | A note on each work item the PR serves, one file per work item per branch: beans/notes/<bean>--<date>--<branch>.md. A note, never an append to the work item def; bean-coordination (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) says why. Then run bun run cat beans:notes, or CI’s beans:notes:check goes red. | One comment on the PR naming the entry and the work items. Before the work items cutover, items 1 and 2 reach main only through the steward’s own PR, a cycle late, so the comment is the ACK the author sees now. After the cutover, write 1 and 2 with state:push; the comment then just points at them. | . A PR whose body names no work item gets the entry with beans: [] and a comment asking the author to name one. The steward does not invent the association.

cfdfed55a819.title: Every open PR has an entry: review the whole list, then triage it
cfdfed55a819.content: merge:steward skips drafts, and a PR that nobody ACKed has no entry, so the queue silently shrinks to the PRs someone happened to look at. On a review, and at least once per working session: . | List every open PR, drafts included, from the API; not from the steward’s table and not from memory. | Every PR without an entry gets one with status: "unknown". A draft gets the placement rule: "draft", class: "hand-back", rank: 99, and its decision names the steward, not the DMN, because the table never placed it. Claiming the table did would be a fact the steward invented. | Triage each one into a status (QUEUE_STATUSES in schemas/sdlc/merge-queue.ts), with the evidence in reason: . | status | when | . | active | its author pushed or commented within 24 hours | . | waiting-on-author | handed back with a named ask, and the author is not back yet | . | blocked | waits on another PR, work item or ruling, named in reason | . | stale | no push and no human comment for more than 24 hours. Bot pushes from merge-main do not count as activity | . | approval-void | the owner approved it, and then its scope changed | . | landed | merged. The entry stays as history; it is never deleted | . | Report the stale ones to the owner as a decision, never close them: closing a PR is the author’s or the owner’s call (deletion-requires-confirmation). | . An approval is for the content that was approved. A branch can change scope after approval. Compare the title and the changed-file count against what was approved before landing. On a mismatch, set approval-void and ask again.

12d0f21eaa51.title: Your merge cadence is an input to the bot’s throughput
12d0f21eaa51.content: Pacing and concurrency are one question, not two. merge-main.yml sweeps the merge-main-labelled PRs on every push to main, so each merge you land starts a sweep — and the per-PR merge job’s concurrency group decides what happens to the sweep already running. A sweep takes 1–15 minutes, and a steward draining the queue can land a merge more often than that. cancel-in-progress is trigger-dependent, so a push sweep QUEUES behind the running one rather than killing it. The rule: . | A sweep in flight is work in progress — do not count a PR as unmergeable while its merge job is queued behind your last landing. Re-read it after the sweep settles. | When you are landing faster than the sweep completes, you are the reason the behind-PRs are not catching up. A merge still carries only main@T(n-1) -> T(n) per sweep; a burst of landings leaves a backlog of steps to carry. | .

64ecae081790.title: A hold has an EXPIRY and a trigger, or it outlives its reason
64ecae081790.content: A hold is a decision, and like every queue entry it records what the steward decided — not a fact. Facts move. So a hold is only valid while the condition that justified it is still true, and the steward re-derives that condition at every sweep rather than inheriting it. Write a hold with three parts or do not write one: . | part | why | . | what it waits on | the condition, stated so it can be checked mechanically | . | what ends it | the observation that lifts it, not a time | . | what it costs | which PRs are being held, so the price is visible | . Two failures that both look like diligence: . | Inheriting a hold across its own justification. Once the condition a hold waited on has passed, the hold must go. A hold whose reason you cannot restate from current facts is not a hold, it is a habit. | Holding to protect a PR that was already conflicted. A head that needs a forward merge whatever happens is protected by nothing. If the thing you are protecting already needs the work your hold is avoiding, the hold is free of benefit and not free of cost. | .

d7906ea6f385.title: Sweep the whole queue; a tracked handful is not the queue
d7906ea6f385.content: Compute the mergeable set from the open-PR list every time, never from the PRs you happen to be following. A PR not in your mental list is in no list at all. The sweep is cheap and mechanical: for every open non-draft PR, read base.ref, run git merge-tree --write-tree origin/main <head> for the rc, and read the check runs on that exact head. Three columns, one pass. A PR with base == main and rc == 0 is a candidate; whether it is mergeable is still the OWED question above, not a count of failures. no failures and nothing pending is NOT green. One completed check out of the full suite reads bad=0 wait=0 because almost nothing has been asked: a gate that did not fire is indistinguishable from one that passed, and a tally of failures cannot tell them apart. So the third column is the owed SET, never a count: compare the check-run names on that head against the set owed for its event, and treat a missing name exactly as a red one. A steward that cannot say why it is not merging a PR which is green on the owed set is holding it by accident; one that merges on bad=0 wait=0 alone is merging unverified. The exact meaning of “all green” for a merge, including the full tier and superseded cancelled jobs, is rule 1 of merge-manager-watcher §”Merge-sweep rules”. bun run cat merge:watch prints that verdict for every open PR.

41bb2a2db7c7.title: Read base.ref BEFORE anything else: a stacked PR is not a main-queue member
41bb2a2db7c7.content: merge-tree origin/main <head> answers a question nobody asked when the PR’s base is not main. Mergeability, independence and placement are all computed against the base, so a stacked PR measured against main is measured against the wrong tree — and the merge button lands it on the wrong tree too. A PR merged onto a stacked base closes as merged while its commits are not on main. The tell is cheap and it is first: gh api repos/<o>/<r>/pulls/<n> --jq .base.ref. A queue sweep must print the base. A stacked PR is not admitted to the main queue. Either its base lands first and the PR is re-measured against main, or it is rebased onto main by its author. The steward’s job is to notice, not to resolve it. GitHub does not retarget a stacked PR when its base PR merges. It retargets only when the base BRANCH is deleted, and these repositories keep merged branches. So “stacked on #N, GitHub retargets to main when #N merges”, a sentence a PR body may well carry, is false here. Read base.ref again after the lower PR merges, and retarget it yourself (PATCH .../pulls/<n> with base=main) before merging.

f66422c4ae3a.title: git add -A after a merge silently reverts the submodule gitlinks
f66422c4ae3a.content: And git submodule status does not catch it. A merge resolves a submodule gitlink like any other path. git add -A then re-records every submodule at whatever the working tree happens to have checked out, overwriting the resolution. If you initialised submodules before merging, and the base advanced them, you have just reverted them to the merge base — and git submodule status shows no + and no -, because the index and the working tree agree with each other. They are simply both wrong. The symptom is usually not a submodule error but regen reporting checks as “a real defect, not staleness”, from a module-load failure such as an export not found in a submodule script. Two rules follow: . | Stage explicitly after a merge, never git add -A, while any submodule is in the tree. | Verify the pins against the ref, not against the working tree. git ls-tree <ref> bootstrap bootstrap-tools is what exposes this; git submodule status cannot, and a check that cannot see the defect is not evidence of its absence. | .

444df48f4abe.title: A local gate run in a contended container is not evidence — and here is the ratio
444df48f4abe.content: A bun test shard in a shared agent container can run about ten times slower than on a dedicated runner, and at that ratio the default 5 s per-test budget stops measuring the code: . grep -c "timed out after 5000ms" -> N grep -cE "^error:|Expected:|Received:|toBe|toEqual" -> 0 . So the signature is cheap to check and worth checking before you believe a red local run: all failures are timed out after Nms and the assertion-failure count is zero. That is contention. Report it as inconclusive under contention — never as green, and never as a defect — and let CI on the exact sha be the authority. What you must not do is “fix” a test that is not broken, and never skip, disable or quarantine a test to get green applies with full force here, because the temptation is strongest when the failure is not real. Two ways to get this measurement wrong: . | A count read from a partial log, before the run ends, is not a count. | A compound command’s exit status is the last command’s, and a test runner’s status has to be captured before anything else runs. | .

5a21974312d5.title: Agentic pre-merge review: warn-only and the would-have-blocked counterfactual
5a21974312d5.content: Agentic merge review is warn-only. Architectural decision: staying WARN-ONLY with measured justification . The decision to keep agentic code review warn-only is governed by empirical evidence, not caution: . | Literature gap: Across five ingested agentic SE papers (CodeAgent arXiv:2402.02172v5, SWE-Debate arXiv:2404.04834v4, SWE-Router arXiv:2507.23348v1, TCAndon-Router arXiv:2601.04544v1, He et al. arXiv:2607.00053v1), zero empirical false-positive rates (FPR) exist for an LLM judge. | CodeAgent’s unconfirmed flag rate: CodeAgent’s own human annotation revealed that 48.6% of GPT-4’s flags were unconfirmed. A reviewer where nearly half of all flags are unconfirmed cannot be a blocking gate. | SWE-Router & SWE-Debate noise boundaries: LLM-as-a-judge suffers from self-enhancement bias, verbosity bias, and positional bias. | Deterministic compile checks stay blocking: G5 (Lean module compilation), G6 (SUSHI FHIR compilation), and G7 (JSON-LD schema validation) are deterministic compile gates that have exact binary outcomes and remain blocking. An agentic reviewer does not share this property. | Backlog inversion: A blocking gate over an active codebase with unreviewed content nodes would fail on existing background patterns rather than PR delta, inverting the order of necessary backfill. | . The counterfactual instrument: why only a warn-only phase can measure FPR . A blocking gate destroys the counterfactual: when a gate blocks, authors modify code, bypass checks, or abandon PRs. It is impossible to determine whether the flagged condition would have actually broken production or represented a false positive. By contrast, a warn-only gate records blocking-severity findings as “would have blocked” (WouldHaveBlockedRecordSchema in schemas/sdlc/merge-queue.ts), pinned to the PR’s headSha. The PR then merges to main. Subsequent monitoring observes whether any defect materialized, enabling humans to adjudicate findings: . | true_positive: Finding correctly identified a genuine defect. | false_positive: Finding flagged benign, correct code. | unknown: Third state (inconclusive, unverified, or cannot be determined). | . The third-state rule: unknown is strictly preserved and never folded into true_positive (which would artificially deflate FPR) or false_positive (which would artificially inflate FPR). Pre-registered promotion criteria . To prevent choosing thresholds to fit data, promotion criteria are registered as numbers and windows before data collection begins (AgenticPromotionCriteriaSchema): . | minimumPrWindow: 50 evaluated PRs. | maximumFalsePositiveRate: <= 0.05 (5% FPR: confirmedFalsePositives / (confirmedTruePositives + confirmedFalsePositives)). | minimumReviewCoverage: >= 0.80 (80% non-unknown adjudication: (confirmedTruePositives + confirmedFalsePositives) / warnedFindings). | . Until all three criteria are empirically proven, the agentic review remains warn-only.

608c667394a8.title: Tool-integrated agentic pre-merge review (CodeAgent / 2402.02172v5)
608c667394a8.content: Codified in research/methodologies/agentic-pre-merge-review.md (opt-in cat-harness.research). Multi-agent tool-integrated code review architectures (Tang et al., arXiv:2402.02172v5) structure automated pre-merge evaluation into specialized roles (Reviewer, Coder, QA-Checker, Consistency, Security) across four sequential phases. Three operational rules govern its integration into this repository’s merge queue: . | The Deterministic vs. Judged Boundary: Deterministic compile gates (Lean formal proofs, SUSHI/FHIR IG AST, JSON-LD schema renders, linter and test suites) answer questions with one computable truth — these MUST BLOCK. LLM-mediated agentic code reviews answer questions with uncalibrated error rates — these MUST WARN (“would have blocked”), exiting 0 and logging structured finding sidecars. | The False-Positive Guard: an automated review gate must never block merge on unverified LLM assertions (see the unconfirmed flag rate above). Promotion from warn to block requires measured calibration against recorded repository defects, per the pre-registered criteria above. | Bounded Dialogue Budgets: Conversational QA-Checker loops must cap at a maximum of 2 adjustment iterations to avoid latency explosions (CodeAgent measured 5 min / $0.122 per review) and context window exhaustion. Deterministic formatters and linters must run directly in CLI gates (bun run cat gates) rather than consuming multi-turn LLM reasoning. | .

166c52b00014.title: What this does not do yet
166c52b00014.content: The train’s size is a fixed cap. Sizing it by risk waits for this process’s own run records, which is why each run is a committed instance under beans/workflows/. The tools named on the steps (merge:overlap, merge:train, merge:leftover) live on branch claude/merge-pipeline-tools until it lands.

0188d51bdff7.title: merge-queue (skill)
0188d51bdff7.content: The skill merge-queue as its source file cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/merge-queue.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

ae2e4de0c709.title: Merge to main — a sub-process with its own gate
ae2e4de0c709.content: Skill merge-to-main: Merging to main is its own step with its own gate: the merge-to-main sub-process, which every process that lands work CALLS rather than inlines. Covers the evidence read live on the head (CI per owed job, mergeability, review state, Claude Approvals where the repository runs it), why a repository with no CI is never green, who may authorise a merge and what does NOT count as authorisation (“fix all issues until green” does not), how the authorisation is recorded, and the post-merge steps: base green, site republished, downstream re-pins, work item and issue. Use for “merge it”, “land this PR”, “merge the green PRs”, and before any write to a default branch in any repository. Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Guideline Updates, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . sdlc/processes/merge-to-main.bpmn (Process_MergeToMain) is the process. Its two gateways are computed by merge-evidence.dmn and merge-authorisation.dmn. Every process that ends in a write to main calls it. Today that is merge-train.bpmn (Call_MergeToMain) and crdm-close.bpmn (Call_MergeToMain, between the recorded sign-off and the issue close). prepare-merge stops before it; prepare-merge-auto Phase 4 runs it. A process that merges without calling it is a process with a hole in it, and the remedy is a call activity, not a paragraph.

ae7dc0955537.title: Why this is a process of its own
ae7dc0955537.content: A merge inlined as the last line of another process cannot refuse, and does not cover a repository with no CI. As its own step it can.

3c38b2d6f444.title: The steps
3c38b2d6f444.content: CI regenerates the harness projections on the head (harness-projections). The merging session then reads the evidence, runs local gates if there is no CI, finds the authorisation and asks for it if it is missing. The owner answers: merge, hold or refuse. The merging session records the answer (not relaxable), merges pinned to the head, confirms main, republishes the repository’s site, re-pins downstream mounts and reports. Each step’s own text is in the diagram. The merging session is the merge-steward lane, and only it merges (owner ruling, 2026-11-13). With none active, the siblings elect one first, and the PR’s own session merges only when it is the one elected (merge-queue §”When no Merge Manager is active”). The gate is the same either way.

8b8205421a1c.title: Evidence — read on the head, live, every time
8b8205421a1c.content: What lands is the head the evidence was read on. Read these facts from GitHub at the time of the merge. Never use a copy from earlier in the session. | fact | values | read from | . | ciState | green, red, pending, none, unreadable | the workflow runs whose head_sha is the PR’s head, per OWED job (merge-queue §”Admission asks which runs are OWED”). Not the PR page, and not the legacy status API. | . | mergeable | clean, dirty, unknown | the PR’s mergeable / mergeable_state. unknown stays unknown after a short re-ask. Only dirty is believed on its own (prepare-merge §Guardrails, step 0). | . | review | clear, blocking, unknown | open CHANGES_REQUESTED reviews, unresolved threads a reviewer marked blocking, a draft PR, a needs-merge-human label, and Claude Approvals where the repository runs it: its required review or check must be present and approving on this head. A repository that runs it and has no approval on the head is blocking, not clear. | . Where the repository has merge:guard (cat-harness and the layers composed with it), its evaluate mode IS this step. Exit 0 means green/clean/clear, exit 1 maps each refused check to its fact, and exit 2 is unreadable, never a pass. Its eight checks are listed in merge-queue §”A PR lands only through merge:guard”. Where it does not exist, read the same facts with the GitHub tools and write each one down with the URL it came from. CI gates a release only (owner, 2026-11-08) . Owner, card Q-CIB-4 A, 2026-11-08, after “CI not gate on non-release merge to main” and “not all CI needs to run unless doing a release build”: . | A non-release merge does not wait for CI. ciState is still read and written into the report, red included, but it refuses nothing. Mergeability, review, the ready: marker, the label and the owner’s authorisation all still decide. Content still needs the owner, and committee content still never merges: those are authorisation rules, and they are unchanged. | A release merge is gated. A merge is a release when the PR carries the release label or the guard runs with --release. Then every owed job must be green, as before. | Main is judged after the merge, by the integration run on main (the full suite on main’s tip, batched; see release-lifecycle §”The release gate”). A red integration run files one fix issue naming the merges in its range. It does not hold the queue. | . This replaces, for non-release merges only: main-green-first (card Q-CIB-1 B, 2026-11-08), the 2026-10-23 ruling that a layer PR merges only on a green index run with it pinned, and “merge non-content when green” in the merge window rules. merge-evidence.dmn then decides, in this order: hand-back on red (a release), dirty or blocking (to merge-refusal, which returns the PR to its owner with the reason); unknown when a fact could not be read (ends, not merged); not-yet while runs are pending or mergeability is uncomputed (ends; re-enter later); no-ci on a clean, clear head with no CI; ready when everything is green, clean and clear, and ready on a non-release merge whose head is clean and clear, whatever CI said (its release input is false).

10be835a9100.title: A repository with no CI is not green (STRICT)
10be835a9100.content: none means nothing tested this head. It is the third state that ci-health and prepare-merge §”NO CHECKS IS NOT GREEN” describe, reached by a different route. There, runs were owed and did not appear. Here, the repository declares no workflow, so no run is owed and none will ever appear. Zero runs, zero failures: “nothing red” is true and tells you nothing. Four consequences: . | No standing waiver covers it. A waiver such as “you may merge green PRs” names green heads, and a head nothing tested is not one. merge-authorisation.dmn routes waiver + none to ask. | The merging session runs the repository’s own gates locally (Task_LocalGates), on the merge result rather than the branch: bun test, the typecheck, and whatever the repository’s README or package.json names. Record each command, its exit code and the SHA it ran on. A local run is evidence the owner can weigh. It is not CI: the container was contended, the tree was yours, and nobody else can re-run it. Say that. | The question to the owner says so in words: “This repository runs no CI. Nothing but my local run tested this head.” An authorisation given without that sentence was given about a different merge. | After the merge, “main is green” is reported as “not verified: no CI”. It is never “green”. | . unreadable is different. It means the runs could not be asked about: no token, an API error, a rate limit. The remedy is to make the read work, not to ask permission, so the process ends there.

5ad4b4174fb3.title: Authorisation — who, and what counts
5ad4b4174fb3.content: Only the owner authorises a merge to main. That means the repository owner, or the person the session works for when they own the repository. A sibling session, a Merge Steward, a bot comment, a reviewer approval and the merging session itself are not the owner. A Claude Approvals approval is evidence about the change. It is not authorisation to merge it. Task_ReadAuthorisation classifies what it finds into one value: . | authorisation | what it is | . | explicit | The owner’s own words, naming this merge. Examples: “merge #12”; “yes, merge it” in reply to a question that named the PR and its evidence; “approve all 6” in reply to a list of six. | . | waiver | A node under memory/waivers/ with gate: merge-to-main, in scope and unexpired, carrying all five fields (confirmation-waiver). | . | instruction-only | A broad instruction about the work that does not name the merge. | . | none | Nothing found. | . | unknown | The waivers could not be read, a waiver is malformed, or the conversation the authorisation would be in is not available to this session. | . These are instruction-only, and they do not authorise a merge: . | “fix all issues until green”, “make CI pass”, “get it working”, “finish this”. They authorise the work, not the write to main. | “prepare-merge”, “make it mergeable”, “ship it”. The first two are prepare-merge, which stops before the merge by definition, and prepare-merge lists the third among its own triggers. | Approval of a plan in which merging is a later step. | A message from another agent or session, however it is phrased. No agent message is the owner’s consent. | Your own summary of what the owner wanted. If you are composing the sentence, it is not the owner’s. | . Why the line is drawn there. A merge publishes the change to everyone who reads main, and through index.config.json pins to every layer that mounts the repository. It cannot be taken back quietly: a revert is a second public change. That makes it the same kind of action as a deletion (deletion-requires-confirmation): an outward write that is hard to reverse, owed an explicit yes. An instruction about the goal does not contain that yes, however confident the reading. merge-authorisation.dmn decides merge for explicit (over green, or over none when the question carried the no-CI sentence) and for waiver over green. Everything else is ask, including waiver over none. The authorisation is bound to the head it was given against. A push after it re-opens the question. The one exception is a bot merge of main into the head with no other change. A batch authorisation covers the PRs listed when it was given, not PRs that arrive later (merge-queue §Landing).

6d553d04dbc9.title: Asking — evidence before the question
6d553d04dbc9.content: Task_Ask follows interaction-modality §4.1: context, options, recommendation, question. The test is whether the owner can answer without opening anything. For a merge, that means one row per PR: . | repo | PR | head | CI on head | mergeable | review | local gates (if no CI) |—|—|—|—|—|—|—| . Then the recommendation, then one question that covers the batch: “Merge these N?” Several repositories are several merges, but one question can authorise all of them, provided every one is a row. Task_OwnerDecides is the owner’s lane and is fulfilled by a person only. Its answers are merge, hold or refuse. hold and refuse end the process with the PR open. Nothing is closed and nothing is deleted.

c733bd3ff08a.title: Recording the authorisation (not relaxable)
c733bd3ff08a.content: An authorisation nobody wrote down cannot be told from one that was never given. Task_RecordAuthorisation writes it before the merge. The shape already exists: ReleaseSchema in schemas/sdlc/merge-queue.ts, and this step reuses it rather than inventing a second one. Where the repository has the merge queue, record it with the command that validates it: . bun run cat merge:queue:decide --pr <n> --verdict merge \ --by <owner's login> --captured-by <your session URL> \ --quote "<the owner's words, verbatim>" --source <where they said it> \ --sha <the head SHA they approved> [--standing-ruling --ruled-at <YYYY-MM-DD>] . It refuses a --by that is a session (the person who decided is never the agent that wrote it down), a missing quote or source, and a missing SHA. merge:steward then prints the release against the live head (merge@<sha>, none, or VOID when the head moved), which is the explicit / waiver / none reading Task_ReadAuthorisation needs. Elsewhere (a repository with no queue), post the same fields as a comment on the PR, signed with the session link, and append it to the work item: . merge-authorised: verdict: merge decidedBy: <owner's GitHub login> decidedAt: <ISO-8601 date-time> authority: explicit | standing-ruling (ruledAt: <date>) | waiver:<waiver node id> quote: "<the owner's words, verbatim>" source: <session link or comment permalink> releasedSha: <the full head SHA being merged> capturedBy: <your session URL> ci: green | none (local: <command> exit <code> @ <sha>; ...) . These fields match index.config.json’s trust consent one for one (by, on, ref, evidence). A quote that is not verbatim is not evidence: a paraphrase is the thing under suspicion, as confirmation-waiver says of a waiver’s quote. The same rule covers a re-pin’s trust.consent.evidence. It quotes the owner’s consent to THAT pin. A goal instruction in that field (“fix all issues until green”) records a consent that was never given.

71d94b704c8f.title: Merging
71d94b704c8f.content: Through merge:guard <pr> --merge --session <id> where the repository has it (it re-evaluates live and pins the PUT to the head); elsewhere with the merge call pinned to the head SHA, so GitHub refuses if the head moved. A merge commit unless told otherwise. Never delete the branch (prepare-merge §Guardrails).

57b22debbeb4.title: After the merge
57b22debbeb4.content: . | Task_ConfirmBase: read main’s CI on the merge commit. If it is red, fix forward (continual-progress §”Two green PRs can merge into a red main”). With no CI, report “not verified: no CI”. Do not report it as green. | Task_Republish: rebuild and republish the repository’s site. A merge that changes what a published site shows is not done until the site shows it. A repository that declares site.build publishes on its own: its .github/workflows/site-publish.yml calls the tools layer’s reusable folio-site-publish.yml on every push to main, so the merge itself starts the publish (owner, 2026-11-10). Your step is to check that run on the merge commit finished green and that the live page shows the change; a red or missing run is fixed forward, never published over. Runs queue one at a time per repository, so two quick merges publish in turn. A repository that declares site.build but has no site-publish.yml gets one from the tools layer’s document templates (templates/document/github/workflows/) in its own PR. Until then, build from the merge commit and publish agent-run (<tools> is the mounted tools layer’s directory): . bun run <tools>/scripts/build-instance-site.ts --root . \ --instance <name> --publish --remote https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> . The build’s gates stay in force either way: an unresolved link refuses the publish, and that refusal goes on the issue and is fixed forward. A repository whose own workflow publishes its site (docs-site-publish.bpmn) needs nothing here. With no site.build, record “no site to republish”. | Task_Repin: re-pin downstream mounts, as PRs, never as part of this merge. Find the layers whose index.config.json names this repository in source.remote.repository. For each, open a PR that moves ref to the merge commit, carries a trust.consent whose evidence quotes the owner’s consent to that pin, and regenerates index.lock.json with mount:remote (remote-mount, index-config). Each re-pin PR is a merge to main in another repository, so it runs this sub-process again. The merge authorisation covers the re-pin only if the owner’s words named the re-pin. When no layer mounts the repository, record “no downstream mounts found” and say where you looked. | Task_Report: a note on the work item with the merge SHA and the authorisation block, and a round summary on the issue (issue-working). Do not close the issue. In CRDM, crdm-close.bpmn closes it after this sub-process returns, and only on the BA’s authorisation. | .

7452f5232e45.title: What this does not do yet
7452f5232e45.content: . | Outside the merge queue, no tool prints authorisation. Where the queue exists, merge:steward prints the recorded release against the live head and check:waivers validates the waiver half. Elsewhere Task_ReadAuthorisation classifies it by reading the conversation, the PR and memory/waivers/. That is a judgement, and the record makes it auditable. | merge:guard does not refuse a merge with no recorded release. releaseCovers exists and merge:steward reports it, but the guard’s eight checks are about readiness. Making the guard require a covering release would turn this rule into a gate. That is a change to merge-guard.ts and is not part of this skill. | It does not change merge:guard’s check 5. In a repository with no workflows, check 5 refuses with “no pull_request run names the head”. Read that refusal as ciState: none and take the no-ci path, not hand-back: the PR has no defect for its owner to fix. | .

709620816ee6.title: Adopting a methodology, and choosing between them
709620816ee6.content: Skill methodology-adoption: How a named external methodology enters the knowledge graph, and how an agent picks which one applies. Read before following a judgement method, before adopting a new one, and before writing a house method instead of adopting one. Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Guideline Updates, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . A methodology is somebody else’s work, adopted whole. It is not a house process with a citation bolted on. The graph carries them as a distinct kind so that adopting one, replacing one and removing one are all ordinary operations. Methodologies are parallel ways of achieving the same process, chosen by context; each is formalised on its own and kept independent, so that other skills can incorporate it as a sub-graph.

872943660150.title: Parallel, not composable
872943660150.content: Two or more methodologies may answer the same question. Do not blend them. A composite — this one’s vocabulary, that one’s record, a third one’s filter — is a house method that cites nobody, and it inherits none of their authority while claiming all of it. So: pick one per decision, name it, and follow it.

31ca984bf1f6.title: Choosing which applies
31ca984bf1f6.content: First: is this a judgement, or a process? . Ask before the ladder. The ladder below is about how to decide something; a request for a change is not yet a decision but work needing agreed requirements before anything is built. Sent down the ladder, it lands on the catch-all rung and produces an options analysis for a question nobody has framed yet. Is somebody asking for a change, such that requirements have to be agreed before it is built? . If yes, the question is who is asking, and does the answer depend on what a folio says? . | A change to the platform’s own capability — a tool, a schema, a pipeline, a skill, a gate — raised by somebody building the tooling, whose answer does not depend on any folio’s subject matter → the software-development process methodology. | Requirements that come from stakeholders who must sign them off, tied to a folio’s domain → the stakeholder requirements methodology. | . Both answer request → agreed requirements, so they are parallel and must not be blended — the refusal below applies to this pair first and hardest. Which is which is stated in each one’s applies-when, not here, for the reason in §”Why this skill does not name them”. If no — the change is agreed and the question is how to decide something within it — continue to the ladder. Then the ladder . Ask in this order. The first yes decides. | Do the criteria recur, with the same inputs having to produce the same answer? → the computable methodology. A one-off tabled as if it recurs asserts a repeatability it does not have. | Is the question the certainty of a body of evidence behind a recommendation? → the evidence-grading methodology. Note this is about evidence, not about a design choice that happens to be uncertain. | Is the context a work item recording a decision? → the decision-record methodology. It constrains the record, not the method, so it composes with (1) or (4) rather than competing. | Otherwise — a one-off choice among candidate options → the decision-analysis methodology. | . If none fits, that is a finding, not a licence. Say which question the decision is and that no adopted methodology covers it. Do not improvise one and do not stretch the nearest fit: either is how a house method gets in. Why this skill does not name them . Naming each methodology here would couple this skill to the set, and the set is meant to be extractable: a methodology can be lifted out, or replaced, without a prose edit here. So the declared set is the contents of the methodology graph, read from the layer’s declaration. Ask for it; do not remember it.

a3c0c9b916df.title: Node, skill, or both?
a3c0c9b916df.content: An adopted methodology can produce up to two artefacts: . | you are writing | it is a node in the methodology graph | it is a skill | . | what the method IS — its vocabulary, its constraints, what it refuses | ✅ | ❌ | . | how to PERFORM it here — the extension element, the gate, the procedure | ❌ | ✅ | . | a house process with no external origin | ❌ | ✅ — and do not dress it as an adoption | . Most adoptions produce both, and the split is the same every time: the node is the method, the skill is this platform’s application of it. The skill names the node and does not restate it, because two files carrying one definition is two copies free to drift. Three worked cases: . | raci — both. The four letters and the one-Accountable rule are the method (node); reading R from the BPMN lane, the cat-harness.processes:raci element and check:raci are this platform’s application (skill). | crdm — both (methodologies/crdm.md). PHII’s three concentration areas (Business Process Analysis, Business Process Redesign, Requirements Definition), the Business Process Matrix, swimlane Task Flow Diagrams, and PATH’s activity-linked requirement structure are the external method (node, backed by library/phii-2023-crdm, library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, and library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm); agentic facilitation, 7-dimension code impact analysis, work-item decomposition, and pull-request merge sign-off are this platform’s adaptation (crdm-requirements-workflow and crdm-requirements-template). | swot — both. | . A methodology in use with no node is invisible to the graph: check:methodology-evidence and every other reader of the methodology graph count nodes, not skills.

6d1990736f43.title: Adopting a new one — the ingestion process
6d1990736f43.content: . | Establish it is external and named. A methodology has an origin: authors, a publication, a standards body. If it has none, it is a house process — write it as a skill and do not dress it as an adoption. | Render it faithfully, and say where the rendering stops. The file carries what the method says, not a summary of what we liked. Where this platform adopts part of a method and refuses part, both halves are stated with the reason — a silent omission misrepresents the standard. | Declare its applicability. applies-when in the front matter, phrased so the selection question above can reach it, and saying what it is not for. | Place it by ownership, not by convenience. A domain-neutral method belongs to the harness; a domain method belongs to the repo that owns the domain. The separation plan decides, and the placement must make extraction literal — the directory lifts out, its declaration entry goes with it, and nothing else moves. | Declare the directory. A methodology outside a declared directory is invisible to every tool that reads the graph. | State its refusals. The part of a method a platform must not do is as load-bearing as the part it follows, and it is the part a later agent will breach first. | Ingest the source and cite it as evidence. origin names the work; evidence: library/<bib-slug> points at a copy a reader can open from this checkout. Use literature-search to find it and library-ingestion to bring it in. Where the source cannot be fetched, that is an outcome to report — a located-but-unreachable document, never a missing one — and the node keeps its origin with no evidence until somebody closes the gap. | .

9d9c027bdc9b.title: Extract the PROCESS, not the paper’s tools
9d9c027bdc9b.content: A source that presents a method through an implementation is presenting two things, and only one of them is the methodology. Render the method first, then decide which tools — existing or to be added — this platform should use to perform it. A node that adopted the source’s tool stack would be adopting an implementation and calling it a method, and it could never be falsified: the tools would work and the method would never be examined. hybrid-llm-deterministic is the worked case. Its source demonstrates the method in one tool with one model and one expression language; the node renders the rule/result inversion, the five safeguards and the bounded-truncation technique, and §”Where this rendering stops” names every tool it declined to adopt and why. The method survives replacing all of them, which is the test of whether you extracted a method at all. Ask it as: what would still be true if they had built it differently? What survives is the methodology. What does not is their engineering, and it belongs in the skill if anywhere — where this platform’s own tool choices already live. And say what the source does NOT establish. A demonstration is not an evaluation. Where a paper shows an approach working once, with no baseline and no measurement, the node records that no performance claim rests on it. Doing otherwise manufactures a finding the authors did not make — the same failure as §”Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured”, arriving through a citation instead.

bbd041ce9105.title: An origin nobody can open is not evidence
bbd041ce9105.content: A methodology’s justification is being somebody else’s named, external work, so its origin must resolve to a source a reader can open. bun run cat check:methodology-evidence is the axis that makes this visible, and test/results/methodology-evidence.qa-results.json is where it is recorded. It reports and does not gate on a missing source: whether a methodology whose source nobody can open may still be used is the owner’s call, and a gate failing on the whole corpus at once would be switched off. It does fail on front matter that does not validate, and on an evidence pointing at a bib-slug no library holds, because a citation that claims to resolve and does not is worse than none. The evidence is an input to SELECTION, not only to adoption. options-analysis.bpmn’s A_CheckEvidence reads it before the chosen methodology is applied. Adoption happens once; selection happens at every decision, and a source can stop being reachable in between. A contested origin is recorded as contested. methodologies/swot.md is the worked example: the usual attribution is repeated everywhere and its own source says no academic reference supports it, so the node declines to name an inventor: flattening that into a fact would carry the authority of a citation while resting on nothing.

5abc1518de02.title: Refusals
5abc1518de02.content: . | Never blend two methodologies into one procedure. Parallel means parallel. | Never adopt a methodology by naming it. A citation with no rendered method is an appeal to authority that no reader can check. | Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured. Where a method scores and sums, this platform adopts the structure and refuses the arithmetic: a total reads as a measurement, and the weights were invented. This is the same rule as never quoting a count from prose as though it were evidence. | Never let a rejected option go unrecorded. Whichever methodology was used, the alternatives and why they lost are part of the output — the same argument bean-coordination makes for scrapped over deleted. | Never write a method from recall and cite a paper nobody fetched. Read the source, or say you read it through another and mark each attribution second-hand. See literature-search §”Never fill the gap with recall”. | .

31e4cbc79089.title: methodology-adoption (skill)
31e4cbc79089.content: The skill methodology-adoption as its source file cat-harness/skills/process/process-core/methodology-adoption.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

23af925c284f.title: Does the prose say what the code does?
23af925c284f.content: Skill narrative-asserts-code: Judge whether the prose side of a declared prose ↔ code pair still says what the code does, when the machine could not settle it. Reads the two mechanical signals first — staleness and resolvable claims — and settles what is left in one of three ways, sending a disagreement with a checker to adjudication. General: the Lean case is a specialisation with its own skill. Named by: Committee review of a content change, Merge and publish a content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Make a decided public comment change, Public comment on a review draft, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate . A reader acts on what the prose says. When prose and code disagree, the reader either avoids a working feature or rebuilds it. This skill is the judgement step. The machine has already done everything it can, and your job is the rest.

4de08026bfa3.title: The pairs this applies to — declared, never inferred
4de08026bfa3.content: | pair | prose | code | declared by | . | diagram ↔ workflow | a .bpmn diagram’s <documentation> | the .github/workflows/*.yml it draws | # bpmn: <diagram> in the workflow (+ # bpmn-node: <id> per job) | . | skill ↔ code | a skill .md | the same-stem .ts beside it | the file sitting there | . | proof ↔ Lean | a paper block’s .md | its lean.ref | the block manifest — see below, it has its own skill | . A pair nothing declares is out of scope. Do not go looking for prose that “seems to describe” some code: an inferred pair is a guess, and a finding on a guess is how a check gets switched off.

ae62c65ce780.title: Read the machine’s output first — it is already in the sidecar
ae62c65ce780.content: Two kg-qa criteria on the subject’s sidecar tell you what is open: . | prose-reviewed-since-code-changed. fail means the code changed and the prose did not. It says nothing about truth, only that nobody re-read the prose. | prose-claims-resolve. Each claim the prose makes about the code comes out holds, false or undetermined. bun run cat pairs:claims prints the whole list, including what it did not check. | . What you judge is exactly the stale pairs, the false claims and the undetermined claims. A claim that holds and a pair that is not stale need nothing from you.

92fa612c1d62.title: Three outcomes, and each leaves a record
92fa612c1d62.content: . | The prose holds. Say why, in one sentence, and attest the pair: bun run cat pairs:attest -- --sidecar <sidecar> --by agent|human --reason "…". A reason is required because an attestation nobody can review is not evidence. Name what you compared: “the TypeScript step describes the repository gates and bun run cat gates derives its list from this job” is a reason; “looks fine” is not. | The prose and the code really disagree. Raise a finding against the side that is wrong. Usually that is the prose, because the code is what runs, but not always: a skill can state the intended behaviour correctly while the code has regressed. Say which side, and why that side. | You disagree with a checker’s false. The machine says a claim is false and you read it as true, or the other way round. Do not overrule it quietly. That disagreement is exactly what adjudication exists for: call Process_CriterionAdjudication (the QA-criterion specialisation of adjudication, whose outcomes are: the finding stands, the criterion is scoped, or a dispensation is granted), and the checker’s entry is kept beneath the verdict, because a disagreement between a checker and a reviewer is information. | .

5d093a62ad3f.title: Lean is the specialisation, not the model
5d093a62ad3f.content: For a proof ↔ Lean pair, a proof assistant can settle the formal claim mechanically, which no other pair kind allows. That work belongs to proof-narrative-lean-equivalence (the science layer): stub-weakening, overreach, hypothesis mismatch and notation drift. This skill states the question for every pair kind, and that one answers it for Lean. Nothing Lean-specific goes here, so a pair kind added later inherits the general question without inheriting Lean’s machinery.

7b23ae034519.title: normative-statements
7b23ae034519.content: Named by: Authoring a document, Data sharing agreement document life cycle . Carry a recommendation, requirement or rule in a document folio — the thing an L1 health-policy guidance note, a standard, or a terms-of-reference document exists to state.

75f40e7647f2.title: The problem this addresses
75f40e7647f2.content: A normative statement is the block readers cite, implementers trace to, and reviewers sign off individually, so it needs a label, a stable identity and a place in the dependency graph. It is not a theorem: nothing proves it, and its authority is the issuing body’s.

67fbd1dfa727.title: What to do
67fbd1dfa727.content: Use a recommendation block: one statement per block, with a label, a title, and its strength as a code. // folio/<slug>/<chapter>/rec-cold-chain-audit.ts import { recommendation } from "@folio/schemas/builders"; export default recommendation({ label: "rec:cold-chain-audit", title: "Audit the cold chain quarterly", strength: { list: "grade-recommendation-strength", code: "conditional" }, uses: ["rec:scope", "prose:cold-chain-terms"], about: ["hi:cold-chain-management"], }); . The block’s .md holds the statement itself, and its label becomes the anchor every cross-reference targets ([see](#rec:cold-chain-audit)). | label: a prefix of your folio’s own choosing, kept consistent across the corpus. The platform reserves none: the kind’s node says prefixEnforced: false. rec: is recognised, never required. Pick a prefix once and write it down in the folio’s own AGENTS.md. | title: the short form the document’s index and any cross-reference will show. | strength: a code in a declared code list, not free text. Core declares two: . | grade-recommendation-strength: strong or conditional, GRADE as the WHO handbook for guideline development applies it; | rfc2119-requirement-level: must, must-not, should, should-not, may, from BCP 14. | . A folio whose issuing body grades differently declares its own folio-code-list/v1 in its code-lists/ rather than editing these. The check is “resolves in the scheme”: strengthFinding in folio-assistant-core/schemas/recommendation-strength.ts. State the strength in the prose too, in the issuing body’s own words, because readers read the prose. | uses[]: the blocks a reader must have read to act on this one. That means definitions of terms it uses, the scope statement it sits under, and the evidence summary it rests on. This is what makes “what else changes if this recommendation changes?” answerable. | about[]: optional labels of the DAK health-interventions this recommendation is about. It is a link, not a merge: the two vocabularies stay separate, and nothing in this one depends on the DAK adapter. | . Keep one statement per block. A block holding three recommendations cannot be cited, reviewed, superseded or traced individually, and splitting it later means renumbering everything that referenced it. Converting a labelled prose block. Change the builder call from prose to recommendation and add strength. The label, title, uses[] and .md stay as they are, so no reference breaks.

11ce46bffe9a.title: When the statement comes from a source
11ce46bffe9a.content: A normative statement or requirement that a SOURCE makes is already a node in that source’s L1 entry (l1-document-ingestion, “Requirements and normative statements”), with the source’s own number in meta.source_number. Cite that node from the block’s meta.source, and keep the source’s number in the title or prose. Do not mint a new id that looks like the source’s: a reader cannot tell the two apart.

b7bd7dcba371.title: What not to do
b7bd7dcba371.content: . | Do not use definition. It is a math kind: its lean field is required, so the block will not validate in a document folio at all. | Do not use a bare prose block. It validates, but no criterion can tell it is normative. | Do not use theorem or proposition for a good-practice statement. They are outside this profile and content_profile_check rejects them. | Do not encode the recommendation number in the label alone. Numbers are renumbered between editions; the label must survive that. Put the published number in the title or the prose. | .
