c29a151db050.title: Prepare-merge — get a feature branch ready to land
c29a151db050.content: Skill prepare-merge: Take a feature branch to a clean, conflict-free, green, pushed state so it can be merged with no surprises: base merged in, generated files regenerated, the folio’s content-type gates run, then pushed. It does NOT merge and does NOT push to the default branch. Use for “prepare-merge”, “make it mergeable”, “ship it”. Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Guideline Updates, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Canonical, repo-agnostic recipe for taking a claude/* (or any feature) branch to a clean, conflict-free, green, pushed state so it can be merged with no surprises. Downstream repositories vendor or sync it rather than maintaining their own copy. “Prepare-merge” is a plain-English ask, not a built-in command, so without one recipe each agent re-derives the steps, inconsistently or unsafely. “Prepare-merge” ≠ “merge”. It makes the branch mergeable and stops. It does not push to the default branch and does not merge a PR. Both are outward-facing, hard-to-reverse actions — do them only on an explicit request. The merge itself is its own sub-process with its own gate, merge-to-main: evidence on the head, the owner’s authorisation for THAT merge, recorded, then the merge. Asking for prepare-merge (or “ship it”) is not that authorisation.

bde9ff840f18.title: fsh-guts must not reach publication
bde9ff840f18.content: Before a branch that touches the knowledge graph ships, the published export must contain no reference to fsh-guts — not the graph typology, not the declared directory, not the skill that documents it, and not an edge naming any of them. scripts/tests/fsh-guts-unpublished.test.ts asserts it against the built artefact and runs in bun test. The mechanism is in kg-export §”fsh-guts NEVER reaches a published graph”.

f3596c0f68b6.title: Recipe
f3596c0f68b6.content: . | Clean + committed. git status --short must be empty. Commit outstanding work first (the container is ephemeral — uncommitted work is lost on resume). | Fetch the base + your branch (retry on network error, backoff 2/4/8/16s): git fetch origin <base> <branch>. | Integrate if the base moved. Compare git merge-base HEAD origin/<base> to git rev-parse origin/<base>: . | Equal → base hasn’t moved; nothing to do (your branch is a clean fast-forward). | Different → bring the base in, resolve conflicts, then re-run the green check. A rebase needs a force-push with lease: git push --force-with-lease — never a bare --force (it clobbers sibling pushes). | . Merge with bun run cat merge:main, never a plain git merge followed by regen. It resolves every conflict a declared pattern covers (glossaries, translated glossaries, UML, viewer pages, site data, QA sidecars), refuses the rest with the tree restored, and runs regen on the result. A plain git merge stops on those same generated files, one by one. After EVERY base merge, conflicted or not, run bun run cat regen — see §”A clean merge can produce a wrong artefact” below. If you merged with bun run cat merge:main, its regen already was that run; do not run a second one. For a merge whose conflicts were all generated, the round is merge-conflict-patterns §”A merge round — run each check ONCE”: targeted checks and a push, with CI’s sharded run as the full gate set in place of a local bun run cat gates or check:merged. An authored conflict, or a merge that touched code, still owes both. A conflict in test/results/ or test/attestations/: see §”Conflicts in test/results/ and test/attestations/” below before resolving either by hand. | Prove it merges cleanly (no assumptions): . | git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/<base> HEAD → success means a clean fast-forward, so conflicts are impossible. This alone is sufficient. | Otherwise dry-run with git merge-tree --write-tree origin/<base> HEAD (exit 0 = clean; non-zero = not clean; add --name-only to list the conflicted paths) and trust its exit code AND its first line. Exit 1 means CONFLICT only when stdout opens with the merged tree’s id — git also exits 1 for a ref it cannot merge (unfetched, mistyped), printing no tree, and that is “could not determine”, never “conflicted with nothing in conflict”. | Capture $? on the line after the command, before anything else runs — git merge-tree … >/dev/null 2>&1; rc=$?, or cmd || rc=$?. echo "base($(git rev-parse --short origin/main)) rc=$?" reports the SUBSTITUTION’s status, always 0 when the ref exists. if ! cmd; then rc=$? is the same trap: inside that branch $? is ! cmd’s status, 0. shell-exit-status.test.ts fails on either shape in a tracked script or workflow. | GitHub’s HTTP 405 “Pull Request has merge conflicts” is a backstop, not a check — it is learned at merge time, after the PR was announced clean. Do not grep the old three-arg output for <<<<<<< / “changed in both”: that false-positives on files which legitimately contain those literals (docs about merge conflicts, test fixtures, this skill). | A clean text merge is not a clean state. merge-tree answers “do the files conflict?”, not “do the gates pass on the result?”. Before asking for a merge, run bun run cat check:merged: it builds the merge with the current base in a throwaway worktree and runs the full bun run cat gates there (exit 0 passes, 1 fails, 2 could not determine — never read as clean). A generated measurement can be green on the branch, green on the base, merge without a conflict, and be stale on the result. | GitHub’s merge queue tests exactly the commit that will land; the gating workflows carry merge_group: so it works once the owner turns it on. Until then, check:merged is the agent’s half. | . | Green check. Run the project’s tests/build (here: bun test, plus bun build <file> --target=bun for type-checking touched files). Report honestly: distinguish failures you caused from pre-existing ones (diff the counts against a baseline run on the merge-base). Do not call a branch green by silently inheriting red. Then run bun run cat security:gate, by name, and quote its result. It runs every security check this repository has (workflow injection, secret leaks, lockfile and toolchain pins, QA reviewer permission, materialised fixity) plus two advisories, and refuses when a blocking check fails OR could not be run. Most of those checks are also inside bun run cat gates; naming the command here makes the merge step cover security explicitly, rather than only when the CI run before it happened to include it. Its advisories (unpinned third-party actions, dependency advisories) are reported in the PR and are not cleared by a green gate. Check the adversarial review verdict with bun run cat check:adversarial-review. On any branch with agent provenance (trailers, claude/* branch, bot committer), it verifies that an independent adversarial review verdict exists, binds to the head SHA, and covers the full diff without silent truncation. Findings are warn-only (“would have blocked”): they are recorded, as data for deciding when to promote the check to a gate, and do not hold the merge. Know what the target covered. Green is a claim about the files the build compiled, which is usually fewer than the files on disk — build targets default to a root plus its transitive imports. Confirm the files you touched were in it (artifact count vs. source count, or build the module by name), and scope any corpus-wide number you quote to what actually ran. For contentType: paper branches that touch content blocks, also run the block_pdf_render gate: . bun run scripts/render-changed-blocks.ts [--upload-drive] . This compiles a standalone PDF for every changed block and scrapes the LaTeX log; --upload-drive additionally pushes clean PDFs to Google Drive when it is configured. Exits 1 on LaTeX errors (fix required); exits 0 with warnings only (advisory); exits 2 on setup problems — including no local latexmk, which is the common case in a container. Exit 2 means the gate did not run; report it that way rather than folding it into a green. For a branch that changes a folio’s blocks, report review coverage. content-change-review.bpmn’s coverage gate (GW_Covered, table decisions/review-coverage-gate.dmn) reads the block counts below and, where the preview published a rendered-impact.json, three page counts (unreviewed pages, undetermined inputs, missed pages; see rendered-impact). Report them in the PR body, in the gate’s own terms, and a page count the preview did not publish as “not known”: . | open defects: review comments of kind defect still open or addressed, from the preview’s review-comments.json; | changed blocks with neither a verdict nor a waiver on their current version. | . Both come from one command, the folio-review-coverage Tool, run on the preview’s published files with --changeset changeset.json --blocks blocks.json --comments review-comments.json [--rendered rendered-impact.json --measured rendered-measured.json]. Its command line is the Tool node’s invoke, declared by the content layer that owns the review process. Quote its stderr summary. If the preview has no review-comments.json, or one with no verdicts field, write “not measured”, never 0. Never count resolved comments as coverage: a resolved comment is not a reviewer’s verdict on the block. This REPORTS; it does not merge or refuse. The gate belongs to the review process, and the committee decides the outcome. Say so when coverage could not be measured, because a branch passed with unmeasured coverage reads as “reviewed”. | Push the feature branch (retry/backoff as in step 2): git push -u origin <branch>. Then ask whether the push produced a run: bun run cat check:head-has-run. The push runs the fast gates first, where the pre-push hook is on. Git’s pre-push hook (installed by cat-harness-tools/scripts/git-hooks/install.sh) and, for agents, a Claude Code PreToolUse hook on git push both run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pre-push-gates.ts on the checked-out tree, before anything leaves the container (work items cat-tools-pp9g and folio-assistant-fn8q). It runs the fast gates minus the whole-suite bun test, plus only the test files whose import closure holds a file the push changed (owner, 2026-11-05: “Affected tests only”). CI still runs the whole suite. What it says: . | refused: a gate or an affected test that is green on the push’s base in this same environment is red now. Fix it, as you would a red CI job. It quotes the gates or tests and the log path; | ? gates not judged: a red it cannot attribute to this push (red on the base too, or no base outcomes recorded here), tracked files that differ from HEAD, exit 2, or no cat runner. The push goes and CI decides. A fresh container reddens some tests CI passes (no publish-time pages, a slower machine), so this is not a local green: report it as not determined, never as pass; | ✓: the fast gates passed on this tree and the affected tests with them. A record keyed by the tree is written; it names bun test as held out, so it never claims the suite. Pushing the same tree again re-runs nothing. | . A push the hook refused is never forced through with a bare --no-verify. If you must push anyway, name the reason, which is logged to .git/cat-gates/push.log: CAT_GATES_BYPASS='<reason>' git push ..., and put the same reason in the PR body. A local pass does not replace step 7: CI still runs every gate. This does not change what you do next — step 7 dispatches either way. It changes what you can honestly SAY. A push can silently produce no run, and a pull request showing zero checks is indistinguishable from one whose checks have not started (§Guardrails, “NO CHECKS IS NOT GREEN”). If the check reports no run, write that in the PR body alongside the dispatched run’s URL. Three states, and the third is not a finding: could not ask (no remote, no network, 403, 404) means nothing was established, and it must not be reported as either answer. | Dispatch the repo’s CI on the pushed branch, and fold the result into the PR. Local green is not CI green — CI runs on a cold cache, its own toolchain, and without whatever build flags you set locally. So after the push, trigger the relevant workflow against your branch (gh workflow run <wf>.yml --ref <branch>, or the actions_run_trigger MCP tool), wait for it, and put the run URL and conclusion in the PR body. Red → fix and re-dispatch. Do not open a PR citing a workflow nobody ran. If you lack actions: write and dispatch returns 403, do not quietly skip it: state in the PR that CI was not run, and give the exact command a maintainer should run. Find the workflow by reading .github/workflows/, not by name. Guessing a workflow name is how this gate gets skipped while appearing to run (a guessed name can be a publish workflow). In a repository whose workflows are all workflow_dispatch-only, nothing runs on push or PR, and “CI is green” is only ever true because someone dispatched it. Check when CI last ran (actions_list → list_workflow_runs): “there is a workflow” is not evidence anything is being checked. Many workflows document a local equivalent in their own header. Run those; they are the same check without the dispatch. Read the workflow before assuming there is no local path. | Stop here unless a PR / merge was explicitly requested. If a PR was requested, see below. | .

6ae08a442644.title: What a green LOCAL run entitles you to claim
6ae08a442644.content: The same commit can fail different tests in CI, in a clean worktree, and when the failing files are run alone, and the sets need not be nested. A green local run is not a weaker version of a green CI run — it is a different measurement, and either can be the one that is wrong. What it entitles you to say, exactly: . The gates I ran passed, on the tree I ran them on, in this environment. And what it does not entitle: . | “CI will pass.” CI tests refs/pull/N/merge, not your head — a tree neither parent holds. A staleness that exists only in the merge tree cannot be seen from any checkout. | “The gate set passed.” Only if you ran the gate set. A subset chosen by hand misses gates such as check:partition (a new script must be classified in scripts/partition/instance-rules.ts) and no check script is unrun (a new check:* needs a SCRIPT_EXEMPTIONS entry when no workflow runs it — or, for a script owned by a layer above cat-harness, a gateExemptions.scripts row in that layer’s <instance>.json). bun run cat gates derives its list from the workflow, so it cannot drift from what CI runs. | “Nothing is failing, so nothing is wrong.” A conflicted head produces no merge ref, so pull_request workflows never fire and the PR shows zero check runs. That reads as untested, not as red. | “It passed in isolation, so the failure is not mine.” Running the file alone removes the only condition under which it failed — for example a test near its time budget that crosses it only under load. | . Your environment is part of the claim, and it can be checked. Run bun run cat check:environment before trusting a run from any hand-built tree, and install dependencies rather than borrowing them: a symlinked root node_modules makes any tool that resolves a real path through it report a location this repository does not contain. Confirming the symlink is git-ignored is not enough; path resolution is a separate confound.

3f47168ba6f3.title: A new gate in a lower layer must pass downstream (STRICT)
3f47168ba6f3.content: A layer that adds a gate or a check:* script takes on its downstream layers too (owner ruling, 2026-11-07, card “Rule 13”: add it): the next re-pin of each one runs it. Twice on 2026-11-07 a lower layer’s main broke every downstream re-pin. New check scripts that no downstream workflow ran failed no check script is unrun (check:test-gherkin, and translation:page-qa:check, which also had a flag mismatch). Checks that walked the file tree without skipping declared build outputs failed too (two such checks in the tools layer). Each time, the re-pin became the P0. So, in the same PR that adds the gate: . | It passes on the layer’s own main. | It says how downstream layers run it: either wired through the shared reusable workflow, or declared opt-in per layer with an exemption row each downstream layer can carry. | A downstream dry run proves it: lay the branch over a fresh mount of folio-assistant main, and run the gate set there. Say in the PR what ran and its result. | . Without all three, the gate waits. It never lands for the next re-pin to discover.

43970a7acfd2.title: A clean merge can produce a wrong artefact (STRICT)
43970a7acfd2.content: bun run cat regen after every base merge. Not only after a conflicted one — after every one. bun run cat merge:main runs it as part of the merge, so after merge:main it has already happened once and a second run re-asks the same tree. Two branches can change one committed generated file in non-overlapping places — say one adds a count field to a projection’s header and the other adds an entry to its array. Git merges them with no conflict and produces an artefact neither side would ever emit (a count that disagrees with the list). A conflict is a question. A clean merge is an assertion that the result is correct — and for a generated file that assertion is worth nothing, because git is merging text it has no way to evaluate. After a merge, RE-RUN THE GENERATORS. Never read the diff to decide whether you need to. bun run cat regen does it by asking each gate first, so its output is the set of artefacts the merge actually broke rather than a wholesale rewrite: . bun run cat regen # repair what is stale in the whole gate set bun run cat regen --fast # ...only the jobs that install no browser bun run cat regen --dry-run # report what is stale, change nothing bun run cat regen --changed <base> # ask only the pairs whose inputs changed since <base> bun run cat regen --explain # say, per pair, why it was asked or not . It asks the gates rather than regenerating everything because the gates (read from the workflow, not package.json) are the list, and because rewriting artefacts that were already correct leaves a diff that says nothing about what the merge broke. The QA working copy is part of the run — do not build it by hand around regen. Generators such as uml:overview and readme:subgraphs read the computed, ignored */test/results/ tree. Before every pass regen asks the copy’s stamp (bun run cat qa:working-copy -- --status) whether it was built from the tree as it stands, and rebuilds it if not. The paths that rebuild changed join the pass’s change set, so any pair that reads them is asked again. A failed build exits 2, and regen never grades a pass over a half-built copy. gates uses the same stamp, so the gates that follows a regen on the same tree builds nothing. It reports four states, and unrepaired is the one to read: a check that still fails after its writer ran is a real defect, not staleness, and the command exits non-zero rather than claiming a repair it did not make. So is a check with no writer. --changed asks less, and says what it assumed. A pair whose declared inputs, script sources and commands meet none of the paths changed since <base> (plus the working tree) is not asked: its answer is its answer at <base>. Undeclared and {tracked} pairs are always asked, as is any pair whose inputs cannot be determined. bun run cat merge:main passes the merge’s fork point, so a skipped pair is one NEITHER side touched, and it is current if the fork point, the branch tip or the base tip was current. merge:main -- --full-regen asks every pair. Separately, every pass after the first asks only the pairs whose inputs the previous pass actually changed (measured from git, not declared). Both cuts are only as good as the task-io.ts declarations — and, for a task owned by a layer above cat-harness, that layer’s own taskIo block in its <instance>.json. task-io.ts collects them and refuses a task declared twice, so declare a row where its script lives, never in both places. The whole-tree pairs (kg:audit:all:check, skill:register:check, kg:audit:check) still run after every merge. Submodules: check the pointers BEFORE you stage the merge (STRICT) . A base merge can roll a submodule back without a conflict, and git add -A is how. git merge updates a submodule’s gitlink in the index but not the submodule’s working checkout. If the checkout still sits at the branch’s old pointer, git add -A during conflict resolution stages that stale checkout, rolling the submodule back in the merge commit. bun run cat regen then runs against the old tools and “repairs” generated files to their old form, and CI fails in code the PR never touched. No step conflicts, and every local check against the stale submodule passes. So, after any base merge and before staging: . git submodule update --init --recursive # move each checkout to the merged pointer git diff --cached --submodule=short -- bootstrap bootstrap-tools # must be empty unless YOU bumped it . Then regenerate. Stage paths by name during a merge, never git add -A, and before pushing confirm the merge carries only your change: . git diff --stat origin/<base> HEAD # should list your files, not hundreds . A diff against the base far larger than your PR is the signal.

64357f930ab2.title: Conflicts in test/results/ and test/attestations/ — regenerate one, read the other
64357f930ab2.content: | tree | holds | durable home | on a conflict | . | <instance>/test/results/** | DERIVED verdicts — every script entry | the orphan qa-reports branch, main/<sha>/ and pr/<n>/<sha>/, written by the CI job qa-publish | take the base’s side: bun run cat merge:main does, then bun run cat regen | . | <instance>/test/attestations/** | JUDGEMENTS — every agent, human and baseline-pair attestation, qa-attestations/v1 | main, as authored content | a person reads both sides; never regenerated, never “take ours” | . test/results/ files are not committed on main, so a base merge conflicts there only for a branch that still carries a copy. merge:main takes the base’s side (the derived-results pattern in merge-conflict-patterns), which is the deletion, and regen rewrites the working copy. Do not hand-resolve one and do not regenerate one in order to “commit the result”: the record of a commit is its qa-reports entry, which no merge touches. Regenerating is a resolution, not a guess, because both writers are idempotent (sameScriptVerdict keeps a reproduced entry verbatim and ignores reviewed_at, reviewed_sha and script_commit_sha), so a sidecar is a pure function of the tree. A conflict in test/attestations/ is two judgements that disagree, and reconciling them is a person’s call. No merge-conflict pattern names that tree, so merge:main refuses it, as does qa:attestations:migrate. Keep both sides’ entries unless they are the same judgement; then run bun run cat qa:attestations:migrate:check, which exits 1 if a judgement is still only in a derived file. There is no qa:resolve-conflicts command: derived sidecars are not committed, so there is nothing for it to resolve.

bf34fc326944.title: A change that moves a cached step’s key — publish what CI can verify
bf34fc326944.content: If the change moves the key of an exact cached step whose producer the determinism audit lists as DETERMINISTIC, run bun run cat cache:publish <step> before pushing, so CI only verifies the entry instead of rebuilding it. Today that is cat-mount when index.lock.json changes. Verdicts are never published this way. The rule, the trust classes and the budget are in cache-first-ci.

bf10c0e00c56.title: Shipping is not merging — hand over on the PR itself
bf10c0e00c56.content: What happens after the handover is merge-to-main, called by merge-train.bpmn for a queued PR and by crdm-close.bpmn for a CRDM feature. When the branch is green and pushed, it reaches the Merge Steward only by its own state: label ready-to-merge, a signed ready: <head sha> comment, and no needs-merge-human. merge-queue §”Handing a PR to the queue” has the six points, and when NOT to spend CI keeping up while far back. The PR’s state is the record. The request to merge is a message: send the merge manager the six-line merge request of merge-manager-watcher §”The merge request: six lines”, with the PR URL, the session URL, what changed, the rendered preview and what to look for in it (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). Never merge it yourself, and never re-pin to make it green: send repin+merge: instead (owner ruling, 2026-11-13). A lone session is elected merge manager alone, so it posts the same six lines in its own chat, then asks the owner by card.

4a4a1283c927.title: Opening the PR (only when asked)
4a4a1283c927.content: GitHub access here is via the GitHub MCP server, whose tools are deferred (lazy-loaded). At session start they appear as names only — you cannot call them until you load the schema: . ToolSearch "select:mcp__github__create_pull_request" . Then call mcp__github__create_pull_request with owner, repo, head (the feature branch), base. This “load-then-call” round-trip is by design, not a failure, and is needed once per deferred tool per session, for every mcp__github__* tool (review, comment, merge, CI status). PR body content: pr-description, written for a first-time reader. PR body convention: end with the Claude Code footer + session link (see the harness git instructions). Do not include the model identifier in the PR.

8805830ebda9.title: Guardrails
8805830ebda9.content: . | Never push to the default branch and never merge a PR without an explicit ask. Prepare-merge leaves the decision to the human. When the ask comes, the merge runs merge-to-main; a broad instruction such as “fix all issues until green” is not the ask. | In folio-assistant an agent never merges to main at all. When CI is green on every job: mark the PR Ready for review, add the label ready-to-merge, and comment ready: <head sha>. The Merge Steward session brings main in, regenerates and merges. If it reports red: fix, then re-label. The policy is in continual-progress §”Green means handed to the Merge Steward”. | Check the change against the skills that govern it before calling it ready, an agent’s PR above all. Green CI says the code does what its tests say; it does not say the change keeps the rules the owner set for that area. Read the governing skills (from the mounted layers when the MCP skill server is unreachable) and hold the diff to them: a step that, say, copies the IG Publisher’s finished HTML into a site passes every test and breaks ig-render-jekyll. A design choice the PR body describes in passing is a question for the owner when a skill already answers it, never an implementation detail to merge past. | --force-with-lease, never bare --force when a rebase rewrote history. | Honest green. Pre-existing red is reported as pre-existing, with evidence; your-change red blocks the “ready” claim. | NO CHECKS IS NOT GREEN — verify against the run list, never the PR page. A PR with zero check runs renders identically to one whose checks have not started. Both are “nothing red”. A push followed by a PR can produce no pull_request-event run for that head, the newest run on the branch being for the previous head. Waiting longer is not the remedy, because how long you wait does not predict whether a run appears, and neither is avoiding force-pushes: plain fast-forwards hit it too. So before calling a branch ready, and before any merge: . | Read mergeable_state FIRST — and believe it only when it says dirty. clean can be served stale (a merged PR’s pre-merge view), and unknown means GitHub has not finished computing it. dirty is the one value worth acting on unilaterally, because its remedy — merging the base in — costs nothing on a PR that did not need it. dirty means the PR conflicts with its base, which is very likely why nothing ran: a workflow on: pull_request: with actions/checkout@v4 and no ref: checks out refs/pull/N/merge, and a conflicting PR has no such commit. When it is dirty, merge the base branch in — do NOT dispatch. A workflow_dispatch run resolves refs/heads/<branch>, so it tests the branch, not the merge result: on a conflicted PR that is a green signal for a tree that will never exist. The workaround in step 3 is for a MERGEABLE PR whose run never fired. | Read the PR’s head_sha. | mcp__github__actions_list → list_workflow_runs, filtered by branch, and find a run whose head_sha matches. | No run for that sha → the branch is NOT ready, whatever the PR page shows. Say so in those words rather than “checks pending”, and re-run them with mcp__github__actions_run_trigger → run_workflow against the branch. | Re-check after every push. A new commit moves the head, and the head is what the absence attaches to. | . An agent holding a standing merge authorisation must not read zero checks as nothing-red: could-not-determine is never rendered as clean, at the merge decision as everywhere else. | One branch. Develop on the assigned claude/* branch; moving work to a different branch needs explicit permission. | NEVER DELETE A FEATURE OR branches/ BRANCH without explicit assent from the user or the repository owner. Not after a merge, not as cleanup, not to quiet a tool that complains about it, and never by passing --delete-branch or its API equivalent. A merged branch is still the record of how the work was done, the base a revert or a follow-up is cut from, and the ref a staging deploy is served under. Deleting it is irreversible from the agent’s side and buys nothing the owner asked for. The same rule is in prepare-merge-auto.md Phase 4 and the anti-patterns, because an agent following either skill must meet it. If you change one copy, change the other. When a tool or hook complains about a branch, fix the tool — for example a reachability check in a stop hook — never delete the branch. | .

dedb9a267fb9.doc: Make a decided public comment change
dedb9a267fb9.title: Steps
dedb9a267fb9.content: Every one of the 4 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Edit the document as decided, on a feature branchTask_AuthorEdits | Author (human or agentic) | public-comment | public-comment edit –branch: the author (human, or an agent in the author role) edits the folio’s blocks as the decision says, on a feature branch for one change-set. Its PR says Closes #N for the change-set issue, and opening it moves that issue’s accepted comments to editing. Before its preview is staged, the author writes the change set’s Disposition (change set) on the Agent tab: one line per comment (No. 136: Accepted. …), starting from each comment’s Blue Disposition on Review Public Comments, after an optional Overall statement. Quality check: every comment number in the change set has a disposition; the sheet flags gaps and words that differ from the people’s. | . | Review the change set on its staging previewCallActivity_ChangeSet | Change set — feature branch and staging | calls Content Change and Reviewstaging-review | The content-change review of the author’s branch: its PR lists the PC refs it answers, and its staging preview is the after side of every deep link. A change the reviewers send back returns to the author inside that process. | . | QA gate: check dispositions against the people and the pull requestTask_QaGate | QA reviewer (independent) | public-comment | Before Ready for merge. Reads: the change set’s Disposition (change set), each comment’s Blue Disposition on Review Public Comments, the PR’s diff at its head commit, and the staging QA report. Checks that every comment number has one disposition; that each agrees with the people’s Blue Disposition; that each Accepted or Partially accepted comment has its change in the diff, and a Not accepted, Noted, Deferred, Duplicate or Out of scope one has none; that the diff changes nothing no disposition accounts for; and that the QA report for the staged commit has no failing gate. Writes: QA gate (change set), first line “Passed <head sha>: …” or “Failed <head sha>: <why>”, and QA report (change set), the report’s link. The sheet shows both under Staging review; a pass for an older commit reads as stale. | . | Mark incorporated when the change set mergesTask_Incorporate | Change set — feature branch and staging | public-comment | public-comment incorporate, naming the branch, PR and staging URL; done by the folio’s workflow when the PR that closes a change-set issue merges. A PR closed unmerged moves nothing. Ready for merge is set only once the QA gate has passed for the PR’s head commit; set earlier, the agent does not merge until it passes. The change set’s Dispositions blurb, as it stands when Ready for merge is set to Yes, is the summary that closes its issue. | .

7625e2e97cf7.title: Public comment channels and intake
7625e2e97cf7.content: Skill public-comment-channels: Set up the channels a public-comment release goes out on (an offline Excel sheet, a Google Form, a GitHub issue form, and the review sheet), each limited to the release’s fixed references, with the editor’s instructions and the announcement, and bring every channel back in through one intake path that ends in agent triage into thematic change-sets. Use when a draft is released for public comment, when a channel is added to a running review, or when returned comments arrive from any channel. Named by: Release a draft for public comment . Process: folio-assistant-core/collab/processes/content/public-comment-release.bpmn (Process_PublicCommentRelease): Task_SetUpChannels and Task_WriteAnnouncement. Intake lands in public-comment.bpmn (Process_PublicComment): StartEvent_CommentsReturned, then Task_Ingest, Task_Triage and Task_ProposeChangeSets. Tool: folio-assistant-core/scripts/public-comment-channels.ts. The comment store, the importer and change-sets are the public-comment skill’s. The review sheet’s script is review-sheet-script. A public-comment release is a frozen, line-numbered draft with an id, for example “Draft for Public Comment Release v0.9” (dpi-h-pc-v0.9). Every comment cites that draft, and nothing else, so every channel offers only the release’s own references: its numbered sections, its printed pages, and its captioned tables and figures. A channel that lets a reviewer type any section number brings back comments that cannot be placed.

b40b9b65ffc4.title: 1. The release’s fixed references
b40b9b65ffc4.content: Once the release is built (Task_BuildPcRelease), make the one list every channel is generated from: . bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/public-comment-channels.ts refs folio/<document>/review-anchors.json \ --release <release id> --title "<release title>" --draft-url <the release's draft link> \ --out review/public-comment/release-references.json . release-references.json holds the release id and title, the sha256 of the frozen PDF and .docx, and three lists: sections as a reader cites them (“3.4.5 Governance”, “Appendix C: Glossary”), printed pages in reading order, and table and figure captions. Commit it beside the comment store. It does not change while the release is open. A new release gets a new file and new channels.

a68df081938d.title: 2. The editor sets up the channels, before anything is announced
a68df081938d.content: The editor chooses which channels the review uses, and sets every one of them up before the announcement goes out, so the instructions can link to each one. Each is generated from release-references.json. Nobody edits a list by hand. | channel | make it | what the reviewer sees | limited to the release by | . | Offline Excel sheet | … xlsx release-references.json --out <release id>-comments.xlsx | Instructions, a Comments tab (their details at the top, one row per comment), a locked References tab | drop-down lists on Section, Page and Comment type that refuse anything else; the Release row | . | Google Form | … google-form release-references.json --out CreatePublicCommentForm.gs, paste into Apps Script, run createPublicCommentForm | “About you”, then one comment per response, with Submit another response | list questions for Section and Page; the release in the title | . | GitHub issue form | … issue-form release-references.json --out .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/public-comment.yml in the folio’s repository | one issue per comment, titled [<release id>] …, labelled public-comment | drop-downs for Section, Page and Comment type; the title prefix | . | Review sheet (committee, not the public) | the review-sheet-script skill, from the release’s template | Review Public Comments and Review Change Sets | the script’s Sections, Pages and Lines links, built from the same review anchors | . Line numbers stay free text in every channel: a line range or “Table 3.1” is one field, and a list of every line would be useless. The importer resolves them against the frozen draft and reports a miss. The editor’s set-up checklist. Done in this order, and every link is recorded for the announcement: . | The release is published: the line-numbered PDF and the comment-period site (its address says it is the public comment release, not branches/, and it is kept, not deleted on merge to main). Record both links. | release-references.json is made and committed. | Each chosen channel is made from it, as above. Record each channel’s link: the Excel sheet’s download link, the Form’s published link, the issue form’s …/issues/new?template=public-comment.yml link. | The review sheet is copied from its template, its Config set for this release, and an agent is asked to watch it (skill review-sheet-script). | Each channel is tried once by someone other than the editor: one comment in, then the check below run on what came back. Delete the trial comment. | The submitter records are ready (§4). The announcement is written last. | .

5504cd72d13c.title: 3. The announcement (Task_WriteAnnouncement)
5504cd72d13c.content: A short communication for the public. It names the release, says what is asked and by when, and links to everything. Keep the process description to a few sentences and link to the published process for the rest. Subject: Public comment: <document title>, <release title> <Organisation> invites comments on <document title>, <release title>, from <open date> to <close date>. Read the draft (line-numbered PDF): <PDF link> Read it online: <comment-period site link> Comment in whichever way suits you: - Online form: <Google Form link> - Offline: download <Excel sheet link>, fill in the Comments tab, and email it to <address> - On GitHub: <issue form link> (comments there are public) Please cite the section, page and line numbers of this draft. Your email is used only to contact you about your comments. Your name is published in the acknowledgements only if you say yes. What happens next: each comment is placed on the text it is about, grouped with related comments into proposed changes, and reviewed by <committee>. The editor decides each one, with a reason. How the review works: <link to the published public-comment process>. Only the channels the editor set up are listed. The links are the ones recorded in §2. Nothing goes out until every link has been opened once.

61134b1f3f35.title: 4. Who submitted: the Public Comment Source tab
61134b1f3f35.content: Submitters are recorded in the review sheet’s Public Comment Source tab, one row per public comment. The columns are No., date received, channel, reviewer name, organisation, country / region, stakeholder type, email, and “Acknowledge by name (Yes/No)”. Every column is Grey: the tab is the external source, copied in mechanically. The tab is locked, and it is the only place a submitter’s name and email are kept (the public-comment skill, §”The live review sheet”). | Each channel asks for the details once per submission: at the top of the Excel sheet’s Comments tab, on the Form’s “About you” page, and from the GitHub login on an issue. At intake, the submission’s details are copied onto every one of its comments’ rows in Public Comment Source, with the comment’s No. and its channel. | A returning submitter is recognised by the importer’s pseudonymous id r-<hash>, which comes from the email or else the name (reviewerId in schemas/public-comment.ts). Someone who comments through two channels with the same email is therefore one reviewer. | The repository gets only that id, the organisation and the country. It gets the name only when the submitter answered Yes to “Acknowledge by name”, and never the email. The importer follows this rule (the public-comment skill, §”Privacy”). | Submitter details are not configuration, so they never go in the Config tab. That tab holds the script’s settings and is written by the agent. | .

d8af723470db.title: 5. Intake: each channel has one path back
d8af723470db.content: All four channels end in the same importer (public-comment.ts import), because each returns a table whose headers are the importer’s own. Before importing, check that every reference is in the release: . bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/public-comment-channels.ts check <returned file> --refs review/public-comment/release-references.json . check lists each row that cites a section or page outside the release, or whose Release row names another release, and exits non-zero. It changes nothing. A flagged row is still imported (it arrives unplaced and triage places it); the list tells the triager where to look. | channel | what comes back | command (from the folio’s repository) | . | Excel sheet | the reviewer’s .xlsx, by email | public-comment.ts import <file> --channel comment-matrix --batch <release id>-<reviewer org> | . | Google Form | the response sheet, downloaded as CSV | public-comment.ts import <responses.csv> --channel online-form --series <release id>-form | . | GitHub issues | issues titled [<release id>] | gh api 'repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues?labels=public-comment&state=all&per_page=100' --paginate > issues.json, then public-comment-channels.ts issues-csv issues.json --release <release id> --out gh.csv, then import gh.csv --series <release id>-github | . | Review sheet | committee feedback, not public comments | the sheet sync (skill public-comment, §”The live review sheet”) | . | A letter or email that used no channel | prose | public-comment.ts import-narrative <file> --reviewer … | . Re-importing is safe: a file already imported is recognised by its sha256, and a form or issue export re-downloaded later adds only the rows (No.) it has not seen, because each carries a --series. Keep the returned files in the review owner’s private store, never in the repository: they hold emails.

55e260c6e2a8.title: 6. Triage into thematic change-sets
55e260c6e2a8.content: After each intake batch, the intake agent proposes change-sets (Task_ProposeChangeSets, the public-comment skill, §”The agent proposes; nobody is notified”): . | public-comment-changesets.ts seed lists the comments in no change-set, bucketed by section. A bucket is a starting point, not a change-set. | The agent groups comments by theme: comments that ask for the same change, or for changes that must land together, wherever they are in the document. A cross-cutting theme (a term, consent, normative keywords) is one change-set across sections. | Each change-set gets a title, requirements (what the text must do, not the new text), and its linked public comments (refs). Record them with propose --file proposals.json. They are proposed: no issue is opened and nobody is notified. | A comment that fits no theme stays out, on the dashboard’s open, in no change-set tile, for a person to place. | . The review sheet then shows the new change-sets on its next sync, and the committee reviews them there or on GitHub.

c67cc2c8619d.title: 7. Closing
c67cc2c8619d.content: At the agreed close: run closePublicCommentForm in the Form’s script, and remove the issue form (.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/public-comment.yml) from main, so nobody is offered a closed release. The kept release site and PDF are not touched. Do a last intake from every channel. A comment that arrives after the close is imported like any other, and the editor decides whether it is considered.
