ce9f41ece569.title: Release epic planning
ce9f41ece569.content: Skill release-epic-planning: Plan and track releases using work item epics. Covers epic creation, story/task decomposition, release readiness tracking, and the relationship between epics and GitHub milestones. Applies to code releases, paper publications, and project milestones. Named by: Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish . A release epic groups all the work for a specific release version. This skill governs how to create, structure, and track them.

e9093f714aa8.title: Epic structure
e9093f714aa8.content: The work items hierarchy for a release: . epic: "Release v0.2.0" ├── feature: "CRDM Phase 4b prioritization" │ ├── task: "Add Phase 4b to crdm-requirements-workflow.md" │ └── task: "Update phase table" ├── feature: "Release lifecycle skills" │ ├── task: "Create release-lifecycle.md" │ ├── task: "Create code-review-process.md" │ └── task: "Create branch-freshness.md" └── bug: "Fix 7 BPMN isMarkerVisible attributes" └── task: "Add isMarkerVisible to 5 files" . Bean types in a release context . | Type | Role in release | Granularity | . | epic | The release itself | 1 per release | . | feature | A capability area / user story | 1 per feature | . | task | A single PR-sized implementation unit | 1 per PR | . | bug | A defect fix included in the release | 1 per fix | . | milestone | A session-scoped work container | Not release-scoped | . Creating the hierarchy . # 1. Create the release epic beans create "Release v0.2.0" --type epic # 2. Create features under it beans create "CRDM Phase 4b prioritization" --type feature beans update <feature-id> --parent <epic-id> # 3. Create tasks under features beans create "Add Phase 4b to workflow" --type task beans update <task-id> --parent <feature-id> . Always check before creating — beans create is not idempotent. See todo-manager.md §”Check before you create”.

c8196073fd83.title: Ordering within a release
c8196073fd83.content: Apply the Phase 4b formalize-first rule from crdm-requirements-workflow.md: . | Structural/organizational work first | Process/policy formalization second | Implementation third | Visualization/UI last | . Within the epic, number features by dependency order. The first feature completed should not depend on any later feature.

c29db86a85ed.title: Release readiness
c29db86a85ed.content: Tracking readiness . The work items visualizer (<base>/beans/) shows open work items grouped by epic. A release is ready when its epic shows 0 open work items. Readiness checklist . Before moving from draft to pre-release: . | All must-have features resolved (all child work items completed) | All should-have features either resolved or deferred to next release | CI green on main (bun run cat gates) | All changed BPMN diagrams re-rendered | All changed docs pages regenerated | Changelog written (see release-lifecycle.md) | BA has reviewed accumulated changes | . Deferring to next release . If a should-have or nice-to-have feature won’t make the release: . # Move the feature bean to the next release epic beans update <feature-id> --parent <next-epic-id> . Record the deferral reason in the work item body: . beans update <feature-id> --body-append "Deferred to v0.3.0: not blocking v0.2.0" .

e663872944aa.title: GitHub milestone integration (optional)
e663872944aa.content: A GitHub milestone can mirror the release epic for stakeholder visibility: . # Create milestone gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/milestones --method POST \ -f title="v0.2.0" -f description="Release v0.2.0" # Assign PRs to milestone gh pr edit <number> --milestone "v0.2.0" . The milestone’s completion percentage gives stakeholders a progress view without needing access to the work items store.

4431627461e2.title: Cross-domain applicability
4431627461e2.content: | Domain | Epic title | Features | . | Code | “Release v0.2.0” | Skills, schemas, pipeline changes | . | Paper | “Publication: Chapter 3 revision” | Section rewrites, figure updates | . | Project | “Deliverable: Phase 1 report” | Analysis sections, appendices | . The hierarchy and readiness tracking are identical.

ca245f3fb454.title: Rules
ca245f3fb454.content: . | One epic per release — if scope creeps, split the epic | Features are independently reviewable — each can be a PR | Tasks are PR-sized — one task, one PR, one review cycle | Never close an epic without BA approval — the epic is the release | Deferred features move to the next epic — they are not deleted | .

00ade0013ec8.title: The release gate: the full suite runs for a release
00ade0013ec8.content: Owner, card Q-CIB-4 A, 2026-11-08: “not all CI needs to run unless doing a release build”, “you can merge to main and not be release build”, “CI not gate on non-release merge to main”. So CI has three lanes, and only the last one gates: . | lane | what runs | gates? | where it shows | . | Pull request | the fast tier: types, lint, and the tests and gates the change can reach; no re-run of main | no: shown on the PR, advisory | a preview at branches/<slug>/, on request, and always for content PRs | . | main | the integration run: the full suite on main’s tip, batched (one run per repository per hour, not one per merge) | no: a red run files ONE fix issue naming the merges in its range | the staging root of the site, not the live root | . | Release | the full tier as an absolute gate: every test, every gate, derive:publish, e2e, the standalone measure, the index at released layer pins | yes: nothing publishes from a red release candidate | the live site, the registry, the GitHub release | . What makes a merge a release: the PR carries the release label (or merge:guard runs with --release). The guard’s check 5 then gates the merge on green owed CI, as it did for every merge before 2026-11-08. A release candidate is cut from main after that merge, and only a green candidate is published (package-release step 3). What does not change: content still needs the owner’s authorisation; committee content never merges; the WHO repositories are not changed without the owner; CodeQL keeps its schedule. Those are authorisation and security rules, not CI tiers. What it replaces: for non-release merges, main-green-first (card Q-CIB-1 B, 2026-11-08), the 2026-10-23 ruling that a layer PR merges only on a green index run, and “merge non-content when green” in the merge window rules. Rollout (phased, owner’s choice A): 1. these skills, the merge DMNs and merge:guard (check 5 advisory unless a release); 2. cat-harness-tools’ layer checks (PR fast tier, the hourly integration run, the release run); . | folio-assistant’s Code-quality gates, previews on request, the site’s staging root; 4. the other layers and the re-pin train. Until a phase lands, its workflows still run in full: they are simply no longer a merge gate. | .

3ea01596c224.title: Remote-mount a harness
3ea01596c224.content: Skill remote-mount: Bring a harness, and every layer it depends on, into a checkout that does not hold it, from another repository at a pinned commit, as declared directories with a lock: a source.remote entry in the downstream’s root index.config.json (legacy: remoteMounts on its declaration) and mountDefaults on the harness. Covers when to mount and when to subscribe instead, why there are no submodules and no .deps/, the transitive closure through needs and gitlinks, overrides by id, the lock, and the three states. Named by: Authoring a document, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Draft, review and publish, Guideline Updates, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Review and publish a folio . How a downstream folio gets the layers it is built on: . | no git submodules, ever; | no .deps/, because a dot directory collides with GitHub’s conventions and with this repository’s own dot-prefix guard; | a remote mount is a declared directory with a remote source, pinned to a full 40-character SHA; | the defaults live in the harness’s own declaration, so a downstream never restates the paths; | a downstream may override them by id, never by path; | mounts are resolved transitively across the dependency closure; | code arrives through the mounted code directories. | . |   | where | . | the process | mount-dependency.bpmn; the per-subgraph view is the remote and npm flows of mount-subgraph.bpmn | . | the schema | cat-harness/schemas/kg/remote-mount.ts, plus the remote, npm and hydrated members of SubgraphSource (schemas/kg/subgraph-source.ts); the per-pin index package is subgraphIndexPackage in schemas/kg/subgraph-manifest.ts | . | the tool | bun run cat mount:remote (--plan to resolve without writing), and bun run cat mount:remote:check (offline) | . | the entry point | bun run cat state:mount, which the session-start hook already runs | .

c83c62e34a1c.title: Mount, subscribe or associate: choose first
c83c62e34a1c.content: | you want | relation | what arrives | . | to build on a harness: run its scripts, import its schemas, read its skills as your own | remote mount (source.remote in index.config.json) | the harness’s declared directories and those of everything it needs, at one pin | . | to read another graph and hold chosen parts of it | subscription (subscriptions): the kg-subscription skill | a snapshot of its declaration, then parts you materialise one at a time through the five gates | . | to know of a harness and link to it | association (associatedHarnesses): the associate-harness skill | nothing | . | to retrieve or distribute as a package | npm distribution (kg-retrieve-npm, source.npm): the npm-kg-distribution skill | an npm .tgz tarball (unhydrated source or hydrated view) | . The test is whether your code imports theirs. If it does, mount. If you only read their content, subscribe: a subscription gates every part through copyright and purpose, and a mount does not, because the code it brings is the platform you are built on.

57aa7cea04e2.title: The two halves of the declaration
57aa7cea04e2.content: The harness side goes in the harness’s own <name>.json and is written once by the harness’s owner: . "mountDefaults": { "path": "cat-harness", "directories": ["schemas", "scripts", "skills"] } . What arrives is what the declaration NAMES: the declaration itself, the chosen directories, and the instance-scoped files in its assets (its README and AGENTS.md). A file the declaration does not name, such as a platform.ts beside it, never arrives. Code the mounted graphs import has to sit in a declared directory. Both fields are optional, and each absence has a meaning: . | path absent means the layer’s home path (livesAt.path, else its directory in its own repository). | directories absent means every declared directory whose content is in the checkout. A branch, family or remote source is somebody’s state, not part of the harness. | . The downstream side goes in the checkout’s root index.config.json, as the source.remote of the layer it brings in. Which layers a checkout instantiates, where each comes from, and the fallback for a folio with no index are index-config’s rule. This skill covers only what a remote source means once it is declared: . { "name": "<harness>", "source": { "remote": { "repository": "<owner>/<repo>", "ref": "<40-character sha>", "overrides": { "cat-harness": { "directories": ["schemas", "skills"] }, "bootstrap": { "skip": true } } } } } . The fields are a remoteMounts entry without its harness, because the layer’s name is the harness (RemoteSourceSchema in schemas/kg/index-config.ts). A folio with no index still reads remoteMounts on its declaration. Declaring a mount in both places is an error: readDeclaredMounts throws and names both files. bun run cat index-config:migrate --write moves the entries across. Every tool that writes mounts writes through writeDeclaredMounts, into index.config.json, and none writes remoteMounts. overrides is keyed by layer name, then by directory id: . | path moves a layer. | directories replaces its default list. An id may be one the layer declares in its <name>.json or from within one of those directories (a "subgraph": true entry of skills/skills.json, such as voices); both are resolved at the pin through instanceDirectories, the resolver every on-disk reader uses. A nested id mounts its own path alone. An id declared in neither place is refused, not dropped, and the refusal says where it looked. The same holds for the harness’s own mountDefaults.directories. An id may also be a concern name, a code from code-lists/concern-group.json such as sdlc. It expands to every kind-first member the layer declares, such as sdlc/processes/ and sdlc/skills/, read from each grouping kind’s own declaration file at the pin. Each member is locked as <directory id>/<code>. A code that none of the layer’s kinds declares is refused like any other unknown id. | After a review of hydrated metadata, `mount:remote –choose [:] --directories a,b --tools x,y` writes the choice into `overrides.` (the choice, never the state), so a fresh clone replays it. It ends the review: that layer mounts as files, so its `hydrated` is dropped. The pin and consent do not move. | skip leaves it unmounted, and the lock records it as an answer. | tools names Tools this layer declares, by id, and mounts each one runnable: its definition, its implementation and their import closure. The next section but one says what that brings. | hydrated: true (here, or on the entry for its harness) mounts each chosen directory as one file: its published index.hydrated.jsonld at the pin, a hydrated source. Read what is there, then choose what to mount as files. No declaration is laid down, and needs is not followed. Where that file comes from is the next section. With no directories, a hydrated mount offers every top-level in-checkout subgraph and ignores mountDefaults.directories on purpose: that list chooses which FILES a downstream gets, and a hydrated mount is the step before choosing. Each top-level file already carries its nested subgraphs inline (hasSubgraph), so a nested one is named only when you want it on its own. | .

f7b900b72503.title: Hydrated: the index files are published per pin, in a package
f7b900b72503.content: A pin’s subgraph index files (index.jsonld, index.hydrated.jsonld under <docs>/subgraph/<HARNESS>/) are published per pin in a package, and a hydrated mount fetches them through the Tool its source names (the hydrated source’s tool, which is remote-mount unless it says otherwise). | Not committed in each repository. The files are builtAtPublish: they are computed over the checkout’s other layers, so no commit can hold them current, and a committed copy turns every re-pin’s check red. | Not generated at mount time. The downstream would need the whole index, kg-export and the framing toolchain to read one file of metadata, which is the cost a hydrated mount exists to avoid, and two downstreams could frame two different files for one pin. | . What that means in practice: . |   |   | . | the package | <harness>-subgraph-index@0.0.0-pin.<sha>: the index files at their published paths, and subgraph-index.json (folio-subgraph-index/v1) giving each file’s sha256 and the repository, pin and harness | . | where | assets of the GitHub release subgraph-index-<sha> in the layer’s repository, with the tarball’s folio-binary-release/v1 record beside it. Every name is computed (subgraphIndexPackage in schemas/kg/subgraph-manifest.ts) | . | who publishes | the subgraph-index-package Tool, run on every push to main by the reusable workflow layer-publish-subgraph-index.yml (the tools layer); a harness opts in with one uses: line | . | what a mount checks | the pin’s git tree first (a commit that does carry the file still works); otherwise the package: the tarball against its record (size, sha256), the manifest against the repository, pin and harness asked for, each file against its sha256, then the same schema and subgraph-IRI check a tree file gets | . | the lock | a directory that came from the package records the tarball’s URL and sha256 and the file’s path in it (package), so mount:lock fetches the same bytes and refuses any others | . No release for the pin is missing, and the detail says the package was looked for. A package that fails a check is missing; one that could not be fetched is could-not-determine. Neither is ever an empty mount. The record travels with the tarball, so its digest proves the transfer, not the publisher: who may publish is the repository’s write access, the same trust the git tree at the pin already rests on.

d24227f7d4ae.title: Tools: choose by id, mount runnable
d24227f7d4ae.content: The workflow: load the Tools’ metadata, review it, then materialise a chosen set. The first step is a hydrated mount of the declaring layer’s tools directory. Its index.hydrated.jsonld holds every Tool whole, and each Tool is its own tools/<id>/ subgraph. The last step is tools on that layer’s override: . "overrides": { "cat-harness": { "tools": ["bean-query", "bpmn-checklist", "agent-memory"] } } . Three rules govern this step: . | A Tool brings both halves. Its definition is <tools dir>/<id>/<id>.ts in the layer that declares it, by the folder convention in schemas/tools/tool-folders.ts. Its implementation is what its invoke names: . | inProcess.module, found in the declarer or in a layer whose needs names it (resolveImplementingPath’s rule; two holders is refused); | the script a bun run cat <key> command resolves to through the layers’ checkoutScripts. | . A bare runtime command (gh, beans) or manual brings no code. Both halves arrive with their import closure. A definition without its code is not a Tool you can run, and code without the modules it imports does not load: either way the checkout is half-working. | One closure walker. The closure is bootstrap-tools’ importClosure (scripts/check-closure.ts). check:tools-closure and the staging cone use the same walk. Do not write a second walker: two of them give two answers to “what does this code load”. | Directory granularity. The mount brings every declared directory the closure touches, whole. It takes the most specific declared directory (a nested one such as skills/voices mounts alone) and never a single file, so the lock schema is unchanged. A closure file in no declared directory, and an import that resolves to nothing, are refused with the file named. Neither is ever dropped. | . With tools named anywhere in a mount entry, each layer of that entry mounts the directories the closure touches, plus any its override names in directories. It does not mount its default list. A whole layer stays whole. A Tool id the layer does not declare at the pin is refused at plan time. tools together with hydrated is refused, because metadata brings no code. What it costs. A Tool folder is not a declared directory: tools/ is, and most definitions import its lib.ts. So a definition arrives with the whole tools directory, which holds every Tool’s definition. The cost that matters falls on the implementation side, which brings the directories its closure touches (in the tools layer, typically scripts and src). Without tools, the tools layer mounts every in-checkout directory it declares. The end-to-end check is the remote-mount test “load tools metadata, choose three Tools, materialise them” in the tools layer.

391b46acffd6.title: Why the default path is the home path
391b46acffd6.content: At its home path, a mounted layer keeps its position relative to its siblings. Two things then follow with no extra machinery: . | instanceRootsIn scans one level deep, so it finds every mounted sibling and needs resolves exactly as it does in the monorepo. | A relative import such as ../../cat-harness/schemas/… finds the file it names. | . Moving a layer by override is allowed, and the overlay still finds it through the lock (mountedInstanceRoots, mountScopeFor). The override is then responsible for any import that climbs out of the moved layer.

a377e4c17782.title: The closure
a377e4c17782.content: . | The harness’s declaration is read from the pinned tree, not from this checkout. | Each needs name is looked for in the same tree. | If it is not there, the planner looks for a gitlink at that tree’s root. A submodule entry is itself a pin, so a need on bootstrap resolves to litlfred/bootstrap at the gitlink’s SHA. The downstream gets the bytes and never a submodule. | A need the downstream already holds as a local layer is local: it is supplied by the checkout and never mounted over. | A need found nowhere is missing. It is never dropped. | .

05ca4ff5c900.title: The lock, and the three states
05ca4ff5c900.content: index.lock.json sits beside the downstream’s index.config.json and is committed. It is generated by mount:remote and never hand-edited, which is why it is a separate file rather than part of the index. Readers also accept the legacy name <name>.mount-lock.json, and both present is an error. It records: . | the pins it was written for; | for each layer: the repository, the SHA, how the pin was found (declared / same-tree / gitlink), the declaration’s digest, each directory’s tree digest, and declared layer assets (such as package.json); | what was not mounted, and why. | . The mounted bytes are not committed. With an index, each mount path is ignored by a generated block in the root .gitignore, written from the index (check:index-ignores is the gate). A path that block does not cover is reported as missing, never patched locally, because a local exclude is invisible to every other clone. In a folio with no index, a path its rules do not ignore goes into the worktree’s info/exclude. Mount path and route collisions. A mount with no path override lands at <name>/ in the downstream root, beside the downstream’s own directories, and its site routes sit beside the site-wide ones. To prevent collisions on disk and in route space: . | Reserved names: RESERVED_ROOT_AND_ROUTE_NAMES in schemas/kg/remote-mount.ts declares the one authoritative list of reserved root directories and site route names: ["skills", "tools", "docs", "assets", "glossary", "api", "payload", "branches/", "beans", "todos", "fsh-guts", "uploads", "test", "build", "_site", "_docs", "_kg"]. | Mount path check: checkMountPathCollisions (run during planning in mount:remote and by bun run cat check:mount-collisions) rejects any remote mount whose effective path (path or <name>/) collides with: . | a directory the downstream declares in its own configuration; | a reserved root or site route name; | another mount’s path. When a collision occurs, the error states how to fix it: “set path” (on the layer’s overrides.<name>.path in index.config.json or source.remote.overrides). | . | Route rules: . | Canonical: every visualiser is reachable at <base>/<harness>/<visualizer>/. Every generated link uses that form unless an alias is declared. | Alias: <base>/<visualizer>/ exists only when a declaration opts in via alias: true or alias: "<alias>" in its Visualisation declaration (coverage.visualiser). The site build refuses an alias that collides with another alias, a harness route, or a reserved site route, and names both claimants. | The route rule itself is in schema-management §”Where a viewer publishes”. | . | . Every layer ends in exactly one state: . | state | means | exit | . | mounted | on disk, hashing to the lock | 0 | . | unverified-approver | mounted, on consent no mountApprovers list checked | 0, reported apart | . | missing | not on disk, edited since mounting, not in the tree, refused, or the lock is for other pins | 1 | . | could-not-determine | the fetch failed, a declaration or lock is unreadable, or a layer is reached at two pins | 2 | . Could-not-determine outranks missing, and missing outranks mounted. A fetch that failed is never an empty layer. A fresh clone: the root’s cat bootstrap . A downstream root’s cat script is bun .github/cat.ts, not the bare runner. The runner (scripts/run-script.ts of the tools layer) is itself a mount, so on a fresh clone it is not on disk.github/cat.ts checks for it and, when it is missing, runs .github/mount-from-lock.sh (which fetches mount-from-lock.ts at the commit the lock pins for the tools layer and replays the lock, verifying every tree digest) before it hands over with the same arguments. So bun run cat <name> works from git clone with no mount step. It checks only that the runner is present, so after a re-pin run bash .github/mount-from-lock.sh by hand to replace the stale mounts. instantiate-harness.ts writes both files from the tools layer’s templates/root-bootstrap/ and sets the cat script. A root set up before that keeps a cat script that runs the bare runner until the two files are copied in. Re-pinning: from a checkout mounted from the lock . A re-pin is mount:remote --seed <name>=<owner/repo>@<sha> (it writes the pin and its consent into index.config.json), then mount:remote (it lays the bytes down and rewrites the lock). Do it in a checkout whose mounts match the lock: a fresh one, or one replayed by .github/mount-from-lock.sh. A mount with local edits is left untouched by the next mount, at its old commit, while the lock’s top-level pin moves, so CI would keep testing the old layer. --seed refuses while a mount it moves has such edits, and mount:check reports a layer entry behind its pin as missing. After the re-pin, check that the moved layer’s sha in index.lock.json is the new pin. A pin only moves forward (owner ruling, 2026-11-06, card “Pin target”, A). When layers pin different commits of a shared layer, align them forward, bottom-up: start at the lowest layer, and move each shared layer to the newest commit that any layer needs. Stop when every lock names one commit per layer. Never move a pin back to an older commit so that two layers agree. A re-pin is a cross-layer set (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). Pin together every layer the change needs, re-pinned to the current mains, and verify on a fresh mount (mount:remote --fresh). A layer can need another layer’s newer commit. For example, cat-harness#1100 removed routes that were listed by hand, because a content layer above it now derives them (builtOnHostSite). So cat-harness at 6dd3746 or later needs that content layer’s change, and the tools layer’s matching one, in the same re-pin. An asset that a layer commits must also match the tools recipe that generates it, such as cat-harness’s edit-links.js. A re-pin is its own PR (owner ruling, 2026-11-07: “keep repins on own PR so easier to stack dependencies”). A re-pin PR changes the pins and nothing else: index.config.json, index.lock.json, the generated uses: pins, and what regenerates from them. It carries no feature change, no workflow logic and no fix. | A feature that needs the new pins is stacked on the re-pin PR (below) rather than riding inside it. | A fix that the re-pin needs lands in the layer that owns it, and the re-pin then only moves the pin. | Counter-example: folio-assistant#2985 carried #2999 (the shared ci-setup move) and its own caches:viz gate line inside the re-pin. | The one exception: mutual dependence (owner ruling, 2026-11-07, card, about 08:43Z, “A. Allow the exception”). A re-pin may share a PR with a change only when neither can pass on its own. The PR body must say why. Example: a content layer re-pinned to cat-harness#1032 failed check:tools without its own PR’s library topic, and that PR alone declared the library topic twice against the old pin. A change that merely needs the new pins is not mutual: it stacks. | . A lower layer’s new gate must not break the next re-pin. A gate or check script added to a lower layer has passed a downstream dry run before it lands, so a re-pin moves pins and nothing else. When a re-pin nonetheless fails on a gate a lower layer just added, the fix goes into that layer, not into the re-pin (prepare-merge (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”A new gate in a lower layer must pass downstream”). Stacking across layers (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). Work that needs an unmerged PR in a lower layer does not wait for it. Develop against that PR’s branch laid over a fresh mount. A draft PR may pin the dependency PR’s full 40-hex head SHA so that its CI sees the change. A branch is never pinned, as for any pin. That draft is never marked ready or merged while it pins an unmerged commit: once the dependency lands, re-pin to its merge commit on main. That move goes forward, so “a pin only moves forward” holds throughout. The re-pin refreshes layer health (owner ruling, 2026-11-07, card “Layer health”, A). When a re-pin moves the tools layer, it regenerates the checkout’s layer health report at the new pins and publishes it. The health check fails a re-pin once the report is more than 26 hours old and the checker has moved. The tools layer implements it. The merge manager re-pins for a merge (owner ruling, 2026-11-13: “send to you as merge manager to handle merge AND repin so you can handle trains and CI”). A session whose PR is green except for a re-pin sends it to the merge manager as repin+merge:, and does not re-pin it just in time. The merge manager makes the re-pin as its own PR and sequences re-pin trains and CI. The rules below are how it does so. The committer re-pins, locally, and CI only verifies. The person or agent who moves a pin does the whole re-pin in their own checkout: --seed, a fresh mount:remote, the regenerated agent surface (skill:commands, agent-memory, index:render), and the local checks. That same mount:remote then publishes the new lock’s layers cache ref (below) alongside the branch, with whatever credential pushes the branch. bun run cat layers:publish retries it, and --no-layers-publish skips it. CI never builds the ref when it exists: it fetches it and verifies it against the lock. Two writers are only fallbacks: . | the re-pin train, for layers nobody re-pinned; | main’s post-merge workflow, which rebuilds the ref for every push that changes index.lock.json. | . The layers cache: one fetch, every byte still verified . Replaying a lock fetches each pinned layer from its own repository. The layers cache is one git commit in the INDEX repository whose tree is the composed overlay a replay lays down: each locked directory at its mount path, each declaration and asset, and nothing an install, a state mount or a publish build wrote. | Ref: refs/cat/layers/<key>, where the key is the sha256 of the lock’s instances. refs/cat/layers/main moves with main’s lock. | Reader: mount:lock, and through it .github/mount-from-lock.sh, the session-start hook and every CI job, first tries ONE shallow fetch of the key’s ref, then of main. A layer whose copy verifies is laid down from it. A layer that does not verify, or a ref that is missing, is fetched from its own repository as before. --no-layers-cache (or CAT_LAYERS_CACHE=0) skips it, and CAT_LAYERS_URL points it at another remote. | Writer: the committer, through mount:remote or layers:publish. It refuses unless every mount reads current, then pushes the overlay. --main also moves main. --prune <n> keeps the newest n lock refs, main, and each --keep <key>, for example the lock of every open PR. | Gate: on an index-mode pull request that changes index.lock.json, the job layers-ref of the tools layer’s layer-pr-checks.yml runs layers:check --changed-from <base>. It only asks (git ls-remote) whether the new lock’s ref is at the repository, and fails when it is not. The build and the push stay on the re-pinner’s machine, never a runner (owner, 2026-11-08). A PR that leaves the lock alone owes nothing. | Shared fallback: an IG whose origin carries no refs/cat/layers/* can name a shared cache in .github/layers-url (one URL). The root bootstrap’s mount-from-lock.sh then sets CAT_LAYERS_URL to it. Only layers at the same pin hit; the rest are fetched as before. | . The lock stays the sole authority. The cache is untrusted. Every byte taken from it is checked against the lock: the declaration’s and each asset’s sha256, and each directory’s treeDigest. These are the same checks a fetched byte passes. So a stale main still serves every layer that did not move, and a tampered ref costs time, never correctness. Trust is unchanged: consent was checked when the lock was written, and the cache cannot add a layer the lock does not name. A replay that fails is reported loudly, not swallowed: a stale mount makes local checks pass falsely.

dc37b0808967.title: A changed lock re-renders the agent surface
dc37b0808967.content: A mount is not done when the bytes are on disk. A newly pinned layer can bring new skills, renamed skills and new agent-memory entries, but an agent does not read the layer: it reads what is generated from it. | surface | generated by | from | . | .claude/commands/<name>.md | skill:commands | every user_invocable skill in the mounted kg graphs | . | .claude/agent-memory/<agent>/MEMORY.md, .agents/skills/, .agents/rules/ | agent-memory | the memory directories the mounted layers declare | . So when a mount:remote run changes the lock, it runs both generators from the checkout root before it exits, and a generator that fails fails the run. A re-pin commit then carries the new layers and the surface rendered from them. --no-agent-surface opts out; --check, --plan and --staging never run it, since they change no lock a commit would carry. The list lives in one place, AGENT_SURFACE_GENERATORS in cat-harness-tools/scripts/remote-mount.ts. A new generator of something an agent reads (a rule file, a settings hook) is added there, not to a checklist: a step a person has to remember is the step that gets skipped. The process step is Task_RenderAgentSurface in mount-dependency.bpmn, between writing the lock and checking against it.

c4f0add76aac.title: Trust: what lets a mount proceed (H8)
c4f0add76aac.content: A real mount needs a person’s consent for that pin (trust.consent); a --staging mount needs none. schemas/kg/mount-trust.ts has the rules. Four things to know: . | The lock records the basis for each layer: staging, or consent with who and when. mount:remote:check re-runs the trust check against the current declaration, so consent withdrawn later reads refused. | A gitlink needs consent of its own. A layer reached through a gitlink is another repository at another commit. Give its consent on overrides.<name>.trust, for the gitlink’s SHA. | Who may consent. Declare mountApprovers and a consent.by not on the list is refused. Without the list, mounts report unverified-approver: exit 0, but never shown as clean. A checkout whose mounts index.config.json lists declares the list there, as its top-level mountApprovers; declaring it on the layer declaration as well is an error. | A one-time consent is recorded where it acts (owner ruling, 2026-11-13). Quote the owner’s card, with its date, in the re-pin PR’s body and in trust.consent’s evidence in index.config.json. Example: folio-assistant#3119 re-pointed a content layer’s pin to that layer’s main under the card “A. Re-point to main”. | A refused mount is not current. Its old bytes stay on disk (an agent does not delete them). The lock records them under unmounted as leftOnDisk, and the check reports them as not mounted. | . Standing consent: a site keeps itself on an upstream branch . Pins stay per site. A site may declare, on one layer’s trust.standing, that a named person consents to following a branch — {follows: "main", consentBy, consentAt, require?: "green"}. The repin tool (cat-harness-tools/scripts/repin-standing.ts, run by its standing-repin.yml workflow) then moves that pin to the branch’s newest (green) commit and writes trust.consent for the new pin, by that person and marked standing. The mount accepts it only while the same rule is still declared: withdraw or edit it and those pins ask again. A pin moved by hand still asks again, rule or not. A standing re-pin never merges itself (owner ruling, 2026-11-13, card “C. No auto-merge”, which replaces “A. MM dispatches, auto-merge OK”). A standing re-pin run, however it is triggered, opens or updates its PR, labels it needs-repin, and stops. The merge manager judges it once CI is green and merges it. The reason was measured: the self-merges landed 3-4 seconds after the PR opened, before any check had run. The tools layer decides the mechanism. A re-pin commit pushed by a bot gets runs held at action_required, and the merge manager approves them, so the re-pin is judged on runs that executed (github-state-inspection). Site repositories (owner ruling, 2026-11-13, card “A. Give MM access”). The merge manager attaches each site repository and runs its re-pin: it dispatches the run, approves the held bot runs, and merges when green. A site’s own sessions do not re-pin it.

26a5f5e0e133.title: Publishing a remote-mounted downstream — provision gh-pages first
26a5f5e0e133.content: A mount brings layers into a checkout; it provisions nothing on the downstream’s remote. A downstream that publishes a site needs a gh-pages branch before GitHub Pages can be switched on, exactly as a new repository does. The step is Task_ProvisionGhPages (“Provision gh-pages”) in the getting-started process (getting-started §5), with the semantics of A_Provision in bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn. Run bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --provision (idempotent, never forced; without the flag it only reports unprovisioned and the exact command), then set Pages to “Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, / (root)”. A worked example is in repo-conversion §5.

7c6d7fd88b3e.title: Never
7c6d7fd88b3e.content: . | Never add a submodule to get a dependency, and never clone into .deps/. | Never pin a branch or an abbreviated SHA. The schema refuses both. | Never move a pin back. Align layers forward to the newest commit any of them needs (§”Re-pinning”). | Never edit a mounted directory and expect a re-mount to keep the edit, or to throw it away. A re-mount leaves edited bytes untouched and reports them as missing. Move the edit upstream, or delete the directory and re-mount. | Never mount over tracked files, or over a directory that no lock says this mount made. Both are refused. | Never read missing or could-not-determine as “that layer has nothing in it”. A layer that is not mounted is absent from every overlay. | .

80d4020ad40e.title: remote-mount (skill)
80d4020ad40e.content: The skill remote-mount as its source file cat-harness/skills/kg/kg-core/remote-mount.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

b60a95967736.title: Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN
b60a95967736.content: Skill render-kg-to-cdn: Render a Knowledge Graph, or a list of its Subgraphs, for publication to a CDN at a publication root URL, and report a status and one message. The same step for a staging preview and for a release — only the root URL and the target differ. Names the target’s Tool, never its steps: GitHub Pages (gh-pages) is one Tool, and it carries its own subprocess. Named by: Authoring a document, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Guideline Updates, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Review and publish a folio . Render the content of a Knowledge Graph, or a list of its Subgraphs, for publication to a CDN at a given publication root URL, independent of staging or release, and report the status of the push with a message. GitHub Pages is one Tool for this general step. Drawn as render-kg-to-cdn.bpmn.

bd6c1ff9453a.title: Inputs and output
bd6c1ff9453a.content: | input | what | . | Knowledge Graph | a layer root — or a tree the caller has already rendered and verified | . | Subgraphs | optional: declared directory ids; absent means the whole graph | . | publication root URL | where the rendering is served | . | CDN target | which Tool performs the push — a Tool that satisfies: ["render-kg-to-cdn"] | . | output | what | . | status | pushed, not-pushed, or could-not-determine — a check that could not look is never pushed | . | message | one line, postable as it stands: what is live (a commit), where, and the QA result | .

423150237453.title: Staging and release are the same step
423150237453.content: A preview is this with a root under the release root; a release is this with the release root. What differs belongs to the caller: who may start it, what must be reviewed or verified first, what else lives on the same host and must survive the push. That is why feature-staging and docs-site-publish both call this process rather than restating it, and keep their own steps — the slug, the render log, restoring the open previews, the publication-manager alert — around the call.

dc8c74c58955.title: Name the Tool, not its steps
dc8c74c58955.content: The general process has one call activity, bound by the Tool: the activity names this skill, the Tool for the chosen target satisfies it, and the Tool lists its own subprocesses — the diagram of its steps (skills-and-tools, bpmn-processes). The general skill never lists them. | target | Tool | its subprocess | its message | . | GitHub Pages | gh-pages | bootstrap-tools processes/render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn | the commit merged onto gh-pages + the QA of what is staged and what is served | . A target may need provisioning before it accepts a push; the Tool’s subprocess owns that. For GitHub Pages a gh-pages branch has to exist before Pages can be switched on to serve it, so the gh-pages subprocess creates it first — the general step does not. Another CDN is another Tool with its own subprocess, and nothing here changes. A CDN in front of an origin is a layer, not a publication host (kg-to-portal): the publication root URL stays the origin’s canonical one even when a CDN serves it.

61c1d383ff12.title: What this is not
61c1d383ff12.content: Not the verification of what a build produced — that is publish-verification, and it runs before a caller hands its tree over. Not the decision to release — the content layer’s publication step and release-lifecycle. This step renders, pushes, and says whether the push landed.

054f41725171.title: Rendered impact — which rendered files a Change Set changes
054f41725171.content: Skill rendered-impact: The list of rendered files a Change Set alters, and how a reviewer approves against it. Each renderer maps the input files a change touched to the rendered files of its site through its dependency cone, before any build; a build diff then confirms the prediction. Use when opening or reviewing a Change Set PR, when asked “which pages does this change”, when a prediction and a build disagree, or when adding a renderer. Named by: Committee review of a content change, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Guideline Updates, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Public comment on a review draft, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate . Skill id: rendered-impact · Package: sdlc-core . A Change Set’s PR is approved against what it does to the rendered site, not only against its source diff. A one-line FSH edit can re-render one page of 722 or all of them, and a reviewer cannot tell which from the diff. So every renderer answers one question, and the PR shows the answer.

877acada16cb.title: Scope
877acada16cb.content: . | Every renderer maps a list of changed input files to the list of changed rendered files, from its dependency cone. | The public-comment Change Set (changeset/1.0.0) is the Change Set for ANY folio change, and the rendered list is one of its fields. | The original stays in library/; a Change Set applies to the folio materialised in folio/, never to the library source. | .

90a5c217b9d3.title: The contract: rendered-impact/v1
90a5c217b9d3.content: Declared in cat-harness/schemas/ui/rendered-impact.ts. A renderer takes the changed input files and returns: . | field | says | . | files[] | each rendered file the change alters: path in the built site, change (changed, added, removed), role (content, data, index) and via, the chain that reached it | . | files[].anchors | for a page that assembles many units (a document page), the fragment ids the change alters; the review list links path#anchor | . | undetermined[] | each input the renderer could NOT place, with its reason, and scope: all when it can change any page | . | method | cone (predicted before a build) or build-diff (measured after one) | . Three rules, each one a refusal: . | Could-not-determine is never “no change”. An empty files with a non-empty undetermined is “not known”, and the PR says so in those words. A renderer that drops an input it cannot map is broken. | Index files are listed and marked, not dropped. The reviewer’s list (reviewList) leaves out role: index (search data, sitemaps, an artefact index) because review is of content, not indexes. The renderer marks the role; the reader filters. | A page whose bytes do not change can still change. An AST artefact page loads its resource in the browser, so the cone names the page AND its data file, and a build diff sees only the data file. That is unconfirmed, not a defect. | .

5af7e767cace.title: Checking a prediction: the one comparison that matters
5af7e767cace.content: comparePrediction(predicted, measured) sorts every file into three groups: . | missed: the build changed it, the cone did not predict it. A cone defect, never a pass. Report it on the PR and fix the renderer: the next Change Set relies on the same cone to tell the reviewer what to open. | confirmed: predicted and measured. | unconfirmed: predicted, not measured. Expected for content pages that load their data (rule 3). For anything else it means the cone is too wide: it is safe, but say so. | .

80553486f6c7.title: The renderers today
80553486f6c7.content: | renderer | maps | how | status | . | fhir-ig-pages | .fsh, .cql, input/pagecontent/*.md | fsh-cone forward cone → SUSHI’s fsh-index.json → AST artefact page + served JSON; a page → itself and every page that includes it | in the FHIR layer, documented with its AST tooling (skill_fetch ig-ast-delta) | . | document-site, public-comment-site, library-site | a block, a document/chapter/section manifest, media/*, the public-comment store, a file in a declared library entry or a folio review-anchors.json naming one (the entry’s Document view and doc.json; its structure.json also the library index) | loaded from the published changeset.json (each changed block’s label and file) and outline.json (the documents), never from source: a block lands on its document’s page, anchored at its label (anchors) — on a LAZY page (outline.json lazy) on its blocks/NNN.json chunk and index.hydrated.html instead, and a block added, removed, renamed or moved reshapes the shell and every chunk from its position on; a file no builder of the site reads is an input with no page: each builder in the folio’s build command exports siteReads (the folio; the comment store; every directory of a typology holding a kind it renders), and a file outside all of them, the submodules, .github/ and the root’s non-Markdown files reaches nothing — so beans/ reaches no page, while todos/, whose pages are rendered, still may. A step that exports no siteReads excludes nothing; never decide it from the layer’s declaration, which also declares what no builder reads | in the document layer, with the ChangeSet Tool | . | docs-site | any file | a file in the COMPOSED Jekyll tree (docsLayers, composedInstances) → its page (permalink, or .md → .html) or asset; an include → the pages that include it, transitively; _data → the pages and includes that read it; a layout, a THEME include (read from the installed theme; unreadable means every include) or an include nothing calls → any page; any page change → the search index; a file outside the tree → undetermined when the staging cone carries any directory, nothing when it reaches none | cat-harness-tools/scripts/docs-rendered-impact.ts | . | published-provenance | a mounted layer’s skill, process or schema (anything a generator renders) | the published root’s own record of what each page was generated from — the “Generated from <path>” note and data-src on the edit link — read back as source → pages; a new source has no page yet and an index names no source, so both stay for the QA diff | cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-changes.ts (predictByProvenance) | . Two builds of one commit differ in every page by a ?v=<build time> cache-buster, so diffBuiltSites blanks BUILD_STAMPS before hashing; without that, every page reads as missed. A renderer’s command line belongs to the layer that owns it; this layer names none above it.

b49a4ec22c82.title: In the review process
b49a4ec22c82.content: content-change-review.bpmn: . | Produce: the staging build writes rendered-impact.json beside the preview and puts the review list in the PR comment. Each entry links to the preview and to main’s copy of the page. | Read: at Compare main vs staging, the reviewer opens every file on the review list, not only the pages the author mentions. Use before-after-preview for the pairs, and visual-diff for figures. | Measure: the staging job diffs its build against main’s published site (measure-rendered-impact.ts, before the banner goes on) and writes rendered-measured.json: what changed, and what the prediction MISSED. Only when that site was built from the PR’s base does it count (status: known); otherwise main’s own changes would read as misses (not-base). No published main site, no file: “not measured”, never “nothing missed”. The review page shows it under the list, as the PR comment does: a run started by dispatch finds its PR from the branch, so the comment is not lost when no pull_request event started the run. | Show: every docs-site preview also carries branches/<slug>/changes/ (cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-changes.ts): the changed sources, with a re-pinned mount in index.lock.json expanded into the files its repository changed between the two pins (a re-pin handed to a renderer as one JSON line predicts nothing); the cone’s files and its undetermined inputs; and the build diffed against the site at the gh-pages root, its missed files listed as changed, not in the cone. That diff folds the preview’s base URL to the root’s, blanks BUILD_STAMPS and compares a page’s <main>, because a preview’s chrome differs on every page; a removed file is listed apart, by directory, since most are parts of the site the preview does not carry. The root records its build commit in build.json; a root not built from the PR’s base is said on the page, never read as this branch’s change. | Gate: review-coverage-gate.dmn reads three page counts beside the block counts, each with a status fact so an uncomputed count is never 0: . | unreviewedPages: review-list files nobody has reviewed at their current pin. A page is reviewed by a page: verdict, or block by block when every block anchored on it has a verdict; a data file goes with a reviewed page that shares its pin. | undeterminedInputs: inputs no renderer placed, until an input: verdict or waiver (with a reason) says somebody looked. | missedPages: measured but not predicted, until a page: verdict. | . A pin is the hash of the git blobs of the changed inputs on a file’s via (pinImpact), never the built bytes, which carry a per-build banner. An edit after review reopens exactly the pages it touched. The tag is in review-comments. | .

44637aa110f6.title: Adding a renderer
44637aa110f6.content: . | Map each input kind the renderer reads to the rendered files it writes, through the dependency information the renderer ALREADY has. Never re-derive a mapping the renderer’s own tool records (SUSHI’s fsh-index is the authority for FSH → resource). | Put every other input in undetermined, unless the renderer cannot read it at all: then it is an input with no file. Decide that from what the layer declares, never from a list of names here. | Test it against a real build with comparePrediction: 0 missed is the bar. | .

265147112de7.title: /repo-conversion — folio-assistant over a repo that already has a life
265147112de7.content: Skill repo-conversion: Lay folio-assistant over a repository that already exists, without losing or silently moving what is in it. Scans the tree read-only, classifies candidate files into library (external source) and content (authored here) with an explicit third bucket for what it cannot classify, scans outside the content tree for mathematical evidence and refutations, lists the content markers (an IG, a DAK, processes, work items, library, Lean, folio manifests) the harness could declare and declares only the ones the person picks, puts the three questions the scan cannot answer to the author as selections, and hands ingestion to one agent or a small swarm. Use when a user wants an existing repo converted to a folio, asks to import what is already there, asks whether their PDFs/notes/drafts can come along, or asks what else in a repository an existing harness could declare. Named by: Getting started, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Process: the content core’s processes/conduct/getting-started.bpmn, Task_ScanRepo, Task_ChooseHarnessed and Task_ConfirmImport (both non-relaxable). Scanner: bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts.

4cc9db83b943.title: 0. The one rule
4cc9db83b943.content: Scan, show, ask, then move — and never in any other order. The author’s repository is the thing of value; the scaffolding is replaceable. A wrong import is not fixed by a git checkout, because the author has to work out what the agent did. Task_ConfirmImport is marked relaxable="false" in the BPMN, and a content package may not declare it away.

f1750c20a69a.title: 1. Scan — read-only, and honest about its limits
f1750c20a69a.content: bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts # human-readable report bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts --json # same, as facts . It walks the working tree (respecting .gitignore) and sorts what it finds into three buckets: . | bucket | means | typical | . | library | external source material — something somebody else wrote, that the folio will cite or ingest | PDFs, papers, scans, datasets, references/, papers/, sources/ | . | content | material authored here, that could become folio blocks | Markdown prose, docs/, notes/, drafts/, .tex | . | unclassified | it could not tell | everything else, and it is reported, not hidden | . unclassified is reported, never forced. A two-bucket scanner’s mistakes arrive as moved files; this one reports what it could not place, and the author disposes of it. The classification is by path convention and extension only. It does not read file contents or call a model, so the author can disagree with any row of it in one word. Outside-content candidate scanning — preserving evidence and refutations . In repositories with formal, analytical, or domain-specific content, crucial verification scripts, macros, and counterexamples often live outside the primary content tree (content/ or folio/); a conversion that carries only that tree drops the evidence that some claims are false. scan-repo-content.ts scans outside the content tree and classifies these artifacts into read-only candidate classifications (defined by the content-type layer’s conversion refinement skill), reporting source location, rationale, and linkStatus (linked when referenced by at least one content block, or unlinked when orphaned). Like the general scan, candidate scanning never writes, moves, or modifies files; it presents the candidates to the author and agent so decisions can be made before importing.

78856cfdf2c8.title: 2. Show, then ask — three questions, all as selections
78856cfdf2c8.content: Present the scan as counts and a handful of examples per bucket, never as a 1,400-line file list. Then three questions, each answerable by picking. Load interaction-modality first. Q1 — import at all? . | Import everything the scan found (recommended) | Import only the library bucket — sources now, prose later | Import nothing; just set up folio-assistant | Let me pick bucket by bucket | . Q2 — where does each group go? Only for groups the scan was not confident about, and only when Q1 was not “nothing”. Offer library/ vs content/ per directory, not per file (a per-file interrogation is the accessibility failure in interaction-modality §0). Q3 — leave in place, or reorganise? . | Leave everything where it is (recommended) — the folio references the files at their current paths. Nothing moves, every existing link still works, and the decision stays open. | Reorganise into library/ and content/ — tidier, and it rewrites paths. Offer this only on a clean working tree, do it in its own commit, and use git mv so history follows. | . Recommend leave in place by default: a broken relative link in somebody’s README is a defect.

b7ca9fc54c4e.title: 2a. Markers — choose what the harness reads (declare, don’t slurp)
b7ca9fc54c4e.content: A harness declares what it reads in a repository; it does not take all of its content. The principle is directory-conventions §”A marker declares what is read, and nothing else is”. The scan’s fourth section, markers, lists the content a harness COULD be told to read: a sushi-config.yaml (an IG: contentTypes.ig), a legacy dak.json (contentTypes.dak), .bpmn processes, a work items store, library/, uploads/, Lean (contentType: paper) and folio manifests (contentType: document). For each it gives the paths, whether it is already declared — declared, not-declared, or unknown when there is no readable index.config.json to ask — and the snippet that would declare it, with where it goes (index.config.json#contentTypes, or a local layer’s <name>.json#directories). Content types come from the registry (defaultContentTypes; an { indexSection } type is checked against contentTypes.<id>), directory facets are checked against the registered graph typologies, and only the evidence the registries cannot state is a short table in cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/content-markers.ts. Where each kind of content lives is directory-conventions. bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts [dir] --markers # the list bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts [dir] --markers --json # same, as facts . A plain command: any agent host (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, Cursor, Copilot) or a person at a shell runs it, with no MCP server. It writes nothing. Q0 — which of these should the harness read? (Task_ChooseHarnessed, non-relaxable). Ask it the interaction-modality way — the full question in the chat, then a tap card where the host has one, otherwise a numbered pick-list with its default stated. Never a typed reply. Offer only the markers that are not-declared (or unknown), one option each: . | None of these for now (the default) — nothing is declared; the scan can be run again any time | contentTypes.ig — sushi-config.yaml, input/fsh/, … (the FHIR IG) | directories: processes — processes/ (7 BPMN files) | Let me pick several — the same options as a multi-select | . The default declares nothing, and the agent never declares a marker the person did not pick. Declare exactly the picks — the scan’s suggestion snippet, at its suggestion.at — in the scaffolding commit, or in its own commit on a layer that already exists. After setup, too. The same question fits any layer at any time: “what else could this harness declare?” is --markers on the layer’s repository, then Q0. Rows already declared are shown for context and are not offered. A content type registered by a higher harness layer appears as a hint when that layer is not loaded, with a note saying where the type lives. Declaring a scoped content type is not a boolean flag: its include list states everything that layer’s readers will read, so confirm the list with the person and consult that layer’s build-pipeline skill for how additional paths are added later.

441e757d1f5a.title: 3. Dispatch the ingestion
441e757d1f5a.content: Ingestion proper is library/processes/document-ingestion.bpmn (and the content layer’s document-intake refinement skill when converting into a content folio). What this skill decides is how much parallelism, and it is a question for the author because it spends their tokens: . | scale | when | how | . | inline | under ~10 documents | do it here, no subagents | . | one agent | tens of documents, one kind | a single background agent, reporting per document | . | small swarm | hundreds, or several distinct kinds | dispatch-agent (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) — 2–4 agents partitioned by directory, never by file count | . Partition by directory because a per-file partition puts two agents in the same manifest, and the conflicts cost more than the parallelism saves. Open one work item per ingestion front before dispatching — running the existence check in todo-manager.md (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) §”Check before you create” first — so a session that dies mid-import leaves a plan behind rather than a half-full library/.

4f9144b4e01c.title: 4. The conversion itself
4f9144b4e01c.content: Once Q1–Q3 are answered, folio_init against the existing directory. It refuses rather than overwrites where a file is already present, which on this branch is the common case (README.md, .gitignore, a docs/). Read its report rather than assuming; the files it declined to write are the ones you now merge by hand: . | AGENTS.md — if one exists, merge; do not replace. It is the most valuable file in the repository for the next agent. | README.md — never replaced. readme-sections.ts only writes inside marker pairs the author has opted into, so offer to add markers rather than content. | .gitignore — append the folio entries; keep theirs. | . If the remote is empty, push main first. A repository with work locally can still have an empty remote, and GitHub makes the first branch pushed to an empty repository its default. Run init-folio or push main before any feature branch. If main has no harness yet, land a setup-only PR first. A fork or an existing repository whose main has no index.config.json and index.lock.json gives the full PR checks nothing to compare against: the base side fails before any test runs, and the PR’s own gates are skipped. So open one small PR with only what folio_init writes and the pins, merge it, and only then branch for content. Draft-tier checks never build the base, so this does not show until the content PR leaves draft. The setup-only PR has a Tool: instantiate-harness. It pins the harness and every layer it needs, mounts them, commits the setup on harness/<harness>, opens that PR, and renders the branch’s preview at gh-pages:branches/<branch>/. On a repository with nothing mounted yet, run it from a fresh clone of the tools layer: . git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness-tools /tmp/cht echo "<where the author consented>" | bun run /tmp/cht/scripts/instantiate-harness.ts \ --repo . --harness <owner/repo> --consent-by <who> [--plan | --local] . The setup also writes .github/cat.ts and .github/mount-from-lock.sh and sets the root’s cat script to bun .github/cat.ts, so after the merge a fresh clone needs no mount step: the first bun run cat … mounts the layers. --plan prints the closure and every step and writes nothing; --local commits on the branch and pushes nothing. The harness’s own adoption steps are its checkout scripts instantiate:<harness> (files it declares, committed with the setup) and prepare:<harness> (what the site is built from, never committed). For an IG on a FHIR harness these declare contentTypes.ig and build the IG’s first AST. A harness built on this platform may add adoption steps of its own for its kind of repository, for example about CI that already publishes a site on every push. Ask skill_list for the skill governing that kind before calling the conversion done.

d77b49282660.title: 5. Publishing — provision gh-pages first; an overlay needs it too
d77b49282660.content: An overlay never reaches getting-started §5 by itself, so this section repeats the one step a publishing route cannot skip: provision gh-pages before GitHub Pages is switched on. The step is Task_ProvisionGhPages (“Provision gh-pages”) in getting-started.bpmn, on the shared path after scaffolding and before the Pages build, and it carries the semantics of A_Provision in bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn. The tool is pages-bootstrap: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts # reports `unprovisioned` (exit 3) and the exact command when gh-pages is absent bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --provision # pushes an orphan gh-pages: placeholder index.html + .nojekyll . --provision is idempotent and never forces a push, and nothing creates a remote branch without it. Then switch Pages on with Source: “Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, / (root)” — the script prints the source it expects. When the repository’s publish workflow pushes gh-pages, “GitHub Actions” is the wrong source: the workflow would push a branch Pages was never told to serve. The same holds for an overlay that remote-mounts its dependencies. A mount brings layers in; it does not provision anything on the downstream’s remote.

21662e6eb052.title: 6. Anti-patterns
21662e6eb052.content: . | Moving a file before Q3 is answered. | Reporting a two-bucket classification. If unclassified is empty on a real repository, suspect the scanner rather than celebrate it. | A per-file confirmation loop. See §2. | Swarming a 12-document import. The dispatch overhead exceeds the work. | Replacing an existing AGENTS.md or README.md. Merge, or leave. | Treating the scan as ingestion. It reads; it never writes. Ingestion is a separate process with its own diagram and its own gate. | Switching Pages on before gh-pages exists, or choosing “GitHub Actions” for a workflow that pushes gh-pages. See §5. | Dropping outside-content math artifacts or unlinked audit refutations. Carrying only the primary content tree (content/ or folio/) drops outside proofs, computations, and refutations showing that some paper claims are false. See §1. | .
