d6b5a08693e3.title: Staging review — before/after comparison
d6b5a08693e3.content: Skill staging-review: Staging preview and before/after comparison for content review. Takes one optional string — what the reader wants to look at, in their own words — and returns a list of URLs, each looked up in the publish ref, with what is published at it and what to review there. Provides before (MAIN) and after (branches/) pairs so reviewers can compare rather than guess. Used by the CRDM feature development workflow, content authoring review sessions, and whenever a staging preview deploys or someone asks to see it. Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Committee review of a content change, Make the content change, Merge and publish a content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Evidence for a recommendation, Guideline Updates, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Public comment on a review draft, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Board: place a note . Skill id: staging-review · Package: sdlc-core . Provide before/after URL pairs whenever rendered content has changed in a feature branch. This is part of every review or feedback session involving visual content. URLs tell the reviewer where to look. The captured, measured pair that goes with them is before-after-preview (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc).

ed118305f749.title: The deep-link rule — every request for feedback
ed118305f749.content: The rule now lives in feedback-deep-links, outside the opt-in sdlc sub-graph, so every layer has it (owner, 2026-11-10, card Q-SG-2 option A). This skill builds the links that rule asks for.

a1c006d0f439.title: Signature — one optional string in, a reviewable list out
a1c006d0f439.content: Other processes invoke this skill, and so does a person typing /staging-review, so the contract is stated formally: one left in prose is one each caller re-derives. Input . |   |   | . | type | string | . | cardinality | 0,1 — optional, and at most one | . | meaning | what the reader wants to look at, in their own words | . | absent | the whole preview: every page this branch changed | . Keep the wording verbatim wherever the output echoes it — the same rule goal-review (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) applies to a goal: a request the agent paraphrased is a different request, and the reader cannot tell which one the list was built for. It narrows; it never adds. “The navbar” gets the pages carrying it, not a page that mentions it. An ask matching nothing that changed is said, not answered with the whole preview — a list that silently ignores its input is worse than an empty one, because the reader believes it was answered. Output . Markdown, in this order. Every part is required; an absent part is stated, not dropped. | What changed, in prose — a short narrative, before any link: what a reader of the site will now see or do differently, in plain sentences, and why (the request it answers, in the requester’s words where there are any). One paragraph per PR or per coherent change. A table of URLs tells a reviewer where to look; only the narrative tells them what they are looking for, and a reviewer who has not read the code cannot reconstruct it from a filename. | Where to start — one line, one URL: the one that best answers the input, or the page with the most change behind it when there was none. A reader opens one thing first whether or not you choose it for them. | The comparison table below — before (main), after (staging), what to review. Links are deep — to the page, and to the anchor on it where the change sits (…/#harness-cat-harness), never the site root with “scroll down”. | The pictures — a before/after pair for each visual change, SHOWN to the reviewer (sent as images where the surface allows it), not only linked. A link asks the reviewer to do the comparison; a pair does it for them. How to make a fair pair is before-after-preview (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc). If a pair could not be made, say which and why — that is part 5, not a silent gap. | What could not be checked, per the three states below. | . The third column is the one with value . What changed must be phrased as something to look at, never as a restatement of the filename. Build it by mapping changed files to published surfaces: . | what changed | which page | what to say | . | a stylesheet or client script | every page that loads it | the affordance that changed, and the gesture to make | . | a template or include | the pages that include it | where on the page to look | . | generated content | the page it generates | what it was generated from — a stale generator and a correct one look identical on the page | . | a schema, a test, a gate | none | say so, and point at the diff | . | folio content (block manifests and prose) | the page each block renders on | the ChangeSet’s aspect: reworded, moved, renamed, added, removed. See below. | . Where a change is only visible after an interaction — a control behind a disclosure, a mode a reader turns on — say WHICH interaction. A reviewer who cannot find the thing reports it as missing, and a gate that sweeps the page without opening the view misses a defect behind it. You can open it yourself — the publish ref is a git branch . Everything above composes URLs for a reader. The agent writing them usually cannot open them. From inside a session container: . | route | result | . | curl https://<owner>.github.io/… | 403 — CONNECT tunnel failed (policy denial) | . | WebFetch | EGRESS_BLOCKED | . | Playwright / Chromium | net::ERR_TUNNEL_CONNECTION_FAILED | . A browser is not a way around it — Chromium is proxy-configured too, so “use Playwright” fails identically. Without another route, nothing in the repository can look at what deployed, and a defect only a click reveals ships past every green gate. But the site is published to the gh-pages BRANCH, and git works. So the deployed bytes are readable with git show, and a Playwright route handler can serve them at their real path: . const blob = (p: string) => { try { return execFileSync("git", ["show", `origin/gh-pages:${ROOT}/${p}`], { maxBuffer: 1 << 28 }); } catch { return undefined; } // absent is a FINDING, not a 200 }; let missing = 0; // REPORT THIS. See below. await page.route(`${ORIGIN}/**`, (route) => { const u = new URL(route.request().url()); let p = u.pathname.startsWith(BASE) ? u.pathname.slice(BASE.length) : u.pathname; p = p.replace(/^\/+/, ""); if (p === "" || p.endsWith("/")) p += "index.html"; const b = blob(p) ?? blob(`${p}/index.html`) ?? shared(p); if (!b) { missing++; return route.fulfill({ status: 404, body: "not in the publish ref" }); } return route.fulfill({ contentType: typeFor(p), body: b }); }); . A preview that shares with the live site falls back to it. A preview (cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-share.ts) stores only the files that differ from the live site, and its staging-sw.js serves the rest from the live root in the browser. So when branches/<slug>/staging-sw.js is in the ref, a file absent from the preview is the live site’s file at the same path, and shared(p) must read it from the root (blob with ROOT set to ""). Without that, every shared file reads as missing. Where there is no staging-sw.js, shared returns undefined and an absent file is a finding. The worker also puts the banner and fa-staging back on a live page it serves, which the route handler does not, so judge banner presence on the preview’s own pages. ROOT is "" for the canonical deploy and branches/<slug> for a preview, so the same handler gives you the before/after pair this skill is about — and a count, not an impression. Fetch the ref first (git fetch --depth=1 --filter=blob:none origin gh-pages); blobs are then fetched on demand. Serve it under the real BASE. A page served at the origin root cannot reveal a missing baseurl, because “composed against the base” and “not composed at all” are the same string there, so an e2e at the root stays green over a missing baseurl. And BASE is NOT the site’s base when you are reading a preview. A preview is published at <origin>/folio-assistant/branches/<slug>/, so that whole prefix is what its pages compose hrefs against — BASE and ROOT carry the same staging segment, one in the URL and one in the ref: . | reading | ROOT (in the ref) | BASE (in the URL) | . | the canonical deploy | "" | /folio-assistant | . | a branches/ preview | branches/<slug> | /folio-assistant/branches/<slug> | . Getting that wrong doubles the segment — branches/<slug>/branches/<slug>/... — and every asset 404s. Report the absent count, and read it before anything else . A run that could not fetch the page’s assets has established nothing, and its other numbers are actively misleading: a wrong BASE on a correct deploy reports zero tiles, which looks like the very defect being checked for. The rule outranks every other number the run prints: . missing > 0 is COULD NOT DETERMINE. Not clean, and not a finding. Discard the run’s other counts rather than reading them, fix the rig, and re-run. Scanning nothing and reporting it broken is as wrong as reporting it clean, and costlier: an agent acting on it goes looking for a defect that is not there, or “fixes” one. What this does NOT verify, and it matters . It serves the bytes in the publish ref. It is not the live host, so it cannot see: . | redirects, headers, or anything else the host decides at request time | Pages’ own 404 handling, or its directory-index rules where they differ from the handler above | whether the deploy has actually published — a ref can hold bytes that Pages has not served yet (§”Say how long”) | . So a green result here means “the published bytes are right”, never “the site works”. Report it in those words. When it stops applying . The technique rests on one assumption: publishing goes to a branch. If publishing moves to the Pages artifact API, git fetch origin gh-pages fails and there is nothing to read. Report that as could not determine, never as a clean run — an empty ref and a correct deploy are opposite facts. The third state, here as everywhere . “Could not determine” is never rendered as clean — and a change with no rendered surface is not a failure, it is the useful answer. | case | report it as | . | not deployed yet | not deployed, with the timing from §”Say how long” — never a link to where it will be | . | a changed page absent from the publish ref | a finding — the build dropped it, or it is not a page | . | no rendered surface | reviewed in the diff, naming the files | . The middle row is the most useful thing this skill can report, and composing its URL anyway would hide exactly that — §”Before you report a staging URL as broken”. The commit in the bot’s comment is NOT your branch head . On a pull_request trigger the stage job builds refs/pull/<n>/merge — your head merged into the base — so the commit the comment names never equals your head and is not even in your clone. Comparing the two reports a stale preview on every PR. Resolve it instead. The merge commit’s second parent is the head it was built from: . git fetch origin "refs/pull/<n>/merge:refs/remotes/origin/pr-<n>-merge" -q git log --format="%h %p" -1 origin/pr-<n>-merge # <merge> <base> <YOUR HEAD> . Stale means that second parent is not your head — nothing else does. This is the same fact bun run cat gates exists around: CI tests the merge, and so does the preview, so a branch behind its base is previewing a tree nobody will have. A stub where a layer should be is the cone, not a broken build . A composed layer the branch cannot reach is replaced by a one-page stub pointing at the published copy. Which layers a preview carries is decided by the staging cone (feature-staging §7), and the build log prints each decision with its reason. Before reporting a missing IG as a defect, read that line. If the cone left out something your change does affect, the fix is a missing writer or derivedFrom on the directory’s declaration, not a rule to always carry it.

d5649d41b1d9.title: Which pages to list: the Change Set’s rendered list
d5649d41b1d9.content: When the change is a Change Set, do not choose the before/after pages by judgement: take them from its rendered list (skill rendered-impact (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)), every content page on it, and say which inputs the renderer could not place. A page the list does not name and you add anyway is fine; a page on the list that you leave out is a gap the reviewer cannot see.

6b5cbdc84580.title: When to provide before/after URLs
6b5cbdc84580.content: Provide before/after URLs in every interaction where: . | Content has changed on a feature branch (authoring, editing, translation) | CRDM feature development — once requirements are agreed and a staging preview exists | Review/feedback sessions — when the user asks to review changes | Translation review — comparing translated vs source pages | .

0fce783b7bfa.title: Before/after URL schema
0fce783b7bfa.content: Every feedback response involving rendered content must include a stagingComparison object: . interface StagingComparison { /** Feature branch name (e.g. "claude/206-staging-preview"). */ branch: string; /** URL to the branch on GitHub. */ branchUrl: string; /** PR number if one exists. */ pr?: number; /** Pairs of before (main) and after (staging) URLs for changed pages. */ pages: Array<{ /** Page title or path. */ title: string; /** URL on the main (production) site. */ before: string; /** URL on the staging preview site. */ after: string; /** What changed on this page. */ summary?: string; }>; } . Example output . When reporting changes to the user: . ### 📋 Staging comparison | Page | Before (main) | After (staging) | What changed |---|---|---|---| Landing page | [main](https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/#languages) | [staging](https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/branches/claude-206-staging-preview/#languages) | Added French translation badge (the landing page itself changed, so its root is the page; the anchor is where the badge sits) | French landing | — | [staging](https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/branches/claude-206-staging-preview/fr/index.html) | New page | Agent onboarding | [main](https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/docs/cat-harness/guides/agent-onboarding.html) | [staging](https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/branches/claude-206-staging-preview/docs/cat-harness/guides/agent-onboarding.html) | Language switcher added | .

7ec0f534a969.title: URL construction
7ec0f534a969.content: Main (before) . https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/<path> . Read from the layer’s config (its index.config.json entry) → readme.pagesBaseUrl, or construct from the repo’s GitHub Pages URL. Staging (after) . https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/branches/<branch-slug>/<path> . The <branch-slug> is the branch name with non-alphanumeric characters replaced by hyphens (the same transform as feature-staging.yml). Deriving the slug . function branchToSlug(branch: string): string { return branch .replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9._-]/g, "-") .replace(/-{2,}/g, "-") .replace(/^-|-$/g, ""); } .

cfb16e749a74.title: Integration with CRDM
cfb16e749a74.content: In the CRDM requirements workflow (Phase 5: implementation), once a staging preview is deployed: . | Post the staging URL on the GitHub issue as a comment. For a folio, post the review page too, branches/<slug>/review/, and name it as the page a reviewer opens first. The folio-staging workflow’s PR comment carries both links. The page lists every changed block, not only every changed page. Posting the site root alone sends a reviewer hunting through a 300-page document for a one-word edit. | Include before/after table for every changed page | Link from the PR body to the staging preview | Remind reviewers that staging uses the magenta “FEATURE BRANCH” banner | . The staging preview is part of the acceptance criteria: stakeholders must review the rendered output, not just the code diff.

901fff9da4bb.title: Integration with content authoring
901fff9da4bb.content: When an author has made content changes on a feature branch: . | Compute the ChangeSet, not a file list, when the branch touches a folio’s folio graph: the folio-changeset Tool, with --folio <folio dir> --base origin/main --head <branch>. Its command line is the Tool node’s invoke, declared by the content layer that defines the folio graph kind; this skill names the Tool, not that layer’s path. It says, per block, whether it was added, removed, reworded (prose), edited (manifest), moved or renamed. A file list cannot: a prose-only edit changes no .ts, and a move changes two files that look unrelated. Rank “where to start” by it. For a large document, the section with the most changed blocks is where a reviewer’s time goes first. | Construct before/after URLs for each changed docs page, and for each page carrying a changed block | Present the change to the author in the Output order above: the narrative first, then the deep-linked comparison table, then the before/after pictures themselves | Offer to run the staging workflow if not already running | . Finding your way on the review page . A 300-page review needs to know where it is, and to move in one key or one click. The review page has a navigation pane, beside the list on a wide screen and above it on a narrow one: . | Outline. Each document’s chapters and sections, in manifest order, from the outline.json the folio’s site build writes. | A section with something to review is a button that moves focus to it, with word badges (“2 changed, 1 comment, QA failing”). | Any other section links to its published page. | It is on the review page only; normal pages carry no table of contents. | . | Minimap. One cell per block, in order. It is one tab stop: Up and Down move, Home and End jump to either end, and Enter opens the block. Each cell is labelled in words and marked with glyphs (Δ changed, + added, ● open comments, ! QA failing), so colour is never the only signal. | Where am I. Every move announces “document › chapter › section › block” in the page’s one live status line. | . Keys, each with a visible button twin: . | key | button | goes to | . | j | Next | the next item | . | k | Previous | the previous item | . | n | Next with comments | the next block with open comments | . | p | Previous with comments | the previous block with open comments | . | u | Next unreviewed | the next changed block with no reviewer verdict on its CURRENT version | . “Unreviewed” means no verdict on this version, not “no comments”. A block whose only verdict is on an earlier version is unreviewed, and says so in words (“1 verdict on an earlier version, not counted”). A build whose review-comments.json carries no verdicts says “No verdict data on this build” rather than treating every block as unread. Typing into a selector is never navigation. Tests. the tools layer’s test/review-nav.e2e.ts drives all of this with the keyboard alone. It uses no mouse, no click and no hover. The review page, and choosing how to see a change . A folio’s preview carries review/index.html: every changed block, grouped by section, with its reviewer comments (the review-comments skill). Each changed block has a “Show this change as” selector, and one at the top applies to every block: . | renderer | shows | the default for | needs | . | Word diff of the source | the Markdown with removed words struck and added words marked: exactly what the author typed | any kind not listed below | the block’s prose | . | Inline, as rendered | the block as a reader sees it now, with the change marked in place | prose, remark, definition, example | the block’s prose | . | Pictures, before and after | a picture of the block on each side, the changed pixels marked, and the share changed in words (visual-diff (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)) | table, figure, diagram, equation, simulator | visual-diff.json from the folio-block-screenshots Tool | . | Side by side | main and the preview next to each other, each scrolled to the block | the same kinds, as the second choice when a build published no pictures | a page on either side | . | Where the data comes from. The ChangeSet step’s --text-out writes changeset-text.json: the source and rendered prose of each listed block, on each side that has it. The pictures step writes visual-diff.json and visual/. With neither file, only side by side is available, and the page says so. | Two renderers may default for one kind. Order is preference: the page opens a block on the first renderer that lists its kind AND can run. | A renderer that cannot run on a block is listed, disabled, with the reason. For example, a manifest-only change has no prose to diff. If the page-level choice cannot run on a block, that block falls back to one that can. | The page-level choice is remembered for this viewer in localStorage. A private window just gets the defaults. | The renderers and the registry are cat-harness-tools/scripts/review-renderers.ts, cat-harness-tools/scripts/word-diff.ts (no diff library; about forty lines, tested) and cat-harness/schemas/ui/diff-renderers.ts. To add one, declare it in the registry with what it needs and which kinds it defaults for, add its function to review-renderers.ts, and add a case to the page’s renderInto. | .

d595e4ba13ed.title: Staging retention
d595e4ba13ed.content: A MERGED pull request’s preview goes away. Everything else is retained by default, subject to the size cap below. The distinction is about where the content lives, not about how confident anyone is: . | the PR was | the preview is | so | . | merged | the same thing the MAIN SITE now shows | redundant on the instant, and removed automatically — no label | . | closed, unmerged | the ONLY rendering of that work | the last copy, and retained unless a person says otherwise | . The store therefore drains: what remains is bounded by concurrent reviews, not by cumulative history, so a size warning stays a signal rather than becoming a permanent verdict. This applies deletion-requires-confirmation; it does not relax it. The merge is the confirmation: a person decided this content belongs on main. What the label guards is the case where nobody decided anything. Removal is one preview directory at a time. Which mechanism depends on whether the PR is still open. Three cases, and the label cannot reach a closed PR: . | Merged — nothing to do. cleanup reads github.event.pull_request.merged off the close event and removes without a label, recording the reason as merged. | While the PR is open, and it will not be merged — add the staging:cleanup label. cleanup in feature-staging.yml fires on pull_request_target: closed and reads the labels off that event, so the label has to be there before the PR closes. | Once the PR is closed unmerged and unlabelled — run feature-staging.yml from the Actions tab with cleanup_slug: <slug> and cleanup_confirm: <slug>. The confirmation repeats the slug so that it names the artefact it confirms, and the job re-checks that nothing is still using the preview before it removes anything. | . Labelling a closed PR does nothing, and re-running its old workflow run does nothing either — a re-run replays the stored event payload, which still carries no label. So for an orphan the health sweep’s staging-preview-orphans finding names, option 2 is the remedy. If you find yourself reaching for a hand-pushed gh-pages commit instead, stop: that is the unilateral removal deletion-requires-confirmation exists to stop, and option 2 exists so you do not have to. The cap — 3 GB of previews in total, the oldest rotated off . Previews are capped by total size, not count, because preview sizes vary widely and a count bounds the total only while preview size holds still. GitHub Pages deploys gh-pages as-is, and past its 10 GB artifact limit the live site stops deploying. Every removal path above is per-preview and event-driven; none bounds the total. What the stage job does, on every deploy, before its one push: . | Sums the size of the previews under branches/, including the one it is staging, and keeps them within 3 GB. The number lives once, as MAX_PREVIEW_BYTES in cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-rotate.ts. | Keeps the newest that fit and removes the rest, oldest first — strictly by recency. An older small preview never outlives a newer one that did not fit, so a preview’s age alone says whether it is still there. One 780 MB preview displaces several small ones; that is what a size budget means. “Last updated” is the branches/<slug>/.staged-at stamp the job writes on every stage, falling back to the latest rendered render-log entry, then the record’s builtAt, then git. The preview being staged is never removed. | Never touches branches/_retired/ or anything that is not a preview directory. | Leaves a record for each removal — a removed render-log entry with the reason, the preview’s staging-preview.json retired into _retired/, and a line in the commit message and the job log giving slug, age and size. | . This DOES reach open pull requests. Under the cap, the oldest preview goes whatever its PR’s state; the owner’s cap is the confirmation deletion-requires-confirmation asks for, given for the class. It is recoverable because a preview is a build, not content: the next push to that PR’s branch re-stages it, and the run that re-stages it can never rotate it off. So when a reviewer’s preview link 404s, check _render-log/ on gh-pages for a removed entry for its slug before calling it broken — if it says “rotated off”, push to the branch (an empty commit will do) or re-run the PR’s Feature Staging workflow. A closed PR is not an abandoned preview . staging-preview-orphans does not ask “is there an open PR?”, and neither should you. A session that reuses one branch across successive pull requests has no open PR for the whole gap between one merging and the next opening. Liveness is three signals, any one of which means leave it alone: an open PR, a branch on the remote carrying work not in the default branch, or a tip commit in the last 30 minutes. scripts/staging-cleanup-preflight.ts --slug <slug> answers the same question on demand, and the dispatch above runs it before removing.

5a586cabfa31.title: Before you hand a staging URL to a person (STRICT)
5a586cabfa31.content: A staging URL is not a deliverable until you have checked the ref, and it is never “live” on your say-so. The bot’s comment says a workflow pushed, not that a site serves. Three states, and conflating any two of them is the defect: . |   | observable from a container? | how | . | the stage job succeeded | yes | the check run on the PR’s head | . | the files are in gh-pages | yes | read branches/<slug>/ on refs/heads/gh-pages | . | the URL serves them | NO | see below | . The third is not available to you, and curl will not make it available. The proxy blocks github.io, so a fetch returns 000 and says nothing either way. And where Pages is configured as Deploy from a branch — as it is here — its builds produce no workflow runs at all (event: page_build returns total_count: 0, and there is no pages-build-deployment workflow to query). So there is no API answer either. So: verify the ref, and report the third state as unverified rather than inferring it. Listing branches/<slug>/ on gh-pages and finding index.html proves the build ran and what it published; it does not prove Pages has rebuilt. Those are different claims and only one of them is yours to make. LIST the directory. Do not FETCH the page. A staging page is ~100 KB of rendered HTML, a context window spent to learn a fact the directory listing gives for free. The listing returns a name and a byte count per entry; index.html present and non-zero is the whole check. Request only the name and size fields. Say how long, and come back . A person handed a URL with no timing either refreshes a 404 or walks away. Give them the number and the follow-up, in the same breath as the link: . | The stage job takes about 22 minutes, plus its wait at the rate limit (derived artefacts, the knowledge-graph export, mounting, Jekyll and checks). Drafts are staged too, from the first push. The job then waits until gh-pages has gone 5 minutes without a staging push and 10 without a main-site one (feature-staging §7), and its PR comment says queued with an earliest push time and a live-by time while it waits. Quote those times; they are the job’s own estimate. | Pages propagation is on top of that, and GitHub documents it as up to ten minutes. Since it is unobservable from here, quote the bound rather than a guess: “give it ~5 minutes; up to 10 if Pages is slow.” | Then actually check back. Schedule it rather than promising it — the same mechanism that watches a PR. Re-list the ref, and if the person reports a 404 after the window, that is a real finding worth chasing; before it, it is the window. | . Never present a URL as though it is already serving. “Deployed to gh-pages, should be live in ~5 minutes” is the honest sentence and costs nothing. Check for newer cleanup commits on gh-pages . Before declaring a preview good, check the gh-pages commit log for any staging(cleanup) commit touching that slug that is newer than the last staging(...) publish: . git log -n 5 --oneline origin/gh-pages -- "branches/<slug>" . If a staging(cleanup) commit appears newer than the last staging(...) publish, or if the directory was deleted within the hour, flag it immediately. A preview whose slug was recently deleted and re-published is vulnerable to cancelled Pages builds: if Pages cancelled the re-publish build, the site continues serving the deletion (a 404) even though the publish ref has the files. A preview whose slug was deleted within the hour is not in the ordinary propagation window. Re-publishing without a code push . When a preview needs to be rebuilt or re-published — because a previous Pages build was cancelled, or because a slug was deleted by cleanup from a preceding PR — you do not need an empty code commit or push. Dispatch the staging workflow directly with the branch name: . gh workflow run feature-staging.yml -f branch=<branch> . This triggers feature-staging.yml via workflow_dispatch for that branch, building and deploying a fresh preview to branches/<slug>/ on gh-pages and queueing a new Pages build.

798c8b1e43b6.title: Do not
798c8b1e43b6.content: . | Do not hand over a staging URL without listing branches/<slug>/ on gh-pages first. The bot’s comment says a workflow pushed, not that a site serves. | Do not declare a preview good without checking the gh-pages commit log for newer cleanup commits. A staging(cleanup) commit newer than the publish means a cancelled Pages build leaves the live site serving a 404. | Do not say a preview is “live”, “up” or “deployed and ready” unless someone has loaded it. You cannot see that from here. | Do not provide before/after URLs without checking the staging workflow has run. A URL that 404s is worse than no URL. | Do not remove a staging preview by hand without confirmation. Apart from a merged PR’s preview and the size cap’s rotation, a person confirms every removal — the label while the PR is open, or the dispatch with its repeated-slug confirmation once it is closed. | Do not read “no open pull request” as “abandoned”. It is true of a live branch for the whole gap between one PR merging and the next opening. | Do not assume all pages are at the root. Guides are under guides/, reference under reference/, French under fr/ etc. | Do not omit the comparison table. Even for a single page change, show the before/after pair — it is the whole point of staging. | .

2ab13ad4ee60.title: Before you report a staging URL as broken
2ab13ad4ee60.content: Look at the publish ref, not the site. A staging URL is LOOKED UP in gh-pages under branches/<branch-slug>/, never composed from the source path — docs/<stub>/proposals/x.md publishes to /proposals/x.html, and composing it from the source path yields a 404 for a page that is there. From an agent container a curl against a Pages URL fails on the proxy regardless, so a failed fetch is not evidence either way. Full rule: github-state-inspection (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc).

78afc665d1be.title: Sub-KG lifecycle — staged here, separated later
78afc665d1be.content: Skill sub-kg-lifecycle: A sub-KG is a knowledge graph staged as a directory inside a harnessed repository, declared as its own layer, that may later leave for a repository of its own. The lifecycle: declare it in place, grow it, stage it for separation (one import seam, the separation guard, a self-contained rehearsal), and then, each behind an explicit owner confirmation, create the repository, copy the staged contents in with history, re-point the declaration, verify on a fresh clone and delete the in-repo copy. The light sibling of kg-separation: use this for a DATA layer that leaves whole, and kg-separation when a graph must split into a content repository and a tools repository. Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Skill id: sub-kg-lifecycle · Package: graph-management Process: sub-kg-lifecycle.bpmn Stages 6 to 13 are drawn as the phases it shares with kg-separation: authorise, move and cut over. A sub-KG created inside a folio or harnessed repository can move to its own repository later: once it is staged for separation, a new repository is created and the staged contents are copied into it.

95e698788646.title: Which skill, this one or kg-separation?
95e698788646.content: | the graph | use | . | holds data — an artefact index, generated pages, a library, a folio — and leaves whole | this skill | . | holds data and the code that writes it, and the two must become a content repository and a tools repository | kg-separation — its fourteen stages, the pair, FR-7 | . | is not yet a graph at all — tangled into its host | graph-detanglement first | . The two share their gates on purpose. Ready to seed? here is the same decision table, seed-readiness-gate.dmn, evaluated by the same command, and the owner’s confirmations here are the same rule, deletion-requires-confirmation. What this skill adds is the part kg-separation does not cover: a sub-KG born in the host, with no tools pair, that leaves in one piece.

fe9bbf33fb87.title: How a sub-KG is born — the intent question
fe9bbf33fb87.content: A content type’s own creation skill asks whether the new thing goes in a new repository or inside this one, and routes here for the second answer. For a folio in general that is getting-started’s add-folio branch. A harness above this one may own a creation skill for its own kind of graph; ask skill_list for it rather than improvising. In-repository is the cheaper default whenever the session is already in a harnessed repository. Every stage up to 6 is reversible with git revert, and nothing outside the repository changes until stage 7. A new repository is the first irreversible, outward-facing act, and this lifecycle puts it behind a confirmation rather than at the start.

3cd46f275a4c.title: The stages
3cd46f275a4c.content: Each stage names its lane (a role in scenarios/roles.json) and what decides that it is done. A stage is done when its check is green, never when the work looks finished. | # | stage | lane | done when | . | 0 | Brief, claim the work item (opening-brief) | authoring-agent | work item claimed with bun run cat beans:claim | . | 1 | Declare it in place | authoring-agent | the declaration parses; instance-repositories.test.ts green | . | 2 | Grow it in place | authoring-agent | the content type’s own gates | . | 3 | Push generic down | platform-authoring-agent | check:import-direction, check:reference-direction, check:process-bindings add nothing | . | 4 | One import seam | platform-authoring-agent | every climb out of the directory goes through <name>/platform.ts | . | 5 | Rehearse self-contained | build-pipeline | bun run cat seed:ready --layer <name> --rehearse | . | 6 | Report what would move | authoring-agent | the report is in the work item (as kg-separation stage 9) | . | 7 | Owner confirms: create the repository | administrator | an answer, recorded in the work item | . | 8 | Create the repository | administrator | it exists, empty, and was read before writing | . | — | Ready to seed? | build-pipeline | seed-readiness-gate.dmn answers settled | . | 9 | Copy the staged contents in, with history | authoring-agent | a reviewed PR on a branch of the new repository | . | 10 | Re-point the declaration | platform-authoring-agent | the host is green consuming the new repository | . | 11 | Verify on a fresh clone | build-pipeline | the new repository’s gates green from git clone in an empty directory | . | 12 | Owner confirms: delete the in-repo copy | administrator | an answer, recorded in the work item | . | 13 | Cutover commit | administrator | one commit, revertable (as kg-separation stage 13) | . 1 · Declare it in place . A directory <name>/ at the host’s root, with <name>/<name>.json: . { "name": "<name>", "repository": "<owner>/<name>", // the PLANNED home; IRIs key on it "livesAt": { "repository": "<owner>/<host>", "path": "<name>" }, // where it sits TODAY "version": "0.1.0", "needs": ["<the harness it instantiates>"], "directories": [ /* only directories that exist, each with its graphTypologies */ ] } . | repository differs from livesAt.repository — that difference is what makes the directory a staged layer, and it is what the separation guard and seed:ready read. Nothing lists the staged layers by hand. | The directory may sit anywhere — a root sibling is the convention, but the tools read livesAt.path, so folio/<name>/ works the same. | Scaffold it with init-folio --staged <path>: . bun run cat init-folio --staged <path> --title "<title>" \ --repository <owner>/<name> --needs <harness> # --host-repository when origin cannot say . It writes exactly two files, <path>/<name>.json and an empty <path>/platform.ts, and nothing at the host’s root; init-folio-staged.test.ts snapshots the whole host tree to hold that. Never --instance inside a host: it writes a repository’s worth of scaffolding (AGENTS.md, .mcp.json, a work items store, a session hook; 15 files, measured with --dry-run). --instance is for stage 8’s repository. | Declare a directory with its files, in one commit: a declared-but-absent directory is scanned as empty and reported clean. | . 3 · Push generic down — before the seam, not after . Move everything generic into the harness below, consolidate what the sub-KG needs into its own harness, and only then seed. The other order copies generic code into a repository that has to give it back. Wrong-direction edges hide in declarations and data, not only in imports: a skill definition naming a package one layer up, a dependsOn, a publication target enumerated in an input schema, prose links, a needs edge to an empty layer. So run all three direction checks, not one. 4 · One import seam: <name>/platform.ts . Every symbol the sub-KG uses from the platform is re-exported from one file, and nothing else in the directory climbs out of it. On the day it leaves, re-pointing the platform is a one-file edit instead of a sweep. cat-harness-tools/scripts/tests/instance-separation-imports.test.ts is the guard. It covers every layer whose repository differs from its livesAt.repository, not only those that opted in, because an opt-in guard is silent for exactly the layer that has no seam. Layers other layers build on are an explicit, checked exemption, and a layer that still climbs has a ceiling that may only fall. Create the seam at stage 1, not here. It costs one file on day one, and every later climb is a reroute. A merge from main is where new climbs arrive, so a red guard after one is the expected signal to reroute, not a regression. 5 · Rehearse self-contained — run the gates, do not scan . bun run cat seed:ready --layer <name> --rehearse --text # exit 0 settled, 1 not yet, 2 unknown . It copies the layer and what it needs into a scratch workspace of sibling directories and runs the tests there. It is a run rather than a reading because: . | a static import scan misses files the gates load at run time — a JSON code list read by URL, for one; | renaming the directory can change every generated page, when a URL prefix or a chrome lookup keys on the directory name. Take the identity from the declaration’s name, never from the path, and check for that before seeding into a different directory name. | . 7 and 12 · The two confirmations . Both are userTasks in the administrator lane, marked relaxable="false", and both follow deletion-requires-confirmation: the agent reports what would happen, how large it is and how it is undone, then waits. Silence is not a yes. The questions are numbered, four options at most, the recommended one first, with a stated default: . Before stage 8: . <name> is staged and rehearses green: N files, M MB, history of K commits. Creating <owner>/<name> is visible outside this repository and is not undone by a revert. May it be created? . | Yes — you create it, and tell me when it exists (recommended) | Yes — I create it (only if this session has that permission) | Not yet — keep it staged here | . Default if you do not answer: 3. Nothing is created. Before stage 13: . <owner>/<name> is green from a fresh clone and the host consumes it. The in-repo copy is N files. Deleting it is one commit, revertable. | Delete the in-repo copy now (recommended) | Keep it until the new repository’s first release | Show me the file list first | . Default if you do not answer: 2. Nothing is deleted. When the repository must be created by someone with credentials this session lacks, the hand-over is agent-handoff: one work item, one sentence for the person to relay. 9 · Copy the staged contents in, with history . The staged directory becomes the new repository’s content with its history: git subtree split --prefix=<name> in the host, then git subtree add (or a merge of the split branch) in the new repository. It goes in on a branch, as a draft PR, never straight to main. The new repository’s own root files — its declaration at the root, its config, its README — are a second commit in the same PR, so the copy itself stays byte-identical and reviewable. Ready to seed? comes first, at seed time, because the tree has moved since the rehearsal: every open PR touching the layer when the copy is taken is orphaned. Its criteria and thresholds are in kg-separation §”Ready to seed?”, and not restated here. 10 · Re-point the declaration . | what changes | how | . | livesAt | removed in the new repository — absent means “sits at the root of repository” | . | the seam | platform.ts points at wherever the platform now is: a remote-mounted path, or a sibling checkout | . | the host | remote mount if the host imports code from the sub-KG — a source.remote layer in the host’s root index.config.json (remote-mount; never a submodule); subscription (kg:subscribe) if it only reads its content | . | pins | the host pins a commit while staging, a version once released (upstream-version-adoption) | . | its site | the new repository publishes and previews itself (feature-staging, Which site): "site": { "agentRun": true } in its index.config.json when an agent publishes it, plus whatever workflow its publisher layer’s own creation skill requires (an IG’s AST-cache refresh, for one) | . | its checks | .github/workflows/harness-pr-checks.yml calling the tools layer’s layer-pr-checks.yml, so its gates run on every pull request | . | its QA record | when it declares a qa directory with storage (test/results/, cat/cat-harness/qa-reports, keyed by commit): .github/workflows/publish-qa.yml calling the tools layer’s layer-qa-publish.yml, so every push to main and every pull request publishes its results to its own qa-reports branch, and test/results/ in .gitignore. A host reads them at the commit it pins. Without the job, the declaration names a store nothing writes | . | .gitignore | the mount block, written by the mount tool between its own markers. Never typed: a hand-written marker makes remote-mount.ts refuse (markers unpaired) | . Copy these from a sibling repository of the same kind; never type them. A repository scaffolded by hand misses them, and its site cannot be built until each is copied in. The host keeps its own copy through this stage. The re-point is additive. 11 · Verify on a fresh clone . bun run cat sub-kg:verify-clone --repo <owner>/<name> --ref <seeding branch> --text # exit 0 green, 1 red, 2 unknown . The Tool sub-kg-verify-clone clones the new repository into an empty scratch directory with its submodules (and each --sibling beside it), installs, and runs its own gates script, else its test script. An empty tree, a failed clone or a repository with no gate is unknown, never green. Nothing in a seed runs standalone until the seam is re-pointed, so a test that climbs out (Cannot find module '../../../<harness>/…') fails here. A rehearsal in the host’s scratch space is not this check; it shares the host’s node_modules and network. The new repository’s own site is part of this check: bun run cat stage:local --repo . --dry-run from the fresh clone must build. A refusal names what stage 10 left out.

135dbcea725f.title: Stage 13: the frozen copy
135dbcea725f.content: After cutover the host keeps a frozen copy in fsh-guts, not a refreshed mirror and not a deletion. Step 12 asks (1) move to fsh-guts now, (2) keep in place until the first release, (3) show the file list first, default (2). Step 13 deposits the directory into the PARENT’s fsh-guts as a verified archive (not plain trees, which CI would audit as live content), then removes it from main. The deposit is the one state:seed --cutover makes for a state graph: an archive that must extract to the exact tree being removed, plus a provenance note (movedFrom, movedOn, sourceCommit, tree), and the removal commit is made only once it has landed. A separation targets the parent’s fsh-guts rather than the departing layer’s, which --cutover does not yet do. The live copy is the remote mount (index.config.json source.remote), npm package retrieval (kg-retrieve-npm), or subscription (kg:subscribe) from stage 10; the frozen one is never refreshed and never rendered. How checks treat a frozen subtree . This is the one place the rule is stated; scanners point here. A frozen subtree is one retired item, and its sibling note is the node that answers for it. Every reader of fsh-guts — the fsh-guts.jsonld export, the fsh-guts page, the render-pipeline and bean-reference tests, check:materialized-fixity — reports the note and does not enter the directory. The page shows it as one row in the via sidecar state. | Recognised by declaration, never by path. A directory is frozen because <name>.md beside it declares $schema: folio-fsh-guts/v1 and kind: separated-instance (isFrozenSubtree in schemas/kg/fsh-guts.ts). A copy dropped in with no note, or under a note of another kind, is walked like any directory, so its files fail self-declaration loudly rather than vanishing from every check. | The note must carry all four stage-13 fields — movedFrom, movedOn, repository, matchesCommit — because it is now the only thing any check reads about thousands of files. Those beyond the common set are exported under the node’s data. | Materialization records inside are not judged. They claim bytes in the repository the graph now lives in, which the copy deliberately does not carry. | The note’s bean: resolves against main’s work plan, with no pending escape. So the deposit lands on the fsh-guts branch in the same step that merges the PR carrying that work item, never before it; a deposit pushed ahead of its PR turns every PR’s CI red. | .

36d9491346ae.title: Anti-patterns
36d9491346ae.content: . | Creating the repository first. It is the one irreversible step; everything that can be done in place is done before it. | A seed with no history. A one-commit seed severs blame for every line, and the history is cheap to keep. | Re-pointing by sweep. If more than one file changes when the platform moves, the seam was skipped. | Reading the rehearsal as the fresh-clone check. They catch different things: the rehearsal catches climbs, the fresh clone catches everything the host’s environment was quietly supplying. | Deleting the in-repo copy because the new repository is green. Green is the precondition for asking, not the answer. | Committing mounted directories to the host repository. Remote mounts populate layer directories locally. If .gitignore does not ignore the mounted paths, external files pollute downstream git status. index.config.json must generate gitignore entries for all remoteMounts. | Breaking dependents when dependencies fold. If a dependency layer folds into another (e.g. cat-openapi into cat-harness), downstreams that still reference the folded layer fail unless FOLDED_INSTANCE_ALIASES maps them. | Separating before resolving withheld asset clearance. If library items are withheld or unpermitted in the separated repository (as with the IRIS replica), materialization results in broken links. Clearance must be verified at seed time. | .

074a0d314d54.title: symbiotic-interaction — the three registers of author input
074a0d314d54.content: Skill symbiotic-interaction: Recognize and respond to the three epistemic registers of author input — Socratic steer (known-answer correction), honest gap (flagged unknown), and intuition seed (tenuous cross-domain identification) — with the coactive-learning measurement spec (per-arc correction quality and turns-to-convergence) and the prompt-lexicon convention. Carries the STRICT rule that a steer correcting a RULE is written into the skill that governs it, in the same turn, quoted and dated — use whenever the author corrects, settles or overrules anything. Generic platform skill. Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch .

a4dc44f5dbf7.title: 0. Why this skill exists
a4dc44f5dbf7.content: Session transcripts show the author’s inputs arriving in three distinct epistemic registers, and mis-classifying them wastes passes in three distinct ways: treating a flagged-gap question as a steer produces sycophantic confirmation; over-verifying a steer wastes the author’s good correction; demanding rigor before cheaply testing an intuition seed kills the division of labor the methodology depends on. The formal backbone is coactive learning (Shivaswamy–Joachims): the author’s feedback is α-informative — an improvement toward the target, not the gold standard — and convergence speed is governed by correction quality.

9e91d7f9c87d.title: 1. The three registers
9e91d7f9c87d.content: | register | seed lexicon (v0 — expanded by transcript mining) | agent protocol | . | steer (author knows or nearly knows) | “isn’t X essentially Y?”, “shouldn’t this be …”, “what about Z here?”, “I think the other point is …” | Treat as a correction near the truth: update the working proposal toward it, verify cheaply rather than relitigate, and do not require the author to repeat the correction. | . | gap (author doesn’t know, and says so) | “I don’t recall …”, “I wish I remembered …”, “is it true that …?”, “not sure”, typed uncertainty markers | The marker REMOVES the presumption of author knowledge: raise the evidence threshold, verify from primary sources or the corpus before adopting, never confirm sycophantically. | . | seed (author suspects a novel link) | “tenuous”, “hunch”, “could A be linked to B?”, “feels like”, any cross-domain identification offered without a citation | Corpus-grep first (is it already known here?); then the cheapest decisive (in)validation — a structural argument or a small probe per the formalize-first discipline — reported fast; survivors get rigorized. Record novelty attribution: author-origin, with a literature-absence check. | . The division of labor the third row encodes: the human is the generator of low-probability / high-value cross-domain hypotheses that exist in neither the literature nor the model’s usable priors; the machine is the fast validator and rigorizer. Once a tenuous identification is made, (in)validation is cheap — so the protocol optimizes for never letting a seed die unexamined and never letting an unvalidated seed masquerade as a result.

fd8cb3c9f3f3.title: 2. A steer that corrects a RULE lands in the SKILL — same turn (STRICT)
fd8cb3c9f3f3.content: §1’s steer row ends “do not require the author to repeat the correction.” Applied to the artefact alone, that clause is broken — just not within the session where it looks kept. The proposal is fixed, the rule that produced the proposal is not, and the next session is a fresh context that never saw the chat. It produces the same proposal, and the author corrects it again. Requiring the correction twice is requiring it repeatedly, and for an author with limited hand function that cost is keystrokes (interaction-modality §0). A steer that corrects a rule is not applied — it is WRITTEN DOWN: in the skill that governs the thing corrected, in the same turn. The rule and its reason go in the narrative; the author’s words, quoted and dated, go in that document’s provenance log. Is this steer rule-level? Three questions . A steer about the artefact in front of you is an edit. A steer about how that kind of artefact is decided is a rule, and the difference is not tone — the author says both in the same register, often in the same sentence. Ask: . | Would an agent with no memory of this chat make the same mistake again? If the correction lives only in a file that agent will not read as a rule, yes. | Does it generalise past this artefact? “Call it voices/ here” is an edit. “Voices belong to the instance that owns them semantically” decides every future placement. | Is there already a rule that this CONTRADICTS? Then the edit is not optional and not additive: the old rule is wrong and stays wrong until it is replaced; a correction filed beside it leaves the next agent two answers. | . Any yes makes it rule-level. A gap or a seed (§1) never is — a flagged unknown is not a ruling, and treating one as a rule is §3’s first anti-pattern with a durable artefact attached. Same turn, quoted, dated — in the provenance log . | Same turn. Not “noted for later” and not a work item saying the skill should be updated. A work item that records a rule is a rule in the wrong graph: beans/ is state, the skills are context, and a reader looking up how something is decided reads the skill. | Quoted. The author’s own words, verbatim, typos included — they are the primary source, and a paraphrase is the agent’s reading of them standing in for the ruling itself. | Dated. A rule with no date cannot be told from a rule that was superseded. | In the log, not the narrative. The quote and its date go in the document’s provenance log, <document>.prov.jsonld beside it (PROV-O), which the renderer shows in the page footer. The narrative states the rule and the reason the author gave, in the present tense, so a reader learns what holds without reading who said it when. | A log may name any layer. It quotes verbatim, so it carries the issue and repository names the original text did, including layers above this one. A log is a record of where a rule came from, not a reference the document depends on, so check:reference-direction exempts *.prov.jsonld. | . You do NOT ask permission to fix a rule the author just corrected . kg-contribution-offer says the agent never picks a destination silently, and that is about manufacturing a node from agreed requirements — work whose shape nobody has ruled on. This is the opposite case: the node exists, it is wrong, and the author has just said so. Asking “shall I write that into the skill?” asks them to repeat the correction, which is the failure at the top of this section. The two do not overlap, and the line is: does the rule already have a home? If yes, the correction goes there now. If the correction implies a skill that does not exist, that is a new node and kg-contribution-offer governs it — except where the author said outright it should be one. Worked examples . | the steer | where it lands | why there | . | “that should be a skill: a collision means coordinate” | the named skill (coordinate (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)), as new triggers | rule-level on all three questions, and the author named the destination | . | “voices belong to the instance that owns them semantically” | the schema module that states voice ownership, replacing the old rule | question 3: it contradicts a standing rule, so filing it beside that rule would leave two answers | . | “the harness handler wins” (a collision between two path rules) | schema-management §”Where a viewer publishes — TWO rules, not three”, beside the two rules | question 2: it settles every such collision, not one generator’s | . A refusal is a ruling. An answer that declines your recommendation carries at least as much rule as one that accepts it — the reason it gives is a durable claim about the domain, and it goes into the governing skill or schema gloss in that turn, with the quote and date in its provenance log.

ff2f32d94574.title: 3. Measurement spec (new sessions and retroactive)
ff2f32d94574.content: An arc is (initial agent proposal y₀; author inputs u₁…u_T with register labels; terminal state ŷ). Metrics, computed offline by a discussion-corpus miner — agents do not annotate live chat: . | T — author turns to acceptance. | α̂ — mean fractional gap closed per steer (successive-proposal distance toward ŷ; the miner’s distance proxy is recorded with the estimate). This is the empirical constant of the coactive bound. | outcome ∈ {converged, abandoned, diverged}. | gap-honored? — after a gap marker, did the agent verify independently before adopting? | seed metrics — validation latency (turns to verdict), verdict ∈ {validated→rigorized, refuted, undecidable-cheaply}, and the literature-absence check for novelty attribution. | . Linkage to artifacts is via the existing commit-trailer ↔ session mapping; no extra ceremony in-session.

fca148e0c02e.title: 4. Anti-patterns
fca148e0c02e.content: . | Treating a gap-marked question as a steer (sycophantic capture). | Relitigating a steer the author has already given (wasted α). | Requiring a derivation before running the cheap probe on a seed — or the inverse, promoting an unvalidated seed into prose. | Flattening the registers: answering every input at the same evidence threshold. | Applying a rule-level steer to the artefact and not to the rule (§2) — the cross-session form of anti-pattern 2. | Filing a rule-level steer as a work item instead of editing the skill. A work item says work is outstanding; the work here is the edit. | .

2ec63dbe5745.title: 5. Lexicon maintenance
2ec63dbe5745.content: Register lexicons above are seeds: a corpus miner’s prompt-lexicon records expand them with observed phrasings, usage counts, and outcomes; updates land as mining PRs citing source sessions. This skill is adapter-generic.

fe05810900f5.title: Test Data Sets & SME Case/Verdict Review
fe05810900f5.content: Skill test-data-sets: Curating fixed (committed, cited, SME-reviewed) and generated (template + params + seed recipe, never stored materialised) test data sets in separately declared graph directories, with per-content-type specialisation as a called subprocess and attributable SME review of decision support and indicator definitions. Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Governs how test data sets are authored, discriminated, specialized per content type, and reviewed by a subject-matter expert (SME) before a test-plan/v1 binds them into test-plan-execution.

45d21faa6802.title: Two kinds of test data, two declared graph directories
45d21faa6802.content: Fixed and generated test data sets do not have the same provenance or audit standing, so they live in separately declared graph directories (test-data-fixed vs test-data-generated in schemas/kg/graph-typology-registry.ts) and carry self-identifying $schema and kind tags in schemas/sdlc/test-data.ts: . | Kind | Graph typology | $schema tag | Discriminator | What is stored | Audit standing | . | Fixed | test-data-fixed | test-data-fixed/1.0.0 | kind: "fixed" | Committed records, optional citations, optional SME review sign-off | Usable as certification evidence (isEvidence in schemas/sdlc/test-plan.ts) once review is present | . | Generated | test-data-generated | test-data-generated/1.0.0 | kind: "generated" | Recipe only: contentType, specialisation, template, params, seed, and canonical sha256 | Never stored materialised; synthesised at run time and hashed into folio-test-run/v1 | . Discriminate from the file content, never from the path . A consumer reading a test data node must call discriminateTestDataSet(doc) in schemas/sdlc/test-data.ts, which inspects $schema and kind inside the JSON document rather than inferring the kind from the directory path: . | FixedTestDataSetSchema is .strict() and refuses recipe fields (template, params, seed, sha256). | GeneratedTestDataSetSchema is .strict() and refuses materialised payload fields (records, cases, path, review), and verifies that sha256 equals computeGeneratedSetDigest({ contentType, specialisation, template, params, seed }). | .

e541f23013c0.title: General curation process and per-content-type specialisation
e541f23013c0.content: The general curation process is sdlc/processes/test-data-curation.bpmn (Process_TestDataCuration): . | Classify the data set (Task_ClassifySet, GW_SetKind) — decide whether the test case needs a small curated fixed set (audit evidence for domain logic) or a deterministic generated recipe (scale, boundary, or combinatorial coverage). | Fixed branch (Task_CurateFixed, GW_NeedsSmeReview, Call_SmeReview) — author the test-data-fixed/1.0.0 node under the layer’s declared test-data-fixed directory; if the set exercises decision support or an indicator definition, invoke sdlc/processes/sme-test-data-review.bpmn (Process_SmeTestDataReview). | Generated branch (Call_ContentTypeSpecialisation, Task_WriteRecipe) — invoke the content-type specialisation as a called subprocess (Call_ContentTypeSpecialisation), then write the test-data-generated/1.0.0 recipe and its canonical sha256 under the layer’s declared test-data-generated directory without committing materialised records. | Verify self-identification and bind (Task_VerifySelfIdentifying) — verify via discriminateTestDataSet and toTestDataRef that the file self-identifies by $schema and kind and bind its digest into the test-plan/v1 case. | . FHIR templating is one specialisation, named as such, not the design . Call_ContentTypeSpecialisation in test-data-curation.bpmn is parameterized by contentType and specialisation (TestDataSpecialisationSchema in schemas/sdlc/test-data.ts): . | fhir-templating (FHIR_TEMPLATING_SPECIALISATION) is one named specialisation for FHIR IG / DAK content (for example, Liquid or FSH/JSON templates producing synthetic patient bundles or MeasureReport cohorts). | Other content types supply their own specialisations — such as markdown-fixture for document folios, lean-counterexample for formal-proof folios, or tabular-cohort for aggregate indicator tables. | Platform schemas and processes never hardcode FHIR resources or DAK structures as the general test-data model. | .

d309f6b8d7b5.title: SME review of decision support and indicator definitions
d309f6b8d7b5.content: When a fixed test data set tests clinical or scientific decision support or indicator definitions, passing is a domain judgement: a subject-matter expert must confirm that the logic produces the right guidance on a worked case or the right value on a cohort. Two units of review in sme-case-verdict/1.0.0 . SmeCaseVerdictKind ($schema: "sme-case-verdict/1.0.0", graph typology sme-case-verdict) discriminates on subjectKind: . | subjectKind: "decision-support" — unit is a worked case (case): . | id, summary, decisionLogicRef, structured input, systemOutput, and optional expectedGuidance. | Refuses cohort. | . | subjectKind: "indicator-definition" — unit is a cohort plus an expected value (cohort): . | id, summary, indicatorRef, populationSize, inputs, expectedValue, computedValue, and optional period, numerator, denominator. | Refuses case. | . | . Attributable SME identity and review date . An audited review without an attributable reviewer and date is not audited. Every sme-case-verdict/1.0.0 node requires: . | reviewer (SmeReviewerIdentitySchema): kind: "human" (never "agent" or "script"), provider (e.g. "github", "orcid"), handle, role (e.g. "clinical-sme"), and optional displayName and actor. | reviewedAt (ReviewedAtSchema): ISO-8601 date (YYYY-MM-DD) or timestamp. | verdict: "pass" | "fail" | "needs-revision", plus a non-empty domain rationale. | . Why the SME lane in sme-test-data-review.bpmn is judgementOnly . In sdlc/processes/sme-test-data-review.bpmn (Process_SmeTestDataReview), the SME review step (Task_SmeJudge) sits in Lane_SME, bound to role clinical-sme (partitionElementRef="clinical-sme"). In scenarios/roles.json, clinical-sme declares "judgementOnly": true and carries no procedural skill on Task_SmeJudge: no procedure yields the clinical or scientific answer, which is the whole reason a person is in the lane. The preparation steps (Task_PrepareWorkedCase, Task_PrepareCohort) and the recording step (Task_RecordCaseVerdict) are mechanical and name test-data-sets; the judgement between them is the human SME’s alone.

7197fa6eb870.title: Theme art intake
7197fa6eb870.content: Skill theme-art-intake: Accept or refuse a set of three theme/avatar layouts arriving through document ingestion, with a named reason for every refusal. Named by: Public comment on a review draft, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Publish extracted statements with source links . Art arrives — three crops for a theme or an avatar — and the answer is either accepted, with the declaration written, or refused, with what to fix.

e55dc630ec79.title: This is a step in document ingestion, not a process beside it
e55dc630ec79.content: Document ingestion already answers the question art arrival poses — something unstructured has arrived; is it acceptable, and if not, why not — with a pipeline and a completeness gate. Theme art is the same event with a different payload, so what exists is a check keyed on the payload, not a second pipeline: a parallel “avatar ingestion” would be a second answer to one question, free to disagree with the first. |   | where | . | the check | schemas/library/theme-art-intake.ts — pure, no I/O, no clock | . | the CLI face | scripts/check-theme-art.ts, bun run cat check:theme-art | . | the arrival | uploads/, per content-acquisition and document-intake | .

6a340a51a36a.title: The constraints
6a340a51a36a.content: Each constraint answers a failure that has happened. Do not add one that has not: a rule with no failure behind it is one whose next maintainer cannot tell whether it still matters. | constraint | verdict | why | . | all three layouts | refuse | resolveThemeBackdrop refuses an incomplete backdrop wholesale, so a theme missing one crop renders with no art — not two thirds of it. | . | distinct content | refuse | two byte-identical files for two named layouts or avatars means one is missing. | . | orientation per layout | refuse | a portrait crop is not a landscape crop scaled down. The quiet area the sticky’s text sits in moves. | . | a declared destination | refuse | art outside a declared directory (at the repository root, say) is seen by no gate: check-declared-assets walks declared→disk. | . | dimensions measured | structural | intake takes bytes and emits the declaration, so there is nowhere for a retyped (or copied) number to enter. | . | weight and format | report | heavy PNGs still render, so refusing them would block work over a bandwidth judgement. | .

d9f4e0385932.title: Refuse, report, or neither
d9f4e0385932.content: . | Refuse when the art cannot do its job, or when intake cannot tell which of two readings is intended. A missing crop and two identical files are both “somebody has to decide something”. | Report when the art works but costs. Weight and format are the cases: a 1.6 MB PNG renders correctly. | Neither — say nothing — for anything intake did not actually measure. | . remedy is a required field on every failure: a refusal that says invalid teaches nobody what to fix. All failures are collected rather than thrown one at a time, because art arrives as a batch, and reporting the first problem of three means three round trips to learn three things.

6e0382c37a40.title: Do not repair somebody’s art
6e0382c37a40.content: deletion-requires-confirmation applies, and so does its spirit. When intake refuses, the outputs are the report and a work-plan item — not a re-crop, not a converted file, and not a quietly removed declaration. What looks like a missing crop may be a duplicate that was uploaded by mistake, and that is a question for the person who has the original. check:theme-art:check runs in CI, so a refusal of declared art is a regression.

15d54ef4246b.title: Reading the report
15d54ef4246b.content: ✓ landing-engineer: 3 layouts accepted · laptop 1672×941 docs/assets/img/harness/landing-engineer-laptop.png ! [heavy] laptop: … is 1560 KB, over the 391 KB budget → convert to webp — the measured gap on this art was about 16× ✗ landing-architecture: refused, 1 problem(s) · [missing-layout] mobile: no file offered for the mobile layout → supply all three layouts … . Three rules for reading it, the same three ci-health states: . | declared-but-absent is not a refusal and not a pass. The declaration names a file that is not on disk. It is reported on its own line because “the file is not there” and “the file is the wrong shape” are different facts, and a reader who cannot tell them apart fixes the wrong one. | A check that fires on every subject is wrong. docs/ is not a declared directory, and should not be — a declared entry names a graph, and the site is the render target — so art under it is not undeclared-destination. When a new check’s first run lights up broadly, ask which of these are correct? before how do I fix the repository?, and test any exclusion in both directions: a test of the excluded case alone passes equally for a check that never fires. A check that fires on legitimate subjects gets switched off, and a switched-off check still reads as coverage. | Warnings do not accumulate into a refusal. Twelve heavy files are twelve reports, not a failure. | .

33daad5fc3f1.title: Adding a constraint
33daad5fc3f1.content: . | Name the failure it answers. No failure, no constraint. | Decide refuse vs report by the line above — can the art do its job? | Write the remedy before the detection. If you cannot say what to do about it, the check is not ready. | Prove it fires, with a test that fails when the check is removed. | Check it against art already shipped. The aspect bands are deliberately wide because the shipped laptop crops run 1.50–1.78; a tighter band would refuse work that is fine. | . The stages of theming, and which owns which question, are in theming.

5dded5d91849.title: What is NOT here
5dded5d91849.content: The theming code — schemas/ui/themes.ts, schemas/library/theme-art-intake.ts, scripts/check-theme-art.ts, scripts/gen-themes-css.ts, scripts/gen-avatars-css.ts — stays where it is. This is the kg graph: the instructions an agent follows, not the implementation. A skill and the code it describes are different node kinds, and moving code beside its documentation would make the partition meaningless.

0cbc1316b9f0.title: theme-art-intake (skill)
0cbc1316b9f0.content: The skill theme-art-intake as its source file cat-harness/skills/ui/theming/theme-art-intake.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

2d3ee627352e.title: At ingestion, and only at ingestion
2d3ee627352e.content: Skill theme-ui-review: Review graphical assets AS THEY ARE INGESTED, in the context of the website or app design they are for — accessibility, branding, languages — to determine what the assets and the UI will be. At ingestion only; called from ingest-theme. Measures rather than asserts, and raises findings rather than fixing them. Named by: Public comment on a review draft, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Publish extracted statements with source links . This skill runs in exactly one place: theme-ui-review.bpmn, called from ingest-theme.bpmn Task_Review, whose agent lane is ingestion-agent. It is not part of a post-MVP SDLC step and is not called from crdm-deliver.bpmn.

ef109d31de01.title: What it reviews
ef109d31de01.content: It looks at the arriving graphical assets laid out in the design they are for, so a finding is a decision about what the assets will be, taken while it is still cheap. The questions: accessibility measured rather than asserted, branding against the layer’s own declaration, and every declared locale. Theme choice is an authoring judgement. There is no role-to-theme mapping (theme.ts records why), so nothing here checks a binding. What gets reviewed is the ingested art in its design context.

da62f59ada70.title: What this gives up — accepted
da62f59ada70.content: An ingestion review answers “what will this turn into?” only as far as the assets can be laid out in their design before the site exists — not how a crop reads in the finished page. That gap is accepted; do not add a post-MVP review call on your own initiative.

5b04cf9b5c3e.title: A person is in the loop, inside ingestion
5b04cf9b5c3e.content: R_Judge is a human step: a person looks at the assets laid out at a web and a mobile width, so ingesting a theme source is attended at that step. Ingesting anything else stays unattended — Gateway_ThemeSource in document-ingestion.bpmn routes non-theme documents past ingest-theme.bpmn entirely.

c65b131bced9.title: Measure; do not assert
c65b131bced9.content: Contrast is computed, against the real ground. A theme with a backdrop has no single ratio — ink over a photograph varies pixel to pixel — so the number that matters is the worst case the art can present. Every shipped scrim in this repository is measured over pure black for that reason, and the check is written so it can fail: without a case that fails at a thin scrim, passing assertions prove nothing about the value. Colour is never the sole carrier (SC 1.4.1). Where it carries meaning, look for the second channel — the priority stripe is a width as well as a hue precisely so a monochrome reader still sees it. An automated pass is necessary and not sufficient: . | axe accepts a non-empty placeholder as an accessible name, so a label removed from the accessibility tree can pass the automated check. | A CSS selector that matches nothing raises no error in any tool, and can leave a backdrop at its intrinsic size across the viewport with every gate green. | . So a person looks at the assets laid out in their design (R_Judge). That is a step in the diagram, not an optional extra, because no automated check catches either case above.

f7cac9b3e977.title: Branding is a question about the LAYER, not about taste
f7cac9b3e977.content: Marks, palettes and art are checked against the layer’s own declaration rather than a remembered style. The sharpest form of the question comes from downstream: would a folio depending on this platform inherit something it did not choose? landing.html states it as a rule — “a downstream folio should not inherit a grumpy cat it did not choose” — and it is why a theme names an image role rather than a path.

b38c6fce72d6.title: Languages: new UI is where untranslated strings enter
b38c6fce72d6.content: Check that every user-facing string reaches the .pot, that each declared locale renders without clipping, and that right-to-left is laid out rather than mirrored by accident. The distinction worth keeping: a name is translatable and a value is not. A theme’s display name goes through the pipeline; its palette does not, because a colour is not language-dependent and translating one invites a locale to diverge on a value the CSS must agree on.

ae282d23c1a4.title: Raise findings; do not fix them
ae282d23c1a4.content: A finding goes back to whoever authored the choice, because the choice was theirs. There is no mapping to correct instead, and a reviewer who quietly re-themes a note has substituted their judgement for the author’s without saying so — which is the same objection decision-audit makes to editing a finding rather than overruling it with a note. The one exception is the one this repository already allows everywhere: a defect that is not a judgement call at all — a selector matching nothing, a string missing from the .pot, a contrast ratio below the floor — is a bug, and bugs get fixed.

771754291102.title: What this does NOT cover
771754291102.content: Not the choice itself. Whether a sticky should be engineer or library is an authoring decision, and this review does not second-guess it; it asks whether what was ingested will render legibly, consistently and in every declared language in the design it is for.

0da9802dc071.title: Both viewports, always
0da9802dc071.content: . | Every surface is inventoried and judged at a web width and at a mobile width. | A review done at one width is incomplete, not passed. | The surface’s wireframe, in wireframe-design-review, states what each layout was meant to be, so the review compares the build against an intent rather than against memory. | .
