e97a5d39a9f5.title: Session Task Manager (beans)
e97a5d39a9f5.content: Skill todo-manager: Maintain and display work-in-progress task lists using the beans CLI issue tracker. Track implementation progress, open tasks, missing artifacts, and blocked items across a session. Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Evidence for a recommendation, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Public comment on a review draft, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Board: place a note . Disambiguation: . | beans (todo-manager, this file) = the agent’s session work-plan. Managed entirely via the beans CLI issue tracker (data stored in beans/). | sidecars (*.qa.json and *.witness.json files) = content state tracking. Work items and sidecars are NOT synonymous! Do NOT convert bulk QA queue items into work items. They are completely separate workflow systems. | todo-review = triage of content feedback stored under feedback/<paper>/ and surfaced via the MCP /todos dashboard. That is paper-content scope, not session scope. | . Instead of an in-memory list or markdown checklists, we manage session work and cross-agent coordination using the beans CLI issue tracker. A work item is a memory record with more structure (owner, 2026-11-03, ruling Q17; the schemas are memory-record-core and bean/1.0.0 in cat-harness-tools schemas/kg/memory-record.ts and schemas/sdlc/bean-graph.ts). It carries what every kept memory carries (an id, a title, tags, when it was made and changed) and adds a status, a type, a priority, a parent and what it blocks. So the memory Tools work on it as on any memory record: memory_note and memory_checkpoint add a dated entry, memory_recall reads them back, and the work-plan store adds what only a work item needs (get, list, create, claiming). The glossary defines the term: Work item, narrower than Memory record. The program and its files keep the name beans; in prose, say work item. This skill holds the work item mechanics: installing the CLI, the STRICT check before beans create, the fallback when the CLI is absent, the status vocabulary, and the coordination rules below. Report formats are elsewhere: . | opening-brief.md (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) — what you say before starting a work item or a topic. | turn-reporting.md — what you say during and after each turn, including the STRICT “next”-line rule. | .

a5c17065e3cc.title: Installing beans (fresh sandbox / cloud container)
a5c17065e3cc.content: beans is the hmans/beans Go binary — a flat-file issue tracker storing issues as markdown under beans/. Cloud sandboxes do not ship it, so reinstall on demand (Go ships in the sandbox): . cat-harness-tools/scripts/install-beans.sh # idempotent; installs into a PATH dir # equivalently, the one-liner it runs: GOBIN="$HOME/.local/bin" go install github.com/hmans/beans@latest . Note: the npm package named beans is an unrelated abandoned tool — do not npm install beans. Verify with beans list && beans check.

8a5424c8380d.title: What the session-start sweep emits, and why in that order
8a5424c8380d.content: A session-start hook runs the sweep where a hook runs at all. It installs the CLI when it is genuinely missing — bounded and quiet, falling through to the degraded reader rather than failing the hook — and prepends the install directory when the binary is already there, so a second session does not reinstall. If the sweep still reports the CLI missing, it could not be installed there. The sweep installs rather than recommends, because an instruction somebody has to act on is weaker than the act itself. The order is not arbitrary: . | Interaction preferences — first, because they change the form of every question that follows. A question asked before them may have to be asked again. | Work-plan priming and the open list. | The roadmap. A flat list of a hundred ids in creation order is data, not a plan; the milestone/epic structure is what lets an end-of-turn report say what is next and why. | The commands the person can run themselves, the interactive browser first. An agent cannot drive a TUI on somebody’s behalf, so the only useful thing to do with one is print it where they will see it — with a copy-pasteable line whose path and branch are computed, never written in. | Default-branch delta, sibling branch activity, CI health. | . Heavy triage of new commits belongs in a background subagent, not the foreground. The sweep’s job is to tell you what changed, not to spend your first minutes reading it.

5a378d95ff3f.title: Core Directives for Sessions
5a378d95ff3f.content: . | A session is a LOG, never an epic or a milestone. Do not create a Session: … work item. What one sitting did is recorded in two places that already exist and are already read: the PR body (## Intent / ## Session results, session-intent) and a work item note on each work item you worked — bun run cat beans:note <id> --title "…", written to the declared notes directory of beans/beans.json and keyed by branch, so it is one file per session per work item by construction (bean-coordination §”Adding to a bean”). See §”A session is a log, not a parent” below for why. | Every todo is a work item, parented by SUBJECT. Each task, probe or action item is a work item (--type task) under the epic whose subject it is — §”WHICH parent” — not under anything representing the session. beans create "<Task Title>" --type task --parent <subject-epic-id> | No manual .md checklists: Never use session-beans.md or raw Markdown - [ ] checklists to track global tasks. Always use the beans CLI to prevent namespace pollution and maintain the official project tracking. | Check before you create: beans create is not idempotent. Run the existence check below before every beans create — no exceptions. | Brief before you work: claiming a work item records which item is taken; the opening brief records what it is taken for. Write it before the first tool call, in the chat. See §”Opening brief” below. | Write work items to the work-plan store, never into a code PR: create, claim, note and status changes go to the store through its Tool. The store’s operations are in work-plan-store; how the Tool in use performs them (today the git state branch, work-plan-store-git-branch) is on that Tool’s page. Do not commit work item files to code PR branches on main. | .

46a91e65abd4.title: Where beans live
46a91e65abd4.content: The work plan is a data store with a contract, work-plan-store, and this skill uses it only through that contract’s operations (get, list, create, update, note, history, positions). Which Tool backs it is the deployment’s choice Today every checkout uses the git state branch; how to mount it, which commands perform each operation and how changes are pushed are on its page, work-plan-store-git-branch. | Never bundle work items in code PR commits. Code PRs touch code and documentation; work item changes go to the store, which keeps the work plan current for every session without merge conflicts or spurious CI runs. | .

9620c9880b0b.title: Check before you create — beans create is not idempotent (STRICT)
9620c9880b0b.content: beans create mints a fresh random ID on every call and dedupes on nothing. Re-running a work-plan step is therefore not a no-op — it creates a second work item. Before every beans create, check whether the work item exists: . T="Prove Foo.bar" beans list --json --search "title:\"$T\"" | python3 -c ' import json, sys t = sys.argv[1] m = [b for b in json.load(sys.stdin) if b["title"] == t] print(f"{len(m)} exact match(es)") [print(" ", b["id"], b["status"]) for b in m]' "$T" . | ≥ 1 match → do not create. Claim the existing work item instead, with bun run cat beans:claim <id> — which reads the shared store first, refuses a work item a sibling holds or one already closed, and records a holder note so the next session’s check can see you. Not beans update <id> --status in-progress. It writes no holder note, so the claim is invisible to beans:claim’s own already-claimed check. Read the outcome — three of them are refusals, and held-unknown means it could not tell a live sibling from an abandoned claim: bean-coordination.md §”bun run cat beans:claim <id> — how it behaves”. | 0 matches → run the semantic check before creating: . bun run cat lsi:near "$T" # add --body "<first paragraph>" when you have one . The exact-title check above catches the same WORDS; this catches the same work in other words. It folds the title into an LSI index of every work item (all statuses — a completed one is often the answer) and prints the nearest five plus the closest epic. Read every hit marked ← (cosine ≥ 0.7) before creating. If one is the same work, claim or reopen it rather than create; if it is related, create and say so in the body. The score proposes; whether a hit IS the same work is your call (method lsi, refusal 3). | A work item ABOUT ONE OBJECT is keyed on the object, not the title. When the work targets a single named thing (a Lean declaration, a block label, a file), titles drift: “Prove Foo.bar”, “PROVE(lean): Foo.bar”, “close sorry in Foo.bar”. Neither check above is guaranteed to pair them, and generator re-runs are the usual source of such duplicates. So write the key into the work item as a line of its own, Target: lean:Foo.bar (or block:<label>, file:<path>), and before creating search the WHOLE store for that line, archive included, because a completed work item is often the answer: . grep -rlF "Target: lean:Foo.bar" beans/defs/ # the archive is beans/defs/archive/ . A hit is the same work: claim it, reopen it with a note, or link to it. A generator that files work items MUST write the key and run this check, since a re-run is exactly the case the title checks miss. | Still new → beans create "$T" --type task, under the epic lsi:near printed if it fits (§”WHICH parent — the criterion nobody wrote down” below). | . --search is a fuzzy Bleve query, so the exact-title comparison inside the pipe is load-bearing — do not drop it and trust --search alone. Why this is STRICT. Because create is unconditional, an agent that re-runs a work-plan step in a loop mints thousands of duplicates: the sweep and the backlog then read mostly noise, duplicates can collide with real work item ids, and corpus searches over beans/ are inflated. An unguarded create is what the rule prevents. It is platform-level so every folio inherits it.

9474b04fee23.title: Check before you UPDATE — --body-file REPLACES the body (STRICT)
9474b04fee23.content: beans create is not idempotent; beans update is not additive. They are different failures and both cost a durable artefact, so they sit together. A work item’s body is an append-only record of who found what, when. Every note in it is dated and signed, and later notes cite earlier ones. Replace the body and you have deleted findings that other work items, commits and issues point at. beans update offers four ways to write one, and only one of them appends: . | flag | what it does | . | --body-append <text> | --body-append - | appends. - reads stdin | . | --body-file <path> | REPLACES the whole body with the file | . | --body <text> | --body - | REPLACES | . | --body-replace-old/-new | replaces one substring; leaves the rest | . --body-file replaces with exit 0, no warning, no diff, no prompt: nothing in the output distinguishes it from an append. For a long, multi-paragraph note, use --body-append -: . beans update <id> --status completed --body-append - <<'NOTE' _2026-09-22T06:51:22Z_ — what you found, and how you know it. NOTE . Do not reach for --body-file because the note is long. (beans create rejects --body-file - with a heredoc, so the two subcommands also disagree about that flag.) . The timestamp prefix is an authored convention, not a CLI feature — no flag adds it. Write it yourself or the note joins the previous paragraph undated. Recovery, if it has already happened. The store is committed, which is the whole reason this is survivable: git show HEAD:<bean-file> returns the body as of the last commit, and the lost notes can be reassembled with the new front matter. Recover from git, not from your own scrollback — a transcript is a copy you made, and the repository is the artefact. Then say plainly what was lost and restored; a silent repair leaves the next reader unable to tell a reconstruction from an original.

aa8165a13102.title: WHICH parent — the criterion nobody wrote down
aa8165a13102.content: A work item’s parent is the epic whose SUBJECT it is, not the epic you happen to be working in. Nothing catches a wrong parent. check-bean-parents tests exactly two things: that an open work item HAS a parent, and that the parent NAMES A WORK ITEM THAT EXISTS. A work item filed under the wrong epic satisfies both, so it is textually clean, the guard is green, and it is only findable by a person reading the roadmap. The check cannot distinguish a right parent from a wrong one, so the criterion has to live here or nowhere. How to choose . | beans list and read the EPICS first — there are many, each with a thematic scope in its title. Do this BEFORE beans create, at the same time as §”Check before you create”; both are questions about where a work item belongs, and both are cheaper before the file exists. | Ask what the work item is ABOUT, not what you were doing when you wrote it. A visualiser whose blocker is an unrecorded ingest relation is an ingest work item. A sticky’s art is a rendering work item. The topic that makes the work hard is usually the right epic. | When two epics both fit, pick the one whose OTHER children you would want read alongside it, and say in the body why the other was not chosen — a parent is a claim about where somebody should go looking. | . A session is a log, not a parent . Do not create a Session: … epic or milestone. It turns the roadmap’s top level into a diary, and: . | An epic is a claim about where to look for a SUBJECT. A session epic points at one sitting, which ended; nobody looks there for the work, so its children are lost to the next agent filing by subject. | It defeats the guards. check-bean-parents passes a task parented to a session epic, because the parent exists and is an epic. The wrong parent is textually clean. | Its status lies. A session epic stays in-progress after its session ends, so it is a stale claim from birth, and the quiet-claim findings fill with logs. | . Where the log goes instead — each already declared, already read: . | what the session wants to keep | where | . | what it intended and what it got done | the PR body, ## Intent / ## Session results (session-intent) | . | what it found about a work item | a note: bun run cat beans:note <id> → beans/notes/<bean>--<date>--<branch>.md | . | a survey of a commit window it read | beans/surveys/ (session-survey) — only if it surveyed one | . | a handover to whoever comes next | a note on the work item being handed over, plus handover-report | . A handover is the same case. A Handoff: … or Handover: … work item typed epic or milestone is a session log with a different title. bun run cat health reports it — the bean-store check’s bean-session-log-roots finding names every OPEN work item whose title starts Session, Handoff or Handover and whose type is epic or milestone. Report-only: the remedy is a person’s (or a reviewed work-plan-restructure plan’s) — re-parent the children by subject, move the narrative into a note, then set the log to completed or scrapped with a pointer. Never beans delete it: other work items, commits and PRs cite its id.

2d5ed4430ce0.title: A GOAL is a milestone bean, and an epic joins one by parenting to it
2d5ed4430ce0.content: A “goal-scoped” queue needs the goal to exist as an object, or every review re-derives the classification from scratch. A goal is a milestone work item, in the owner’s own words, and the epics serving it are parented to it. beans create "<the goal, verbatim>" --type milestone # after the existence check above beans update <epic-id> --parent <milestone-id> . Three properties make this the cheap answer rather than a new mechanism: . | The type exists and check-bean-parents permits an epic under a milestone. | beans roadmap groups by parent:, so the goals become the roadmap’s top level the moment the epics are parented — which is what a roadmap was always for. | “Prioritise against the goals” becomes a query: walk down from the milestone. An item under no goal is then visible as such, which is itself the finding a review wants. | . Verbatim, and this is not a style note. A goal is the owner’s sentence, and a tidied paraphrase is a different claim that nobody agreed to — the same rule confirmation-waiver applies to a waiver’s quote, and for the same reason: the reader auditing the classification has only that string to check it against. If you do not have the owner’s words, you do not have the goal — record the paraphrase as a paraphrase, say so, and ask. This does not conflict with filing by subject (§”WHICH parent”). A milestone sits ABOVE the epics; a work item is still parented to the epic whose subject it is, and the epic is parented to the goal it serves. Two levels, one criterion at each.

f7a4412cf101.title: A WORK PLAN is an epic or milestone that names the process it runs
f7a4412cf101.content: Owner, 2026-11-05: “At the beginning of a large process (like creating a new collaborative document, or adding software features,) there should / may be a work plan. Not every process needs a work plan. Docs/proposals/ once approved become workplans”, and on the card, “Epic is the plan”. So a work plan is not a new kind of file. It is the epic (or milestone) that already groups the work, with two tags saying what it runs and where it came from: . beans update <epic-id> --tag process:<bpmn:process id> # what it instantiates; repeat for several beans update <epic-id> --tag proposal:<repo-relative path> # the approved proposal it was made from beans list --tag process:<bpmn:process id> # every plan that runs that process . | Tags, not front-matter fields. The beans CLI drops every front-matter key it does not know on its next write (measured 2026-11-05), and keeps tags. | A process: tag is what makes it a plan. A proposal: tag alone does not: a proposal with no process to run is not a plan yet. A plan filed as a feature or a story is reported, not refused (the work-plan schema in the tools layer reports it). | Start the process under the plan: workflow_start with plan: <epic-id> (bun run cat workflow:start <process> <subject> --plan <epic-id>). The instance names its plan, as it names its work item; the plan does not list its instances, because where the work is lives in the instances. | Not every process needs one. A small process tracked by one work item runs with no plan, exactly as before. | The work items under the plan are its work: parented to the epic, as always. A work item is a memory record with more structure; a work plan is a work item that says which process it runs. | . The work-plan page marks each plan in its tree with its process, its proposal and how many instances are running under it. Approving a proposal seeds its plan . When the owner approves a proposal (owner, 2026-11-05, card “Proposal seeds plan”), one command writes both ends, so neither is kept by hand: . bun run cat proposal:approve <path/to/proposal.md> --process <bpmn:process id> [--process …] \ [--plan <epic or milestone id>] [--parent <goal id>] [--dry-run] . | With no --plan it creates an epic titled as the proposal. With --plan it tags that epic or milestone instead; a feature or a story is refused. | The plan gets the process: and proposal: tags. The proposal’s front matter gets status: approved, approvedOn: <date> and plan: <id>. | At least one --process is required, unless --plan already names one: a plan is defined by what it runs. | Approve only on the owner’s word. The command records an approval; it does not decide one. Run it with --dry-run first and show the owner what it will write. | bun run cat proposal:approve --check <proposals dir> checks the two ends against each other and reports rather than fails: an approved proposal with no plan, a plan id that is no work item, a plan that names no process, or a plan whose proposal: tag names another file. | .

df1c628a5fa6.title: After you create — parent it, and re-run the guard before you push
df1c628a5fa6.content: check-bean-parents fails on an open work item with no parent, because such a work item lands in the roadmap’s Miscellaneous section where nobody looks for it. Two ways past it: . | A multi-flag beans update can apply only some of its flags and still report success (-s in-progress --parent <epic> can set the status and leave the parent unset). After setting several properties at once, read the front matter back — grep -n "^status:\|^parent:\|^priority:" beans/defs/<file>.md — rather than trusting the “Updated …” line. | A work item created after your last test run is an unguarded work item. | . So: beans create and the --parent that follows it are one action, and touching the work item store invalidates your last test run. Re-run at least bun test cat-harness-tools/scripts/tests/check-bean-parents.test.ts before pushing. A green suite is green for the tree you ran it against. A new bean also owes readme:subgraphs — and this is the most-missed step . beans/README.md is GENERATED and carries per-subdirectory counts, so creating or archiving a work item makes it stale. Nothing in the beans CLI regenerates it, and the gate that catches it is named for the generic case rather than for work items: . Repository gates (hard) · step 65: "Every declared directory's README is current" . That is readme:subgraphs:check. Run its writer before you push: . bun run cat readme:subgraphs # updates beans/README.md; push state via the store Tool bun run cat readme:subgraphs:check # must exit 0 bun run cat state:push # when the store Tool is git-branch (work-plan-store-git-branch.md) . The check’s name gives no hint that adding a work item dirtied it, so a session that reads only the name looks at directories and never at the work item it just created. Read the failing STEP, and remember that beans/ is a declared directory like any other. The same shape applies one door along: editing a skill owes bun run cat skill:register, which skill-registration carries in full. Both are instances of one rule — a declared artefact has generated neighbours, and the CLI that writes the artefact does not write them.

b3a3da674c7e.title: When the beans CLI is not there — you are still not read-only
b3a3da674c7e.content: scripts/beans-fallback.ts writes the same store in the same layout: same files, same front matter, same id shape, read from .beans.yml. The CLI reads everything it writes once installed. There is no import step and no second store. bun run cat beans:fallback list --status todo bun run cat beans:fallback show <id> bun run cat beans:fallback claim <id> bun run cat beans:fallback create "<title>" --status in-progress bun run cat beans:fallback note <id> "<what you found>" . A read-only fallback would let a session see its plan but not claim it, so it would do its work unclaimed. Its create refuses an exact duplicate title and names the work item to claim instead; the CLI’s create does not. --force exists for a genuinely intended duplicate and has to be typed.

d9b5ca205c33.title: Check before you WORK — a checkbox is a claim, not a measurement (STRICT)
d9b5ca205c33.content: beans create is not idempotent, and §”Check before you create” above is the guard. This is its twin at the other end: a work item’s stated state is a claim somebody wrote down once, and the code has moved since. Re-measure a work item’s open items against the code before you act on them. The cost of skipping this is not wasted effort; it is acting on a stale claim. The two failures this prevents, and they are different . 1. Doing work that exists. Siblings finish items without ticking the box. 2. Undoing a decision that was recorded elsewhere. An open item can read like a gap when the absence is deliberate and explained in a comment in the file the work item is about. Doing the obvious thing then re-introduces the defect the decision avoids. The decision is in the file, not the work item. What “re-measure” means, concretely . | Run the thing — the audit or check that measures the item. | Read the body, not just the boxes. | Date it. git log -S on the symbol or the file against the work item’s created_at separates fixed since from wrong when written. | Read the file the work item is about, for a comment saying why it is the way it is. That is where a deliberate absence lives. | . And a bean you re-measure, you record . Leave what you found in the work item, with the commits and the times — a stale checkbox you silently worked around is one the next agent meets unchanged. Tick what is done and name who did it; withdraw a done-when you no longer believe, with reasons, rather than leaving it unmet. Where the work item and the code disagree, the code is what is true and the work item is what is wrong — the same rule AGENTS.md states for a skill against that file. This is the work-plan half. The cross-session half is bean-coordination §”Claims are global via the branch store”.

2939c37ee1fb.title: Working with Beans
2939c37ee1fb.content: 1. Finding Tasks & Graph Analytics (beans:query / bean_query) Use beans list for simple listing, or bun run beans:query (and the bean_query MCP tool) for fast in-memory SPARQL 1.1 analytics over the work item store (loads ~1,000 work items into an Oxigraph store in ~70 ms): . | bun run beans:query --named safe_drain_candidates: leaves with >= 2 open siblings under their parent container (safe against check:bean-rollup) | bun run beans:query --named actionable_leaves: open/todo leaf work items with zero open blockers, ready for an agent to claim immediately | bun run beans:query --named critical_path_blockers: blockers ranked by how many open work items they directly hold up | bun run beans:query --named epic_burndown: per-epic child status breakdown (total, open, completed, scrapped, and completion percentage) | bun run beans:query --named rollup_invariant_violations: completed containers with open children, or in-progress containers with 0 open children | bun run beans:query --named stale_claims: in-progress work items whose updated_at timestamp is older than 7 days | bun run beans:query --named unparented_open_tasks: open non-epic work items that have no epic or milestone parent | bun run beans:query --named circular_blockers: circular blocking deadlocks | bun run beans:query --named high_fanout_epics: epics with high fanout (>= 15 direct children) that may need decomposition | Arbitrary SPARQL: bun run beans:query --sparql "SELECT ?id ?title WHERE { ?b bean:id ?id ; bean:title ?title }" | Export RDF graph: bun run beans:query --export-nq beans.nq | . 2. Setting Dependencies You can map out sequence blockers using: beans update <id> --blocked-by <blocker-id> beans update <id> --blocking <blocked-id> . 3. Updating Status & Adding Comments . | When starting work: bun run cat beans:claim <id> — a claim goes through the claim tool, never through beans update, so it is visible to the next session’s check | When completed: beans update <id> --status completed | To add notes or discussion: beans update <id> --body-append "Your note", or --body-append - with a heredoc when it runs to paragraphs. Never --body-file — it replaces the whole body, silently, exit 0: §”Check before you UPDATE”. | . 4. A work item that delivers a requirement copies its success criteria When a work item is part of a work plan — it delivers one or more req: statements (or a plan’s REQ-### / FR-###) — it names them in its body and its ## Done when is copied from their success criteria, one checkbox per criterion, with the criterion’s key. Closing the work item is then judging those criteria. The work item ids are also listed in the requirement set’s workPlan — a set at planned with none is refused by check:requirements. The rule and an example are in the content layer’s requirement-definition skill (skill_fetch requirement-definition) §”The work plan is beans”.

16b01d8b3aec.title: Archiving — two dispositions, and they answer different questions
16b01d8b3aec.content: beans archive moves every completed or scrapped work item out of the working set. It moves, never deletes: an archived work item is still resolvable by id, which is what makes it a disposal an agent may perform at all (deletion-requires-confirmation). There are two ways it can be driven, they are not alternatives, and a process author needs to know which one they are reaching for. |   | a per-activity op | a periodic sweep | . | what it is | a step inside one process — a fourth <cat-harness.processes:bean op> beside claim, note, resolve | a scheduled run over the whole store | . | the question it answers | is this item’s work over? | is the store still readable? | . | what decides | the process reaching a step that means completion | a uniform, process-independent criterion — completed or scrapped | . | what the archive then records | why — “archived because the release shipped” | when — “archived in the sweep of that date” | . | what it cannot do | reach a work item no process resolved | know that this release is what terminated this item | . Why neither replaces the other . The op cannot cover the store. A work item resolved by a process with no archive step, by hand, or by a sibling session, is never reached; coverage would depend on every path having been drawn, and paths are added faster than they are wired. The sweep cannot carry authority. It knows only status. It cannot say that a requirement was archived because the stakeholder signed off, which is the fact an audit of the CRDM close would want — and crdm-close.bpmn is precisely where that authority exists. So the honest shape is: the sweep is the floor, the op is the exception. The sweep guarantees the store stays readable whatever anyone forgot; an op is worth adding only where a process’s completion is itself the reason, and recording that reason is worth the extra edge on the diagram. Where this sits against resolve — two layers, not two spellings . resolve is the process saying “I am done with this item.” Archiving is the store saying “this is no longer in the working set.” They are different layers and they are allowed to be far apart in time — which is why resolve must never imply an archive, and why the sweep is still needed. The per-activity op: a step carrying <cat-harness.processes:bean op="archive"/> moves the instance’s work item into beans/defs/archive/, with a line saying which process closed it. It does so only once the process has finished and the work item is completed or scrapped; otherwise it leaves the work item in place with a note saying why, because check:bean-archive allows only terminal work items in the archive. Where the bean ops live — OPEN and CLOSE, called by every process . The claim, resolve and archive ops live in two called processes, and nowhere else, so no process can open a work item it never closes: . |   | process | what it does | ops it carries | . | OPEN | Process_BeanOpen (sdlc/processes/bean-open.bpmn) | check before you create, create, whose work item, claim — or leave it alone | claim | . | CLOSE | Process_BeanClose (sdlc/processes/bean-close.bpmn) | outcome: complete, or scrap with reasons, then one shared archive step; or record the blocker and hand back | resolve, archive (and a note for the blocker) | . Process_BeanLifecycle is OPEN → work → CLOSE, calling both. Process_BeanDrain (sdlc/processes/bean-drain.bpmn) is the same over a queue: build the queue grouped by owner, then for each work item OPEN → work → CLOSE, and refill when a drainer’s list runs dry. A work item OPEN finds is someone else’s is marked skip on the queue, not worked. How a process uses them. Call Process_BeanOpen where the work item becomes the process’s own — usually its first step — and follow it with a gateway (claimed / not yours): the engine hands a called process the caller’s work item but not its end event, so the caller reads which end OPEN reached, and not yours stops at an end of its own without touching the work item. Call Process_BeanClose straight before each end the process reaches after OPEN. Straight before matters: resolve counts the process as finished when nothing but archive steps is left (onlyArchiveLeft), and a CLOSE followed by more work turns its resolve into a note. note ops stay where the work happens. A called phase does not open or close again. A process only ever called by another (the CRDM phases under crdm-requirements.bpmn) runs on its caller’s work item, so the caller opens and closes it. A process that is both run on its own and called (code-change-review, upstream-version-adoption, editing-hci-validation) keeps its own pair: nested, OPEN’s claim is idempotent and CLOSE notes instead of closing while the outer process still has work. The check. check:bean-calls (also run inside check:workflow-refs, which CI gates) fails on a claim, resolve or archive op outside OPEN and CLOSE, on a process that calls one of them without the other, and on an entry process that names a work item by ref without calling both. A process whose only marks are note (or a bare <cat-harness.processes:bean/>) and that nothing calls is reported, not failed: it writes on whatever work item its instance was started with and never decides that work item’s fate. The sweep is still beans archive, run deliberately — the floor under every process that never reached CLOSE. Note the CLI prints .beans/archive/ but honours path: from .beans.yml; here that means beans/defs/archive/.

f5d4bf5ecbec.title: Status Display Format
f5d4bf5ecbec.content: When the user asks “status” or “show beans”, run beans list and display the work items this session touched under their subject epics — the epic is the heading because it is where the work lives; the session is a filter, not a node: . ## Beans this session touched (branch <branch-name>) - [abcd] PROCESS: how an agent decides what it is doing (epic) - [task-124] Task A (completed) - [task-125] Task B (in-progress) - [efgh] QA: verdicts, sidecars and the audited review record (epic) - [task-126] Task C (todo) .

b180d1cd0bf0.title: Coordination discipline
b180d1cd0bf0.content: . | Claim before you work, with bun run cat beans:claim <id>, so sibling sessions working the same goal do not duplicate the effort. Also check the open PR list for the work item id and its subject before you start: a claim announces the item is taken, but a sibling may already have a PR. Full rule: bean-coordination.md §”Claims are global via the branch store”. Brief it in the same turn you claim it — opening-brief.md. The claim tells a sibling the item is taken; the brief tells them, and the author, what it is being taken for. | One source of truth per concern. Do not fork a work item into a parallel todos/*.json queue; link to the queue from the work item instead. | Move wiring and script together. When relocating a hook-backed script, move its hook reference in the same change — a script without its wiring, or a hook reference without its script, leaves a dangling reference. | Close on landing. When the work lands, close the tracking work item and update any cross-repo ownership note. | .

7c5a91b332eb.title: Relationship to other surfaces
7c5a91b332eb.content: . | bean-coordination.md — the cross-session claim and handoff lifecycle, and why a claim is not a lock. | bean-blocking.md — a real block carries what it waits on, since when, an expiry and a handoff. | scripts/session-start-coord-sweep.sh — the CLI-independent session-start surface: fetches origin/main and summarises sibling branch activity. Works even when the beans CLI is absent. | cat-harness-tools/scripts/install-beans.sh — provisions the CLI. | .

99f50fb94580.title: todo-manager (skill)
99f50fb94580.content: The skill todo-manager as its source file cat-harness/work-plan/skills/work-plan/todo-manager.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

dfcb65165dcb.title: Todo Review Skill
dfcb65165dcb.content: Skill todo-review: Monitor and triage open feedback across all content blocks. At session start, ask the author if they’d like to work on feedback. Provide overview, let them pick a chapter/section, then review and iterate until done. Named by: Public comment on a review draft . Disambiguation: . | todo-review (this file) = triage of content feedback stored under feedback/<paper>/ (paper-scope; persistent across sessions; surfaced via /todos dashboard). | todo-manager = the agent’s session work-plan via work items (durable, committed under beans/). | . Both can be active in one session: the agent’s work-plan (todo-manager) may include “process N feedback items via todo-review” as a single task.

e18600cbdda4.title: Where the feedback came FROM — this skill starts mid-air without it
e18600cbdda4.content: Materialized content (held by reference or materialized from elsewhere) is read-only; a reviewer cannot annotate it in place. The first step of review is copy-out-materialized (diagram: library/processes/copy-out-materialized.bpmn): the reviewer copies the materialized sub-graph into their own folio/, carrying provenance.local back to the original, annotates the copy, and those annotations arrive here. While triaging: . | Feedback is on the COPY, not on the original. Resolving an item edits the copy. The original still hashes to its recorded digest, and check:materialized-fixity fails if somebody annotated held content in place. | provenance.local makes a resolved item traceable to the thing it was about; without it the copy is indistinguishable from original work one rename later. | .

3cd5e7b6d631.title: Role
3cd5e7b6d631.content: Monitor open feedback across the manuscript. At session start, offer a structured todo workflow. Provide triage, context-aware selection, and a feedback cycle until the author is satisfied.

d474979a1461.title: When to Use This Skill
d474979a1461.content: . | Session start (automatic): ask if author wants to work on feedback | User asks: “show todos”, “what feedback is pending”, “review todos” | User asks: “what needs attention”, “any open items”, “work on todos” | After completing a block of work, to check if related items can be closed | .

a31c127fe29f.title: Feedback Storage
a31c127fe29f.content: Feedback lives in feedback/<paper-dir>/ (tracked in git, committed to main via worktree). Each content block with feedback has a TypeScript file: . feedback/ <paper-dir>/ <block-a>.ts <block-b>.ts ... Each file exports an array of FeedbackItem (extends TodoItem with author/authorEmail): . import type { FeedbackItem } from "../../schemas/types"; export default [ { "id": "todo-mn159z53", "summary": "short description of the issue", "comment": "longer description of the issue", "status": "open", "priority": "medium", "origin": "human", "assignee": "editor-agent", "createdAt": "2026-03-22T02:35:33.543Z" } ] satisfies FeedbackItem[]; .

98fbee480575.title: Session Start: Todo Workflow
98fbee480575.content: When the editor skill enters the session start protocol and open feedback exists, follow this flow: . Step 0 — Offer the todo workflow . Present a brief overview and ask: . You have N open feedback items (X critical, Y high, Z medium). Would you like to work on feedback today? . Options: . | Yes, let’s review feedback → proceed to Step 1 | No, I have something else in mind → exit to normal triage | . Step 1 — Overview and scope selection . Show a quick summary grouped by chapter: . ## Feedback Overview | Chapter | Open | Critical/High | Sample |---------|------|---------------|--------| Ch 1: Introduction | 12 | 3 | "this does not need to hold in general" | Ch 4: Methods | 4 | 1 | "missing cross-ref to prior section" | Ch 11: Results | 6 | 0 | "clarify the derivation" | . Then ask: . Where would you like to start? . Options (dynamically generated): . | High priority first — all critical + high items across paper | **Ch N: ** — one option per chapter that has feedback | Show all — flat list sorted by priority | . Step 2 — Present the selected feedback . Show the filtered items as a table: . ## Open Feedback — Ch 1 (12 items) | # | Priority | Block | Summary |---|----------|-------|---------| 1 | high | initial-conditions | this does not need to hold in general | 2 | high | main-point | need a supporting statement for the claim | 3 | medium | core-definition | clarify notation convention | ... | . Ask: Which item(s) would you like to address? (pick by number or “all”) . Step 3 — Review and address each item . For each selected feedback item: . | Show the feedback — full comment, author, date, priority | Read the block — load content/<paper>/<chapter>/<rootName>.md and .ts manifest for context | Propose a fix — suggest specific edits to the .md content | Ask for approval — show the proposed changes and ask: Does this address the feedback? (yes / revise / skip) . | Apply if approved — edit the file, mark todo as in_progress | Iterate if “revise” — ask what to change, re-propose | . Step 4 — After each item, offer next steps . After completing (or skipping) an item: . Done with “this does not need to hold in general”. What next? . Options (context-aware): . | Next item on this block (if more exist) | Next item in this section/chapter | Back to overview — re-show the chapter summary | Done for now — exit todo workflow | . Step 5 — Wrap up . When the author says “done” or all items in scope are addressed: . Session feedback summary: . | Reviewed: 5 items | Addressed: 3 (edits applied) | Skipped: 2 | Remaining open: 9 | . The addressed items are marked in_progress. You can resolve them from the viewer feedback panel when you’re satisfied with the changes.

858142afbee3.title: Resolving Feedback
858142afbee3.content: Only the human author may resolve or remove a FeedbackItem. Agents must never set status to resolved or wontfix, and must never delete items. Agents may set status to in_progress after making edits. Resolution happens in the viewer’s feedback panel (click the status badge on any feedback item).

8785f8af9d18.title: Seeding Feedback

0b3d76d20a44.title: The two-axis model
0b3d76d20a44.content: A content node varies along two axes: . | Format — .md (Markdown), .lean (Lean 4), .tex (LaTeX), .bpmn, .dmn, etc. | Language — BCP 47 locale tags (en, fr, es, ar, zh, ru). | . The format axis is handled by companions. The language axis is handled by the PO/POT pipeline with TranslationNode manifests in translations/<locale>/.

b74a086cb5dc.title: TranslationNode — .po/.pot files as KG nodes
b74a086cb5dc.content: Each .po/.pot pair is wrapped by a .ts manifest that makes it a first-class node in the knowledge graph: . import type { TranslationNode } from "../../schemas/translation"; const node: TranslationNode = { label: "trans:fr/index", locale: "fr", sourceFile: "docs/index.md", potFile: "translations/fr/index.pot", poFile: "translations/fr/index.po", status: { locale: "fr", official: false, generatedBy: "agent" }, coverage: { translated: 37, total: 37, pct: 100 }, }; export default node; . The manifest carries the status, coverage, and QA results inline — no separate status.json or .qa.json files.

9ea244dbaeb3.title: PO source resolution (fallback behavior)
9ea244dbaeb3.content: Content blocks can declare explicit PO sources via poSources[] on BlockBase. When not declared, the pipeline resolves by convention: . | Block-level: translations/<locale>/<block-stem>.po | Chapter-level: translations/<locale>/<chapter-slug>.po | Folio-level: translations/<locale>/global.po | Dependency walk: walk <name>.config.json dependencies depth-first | . When poSources is declared, only the listed files are consulted (no fallback). Later entries override earlier for the same msgid.
