d1bbe96ecb0d.title: Visual diff — see a figure change
d1bbe96ecb0d.content: Skill visual-diff: Pictures of a changed figure, diagram or table, before and after, and how much of it changed. Says when to use it, what the percentage means and must NOT be read as, what a missing picture means, and how the staging job and the review process call it. Use when a reviewer asks “what does this figure look like now”, when a table’s markup diff is unreadable, or when a staging preview’s pictures are missing. Named by: Committee review of a content change, Merge and publish a content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Public comment on a review draft, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate . Skill id: visual-diff · Package: sdlc-core . For a figure, a diagram, a table, an equation or a simulator, the change a reviewer must judge is how the block LOOKS. The Markdown or SVG diff of a recoloured bar chart is noise. So the staging job pictures each such block on both sides, and the review page shows the pictures. For a before/after of anything the staging job does not picture (page chrome, scroll behaviour, a PDF page, an IG page, a slide), and for the rules every reviewer-facing pair follows, see before-after-preview.

ddfc2dcba6be.title: Design rules
ddfc2dcba6be.content: . | A Skill and a Tool, built into the processes. The steps live in the folio-block-screenshots Tool and in this skill. The staging workflow and the review process CALL them; nobody copies them. | No new dependency. The pictures are taken with Playwright, which the platform already uses, and the comparison runs in Chromium’s own canvas, so nothing new needs a licence. | One key or one click; never a drag. The page offers four views as radio buttons, not a slider. | .

32efe71ed6f6.title: What the reviewer sees
32efe71ed6f6.content: On the review page, a visual block opens on “Pictures, before and after”. It shows: . | a sentence stating how much changed: “12.3% of the block’s pixels changed”, or “No pixel changed beyond anti-aliasing”, or “Only one side could be pictured”; | four views, each one click (or an arrow key): | . | view | shows | . | Changed pixels | the after picture faded to grey, with every changed pixel marked in magenta | . | Before | the block on the published site | . | After | the block on this preview | . | Both | before and after side by side | . When a build published no pictures, the block opens side by side (the live pages in frames) instead, because the page takes the first view that can run and lists the block’s kind.

8cfdbfb4e38f.title: What the percentage means, and must NOT be read as
8cfdbfb4e38f.content: | it is | it is not | . | the share of the block’s pixels, in the larger of the two pictures, that differ by more than a small tolerance (24 of 255 per channel, to absorb anti-aliasing) | whether the change is right. A one-pixel line through a chart can be the whole point | . | counted over the larger picture, so a block that grew counts the new area as changed | a measure of text change: a reworded caption moves many pixels | . | of the light theme only | a check of dark mode | . Zero means nothing changed that the eye would see. A block the ChangeSet lists as changed with 0% is still worth a look at its markup: the change may be in alt text, a label or a link.

e24ed8489763.title: When a picture is missing
e24ed8489763.content: A missing picture is said, never drawn blank: . | message | means | what to do | . | “Not on main: this block is new.” | an added block has no before | nothing: there is nothing to compare | . | “Its page is not in the published site” | the before side has no page for the block’s document | the document is new, or main was never published. A folio publishes main when its staging caller lists push to main; the build log warns when _main-site.json is absent | . | “Its anchor is not on the … page” | the page exists, but has no <a id="<label>"> for the block | the block was renamed without renamedFrom, or the build dropped it. Check the id-stable QA criterion | .

5bd28b240d07.title: How a picture is taken
5bd28b240d07.content: The site build writes an empty <a id="<label>"> before each labelled block. There is no element that wraps the block. So a block’s picture is the region from its anchor down to the next anchor, as wide as the anchor’s container. A page with anchors out of order pictures the wrong region, so if a picture looks wrong, check the anchors first.

8279283ab0cd.title: The Tool
8279283ab0cd.content: # how many blocks would be pictured (no browser needed) bun run <platform>/cat-harness-tools/scripts/block-screenshots.ts --changeset _site/changeset.json --count # picture and compare bun run <platform>/cat-harness-tools/scripts/block-screenshots.ts \ --changeset _site/changeset.json --base pages --head _site --out _site . It writes visual-diff.json (folio-visual-diff/v1) and visual/*.png next to the site. The review page reads ../visual-diff.json.

46acbfdfa578.title: Where it runs in the processes
46acbfdfa578.content: . | folio-staging.yml, step “Picture changed figures, diagrams and tables”. It runs after the step “Choose the before side”, which picks: . | main’s site, at the publish branch’s root, published by the same workflow’s publish-main job on every push to main; | for a stacked PR, its base branch’s preview, branches/<base-slug>/, so the pictures and the ChangeSet compare with the same branch. When the base has no preview, main’s site is used and the banner, the review page and the PR comment all say so. | . It installs Chromium only when --count is above zero. | publish-main (same workflow) deletes only files its own manifest, _main-site.json, lists. branches/, _render-log/ and anything a person put at the root are never touched, and the first publish removes nothing. | content-change-review.bpmn, task Compare main vs staging. The reviewer’s comparison names this skill beside staging-review, so a reviewer handed that task is told the pictures exist. | .

1c2fc5c8e97e.title: Tests
1c2fc5c8e97e.content: . | cat-harness-tools/scripts/tests/block-screenshots.test.ts: the pixel compare, the tolerance, a size change, block selection, and page paths (including .. being refused). | the tools layer’s test/block-screenshots.e2e.ts: the whole Tool in Chromium. It covers a recoloured block, an unchanged block, a new block, and a missing anchor. | the tools layer’s test/review-visual.e2e.ts: the renderer, keyboard only. | .

1343762b0ed5.title: Visualizer loading — the page is layout, the graph is fetched
1343762b0ed5.content: Skill visualizer-loading: The general strategy for a complex visualizer: the generated page carries identity, layout and a pointer, and its bulky or repeated content is fetched from the Knowledge Graph in the browser rather than baked into every page. What must stay server-side, how to fetch, how to stay equivalent to the render being replaced, and how to verify a page whose content is not in its HTML. Read before generating any page that shows a KG node’s data at length: an IG artefact view, a graph viewer, a schema or sidecar view. Named by: Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Skill id: visualizer-loading · Package: ui-core .

6bbd1d5fe9f7.title: The rule
6bbd1d5fe9f7.content: A generated page for a complex visualizer holds three things: . | Identity: the title, description and front matter that navigation, search and a link preview read. | Layout: headings, tabs and links, arranged by a template (liquid-templates). | A pointer: the KG file the content comes from, resolved by the generator. | . The content (a sidecar file, a node’s properties at length, a table derived from the graph) is fetched by the browser from the committed KG artefact. It is never copied into the page. Each copy is a second answer, free to drift from the first, and copied into a thousand pages it is most of the site’s bytes. kg-viewer is an instance of the pattern: one page that fetches its sibling graph document and computes back-links at load.

ae9e084bd02c.title: What stays server-side
ae9e084bd02c.content: Moving content client-side has costs: a reader without JavaScript loses it, a search index loses it, and so does the first paint. So these stay in the page: . | What navigation and search need: title, description, headings, and the link labels a reader scans for. | The way to reach the data without JavaScript: a link to the raw file, under <noscript> if nowhere else. A view that renders nothing without scripts must still say where its content is. | Anything short and unique to the page. A one-line value is not bloat, and fetching it costs a request to save a few bytes. | . Move a block when it is large or repeated and already a KG file. A block that would need a new file published just to be fetched is a design question for the owner, not a default.

f6b99b42a6c6.title: Where the data is served from — served: true
f6b99b42a6c6.content: The fetched file is the KG’s own, published verbatim. A directory declares served: true in its layer’s <instance>.json, and mount-instance-docs copies its bytes to /<instance>/<path> after Jekyll: no Liquid, no layout, no index page. Pages under the layer’s composed docs then reach it with a relative path. Never copy the file into docs/ beside the page instead — a gate flags it as an unknown file family in a docs directory. A generator whose data is not served writes no page that would fetch it, and says why.

53daf7dcacb3.title: How to fetch
53daf7dcacb3.content: . | Relative to the page’s own location, never via a configured base URL, so the same bytes work in production and in a staging preview (kg-viewer §”The page is generated, not committed”). | One shared loader per visualizer kind, published once and referenced by every page, never inlined in each page. | No dependencies: no CDN or framework. Same reason as kg-viewer: the data is this repository’s, and a third party in its trust boundary is at odds with that. | Three states on the page: loading, loaded, and could not load, which names the file and the error. A failed fetch that leaves a blank or a permanent “Loading…” is the silent-gap defect in another form. | .

e6a395d08351.title: Stay equivalent to the render you replace
e6a395d08351.content: When the page replaces another renderer’s page (for example the IG Publisher’s, which every phase must render equivalent to), compute the display the same way that renderer does, and then check it. For example, a page that shows a file as JSON.stringify(parsed, null, 2) differs from the file’s own bytes whenever the file has integer-like keys, which JavaScript orders first; showing the raw bytes would look right and be wrong.

6409dfcb2a53.title: Printing and PDFs
6409dfcb2a53.content: A browser prints the page as it is at that moment, so fetched content prints once it has loaded and not before: a PDF taken at domcontentloaded holds “Loading…”. | Every loader signals completion. Each counts itself in and out of window.__kgLoads, and the last one to finish sets <html data-kg-loaded>, on success or failure. A failed fetch still ends the wait, and its message is what prints. | Anything that prints or renders a PDF waits for that attribute, never for a fixed delay. That includes a Playwright page.pdf(), a PDF build step and a screenshot test. A page with no loader never sets it, so a tool that waits must first check whether the page loads one of the loader scripts. | A reader pressing Ctrl+P gets the page as loaded. The loaders are fast, but a print from a cold cache can still catch “Loading…”. That is a visible, honest state, not a blank. | .

2b2854947623.title: Verify in a browser, not in the HTML
2b2854947623.content: A static check cannot see fetched content: the built HTML holds only “Loading…”. Verification therefore means loading each page in a browser (Playwright, with the pre-installed Chromium) and comparing what it displays against the reference, as rendered-verification requires of any rendered artefact.

0112f1d69e0d.title: Finding what to move
0112f1d69e0d.content: A QA review over a built site: . | The mechanical half measures per-page bytes, blocks repeated across pages, and blocks matching a committed KG file, and writes a QA sidecar. | The agentic half judges each candidate against §”What stays server-side”. | . Repetition is a measurement, but whether a block may leave the page is a judgement.

ad3f6031d463.title: Do not
ad3f6031d463.content: . | Bake a KG file’s text into a page “for now”. That copy is what the next person will have to find and remove. | Move navigation or search terms client-side to save bytes. The saving is small and the loss is the page being findable. | Add a framework to fetch a JSON file. fetch and textContent are the whole loader. | .

cea60de568b3.title: Voice overlay review
cea60de568b3.content: Skill voice-overlay-review: Review a block against the active voices’ rules and record the verdict on its QA sidecar. The human/agent half of the voice overlay; the mechanical half is whatever patterns and terminology a rule carries. Named by: Committee review of a content change, Merge and publish a content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Make a decided public comment change, Public comment on a review draft, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate .

b78690f07af5.title: What you are reviewing, and against what
b78690f07af5.content: One block, against the rules of the voices the folio has activated — not every voice it ships. The layer’s config (its index.config.json entry) holds the list; an empty list means there is nothing for this skill to do and that is a pass, not a gap. bun run cat check:voices # the voices, their rule counts, and that every citation resolves .

0c9747d1c88e.title: The rule’s citation is the argument, so open it
0c9747d1c88e.content: Every voice rule carries a source that resolves to a real file — a library/<doc>/sections/<section>.md for a rule read from an ingested document, or a path for a house standard. It also carries the quote the rule was read from. Open the citation before upholding a finding. | A reviewer who has read the source can say why the rule applies to this block. | The rule may be wrong. A rule derived from a document can misread it. If the quote does not support the rule, the rule is the defect and the work item goes against the voice, not against the block. | .

e941bf730485.title: Three outcomes, as with the house voice axis
e941bf730485.content: Identical to voice-editorial-review: . | The finding stands — the register is wrong for this block. Fix the prose. | The rule does not apply to this content — record it, and consider whether the rule needs appliesTo scoping on the voice. One scoping edit beats many per-block overrules. | The rule applies and this block is an exception — a reviewer entry on the sidecar saying why. It leads the criterion, so the block reads pass with the reasoning attached and nothing is silently rewritten. | .

6232d6ced718.title: A mechanical match is a question
6232d6ced718.content: A pattern is a regex over text; it does not know what the block is about. Examples of non-defects it matches: . | voice-scholarly-default on documentation pages whose register is correctly second-person. | voice-editorializing on merely inside a comparative, where the contrast is the block’s claim. | voice-editorializing on clearly used as proof economy. | . Verify before upholding, and when a rule fires repeatedly across a corpus on the same non-defect, that is evidence about the RULE.

2f5ca985ae48.title: Recording the verdict
2f5ca985ae48.content: Voice findings go on the block’s QA sidecar like any other, through the same writer, so the icon and the published witness agree with what you decided: . bun run pipeline/qa-merge-findings.ts --file findings.json . insertAdjudication places your entry ahead of the script entry, because list[0] is a criterion’s effective verdict. The script’s entry is kept beneath yours, because the disagreement between a checker and a reviewer is information.

3cfcb4c37824.title: Do not
3cfcb4c37824.content: . | Do not uphold a finding you have not traced to its quote. A rule that misreads its source is the failure this design exists to prevent. | Do not review against a voice the folio has not activated. | Do not delete a script finding from a sidecar. The sweep rewrites its own entries; a hand-removed one returns with no record that anyone looked. | Do not resolve a conflict between two active voices in the prose. Both rules stand: name them and let the editor decide. | .

c19b0ee1324d.title: /watch — background watcher with integration check
c19b0ee1324d.content: Skill watch: Background-watch a branch (default origin/main) or a GitHub PR for new activity while you work, and on every event report whether to integrate / whether it conflicts with the current branch / whether it lets you simplify exposition / proofs / computations . Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Record agent step, Review-log watch . A unified watcher that handles branches (poll git ls-remote) and change proposals — pull requests, PRs — (subscribe to their activity through the session platform; subscribing is not a forge operation). On every event, walk the §3 integration checklist and either act, defer, or flag the user.

d29c88cb8cb4.title: Invocation
d29c88cb8cb4.content: The user’s request maps to one of three modes; pick the right one without asking: . | user phrase | mode | how | . | “watch main” / “watch upstream” / no target | branch:main | poll origin/main every 5 min | . | “watch PR 516” / “watch the PR” / “watch this PR” | pr:N | subscribe to its activity — the session platform’s subscription (event-driven) | . | “watch branch foo/bar” / “watch claude/x-y” | branch:foo/bar | poll origin/foo/bar every 5 min | . | “watch foo/bar PR 42” | pr:42 + maybe branch | subscribe + poll | . If ambiguous, default to branch:main.

7f23cf205367.title: 1.  Stash the baseline
7f23cf205367.content: Before arming anything, record the current state so the §3 review compares cleanly: . # Explicit refspec, ALWAYS. `git fetch origin <BRANCH>` writes FETCH_HEAD and # refreshes refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH> only when the clone's configured # refspec covers it — and exits 0 either way. A baseline read from a tracking # ref that was never updated is not a baseline. git fetch origin "+refs/heads/<BRANCH>:refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH>" 2>/dev/null # Sanitize branch name for use in a file path: replace `/` with `_` # (e.g. `feature/foo` → `feature_foo`). Without this, branches with # slashes silently land in non-existent directory trees. SAFE_BRANCH=$(printf '%s' "<BRANCH>" | tr '/' '_') git rev-parse "origin/<BRANCH>" > "/tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE_BRANCH}.sha" . For PR mode, instead capture the latest PR head SHA: read PR N with the read change proposal forge-operation Tool and stash its head commit SHA.

90853bffe079.title: 2.  Arm the watcher
90853bffe079.content: Branch mode — Monitor with poll loop . Use the Monitor tool, persistent: true, 5-minute poll: . Monitor: description: "origin/<BRANCH> new commits" persistent: true command: | BRANCH="<BRANCH>" last=$(git ls-remote origin "$BRANCH" | cut -f1) while true; do cur=$(git ls-remote origin "$BRANCH" 2>/dev/null | cut -f1) if [ -n "$cur" ] && [ "$cur" != "$last" ]; then git fetch origin "$BRANCH" 2>/dev/null # one line per new commit, oldest first git log --reverse --oneline "$last..$cur" | head -20 last=$cur fi sleep 300 done . Each new commit becomes one notification line. PR mode — activity subscription . Subscribe to the PR’s activity through the session platform (in a Claude Code remote session, its PR-activity subscription). This is not a forge operation, so no forge Tool node offers it. Already event-driven — no polling needed. The harness delivers <github-webhook-activity> events for comments, CI status, reviews, and merges. See the existing PR-subscription guidance in the system prompt for handling.

7cbb0df9cd56.title: 3.  Per-event integration checklist
7cbb0df9cd56.content: For every notification (branch commit or PR event), run through these four questions in order — stop at the first “no” or “no action”: . Q1 — Should we integrate? . | Is the change on a file we touch in this branch? Quick check: git diff --name-only HEAD <NEW_SHA> -- $(git diff --name-only $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)..HEAD). | If yes and the change is small, rebase / pull now. | If yes but large, defer until the immediate task ships and add a TODO. | If no overlap, skip Q2/Q3/Q4 and acknowledge with a one-liner. | . Q2 — Does it conflict? . | Try a dry rebase in a fresh worktree. Use mktemp -d so the path is unique (avoids collisions with previous failed runs and with parallel /watch invocations) and clean up unconditionally via trap: . PROBE=$(mktemp -d /tmp/rebase-probe.XXXXXX) trap 'git worktree remove --force "$PROBE" 2>/dev/null; rm -rf "$PROBE"' EXIT git worktree add "$PROBE" HEAD >/dev/null ( cd "$PROBE" && git rebase "origin/<BRANCH>" ) status=$? # trap fires on EXIT . | Conflicts (status != 0) → first attempt auto-resolve for the recurring drift-conflict pattern (see §2a below); only flag the user if auto-resolve fails or the conflict is non-trivial (overlapping logic edits, schema rewrites, etc.). | . §2a — Auto-resolve drift-conflict pattern (CI-regenerated artifacts) . Some artifacts (*.witness.json sidecars, generated caches, derived reference files) are routinely regenerated by the CI validate job and frequently conflict on rebase against fast-moving main. These conflicts are always the same shape: our branch’s committed artifact was regenerated against an older main; main now has a fresher version. Resolution is mechanical: regenerate against current main and recommit. The recipe (run on the real branch, not the probe worktree): . # When `git rebase origin/<BRANCH>` halts with a regenerated artifact # in the conflict list, do NOT hand-merge the JSON. Instead: # 1. If the conflicting commit was a pure regen of these generated # artifacts (no other changes), skip it — main already has the regen: git diff --name-only --cached | grep -qE '\.witness\.json$' && \ ! git diff --name-only --cached | grep -vE '\.witness\.json$' && \ git rebase --skip # 2. Otherwise, abort the rebase, regenerate the artifacts # on the rebased branch, then re-rebase. This produces a clean # apply because the regenerated artifact now matches main. git rebase --abort git rebase origin/<BRANCH> # re-rebase, skipping bad commits as above # regenerate the affected artifacts via the project's generator(s), e.g. bun run cat regen git add <regenerated-artifact-paths> git commit -m "Regen generated artifacts post-rebase against latest main" git push --force-with-lease . Only flag the user if: . | The conflict is in a source file (.py, .lean, .ts, .md) — those are real semantic conflicts that need human judgment. | The conflict is in a generated artifact whose regenerated content differs substantively from a simple drift (e.g. a numerical value changed, not just a timestamp/hash) — that means a CI-run generator on main produced different output, which deserves a closer look before blindly accepting. | The auto-resolve recipe itself fails (regen script errors out, push rejected for non-fast-forward reasons, etc.). | . For generated artifacts specifically: if upstream regenerated files our branch also touched, prefer rebase-and-regenerate over hand-merging. Drift is structural; merging is fragile. Q3 — Can we reuse? . Apply four reuse questions: . | Definitions / lemmas / helpers / witnesses — does the new commit add something our branch is duplicating, paraphrasing, or reinventing? Replace with uses[] / a citation and delete the local stand-in. | Proofs — does a new lemma or tactic discharge a hypothesis, collapse a chain, or close a gap? Apply via the project’s proof-simplification / build-fix skills. | Exposition — does our .md re-derive what main now defines upstream? Replace with a forward-reference; route through the project’s accuracy / readability skills. | Computation — does a new script or witness supersede a hand-rolled loop or stale witness in our branch? Swap in and regenerate the artifact. (See §2a for the routine drift-conflict pattern.) . | When the upstream commit adds or modifies a prop: / thm: / lem: / cor: block (or its sibling formalization), delegate to the project’s compute-integration watcher to check whether the new claim is wired into the production compute chain. Capture the verdict here and feed it into Q4. | . | . Q3a — Did upstream land a new skill file? . For each main-refresh, check whether a skill directory the layer declares in its kg graph (skill_list names them) gained a new file between this branch’s prior baseline and the new origin/main: . git diff --name-only --diff-filter=A "$LAST_BASE..origin/main" -- <skill-dirs> . For each new skill file: . | Read its frontmatter — extract name, roles, description, and any inherits field. | Match against branch scope — does the skill’s description overlap with what this branch is doing? Heuristics: . | skill description mentions a file kind / domain / pattern that appears in this branch’s git diff origin/main..HEAD --name-only, OR | skill is a new integration-watcher child (inherits: local/integration-watcher) and your branch is itself an integration-watcher PR, OR | skill is a content-block QA skill (e.g. one-voice-*, proof-*, compute-*) and your branch touches .md / .ts / .lean content blocks. | . | Surface to the user via AskUserQuestion with the standard 3-chip pattern: . New skill <name> landed on main: . <one-line description from frontmatter> . This branch’s scope overlaps because <one-line match rationale + file paths>. 1) Adopt now — invoke the skill on the relevant subset of this branch’s diff before continuing. 2) Defer to follow-up branch — record the decision and note for the next branch; don’t change this branch. 3) Not relevant — record so the watcher doesn’t re-prompt on future main-refreshes. | Record the decision as a note on the watcher’s work item (or in chat for the bare /watch flow) so subsequent main-refreshes don’t re-prompt for the same skill. | . This rule applies to skill files only. Skills landing on sibling PRs that haven’t merged yet do NOT trigger this check — only main commits count, mirroring the §2 “watch origin/main” scope. Q4 — Report or act? . | Acted (made the change): one-line summary + the new commit SHA. | Will act after current task: add a TODO with what + why. | Skipped: one-line reason (“no overlap”, “blocked on $TASK”). | .

7fad2244a8a6.title: 4.  Stop the watcher
7fad2244a8a6.content: Stop when the branch ships (PR merged, or you switch branches): . | Branch mode: call TaskStop on the Monitor task ID. | PR mode: the harness auto-unsubscribes when the PR merges/closes; otherwise unsubscribe through the session platform. | .

38fad4e57c6a.title: 5.  Common upstream patterns (heuristics)
38fad4e57c6a.content: . | Artifact drift: upstream regenerated generated artifacts (*.witness.json, caches) while we also modified them → rebase-and-regenerate, never hand-merge. | Toolchain version bumps: a dependency/toolchain hash changed → check our branch’s toolchain pin aligns before continuing a build. | Schema or generator changes: run bun run cat regen before continuing. | Routine review-cycle commits (Gemini/Copilot fixes on unrelated PRs): almost always Q1 = no overlap = skip with one-liner. | .

de68d1b4bfe8.title: 5b.  Monitor-timeout recovery (MANDATORY when re-arming)
de68d1b4bfe8.content: Background Monitors time out ([Monitor timed out — re-arm if needed]). Do not just re-arm and continue — between the last event and the timeout, main may have moved substantially. Mandatory steps on timeout-recovery: . # Compare the stashed baseline against the WATCHED BRANCH's actual head. # # This fetched `main` and then measured `origin/<BRANCH>` — a different ref # from the one it refreshed. The recovery step that exists to catch what was # missed while the watcher was down therefore compared the baseline against a # tracking ref nothing had updated, found them equal, and reported 0 missed # every time. Fetch the ref you are about to read, with an explicit refspec so # the tracking ref is actually written. git fetch origin "+refs/heads/<BRANCH>:refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH>" 2>/dev/null SAFE=$(echo "<BRANCH>" | tr '/' '_') LAST=$(cat /tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE}.sha 2>/dev/null || echo "") CUR=$(git rev-parse origin/<BRANCH>) if [ "$LAST" != "$CUR" ]; then MISSED=$(git log --oneline "$LAST..$CUR" 2>/dev/null | wc -l) echo "MISSED $MISSED commits while watcher was down" git log --oneline "$LAST..$CUR" | head -10 # Update baseline AFTER reporting git rev-parse origin/<BRANCH> > /tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE}.sha fi . If MISSED >= 5 OR any missed commit touches a file in your branch’s diff, run the §3 integration checklist on the missed range BEFORE arming a fresh monitor. This catches main moving many commits ahead during a long focused session while the watcher is timed out.

535462be864a.title: 6.  Output style
535462be864a.content: Follow interaction-modality: . | One sentence per commit / event by default | Numbered choices when integration is non-obvious | Run small fixes proactively; flag big ones | .

7a14c1f38bf0.title: Wireframe design review
7a14c1f38bf0.content: Skill wireframe-design-review: Design a user interface (a page, a visualiser, a navbar) by the WireGen methodology: a written design intent, at least two mid-fidelity HTML candidates, each with a web AND a mobile layout, mechanical checks at both viewports, a blind per-criterion review, adjudication where reviewers disagree, and a recorded choice. Also how an EXISTING visualiser is wireframed as-is, so that every declared visualiser has a wireframe with a QA sidecar. Process: processes/ui/wireframe-design-review.bpmn. Called for Design use from CRDM (Process_CRDM_Requirements, Call_Wireframe) whenever a requirement changes a rendered surface, before anything is built. Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Guideline Updates, Public comment on a review draft, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Method: wiregen. Process: processes/ui/wireframe-design-review.bpmn.

f5e4fd68abb0.title: Where wireframes live
f5e4fd68abb0.content: | use | directory | . | As-is | <instance>/docs/wireframes/<topic>/, in the layer that declares the visualiser: cat-harness/docs/wireframes/<topic>/ for this harness’s own pages, and a content layer’s own docs/wireframes/<topic>/ for a page it declares | . | Design, from a CRDM request | docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/, beside the request’s proposal docs/proposals/<slug>.md: the candidates are assets of the proposal. When the proposal is filed (git mv to docs/requirements/, crdm-requirements-workflow (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)), its asset directory moves with it in the same commit. | . Either directory holds: . | intent.md | one HTML file per candidate | authors.json, which reviewers are not shown | checks/: screenshots and the checker’s report | reviews/: one file per reviewer | . Each layer’s docs/wireframes/index.json maps the visualiser refs that layer declares to the wireframe that covers each. bun run cat check:wireframes reads every such index in the checkout, writes the QA sidecar (test/results/wireframes.qa-results.json) and fails on any gap. A wireframe sits with its page because an index naming another layer’s page reads as an undeclared ref wherever that layer is not mounted; another layer’s wireframes are reported as <instance>/<topic>.

629aaffc305e.title: Input and output
629aaffc305e.content: The contract is input.schema.json and output.schema.json. | In: the use (design or as-is), the topic (for CRDM, the proposal slug), the surface, and, from CRDM, the requirements that change it, the proposal path, the humanReviewer (requester or BA), the channels the candidates are shown in, and the branch. | Out — the renderings: assetDir, intent, and one candidates[] entry per candidate: its source HTML path, its screenshots.web and screenshots.mobile paths (from wireframe-check), their staging deep links, its per-criterion entries, and its outcome with the reason. chosen names the candidate, who chose it and the comment that records it; it is absent until a person chooses. | Out — as changed assets: changedAssets[] lists every wireframe file the branch adds, changes or removes (candidate HTML, screenshots, intent, reviews) in the record shape a staging preview’s graph carries (change, kind, title, before, after, source, pages or pagesUnknown; ChangedAsset in cat-harness-tools scripts/kg-changed-assets.ts). The review therefore lists the drawings the same way it lists every other changed asset. | Out — staging links: stagingLinks, the shape every request for feedback carries (staging-review), copied inline as definitions.stagingLinks. | .

b3d1b51d2d7b.title: Two uses
b3d1b51d2d7b.content: | use | candidates | review | . | Design: a new or changed UI | at least two, compared blind | per-criterion, then adjudication, then options analysis | . | As-is: an existing visualiser, drawn as it renders on main | exactly one, marked as-is | the same criteria. A finding becomes a work item against the visualiser, not a redesign | .

81add79c9dbe.title: 1. Intent
81add79c9dbe.content: A few sentences: who the screen is for, what they need to do, and what it must show. For an as-is wireframe, the intent is read off the visualiser’s own declaration and generator, not invented.

f3afb03cd68a.title: 2. Candidates
f3afb03cd68a.content: . | Mid-fidelity HTML: monochrome, real content from the graph it shows, semantic icons, and no placeholder text. | Web and mobile in every candidate, through responsive CSS or two layouts. A candidate with one layout does not enter review. | .

ca6e65b47b4a.title: 3. Mechanical checks (wireframe-viewport-check)
ca6e65b47b4a.content: bun run cat wireframe:check --use as-is --topic <topic> --surface <visualiser ref> bun run cat wireframe:check --use design --topic <slug> --surface <surface> . The three flags are this skill’s input. --topic picks the directory in the table above and every candidate in it (name candidates to check fewer; one outside it is refused), and the report goes to its checks/. --use design needs at least two candidates; --use as-is needs each marked as-is in its file name, and a --surface that is the topic or a ref index.json says it covers. The use, topic and surface are recorded in report.json. This renders each candidate at web (1280×800) and mobile (390×844) sizes. It records script entries for renders, no-overflow and no-placeholder, each pass or fail with a note, and writes a screenshot per viewport. Any fail sends the candidate back to step 2.

73f28e59c9ff.title: 4. Blind review, per criterion
73f28e59c9ff.content: Reviewers include at least one agent that did not author the candidate and one human. For Design use called from CRDM, the human is the requester or the BA who owns the request: the person who will accept the delivered feature chooses its design. They see the intent, the screenshots and the HTML, without the authors. For each criterion they record pass, warn or fail, with a reason: . | criterion | question | . | intent-fit | Does it do what the intent says, for the person it names? | . | web usability | Can the task be done at desktop width? | . | mobile usability | Can the task be done at phone width, by touch? | . | accessibility | Contrast, a non-colour channel, accessible names, keyboard, reading order | . | alternatives | Do the candidates differ in the ways that matter? (Design use only) | . There are no scores and no averages (methodology-adoption, Refusals).

91c019c3d9b6.title: 5. Adjudication and choice
91c019c3d9b6.content: . | When entries for one criterion disagree, call Process_Adjudication. The adjudication leads, the checker’s entry is kept, and a dispensation needs its reason. | The choice between surviving candidates is Process_OptionsAnalysis. Rejected candidates stay, each with the reason it lost. | .

401ba143cd39.title: Staging links
401ba143cd39.content: When a staging preview exists, every request this skill makes for feedback, review or sign-off carries it: one deep link per changed page, to the anchor where the change sits, with the same page on main as before. Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: feedback-deep-links.

94e5f49d9197.title: Showing it to the requester
94e5f49d9197.content: Design use from CRDM ends in a person’s choice, so the candidates must be in front of that person before implementation starts: . | Commit the candidates, intent.md, checks/ (screenshots) and reviews/ under docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/ on the feature branch, so feature-staging publishes them with the rest of the branch. | Show them where the requester will look, chosen from context: the conversation, the issue the request came from, the pull request, or more than one of these. Where it goes is a judgement (feedback-deep-links, point 5); every place chosen carries the same content: a short narrative of what each candidate does differently; branches/ deep links to each candidate’s HTML (not the site root); and its web and mobile screenshots shown as images, not only linked. Say which could not be linked or rendered, and why. | Ask the requester or BA to choose, with the comparison (one row per candidate, from A_CompareOptions) and a recommendation, per interaction-modality where it applies. | Record their choice in the proposal and in the output’s chosen. An agent never chooses on their behalf. Implementation (CRDM Phase 6) builds against the chosen candidate, and the delivery summary links it beside the after-screenshot. | .

15db5aac71a3.title: The work plan’s contract
15db5aac71a3.content: Skill work-plan-store: The contract the work plan (work items) keeps as a data store, as operations any Tool must provide: get, list, create, update with ifMatch, note, history, and where a work item is in its processes. Give back a work item exactly as written, keep ids unique and links whole, keep status and type to their closed lists, lose nothing to concurrent writers, and answer a work item’s history. A mechanical Actor plays this Role through whichever Tool the deployment names. Named by: Authoring a document . The work plan is a data store, and this is its contract. work-plan in scenarios/roles.json is a mechanical Role with a store block: what it holds, and how it is reached. This skill is the other half, what it must do. How an agent USES the plan is todo-manager; this file says what the plan promises back. This contract names no Tool. A process or skill that touches the work plan says which operation below it performs (“note the bean”, “claim it”), never which command does it. How one Tool performs an operation belongs on that Tool’s page, listed in §”Tools”. The Tool in use is chosen by the deployment description, per checkout. A diagram draws the store as a data store, never a lane: a dataStoreReference with dataStoreRef="work-plan", declared once in processes/global-tasks.bpmn. A task that opens or closes a work item writes to it with a dataOutputAssociation; a task that reads the plan has a dataInputAssociation from it. The task sits in the lane of whoever does it.

084ed0461a00.title: What it holds
084ed0461a00.content: | Kind | What | . | bean-defs | work items ($schema: bean/1.0.0), shaped by schemas/kinds/bean-defs.schema.json | . | bean-notes | addenda to a work item, one per writer, never rewritten | . | workflow-state | running and finished BPMN instances (folio-workflow-instance/v1) | .

313e34706135.title: Operations
313e34706135.content: Every Tool provides these. Each line says what a caller can rely on. | Operation | Guarantee | . | get(id) | the work item as last written, or “none”. A short id resolves to exactly one work item or to none | . | list(filter) | work items by status, type, tag or parent; archived work items only when the filter asks for them | . | create(bean) | the id is unique; the work item is readable by get once create returns | . | update(id, change, ifMatch) | refused when ifMatch names a version that is no longer current; a retry on the current version lands. archived: true archives the work item | . | note(id, text, by) | appended to the work item’s notes, never rewriting earlier ones | . | history(id) | every change to the work item, oldest first: when, by whom, what changed, and which process step made it when one did | . | positions(id) | every workflow instance that names the work item: process, step(s), instance status, last move | . | beansAt(process, step?) | the work items with a token at that process (and step) | . Archiving is a field, not an operation. update(id, { archived: true }, ifMatch) is refused unless the work item is completed or scrapped, and the work item keeps its status. get still finds an archived work item; list leaves it out unless asked. Where an archived work item lives is the Tool’s choice, stated on its page. A work item’s position lives only in the workflow instances. The work item records no process or step of its own; positions and beansAt read the instances the store holds. A tag such as process:code-change-review may label a work item for people, and is never read as its position.

6653a4daff58.title: Responsibilities
6653a4daff58.content: Each line is something a test can check against any Tool. | Give back what was written. get after create or update returns, byte for byte, the work item written. | Keep ids unique. No two work items share an id. | Keep links whole. parent, blocking and blocked_by name work items that exist. | Keep the lists closed. status and type take only the values the schema declares. | Lose nothing to a race. Two writers at once both land: the second update with a stale ifMatch is refused, retried on the current version, and lands. Nothing is overwritten unread. | Keep the history. history(id) answers who changed what and when, and which process step did it. | Archive only what is finished. archived: true on a work item that is not completed or scrapped is refused. | Know where a work item is. positions and beansAt agree with the instances the store holds. | .

3c18b2c99a49.title: Tools
3c18b2c99a49.content: | Tool | Backed by | Page | . | git state branch | a branch per graph (cat/<harness>/beans), mounted at beans/, written with the beans CLI (beans-cli) or by hand (beans-manual), read with bean-query | work-plan-store-git-branch | . | work items server | beans-serve GraphQL (schema); its mutations already take ifMatch | proposed | . | MCP service | an MCP server over the same operations | proposed | . | run-scoped store | in memory or a scratch branch, one per benchmark run, never the real plan (req:model-benchmark) | proposed | .

3d40c58b142f.title: Tests
3d40c58b142f.content: The conformance suite lives in the tools layer (scripts/tests/sdlc/work-plan-store-conformance.ts, one describe per responsibility above) and runs against both of the git Tool’s access modes. Until this file carries a tested-by: line, kg-audit reports this role as mechanical-role-untested.

64f5c874f933.title: State in a running process
64f5c874f933.content: Skill workflow-state: Where a running process keeps what it knows, and which store answers which question. The three records a step may touch, the one it may not, what <cat-harness.processes:bean op> actually performs, and why an instance and a work item must be one answer rather than two. Named by: Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . A process instance is not self-contained. It walks a diagram that lives somewhere else, records its position somewhere else again, and reads facts it must not change. Five stores; confusing any two of them is how a work plan comes to disagree with itself.

8677423a0f25.title: Which store answers which question
8677423a0f25.content: | question | store | graph typology | layer | . | what does this process DO? | processes/**/*.bpmn | cat-harness | content | . | where did this instance GET TO? | the workflow-state node of the work item graph | workflow-state | state | . | what is being worked on? | the bean-defs node of the work item graph | bean-defs | state | . | what does a PERSON still owe? | todos/ | todo-items | state | . | what do I already know? | agent memory | memory | context | . The layer column says what a step may do. A step may write to a state graph; that is what state is for. A step that writes to context is a defect, not an update: memory changes when a human directs an authoring act, outside any instance. content-context-and-state-graphs carries the axis; processMayWrite() is the predicate.

3000ef28b445.title: The diagram is content and the instance is state, and that is the whole model
3000ef28b445.content: A .bpmn is authored, reviewed, versioned and read by anyone — it stands on its own. An instance is a token position in that diagram plus a history: it means nothing detached from the file it walks. That is why the two live in different graphs and why an instance names its process rather than embedding it. Two consequences: . An instance is never edited by hand. It carries "$schema": "folio-workflow-instance/v1" and the interpreter owns it. Hand- editing a token is asserting a step happened, which is precisely what the gate exists to refuse. A diagram change does not rewrite history. An instance records where it got to under the diagram as it stood. If a step is renamed, the honest answer is that the old instance names a node that no longer exists — not that it retroactively took a different path.

a18eaf7f57b7.title: Beans and instances are ONE answer, not two
a18eaf7f57b7.content: bean-defs says what is being worked on; workflow-state says where it got to. Those must be one answer or they diverge, and a work plan that disagrees with itself is worse than one that is merely coarse. The loop is closed by <cat-harness.processes:bean op="…"> on an activity. A bean-marked step is not a step about the work plan — it IS the work-plan operation, so completing the step performs it: . | op | on completing the step | . | claim | status → in-progress, idempotent | . | note | append the caller’s note to the body | . | resolve | status → completed, only if the instance itself finished (or only archive steps are left) | . | archive | move a completed or scrapped work item into the archive, only once the instance finished | . claim is drawn only in Process_BeanOpen, and resolve and archive only in Process_BeanClose; every process that works on a work item calls both (check:bean-calls). note is drawn where the work happens. resolve is the careful one. A work item is never closed on somebody else’s judgement, so it does not fire on the caller’s say-so: the work item completes only when the instance tracking it has completed, which is a fact derived from the process rather than asserted by the agent calling it. A still-running instance gets a note. An op the build does not implement fails at process load. A step that says it resolves a work item and quietly does nothing is exactly the divergence the extension exists to close.

8f4299b403e0.title: What state does NOT buy you
8f4299b403e0.content: Ordering is not quality. A completed instance means the gates ran in order and a person saw the findings. Whether the content is correct is what the QA axes, the build and the validators are for. A green process must never be read as a reviewed artefact, and any dashboard built on this has to say so. A position is not a claim. An instance at Task_Commit says the token arrived, not that the commit is good.

4337ac605cd4.title: Where running instances live — the state graph on the branch store
4337ac605cd4.content: Running instances are part of the work-plan store (workflow-state graph typology; positions in work-plan-store (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan)). Where the deployment uses the git state-branch Tool, the store is mounted and pushed as described in work-plan-store-git-branch. The container is ephemeral and a work plan only one agent can see is not a work plan. Instance state lives in the shared work-plan store for the same reason work item definitions do: a sibling session, or the same session resumed in a fresh container, reads the store to find the position that exists rather than starting a second one beside it. When an instance advances, its state is written through the store’s Tool (bun run cat state:push when backed by the git state branch). This keeps instance state globally visible without cluttering code PR diffs on main. Instance ids are derived from the subject rather than random, so re-entering a step finds the instance that is already there: beans create is not idempotent and dedupes on nothing, so an id you can recompute is what prevents duplicates.

2a5483ef050f.title: Reading the state you did not write
2a5483ef050f.content: Before acting on an instance you did not start, ask what it is waiting on. A work item’s status defaults to non-blocking; a real block carries what it waits on, since when, an expiry and a handoff — because a block with no expiry cannot be told from abandoned work. bean-blocking carries that, and bean-coordination carries the rule that a claim announces rather than reserves until your PR exists.
